items.title: Why the best work comes from people who trust you
items.excerpt: Why the best creative work comes from people who already trust you, and how to stay in touch without pestering: no-agenda check-ins and small useful things.
items.coverAlt: A man laughing with a colleague on an exhibition stand
items.body:
The best work tends to come from people who already trust you, because trust makes everything easier. They tell you the real budget and the real worry. They give you proper access. They make decisions quickly and back your judgement on the day. You earn that by staying in touch without asking for anything, doing small useful things, and treating every project as one chapter in a longer conversation.

I'd go further and say that for a documentary studio, trust is most of the job. We're asking people to let us into their workplace, put a microphone on them and talk honestly about something they care about. That's a lot to ask of a stranger.

Why does the best work come from people who already know you?

Because the first project with anyone spends a lot of energy on working each other out. Will they deliver? Do they get what we do? Can I say what I actually think in this meeting? All reasonable questions, and all time not spent on the film.

Once that's settled, the brief gets honest. A client who trusts you will tell you the thing they'd normally keep back, like the part of the business they're nervous about showing, or the person who'll freeze on camera, or the budget they really have. Those details are what a good film gets built on. You can't plan around a worry nobody's mentioned.

And it shows on screen. People talk differently to someone they've met before. Interviews loosen up faster, staff stop performing sooner, and the moments that make a documentary feel true turn up earlier in the day.

What's the difference between a relationship and a transaction?

In a transaction, the conversation ends when the invoice is paid. In a relationship, delivery is somewhere in the middle.

The difference is mostly in what happens after the film goes out. Do you ask how it's landing? Do you notice they've posted it in the wrong shape for a platform and send them the right cut? Do you remember that the launch was this week and drop them a line? None of that takes long, and almost none of it is billable. It's also exactly what people mention when they recommend you.

I want any deal we do to feel fair to both sides, and a relationship is what makes that possible over time. When you know you'll be working together again, nobody's trying to squeeze the last drop out of one job.

How do you stay in touch without pestering?

Only get in touch when there's a reason that's about them. A good test is whether they'd be glad to get the message even if they never bought anything from you again. If the honest answer is no, don't send it.

"Just checking in to see if you've got any projects coming up" fails that test every time. It's a sales email dressed up as a hello, and people can tell. They start reading everything you send as a pitch, which is a hard habit to undo.

If you only write to someone when you want something, they'll learn to read every email you send that way.

Spacing matters too. There's no fixed rule, but every few months is plenty for most people unless you're actually working together. Silence in between is fine. Silence isn't rude, and nobody's sitting there wondering why you haven't emailed.

What does a check-in with no agenda look like?

Short, and it says outright that there's no agenda. Then it means it. It asks how they are, or how something they mentioned turned out, and it ends there. No link, no "while I've got you", no call to action tucked into the last line.

This matters most when someone's going through something hard. Illness, a bereavement, a rough year for the business. Work can wait, and it should. If there was a project on the table, the kindest thing to say is that nothing has changed or expired at your end and there's genuinely no rush. Then leave them to it. People remember who checked on them when they had nothing to offer back.

The most underrated business tool I know is remembering what someone told you last time. No subscription required.

What small, useful things actually build trust?

Most of them take five minutes. A few that tend to go down well:

  • Sending a cut they'll need before they ask for it, like a vertical version for a campaign you know is coming.
  • Pointing out a broken video link or an old film still sitting on their homepage.
  • Introducing them to someone who can genuinely help them, with no angle for you.
  • Tagging and crediting them properly when you share the work, so they get the attention as well.
  • Passing on something you read that's relevant to their sector.
  • Remembering the detail, whether that's the launch date, the new hire or the event they were dreading.

None of these are tactics if you do them because they're useful. They only become tactics when you do them while counting.

Doesn't this take too long for a small business?

Honestly, yes, it's slower. Relationship work doesn't show up in this month's numbers, and there are weeks when it feels like a luxury. I'd be lying if I said I never wondered whether the time would be better spent sending more cold emails.

But cold outreach is hard work for a small studio, and most of it goes nowhere. Work that comes back from people who already know you takes less convincing, starts from a better brief, and usually ends in a better film. Over a few years, that adds up to most of what keeps a studio going. It's also a much nicer way to spend your days.

How does this show up in the films themselves?

In the access. On a second or third shoot with the same people you know where the light's good at that time of day, who'll talk for an hour and who needs a quiet word first, and which corner of the building nobody wants on camera. All of that time goes back into the film.

It's also why we like ongoing work as much as one-off films. When you film the same business regularly, you start to see the stories they're too close to notice. Our post on turning one film into a year of content goes into how that works in practice.

If you'd like to see the kind of work that comes out of that trust, have a look at our films. And if you've a story in mind, even a vague one, drop us a line. No pitch, just a conversation.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How often should a small business contact past clients?
faqs.a: Every few months is plenty for most past clients, as long as each message has a reason that's about them. A film relevant to their sector, a note on something they launched, or a simple hello all count. If you're working together on an ongoing basis you'll naturally talk more, but for everyone else, less often and more useful beats a regular newsletter they don't read.

faqs.q: Is a newsletter a good way to stay in touch with clients?
faqs.a: It can be, if it's genuinely useful and people chose to get it. But it doesn't replace a personal message. A newsletter goes to everyone, so it can't remember that someone's launch was this week or that they mentioned a new hire. Use one for broad updates if you like, and keep the personal notes personal.

faqs.q: How do you ask a happy client for a referral without it feeling awkward?
faqs.a: Ask once, specifically, at a natural moment such as just after they've told you they're pleased with the work. Name the kind of person you'd love to meet rather than asking if they know anyone at all. Then make it easy to say no. Most people are glad to help someone who's looked after them, and a light ask respects that.

faqs.q: Should you send clients gifts to build the relationship?
faqs.a: Small, thoughtful gestures are fine, but they're no substitute for being useful. A handwritten note or something connected to a conversation you had will mean more than a branded hamper. Be careful with public sector and larger organisations, as many have rules on accepting gifts. When in doubt, a useful introduction or an extra cut of their film is the better present.

items.title: What is narrative in marketing?
items.excerpt: Narrative in marketing is the ongoing account of who a brand is and what it believes, running through every story. Here's how it differs from story and messaging.
items.coverAlt: A military band in black and white uniforms marches down a village road led by a drum major in a red tunic, bunting along
items.body:
Narrative in marketing is the overall, ongoing account a brand gives of who it is, what it believes and what it's trying to change. A single story is one episode. The narrative is the thread that runs through all of them and makes them recognisably yours, whatever the format, channel or campaign.

The words get used loosely, so this post sorts them out. I'll cover how narrative differs from story and messaging, what a brand narrative is made of, a few well known examples, how to build your own, and how it shapes a brand film. For the definition of storytelling itself, see what brand storytelling is, and the rest of the series is gathered in the complete guide to brand storytelling.

What's the difference between narrative, story and messaging?

I find it easiest to think of them as three levels, from the big picture down to the sentence.

  • Narrative is the big idea. It's the worldview your brand keeps coming back to: what's wrong with how things are done, what you believe instead and what you're working towards. It lasts for years.
  • Story is a specific example. A customer, a job, a founder's decision. Stories prove the narrative, one at a time, and you'll tell dozens of them.
  • Messaging is the wording. The headlines, the taglines, the lines on a sales deck. Messaging should be an expression of the narrative, and it changes most often.

Get the order wrong and things go sideways. A business that starts with messaging ends up with slogans nobody believes. One that starts with stories but no narrative ends up with a pile of nice anecdotes that don't add up to a reputation. Narrative gives the stories somewhere to go. For how a single story is put together, you want how to tell a brand story, which sits one level down from this post.

What does a brand narrative actually contain?

It doesn't need to be complicated. A working narrative usually answers four questions, and if you can answer them in a few plain sentences, you have one.

What's the problem in the world?

Something in your field that frustrates you and your customers. Cheap work that doesn't last, an industry that hides its prices, a craft that's dying out. This gives you something to stand against and gives people a reason to care.

What do you believe instead?

Your position. "Work should be done once and done properly." "People deserve to see how things are made." It should be specific enough that some people would disagree with it. If everybody agrees, it isn't telling anyone anything.

What do you do about it?

The practical ways your business acts on that belief. Your methods, your standards, the things you refuse to do. This is where the narrative turns into evidence.

What changes for the customer?

The result in their life or business, described in terms they'd recognise. Narrative that ends in "and that's why we're great" is a brag. Narrative that ends in "and that's how your day gets better" is a promise.

A story is something you tell once. A narrative is what people say about you when you're not in the room.

What are some well known examples of marketing narratives?

The big brands show the idea at scale, and it's worth knowing what they did, as long as we're careful not to over-read it.

Apple's "Think Different" campaign in 1997 didn't describe a single product. It set out a view of the people who change things and positioned the company alongside them, at a time when the business needed a reason to exist. Dove has run its Campaign for Real Beauty since 2004, an idea about how women are portrayed that has driven everything from billboards to the Real Beauty Sketches film. Patagonia's "Don't Buy This Jacket" advert, which ran in the New York Times on Black Friday 2011, made a point about overconsumption in the middle of the biggest shopping day of the year, and the point was consistent with how the company already behaved.

What those share is consistency over a long period and a position someone could argue with. The campaigns changed. The narrative underneath stayed put. For more examples of businesses that do it well, what brands use storytelling goes through them.

Narrative isn't only for giants, though. A small London goldsmith who works only in recycled metal has a narrative handed to her. It says something about where materials come from and what care looks like. We built the film for Catherine Marche around the way she works instead of the pieces in the case, and the narrative came through without anyone saying it outright. The viewer finishes knowing what she stands for.

If your narrative could belong to any competitor on your street, it's a tagline with ambitions.

Why does narrative matter when people are watching so much already?

Because attention is crowded, and people file brands quickly. IPA and System1 research found the most consistent brands get 27% more Very Large Brand Effects and 28% more Very Large Business Effects. People are surrounded by other people's stories all day. In that setting, the brands that get remembered are the ones that mean something clear and stay consistent, so a person can sum them up in a sentence and repeat it.

That's what a narrative does. It makes you easy to describe, and being easy to describe is what lets people recommend you. When a customer tells a friend "they're the ones who still do it all by hand" or "they actually show you what's going on", they're repeating your narrative. That's word of mouth, and it can't be bought directly.

How do you build a narrative for your business?

Start with evidence, not slogans. Here's the process I'd use, and it works with nothing more than a notebook and a few conversations.

  1. Collect the raw material. Ask five recent customers why they chose you and what they'd say to a friend. Write down their exact words. Ask your team what they're proudest of.
  2. Look for the pattern. The same two or three themes will keep appearing. Reliability, craft, honesty, speed, care. Those are where your narrative lives.
  3. Find the thing you push against. What does your industry do that you refuse to do? That's your problem in the world.
  4. Write it in plain language. Four or five sentences, as you'd say them to a customer. No jargon. Read it aloud, and if it sounds like a brochure, start again.
  5. Test it against your behaviour. If the narrative says you're transparent, does your pricing page prove it? A narrative your business doesn't live up to is worse than none.

Once it's written, the stories follow naturally, because you can pick the examples that prove it. The article on what makes a good brand story will help you choose which ones.

How does narrative shape a brand film?

It decides what gets filmed and what gets left on the cutting room floor. Without a narrative, a film becomes a tour: here's the office, here's the team, here's the logo. With one, every scene has a job, and you can cut anything that doesn't support it.

In practice, I ask clients to tell me their narrative in a couple of sentences before we plan a shoot. Then we look for the people, places and moments that show it rather than state it. A founder explaining why they do the work the slow way. A customer describing the difference. The work itself, filmed carefully. Nobody on screen has to recite the narrative, because the viewer should be able to work it out. I explain the difference between this and a standard promotional film in brand documentary versus corporate video.

It also helps with consistency across the edit. When you cut a long film into short clips, each clip should still feel like it belongs to the same brand. A clear narrative is what makes that possible. And it explains how you can make a lot of different content without it feeling scattered, a point I come back to in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

Does narrative mean something different in PR and media?

A little. In communications, people talk about "the narrative" around a company, meaning what the press, analysts and the public are saying about it. That one isn't entirely in your hands. You can influence it, but a brand narrative in the marketing sense is the version you're putting forward and living up to. When the two line up, you're in a strong position. When they pull apart, say a brand claims to be transparent while the press reports otherwise, the outside narrative usually wins.

There's also the idea of a category narrative, which is the story an entire market tells about itself. "Fast fashion is cheap and disposable" is a category narrative, and so is "solar panels pay for themselves". Challenger businesses often succeed by telling a different one: a better way to do the thing everyone else does. If you work in a trade where customers have been let down before, you probably have a natural category narrative sitting there.

How do you keep a narrative alive over time?

Treat it like a habit. Every few months, look at what you've published and ask whether a stranger could work out what you stand for. If they couldn't, the stories are drifting from the narrative. Pull them back by choosing the next customer story, shoot or post to prove a point you haven't proved recently.

Brief everyone who speaks for the business. If your salespeople describe the company one way and your website another, the narrative breaks at the first conversation. A short, plain version that the whole team can say in their own words does more than any brand guideline, and it makes it far easier for people on camera to talk naturally about what you do.

Finally, let it evolve honestly. If your business grows, changes direction or learns something new about what customers value, adjust the narrative to match. Customers will forgive a company that changes its mind and explains why. They won't forgive one that keeps telling a story it's stopped living.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Making it too vague. "We care about quality and customers" fits every company on earth. Say what you actually do differently.
  • Making it up. Narrative has to come from what's true. Customers test it every time they deal with you.
  • Changing it every year. A narrative works through repetition. Revisit it when your business really changes, and leave it alone otherwise.
  • Keeping it in a document. A narrative nobody sees in the work isn't doing anything. It has to show up in what you film, publish and do.
  • Treating it as a campaign. Campaigns end. The narrative is what they all point back to.

If you want to see how a narrative translates onto film, or you'd like help working out yours before you commit to a shoot, have a word with us. The finished work is on our films page, and the explanation of brand storytelling in marketing fills in the surrounding picture.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a brand story and a brand narrative?
faqs.a: A brand story is one specific account, like a customer's experience or a founder's decision. The brand narrative is the larger, lasting idea those stories add up to: what you believe, what you're against and what you're working towards. You'll tell many stories over the years, but the narrative stays consistent and gives them a common thread.

faqs.q: What is a narrative in advertising?
faqs.a: In advertising, narrative means the way a campaign unfolds as a sequence, from setup through complication to resolution, and also the bigger idea a brand keeps returning to across campaigns. The first sense is about a single advert's structure, while the second is about the brand's long-running position. Good brands manage both.

faqs.q: Can a small business have a marketing narrative?
faqs.a: Yes, and often a clearer one than large brands, because the founder and the work are visible. A small business narrative can be as simple as a belief about how the job should be done and the evidence that you do it that way. It needs to be true, specific and repeated consistently in everything you publish.

faqs.q: How do I write a brand narrative?
faqs.a: Interview your customers and team, note the themes that repeat, identify what your industry does that you refuse to, and write four or five plain sentences covering the problem, your belief, your action and the customer's result. Then test it against how you actually behave. If your business doesn't live up to it, change the business or the narrative.

items.title: What is storytelling in social media marketing?
items.excerpt: Storytelling in social media marketing means telling short, repeatable stories in each platform's native format. Here's what works in a feed and how to plan it.
items.coverAlt: A smiling man and a laughing woman hold red party cups at an outdoor summer party under bunting
items.body:
Storytelling in social media marketing means using short, repeatable stories, told in the formats each platform favours, to build recognition and trust with people who weren't looking for you. It swaps the single polished film for a steady run of real moments, people and small turns that make a feed feel like it has someone behind it.

Social storytelling plays by different rules from a brand film on your website, and most of the mistakes come from forgetting that. This post covers how the rules differ, which story shapes work in a feed, what each main platform rewards, and how to plan it without spending your life posting. For the wider question of how stories behave in marketing, start with the brand storytelling complete guide.

How is storytelling on social media different?

On your website, someone has chosen to be there. On social, you're interrupting something else. Nobody opened Instagram to watch your brand, so the story has to earn attention in the first second and keep earning it. That changes almost everything about how you build it.

The audience is huge, which is part of the appeal. DataReportal's Digital 2026 report counted 55.5 million social media user identities in the UK in October 2025, equal to 79.7% of the population. Those figures count accounts rather than unique people, since plenty of us have several, but the scale is clear. Most of your customers are somewhere on these platforms, and they're scrolling fast.

Three things follow from that:

  • The hook comes first. There's no slow build or logo opener. You start on the most interesting moment, face or line.
  • Stories get serialised. A single post is a scene, and the story is the run of them. People follow along, and the picture of your business builds over weeks.
  • The audience talks back. Comments, replies and shares are part of the story. Answering them in the same voice keeps it alive.

If you want the video side in detail, I've covered it in social media videos for business, and the visual craft in what visual storytelling in marketing is.

What kinds of story work in a social feed?

You don't need to invent anything. The stories that do well are usually the ones that already exist in your business, told in small pieces.

The customer story

A real customer, a real problem and what changed. On social this is often a thirty to sixty second clip of them explaining it in their own words. It works because it's somebody else vouching for you, which carries more weight than you vouching for yourself. For a longer treatment, see customer testimonial videos.

The craft and process story

Hands doing something skilled. A job being done properly, a product being made, a repair being finished. People watch other people being good at things, and it quietly makes the case for your price. Signwriters, shoemakers, cheesemongers and builders all have this, and it's usually underused.

The behind the scenes story

The messy middle that nobody normally sees: the early start, the thing that went wrong, the argument about which approach to take. It's honest, which is exactly why it works in a space full of polish.

The founder story

Why you started, what you got wrong, what you'd do differently. Told in small pieces over several posts it builds a relationship. Told as a single long speech it gets skipped. Remember that the viewer is meeting you for the first time, so keep it personal and brief.

The ongoing story

A project that unfolds over weeks, like a build, a launch or a season. This is the most powerful and the least used, because it gives people a reason to come back. Each post is a chapter, and following the project becomes a habit.

On social, a story isn't one big film. It's a reason for someone to look for your next post.

What does each platform reward?

I'd be wary of anyone who gives you precise rules for algorithms, since they change constantly and the platforms rarely explain them. These are the broad habits that have held up on shoots and in the work we've delivered.

  • Instagram. Short vertical video and carousels. Carousels suit stories with a beginning, middle and end, since each swipe is a beat. Reels suit the hook-first moment.
  • TikTok. Native, unpolished and quick. The person in the clip matters more than the production. Trends are a way in, but your own angle on them is what gets remembered.
  • LinkedIn. Personal accounts do better than company pages for storytelling. A lesson, a mistake or a client moment told plainly by a named person tends to get read. Video does well when it's a real voice rather than a promo.
  • YouTube. The place for longer stories and for Shorts. Ofcom's Online Nation 2025 research found Britons spend about 51 minutes a day on YouTube, so people will happily watch something with substance if it's worth their time.
  • Facebook. Still strong for local and community businesses. Stories about people in a place, and anything that gets shared among neighbours, do well.

You don't need all five. Pick the one or two where your customers already are and do them properly. A thin presence everywhere is worse than a good one in the place that matters.

Posting on six platforms with the same dull clip isn't a strategy. It's a very efficient way to be ignored six times.

How do you make one story go a long way?

This is where most small businesses either win or burn out. The answer is to film once and cut many ways. A single day on a job can produce a long film for YouTube, a run of vertical clips, a couple of carousels and a set of photographs. We did exactly this on a day filming one drainage job in Enfield, where one shoot became a longform film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels, with the channel set up so it kept working afterwards.

It's far cheaper than making each piece from scratch, and it keeps the story consistent across platforms. The method is in how to turn one brand film into a year of content, and if you're filming it yourself, phone video for business content shows what you can do with the kit in your pocket.

Plan the cuts before you film. Know that you want a clip of the customer's key line, a close shot of the work and a moment of the founder laughing at something, because those are the pieces that'll become posts. It's much easier to capture them on the day than to hunt for them afterwards.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Treating it as advertising. A feed full of offers and logos isn't a story. People scroll past anything that looks like an ad.
  • Starting slowly. Intros, greetings and title cards cost you the viewer. Begin on the interesting part.
  • Posting without a thread. Ten unconnected posts don't add up. Know what the running story is, even if it's simply "this is how we do the work properly".
  • Ignoring sound and subtitles. Many people watch with the sound off, so add captions as standard. Our guide to repurposing a film has the numbers on how many viewers do.
  • Going quiet. A story that stops mid-chapter loses the people who followed it. It's better to post a little less often and keep going than to burst and vanish.
  • Faking it. Staged enthusiasm and invented customers show. Real people reading from a script look nervous, and that undoes the trust you're after.

How do you write a hook that stops the scroll?

Treat the first line of a caption and the first two seconds of a clip as the whole pitch. Everything else is a reward for those who stay. A few approaches hold up well.

  • Start with the outcome. "This kitchen was finished a day early" gives people the result and makes them want the route.
  • Start with a person mid-sentence. A face already talking, with a line that sounds like something real, beats any title card.
  • Start with something slightly wrong. A mistake, a surprise or a thing that shouldn't work draws people in because they want to see how it ends.
  • Start with a specific detail. "Two hundred and ten steps to make one pair of shoes" is a better opening than "Handmade shoes".

Then keep the promise. A hook that the clip doesn't pay off teaches people to scroll past you next time, and that costs more than a dull opening would.

What does a month of social storytelling look like?

Here's a realistic pattern for a small business posting twice a week, built from one day of filming and a handful of phone clips.

  1. Week one. The founder or lead person introduces what the work really is, with one short clip, plus a carousel that walks through a single job from start to finish.
  2. Week two. A customer clip, using their own words, and a behind the scenes moment from the shoot or the job.
  3. Week three. A craft or process clip with no talking, just the work and good sound, and a post answering a question customers keep asking.
  4. Week four. The longer film goes up on YouTube and the website, and the week's posts point to it with short cuts from it.

That's eight posts, all from the same underlying story. Nobody has had to invent anything, and the posts support each other. If you can do that month after month, you'll have a body of work that a new customer can scroll through and understand your business in ten minutes.

How do you know if it's working?

Likes are the weakest signal. Look for the ones that point towards trade: replies and direct messages from people who match your customer, saves and shares, profile visits, and new enquiries that mention something they saw. Ask every new customer how they found you, and write the answer down. Over a quarter, those answers tell you which stories earn their place.

Be patient with the numbers. A story-led feed builds slowly, and small accounts can still be very effective if the right fifty people are watching. Reach is a vanity figure until it turns into conversations.

How do you start without it taking over your week?

Start small and fixed. Choose one story thread, one or two platforms and a rhythm you can keep up, such as two posts a week for three months. Film in batches, so one morning produces a month of material. Write down every question a customer asks you, because each one is a post waiting to be filmed.

Then look at what people respond to. A clip that gets replies tells you what your audience wants more of. Do more of that and less of what gets silence. The guide to using storytelling in marketing shows how social fits with your website and sales material, and what digital storytelling in marketing is covers the wider picture.

If you'd rather have a proper film as the foundation for your social, with the cuts planned from the start, get in touch. Our films page shows what that looks like.

faqs.q: What is storytelling in social media?
faqs.a: It's using short, connected pieces of content to tell a story about your business over time, rather than posting isolated promotions. Each post is a scene from a larger story about your people, your work or your customers. Because people follow along, the story builds recognition and trust that a single advert can't.

faqs.q: How often should I post stories on social media?
faqs.a: Pick a rhythm you can keep up for at least three months, usually two or three posts a week for a small business. Consistency matters more than volume, because a story only works if people can follow it. Film in batches so one session produces several weeks of material, and don't burst then vanish.

faqs.q: Which social platform is best for brand storytelling?
faqs.a: It depends where your customers already spend time. Instagram and TikTok suit short visual stories, LinkedIn suits personal stories from named people in B2B, YouTube suits longer pieces, and Facebook suits local and community businesses. Do one or two properly rather than being thinly present on all of them.

faqs.q: Do I need professional video for social media storytelling?
faqs.a: Not for every post. Phone video is fine for behind the scenes and quick updates, and it often feels more authentic. A professionally shot film is worth it as a foundation, since it gives you high quality interviews and footage to cut into dozens of social posts. The mix of the two usually works best.
