items.title: Which storytelling structure is most effective in marketing?
items.excerpt: No structure wins everywhere. Here's how the three-act, ABT, hero's journey and problem-solution patterns compare, and which fits each kind of marketing video.
items.coverAlt: Two men in navy overalls stand in a field facing a tall rocket against a blue evening sky
items.body:
No single storytelling structure wins in marketing. The three-act structure and the "and, but, therefore" pattern work best for short brand films, the hero's journey suits longer documentary pieces, and problem, agitate, solve is strongest in direct response. What matters is matching the structure to the length, the audience and what you want people to do next.

I've cut a lot of films, and I haven't seen any structure rescue a story that has nothing in it. This post compares the main structures honestly, says where each one helps and where it gets in the way, and gives a rule for picking. For the general question of how a brand story is put together, see how a brand story should be structured, and there's more in the brand storytelling complete guide.

Is there one storytelling structure that's proven to be most effective?

No, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling a framework. I've looked, and I can't find robust research that tests story structures against each other in real marketing and ranks them. What exists is plenty of craft wisdom, a handful of experiments with small samples, and a lot of confident blog posts.

What I can say is that structures survive because they solve the same few problems. They get attention early, give the viewer a reason to keep watching, build towards a change and give them a place to land. Different structures do those four jobs in different orders and at different speeds, which is why the right one depends on how long you've got.

What are the main storytelling structures used in marketing?

The three-act structure

Setup, confrontation, resolution. Someone is in a situation, something goes wrong or changes, and they come out the other side. It's the backbone of most films you've seen, and it works at almost any length from thirty seconds to two hours. For brand films it's the safest choice, because it matches how people already expect stories to go. You can hear it in how a customer describes their own experience: here's how things were, here's what happened, here's how it is now.

And, but, therefore

Marine biologist and filmmaker Randy Olson popularised this as the ABT template. "We started doing this, and it was going well, but then this happened, therefore we did that." It forces cause and effect into a single sentence, which is why I find it useful for checking a script before filming. If your story is a run of "and then, and then", it hasn't got a spine. It works particularly well for short pieces and social clips, where there's room for one turn and no more.

The hero's journey

Joseph Campbell's pattern, later boiled down for screenwriters, has a hero leave the familiar world, face tests, hit a low point and return changed. It's a grand template, and it can make a customer story feel important. It's also easy to overdo. A plumber's customer doesn't need to slay a dragon. Used lightly, with the customer as the one who changes and the brand as the guide, it helps in longer films. Used heavily, it gets pompous.

Problem, agitate, solve

A copywriter's formula: name a problem, make the reader feel its cost, then offer the fix. It's quick and it pushes people to act, which is why it's common in adverts and sales pages. Because it leads with discomfort, it can feel heavy-handed in a brand film, where you're trying to build trust more than prompt a purchase. It's a good fit for a sales video and a poor fit for a documentary.

Before, after, bridge

Show the world as it is, show the world as it could be, then explain how to get there. It's the cousin of problem, agitate, solve with a more hopeful tone. It suits product and service explainers where the change itself is the point.

Starting in the middle

Open on the most interesting moment, then go back and explain how it got there. Documentary makers do this constantly, since it gives you a hook without having to explain anything first. It's the nearest thing to a universal technique for online video, and I'll come back to why.

The best structure is the one the viewer doesn't notice, because the story just seems to be going somewhere.

Which structure suits which kind of marketing video?

This is the part that actually helps. I choose by length and by job.

  • Under a minute, for social. Start in the middle, then use a single ABT turn. Put the interesting moment in the first two seconds and skip any introduction. You don't have time for three acts.
  • One to three minutes, for a website or case study. Three acts, compressed. A situation, a complication and a result, told by the customer or the founder. This is the workhorse length for brand film.
  • Three to ten minutes, for a documentary-style brand film. Three acts with room for a second turn, or a light hero's journey if there's a real transformation. You can afford to let people breathe and show process.
  • Sales and conversion videos. Problem, agitate, solve, with a clear next step at the end. Honest about what you're doing: this is persuading, not documenting.
  • Launches and explainers. Before, after, bridge, so the change is the star.

If you're unsure how long yours should be, how long a brand story should be and how long a brand film should be will settle it, since length decides structure more than any other factor.

Why does the opening matter more than the structure?

Because you can have a perfect arc and lose the viewer in the first ten seconds. Researchers who analysed the emotional shape of 1,327 stories found six core arcs, and the lesson holds for any of them. Put the most compelling material early. That's a structural instruction in a single line: don't save your best material for the end, because many people won't reach it.

I'd take that further. Whatever structure you use, build the first fifteen seconds as if it were a trailer for the rest. Show a face, a line of speech or a striking image that raises a question, and let the rest of the film answer it. If you want to see how that's done, how brand storytelling should always begin is a closer look, and how to make a brand video people watch covers the mechanics of holding someone to the end.

I've seen clients agonise over three-act versus hero's journey and then open their film with forty seconds of logo animation.

What does a good structure look like in a real film?

Take the Tooting house film. A Victorian house had sat empty, a couple bought it, they renovated it in eight weeks with a baby on the way, and then they told the story. That's a three-act structure that arrived ready-made: the setup of a neglected house, the pressure of a deadline you can't move, and the resolution of a family in a finished home. We didn't impose it. We found it by listening to what happened and putting the moments in the order a viewer would want them.

That's the approach I'd recommend to most people. A documentary approach means the structure usually comes out of the material. You ask the right questions in the interview, you film the work as it happens, and the shape emerges in the edit. Compare that with a scripted film, where you have to invent the tension, and you can see why real stories are easier to structure.

Another example is the film about hand painted signwriting, where the structure is simpler. It follows the work from the workshop out to the shopfront, so the sequence of the craft is the story. Not every film needs a dramatic turn. Sometimes a clear process with a person you want to watch is the whole thing.

How do you test a structure before you shoot?

I use three checks, and they take about ten minutes with a pen.

  1. The one-sentence test. Write your story as "We started with X, and Y, but Z, therefore W." If you can't fill in the "but", the film has no tension.
  2. The cut-the-middle test. Imagine only the first and last ten seconds. Is the change obvious? If the opening and ending look the same, nothing has moved.
  3. The friend test. Tell the story out loud to someone who knows nothing about your business. Watch where their attention drops, and that's where the film will lose people too.

If it passes, you can shoot with confidence. If it doesn't, no structure will fix it, but you can often find the missing piece by asking one more question in the interview. What makes a good brand story will help you judge whether you have enough material to begin with.

What mistakes do people make with structure?

The first is following a template too literally. A framework is a checklist for your draft and was never meant as a script. When every beat arrives exactly on schedule, viewers feel the machinery, and the film starts to sound like every other one.

The second is putting the company at the centre. Nearly every structure above works because a person wants something and meets resistance. If that person is your business, you've written a brochure with a plot. Put the customer, the maker or the founder in that position and keep the brand as the thing that helps.

The third is cramming. A ninety second film can hold one turn. If you try to fit the founding story, three services, a testimonial and a call to action into it, the structure collapses into a list. Choose the one moment that matters, and save the rest for another cut. That's one reason I plan a shoot to produce several lengths, as I describe in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

The fourth is ignoring the ending. Plenty of films have a strong opening and a limp finish, which is a pity, because the end is what people carry away. Finish on the change, on an image or on a line that sounds like a real person, and then stop. Resist the urge to summarise what the viewer has just watched.

What's the practical answer?

Pick the structure that matches your length. For most small business films that means a compressed three-act arc, opened on the most interesting moment, with a single clear turn. Use ABT to check it. Keep the hero's journey for longer pieces where somebody really does change. Keep problem, agitate, solve for sales videos. And spend more time on what happens in the first fifteen seconds than on which framework you've chosen.

If you've got a story and you're not sure how it should be told, send us the outline and we'll tell you how we'd shape it. Our films show how the finished work comes together.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the most common storytelling structure in marketing?
faqs.a: The three-act structure is the most common: a situation, a complication and a resolution. It matches how people naturally tell stories, so it feels familiar at almost any length. In short marketing videos it's usually compressed, with a quick setup, one clear turn and a result. Problem, agitate, solve is the other staple, mostly in adverts and sales pages.

faqs.q: What is the ABT storytelling structure?
faqs.a: ABT stands for And, But, Therefore, a template popularised by scientist and filmmaker Randy Olson. You say what's happening, introduce the complication with 'but', then give the consequence with 'therefore'. It forces cause and effect into a single sentence, which makes it a quick way to check whether a story has real tension before you film.

faqs.q: Should a brand story follow the hero's journey?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It suits longer pieces where someone really does change, such as a customer whose situation was transformed. Used lightly it gives a film weight. Used heavily, it makes ordinary businesses sound grandiose. A good rule is to make the customer the one who changes and the brand the guide, not the star of the journey.

faqs.q: Does the structure matter more than the content?
faqs.a: No. A well structured story with nothing in it stays empty, while a real story with a rough structure often still works. Content comes first: a person, something at stake and a change. Structure then helps you order that material so people keep watching, which is why the opening seconds matter as much as the overall shape.

stat.title: Core emotional arcs found across 1,327 stories
stat.takeaway: Researchers analysed the emotional shape of 1,327 stories and found six core arcs, so there are only a few shapes worth choosing between.

source.name: Reagan et al., EPJ Data Science (2016)

items.title: Is storytelling a marketing strategy?
items.excerpt: Storytelling is an approach that serves a marketing strategy, and it can sit at its centre. Here's how to tell the difference and plan it properly.
items.coverAlt: Aerial view of a long low bridge crossing a calm Norwegian fjord with small islands and hills under a blue sky
items.body:
Storytelling is a marketing approach rather than a marketing strategy on its own. A strategy decides who you're trying to win, what you want them to think and which channels you'll use. Storytelling is how you carry that message so people remember it. It can sit at the centre of a strategy, but it needs the strategy underneath it.

This post is about where storytelling sits in your plan and how to tell if you're using it as a strategy or only as a tactic. I'll cover what a strategy is, when story becomes the core of one, a simple test, and the mistakes I see when businesses skip the planning. If you want the general how-to, see how to use storytelling in marketing, and the full set of guides starts at the brand storytelling complete guide.

What's the difference between a strategy and a tactic?

A strategy is a decision about where you'll compete and why you'll win there. A tactic is something you do to carry it out. The strategist Richard Rumelt, in his book Good Strategy Bad Strategy, boils a good strategy down to three parts: a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it and a set of coherent actions that follow. A list of things you'd like to do isn't a strategy, however long it is.

Put that next to storytelling and the answer gets clear. "We'll tell stories" doesn't diagnose anything, and it doesn't tell you what to say no to. "We're the only firm in our trade that shows its work, so we'll let customers and craftspeople explain what we do in their own words" does. That sentence names a gap, makes a choice and implies the actions. The story is how it gets delivered, and the choice behind it is the strategy.

That's why you'll hear two opposing opinions about this question and both can be right. People who say storytelling is a strategy usually mean the brand is built on a distinctive narrative. People who say it's a tactic usually mean a business has made a film or posted some stories without any plan behind them. They're describing different situations.

When does storytelling become the strategy?

It becomes the core of a strategy when your difference is something people can only understand by hearing it told. That's more common than it sounds, and it shows up in a few places.

  • Craft and heritage. When what you offer is slower, more careful or more personal than the alternative, the story is the product's justification. Without it, you're just more expensive.
  • Founder-led businesses. If the reason people buy is the person, the story of that person is your positioning.
  • Trust-heavy services. Where buyers are nervous, such as a big renovation, a care provider or a professional adviser, seeing real people and real outcomes does the persuading that claims can't.
  • Commodity markets. When everyone sells much the same thing at much the same price, the story is often the only thing left to choose between.

Take the Easee films we've made, built around moments real people recognise, such as moving house or passing a driving test. They sit inside a set of brand films built around the moments people actually get a charger. The thinking came first (who is buying, and when) and the story followed. That order matters. It's what turned three films into a plan.

A story with no strategy behind it is a nice film. A strategy with no story is a spreadsheet nobody remembers.

What does a strategy that includes storytelling look like?

It answers five questions before anyone picks up a camera or opens a document. I use these with clients, and they fit on a page.

1. Who exactly are you trying to reach?

Not "everyone who might need us". Pick the buyer you'd most like more of, and describe their day. A story told to nobody in particular lands with nobody in particular.

2. What do you want them to think, feel or do afterwards?

Be specific. "Remember us" isn't enough. "Trust that we'll turn up and finish the job" is. "Book a survey" is better again. The answer decides the story you choose. If you haven't read it, why a brand film needs a business goal goes into this in more detail.

3. What's true about you that competitors can't copy?

This is where the story comes from. It's usually a person, a place, a process or a decision. You can find it by asking what you'd say if a customer asked why you do it this way.

4. Where will people meet it?

Your website, your social feeds, a sales meeting, a tender, an email. Each has different needs. A film at the top of a service page does a different job from a vertical clip on Instagram, and both do a different job from a case study sent after a call.

5. How will you know it's working?

Choose one or two signals before launch. Enquiries that mention the film, branded search, time on the page, win rate on proposals. If you can't think of a measure, the strategy isn't finished.

Notice that none of these are about the creative. The strategy decides what story is needed, and only then does anybody write or film it.

Is storytelling worth building a strategy around?

For many businesses it is, and the reason is basic. The Content Marketing Institute's 2026 research found that 97% of B2B marketers have a documented content strategy, and that 74% of marketers credited refining that strategy as the biggest driver of better results, ahead of adopting new technology at 51%. Their own summary line was that strategy beats scale. The same logic applies to story. A modest, well planned set of films beats a pile of unplanned ones, and you don't need a big budget to start.

That research is B2B, and it's about content in general, so I wouldn't stretch it too far. Still, it matches my experience from the production side. The projects that perform are the ones where the client could say, before the shoot, who the film was for and what it should do.

If your strategy is "post more", you don't have one, you have a calendar.

What goes wrong when storytelling is treated as the strategy?

The most common failure is starting with the story and hoping a purpose appears later. A business commissions a handsome film because a competitor has one, then wonders why nothing changed. The film was fine. Nobody had decided who it was for.

The second is telling one story once. A strategy needs repetition. People don't build a view of a business from a single film, and the effect comes from the same few ideas turning up across the website, the sales deck, the social feed and the way staff talk about the work. I'd plan the shoot so that one day of filming becomes a long film, a short cut and a run of clips, as I describe in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

The third is mixing up the brand story with campaign messages. Your brand story is long-term and stays roughly constant. A campaign is a short push with a date on it. The two should fit together, but they shouldn't be confused. For the difference between the story and the wider narrative around it, see what narrative in marketing means.

The fourth is waiting for permission to measure. Many businesses can't prove a film caused a sale, and that's fine, because very few marketing activities can be proved that cleanly. What you can do is watch the leading signs and ask new customers how they heard about you. A simple question on an enquiry form tells you more than most dashboards.

It's worth saying that a strategy can change. Plenty of businesses start with a clear plan, learn from the first film what their customers respond to, and adjust. A line that gets quoted back on calls tells you what to say more often. A clip that nobody watches tells you what to drop. Treat the first piece as a test with a real audience and not as a verdict on the whole approach, and keep the plan short enough that changing it takes an hour.

How do you decide if you're ready to build on it?

Here's the quick test I'd run on any business before suggesting a film. If you can answer yes to all four, storytelling is a sensible centre for your plan.

  1. Can you describe your ideal customer in a sentence?
  2. Do you have a real person or place that explains why you're different?
  3. Will that person speak on camera, or can we film the work instead?
  4. Can you commit to using what we make in more than one place for more than a month?

A no on any of them isn't a stop sign. It just tells you what to fix first. If you haven't got a person who'll talk, we film hands and process. If you haven't settled the customer, that's a conversation to have before spending anything.

For smaller businesses in particular, a documentary film is a good fit as the anchor piece. It's the one asset that works as your strategy's evidence: it shows the real people, the real place and the real work, which is hard to fake and hard for a competitor to copy. For an example of how that plays out on a single project, have a look at the La Fromagerie documentary brand film, and the explanation of brand storytelling in marketing if you want the definition first.

What does the difference look like in practice?

Picture two renovation firms, both with a film on their site. The first made it because a friend said they should. It runs three minutes, opens on a drone shot of a roof and finishes on a logo. It's been viewed a few hundred times and nobody on the team could tell you why it exists.

The second decided its buyers were couples nervous about handing over a big budget, and that the thing which calms them is hearing from people who've been through it. So it filmed a homeowner explaining the whole job from their side, cut a two-minute version for the service page, pulled three short clips for sales emails and asked every new enquiry how they'd heard about the firm. Same technique, completely different result, and the only thing separating them is the planning. We took that customer-side approach on a renovation explained by the person who lived through it.

That's the point to hold on to. Story is a good thing to build a strategy on, and a poor thing to use as a substitute for one.

Where should you start this week?

Write the five answers above on one page. Don't make them neat. If you struggle with the third one, ask three recent customers why they chose you and write down their exact words, since those words are usually your story. You can do all of this in an afternoon, with no budget, and it will make any film you commission better.

If you've got the page and you'd like a second opinion on whether a film is the right next step, tell us where you've got to. We'll say so if we think something else should come first. You can also look at our films to see what the finished work looks like.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is storytelling a strategy or a tactic?
faqs.a: It can be either. As a tactic, it's a film or a post you make to carry a message. As the centre of a strategy, it's a decision to compete on a distinctive narrative, such as craft, heritage or a founder's story. The test is whether a clear audience, goal and measure sit behind it. Without those, it's a tactic.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a content strategy and storytelling?
faqs.a: A content strategy decides what you'll publish, for whom, where and how you'll measure it. Storytelling is the approach you use to make that content memorable. You can have a content strategy without much story, but a story-led one needs the strategy underneath to stop it becoming a collection of nice but unconnected pieces.

faqs.q: Do small businesses need a storytelling strategy?
faqs.a: They need a clear one, not a big one. A single page covering your audience, goal, difference, channels and measure is enough. Small businesses often have the strongest material, because the founder and the work are visible and real. The plan just makes sure that material gets used on purpose and in more than one place.

faqs.q: How long does a storytelling strategy take to work?
faqs.a: Expect months rather than weeks. Stories build recognition and trust through repetition, so a single film on its own won't shift much. Leading signs like enquiries mentioning the film or more people searching your name tend to appear first. Judge it over at least a quarter, against a measure you chose before launch.

stat.title: What B2B marketers say drove better content results
stat.takeaway: Marketers credit a better plan above new tools, so decide who a story is for and what it should do before anyone picks up a camera.

source.name: Content Marketing Institute, 2026 B2B Content and Marketing Trends

items.title: Shotgun microphones explained for interviews
items.excerpt: What a shotgun mic is, how polar patterns work, boom versus on-camera, indoors versus outdoors, wind protection, and why interviews pair it with a lav.
items.coverAlt: A panel talk in a marquee at the Southwick D-Day 80 event
items.body:
A shotgun microphone is a long, thin mic that mostly hears what it's pointed at and turns down sound coming from the sides. It's the mic you see on the end of a boom pole on a film set, held just above the frame and aimed at the speaker's mouth. It works best close to the voice, outdoors or in rooms that aren't too echoey, and it struggles when it's sat on top of a camera several metres away.

I've written about lav mics and wireless systems already. This is the other half of interview sound: what a shotgun actually does, where it goes, and why it's so often paired with a lav.

How does a shotgun microphone work?

Inside the long tube is a fairly normal directional capsule. The tube is what makes it a shotgun. It's called an interference tube, and it's covered in slots or holes along its length.

Sound arriving from straight ahead travels down the tube cleanly and reaches the capsule in one go. Sound arriving from the side comes in through the slots at lots of slightly different points, so the pieces arrive at the capsule out of step with each other and partly cancel out. The result is a mic that's noticeably more sensitive in front than at the sides.

Two things follow from that. First, the trick works better at higher frequencies than lower ones, so a shotgun is less directional for low rumble like traffic and air con than it is for voices. Second, sound from off to the side gets quieter and also coloured, sounding thin, hollow and a bit phasey. That colouring matters a lot indoors, which I'll get to.

Length changes things too. A short shotgun is the everyday film and TV mic, easy to boom and forgiving. A long shotgun reaches further and rejects more from the sides, which suits outdoor work and documentaries where you can't get close, but it's heavier, harder to aim and less forgiving when the speaker moves.

What are polar patterns?

A polar pattern is a map of which directions a mic hears best. They're drawn as a shape around the mic, and the ones you'll hear about most are:

  • Omnidirectional. Hears equally in every direction. Most lavs are omni, which works because they're so close to the mouth.
  • Cardioid. A heart shape. Hears the front well, the sides less, and the back hardly at all. Common on vocal mics.
  • Supercardioid and hypercardioid. Tighter at the front than a cardioid, with a small sensitive patch at the back. Good indoors on a boom.
  • Lobar. The narrow, stretched shape of a shotgun, very tight at the front with smaller lobes elsewhere, including at the back.

That little patch at the back catches people out. A shotgun pointed down at someone from above is also listening, faintly, to whatever's above it. A shotgun on a camera pointed at a speaker is also listening to the camera operator breathing behind it.

A shotgun hears the sides a bit less. Distance still decides how it sounds.

Does a shotgun mic pick up sound from far away?

Not in the way most people think. It doesn't zoom. It hears a distant voice no louder than any other mic would, it just hears less of the room around it. Distance still wins.

Every time you double the distance between a mic and a mouth, the voice drops by around six decibels, while the room noise stays where it was. So a shotgun at three metres sounds roomier and thinner than the same mic at half a metre, however good it is. On a sit-down interview, the boom wants to be as close as the frame allows, usually somewhere between a forearm and an arm's length from the mouth.

Boom or on-camera: which is better?

For an interview, the boom, by a long way. A boom pole lets the mic sit just out of shot, close to the voice, aimed exactly where it needs to be. The camera can be wherever the picture needs it to be.

The usual position is overhead, angled down at the mouth or upper chest, just above the top of the frame. From there the mic hears the voice, and its less sensitive sides face the walls. Booming from below, pointing up from under the frame, is sometimes used to get away from noise above, like a ceiling full of air con, though it tends to pick up more of the body and the floor.

A good boom operator is doing a real job. They watch the frame edge so the mic never dips in, follow the speaker as they lean and turn, and keep the pole steady for an hour. It's more tiring than it looks.

An on-camera shotgun is fine for what it's for: picking up sound you'll use to line up audio in the edit, recording atmosphere, and grabbing quick moments when you're right next to someone. For a proper interview it's usually too far away, pointed wherever the camera's pointed rather than at the mouth, and it hears the operator's every move. It's better than the camera's built-in mic. It's still the wrong tool for the job.

The camera-top shotgun is the mic equivalent of shouting your order from the back of the queue. Technically it gets there.

Should you use a shotgun indoors or outdoors?

Outdoors is where a shotgun is happiest. There are no walls to bounce sound back, so the tight front pattern works exactly as intended. Point it so the noise you don't want, a road or a building site, is off to the side or behind, and angle it down so the background is the ground rather than the street.

Indoors is trickier. In a small room with hard walls, your voice bounces around and arrives at the mic from every direction. The shotgun hears those reflections through its sides and colours them, so the voice can come out hollow and boxy. That's why many sound recordists switch to a hypercardioid mic for interiors. It's shorter, handles reflections more gracefully and is easier to swing in a cramped space. Soft furnishings, rugs and curtains help either way, and picking the least echoey room for the interview is one of the easiest wins there is.

Why do interviews often use a boom and a lav together?

Because they fail in different ways. The boom sounds open and natural, like you're sat across from the person, but it can be caught out by a bus going past or the speaker leaning out of its sweet spot. The lav is right on the chest so it holds up in noise, but it can rustle and sometimes sounds a bit close and boxed in.

Recording both to separate tracks means the editor can pick the better one moment by moment, or blend them. When they're blended, the two need lining up carefully, because the boom is further away and its sound arrives a fraction later, which can make the mix sound thin if it's ignored.

Our coverage of the D-Day eightieth anniversary in Southwick is a good reminder of why sound gets planned in layers. It included a full panel talk recorded end to end in front of a packed marquee, at an event that couldn't be asked for twice. When nothing can be repeated, two sources for every voice is the sensible default.

How do you stop wind noise on a shotgun mic?

With layers of protection, and the more wind there is, the more layers you need.

  • Foam. The grey sleeve most shotguns come with. Fine indoors, and for the small rush of air when a boom is swung. Close to useless in a real breeze.
  • Slip-on fur. A furry sleeve that fits straight over the mic. Good for on-camera mics and light wind.
  • Basket windshield. A cage, sometimes called a blimp or zeppelin, that surrounds the mic with a pocket of still air. Wind hits the cage, not the capsule.
  • Fur over the basket. The fluffy grey thing on a pole you see at outdoor shoots. The fur slows the air before it reaches the cage, and together they deal with strong wind.

A low-cut filter, on the mic or the recorder, trims the very low rumble that wind and traffic produce without touching much of the voice. A shock mount, the cradle of elastic the mic sits in, stops knocks on the pole travelling into the recording. Neither replaces proper wind protection, but both help.

The lav needs protecting outdoors as well. I use URSA Fur Circles on lav mics, small furry discs that sit over the capsule under or on the clothing, because a lav catches wind just as easily as a shotgun does. If you want to see how sound fits into everything else on a shoot, what a shoot day looks like walks through it, and our free guide covers the planning before it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a shotgun mic for a podcast or voiceover?
faqs.a: You can, but it's rarely the best choice. A voiceover is usually recorded close up in a treated space, where a large diaphragm cardioid studio mic sounds fuller and warmer. Shotguns are built for film sets, where the mic has to stay out of shot. If a shotgun is all you have, get it close, point it at the mouth and record in a room with plenty of soft furnishings.

faqs.q: Do shotgun mics need phantom power?
faqs.a: Most professional shotguns are condenser mics and need 48 volt phantom power, supplied by the recorder, mixer or camera through the XLR cable. Some can also run on an internal battery. Small on-camera shotguns often take power from the camera's mic socket or have their own battery. Check before the shoot, because a mic with no power records nothing at all.

faqs.q: How far should a boom mic be from the speaker?
faqs.a: As close as the frame allows, which for a sit-down interview usually means roughly half a metre to a metre from the mouth, just above the top edge of the shot. Closer means more voice and less room. A wide shot pushes the mic further away, which is one reason many crews frame interviews in mid shots or close-ups and rely on the lav for wider angles.

faqs.q: Is an expensive shotgun mic worth it?
faqs.a: Up to a point. Better shotguns tend to have lower self-noise, smoother off-axis sound and better handling of humidity, which matters on long outdoor days. But placement and wind protection make a bigger difference than price. A mid-range mic on a boom half a metre from the mouth will beat an expensive one sat on a camera across the room every time.

items.title: Why does storytelling work in marketing?
items.excerpt: Storytelling works in marketing because people remember and trust stories more than claims. Here's the psychology, the IPA evidence and where it falls short.
items.coverAlt: A crowd gathers around a vintage car in the village, a hand raising a phone to film as veterans in tweed greet each other
items.body:
Storytelling works in marketing because people remember and believe stories far more readily than lists of claims. A story gives the brain a sequence to follow, a person to care about and a feeling to attach the facts to. That's why an emotional film tends to build trust and recall that a feature list can't.

This post is about the reasons behind that, not the how-to. I'll go through what's happening in a viewer's head, what the advertising evidence says, where storytelling stops working, and what it means if you're about to commission a brand film. For the definition, start with what brand storytelling is, and the full picture lives in the complete guide to brand storytelling.

What actually happens when someone watches a story?

A claim asks the viewer to do the work. You say "we're reliable" and they have to decide whether to believe you. A story does the work for them, because they watch someone be reliable and reach the conclusion on their own. People hold on to conclusions they've reached themselves far more tightly than ones they've been handed.

There's some decent research behind this. Psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock described what they called transportation in 2000: when people get absorbed in a narrative, they tend to question it less while they're inside it, and the beliefs they take away often stick. You've felt it yourself if you've ever realised you were three episodes deep into something you only meant to glance at. The same absorption is what makes a good brand film feel shorter than it is.

A Princeton team led by Uri Hasson found something related in 2010. When one person told a story and another listened, their brain activity lined up, with the listener's patterns following the speaker's. The closer the match, the better the listener understood. I wouldn't build a marketing plan on one study, and neither should you, but it fits what I see on shoots. When a founder tells their story properly, the room goes quiet and the crew stops looking at their phones.

Paul Zak, a neuroeconomist, has written about character-driven stories and the release of oxytocin, the chemical linked to empathy and trust. Take that one with a pinch of salt, since the science of single hormones is messier than the headlines make out. The practical point survives anyway: people respond to other people with a problem, a want and something at stake, and they respond far less to a company describing itself.

Why do stories stick when facts slip away?

Facts arrive one at a time and have to be filed one at a time. A story hangs them on a thread. Order, cause and effect, a before and an after, all of that gives the memory something to grip, so when someone later thinks of your brand they recall the scene and the facts come with it.

Think about the adverts people still talk about. Cadbury's gorilla playing the drums to Phil Collins in 2007 sold chocolate without mentioning a single ingredient. Guinness's Surfer, from 1999, never explained the beer. Dove's Real Beauty Sketches in 2013 had a forensic artist drawing women twice, once from their own description and once from a stranger's, and the gap between the two pictures did all the persuading. You can recall each of them in detail years later. Now try to recall the last three product feature adverts you scrolled past.

The same effect shows up at a much smaller scale. A cheesemonger who tells you the cheese in front of you came from a particular farm, was turned by a particular person and has been aged for a particular length of time is selling you a story, and you'll remember it when you taste it. It's what we found when we made the film for La Fromagerie. People remember a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed long after they've forgotten the price list.

Nobody has ever described a brochure to a friend at dinner. They've retold a story from one.

What does the advertising evidence say?

The most useful body of evidence in the UK comes from the IPA, the trade body for advertising agencies. Les Binet and Peter Field spent years analysing the IPA Effectiveness Awards entries, which are real campaigns with audited results. They published the findings in The Long and the Short of It in 2013 and have been updating them since.

Their headline finding on this question is plain. Emotional campaigns beat rational ones on every brand measure they tracked: awareness, commitment, trust, differentiation, perceived quality, fame and image. Rational campaigns averaged 1.0 brand effects. Emotional ones averaged 1.7, which is 70% more. Stories are the most dependable route to emotion we have, because a story gives people someone to feel something about.

There's a caveat that Binet and Field make themselves, and I'd be misleading you if I skipped it. Rational messaging still wins in direct response, where someone is ready to act and needs a price, a date or a phone number. Emotion does its best work over the long term, building the memory and preference that make people pick you when they're ready. Both have a job, and storytelling is the long-term one.

A claim tells people what to think. A story lets them get there themselves, and they hold on to it harder.

Why does this matter more for a smaller business?

Big brands can buy repetition. A national advertiser can show you the same thirty seconds fifty times until it sinks in. A founder-led business in London or Leeds can't, and that's where story earns its keep, because a good one needs fewer showings to be remembered. It gets passed on, quoted and shared. You're borrowing other people's attention instead of paying for every impression.

It's also the best answer I know to the sameness problem. Most firms in a given trade can say they're experienced, local and professional, and most of them do say it. What none of them can copy is the actual history of how you ended up doing this, the specific person who does the work, or the moment a customer's problem got solved. That's the material that makes you different, and it's available only to you.

Where does it show up in the numbers?

Be careful here, because the claims around storytelling get inflated fast. You'll see confident figures about stories being twenty times more memorable than facts, and nearly all of them trace back to an unsourced line repeated until it sounded like research. I wouldn't quote them. What you can say honestly is that the IPA data points to stronger brand effects for emotional work, and that you can measure your own version by watching branded search, direct enquiries and how often prospects mention the film on a call. I've written about measuring this properly in why a brand film needs a business goal.

When does storytelling not work?

It fails more often than the evangelists admit, and usually for the same few reasons.

  • The story is about the company. A founding history with no stakes or tension is a timeline with music on it. People engage with a problem, a person and a change.
  • It's made up or inflated. A viewer can sense a performance. If the customer on screen sounds scripted, the trust you were building turns into suspicion.
  • It has no connection to what you sell. A lovely story that doesn't lead anywhere near your service is entertainment that someone else gets the benefit of.
  • Nobody sees it. A beautiful film on a page nobody visits does nothing. Distribution is part of the plan, and I'd cover it before the shoot, not after.
  • It's the wrong job for the moment. Someone ready to buy this afternoon wants clear information. Story works earlier and keeps working later, but it won't replace a clear price page.

The honest version is that storytelling is a tool for being remembered and trusted. If you need a sale by Friday, it won't help much. If you want to be the obvious name in your trade in two years, it's among the best things you can do.

What does this mean for a brand film?

A documentary approach is the most direct way I know to turn this into something you can use. Instead of writing a script and casting an actor, we film the real people at the real place doing the real work, and then interview them. The tension and the stakes are already there, because they're real. That's also why it holds up. A real person telling the truth about their work is very difficult to fake, and viewers know it.

Take the shoemakers we filmed at the Oxo Tower, Carréducker. A pair of hand sewn shoes takes two makers 210 steps and about six months. You could put that in a bullet point and it would be a fact. Filmed, with the makers explaining why they do it the slow way, it becomes a reason to pay for it. Same information, but one version gets remembered. I made a similar point in brand documentary versus corporate video, if you want the comparison.

Preparation matters as much as the shoot. The people on camera need to feel at ease enough to talk the way they do over a cup of tea, which is why I'd read how to prepare for a brand film interview before the day. And once you have the film, it shouldn't sit on one page, so turning one film into a year of content is where I'd go next.

One more thing I'd say from the edit suite. The strongest moments in a film are almost never the ones anyone planned. They're the offhand line about the first customer, or the pause before someone admits what went wrong. Those moments are why story works: they show a person being honest, and honesty is what a viewer reads as trust. You can't script that, but you can set up a shoot so it has room to happen.

How do you put this to work without overthinking it?

Start with a single real story that your best customers would recognise. The day a job went wrong and you fixed it, or the reason you started, or the customer who changed how you work. If you can't think of one, ask your team. Someone always has it.

Then check it against three simple questions. Is there a person in it? Is something at stake for them? Does the outcome say something true about what you do? If all three are yes, you've got the raw material, and the rest is craft. For how to build it from there, how to tell a brand story is the practical follow-up, and what makes a good brand story will help you judge your own draft.

If you'd like to talk through whether you've got a story worth filming, get in touch and tell us what it is. See our films for what the finished thing looks like.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is there scientific proof that storytelling works in marketing?
faqs.a: There's good supporting evidence rather than a single proof. Research on narrative transportation shows people question stories less while absorbed in them, and the IPA's analysis of real UK campaigns found emotional work produced 1.7 brand effects against 1.0 for rational work. No study guarantees a result for your business, so measure your own.

faqs.q: Does storytelling work for B2B as well as consumer brands?
faqs.a: Yes. B2B buyers are people, and they remember a clear story about a supplier more easily than a list of capabilities. Long buying cycles make it more useful, since the story keeps working between meetings. Keep it specific to the problem the buyer has, and use real people from the business instead of generic imagery.

faqs.q: How quickly does storytelling start to work?
faqs.a: Brand effects build over months rather than days. You'll usually see early signs sooner, such as prospects quoting the film on calls or more people searching for you by name. Anything that needs a sale this week is a job for clear direct response, with the story supporting it in the background.

faqs.q: Can storytelling backfire?
faqs.a: It can, mostly when it's invented or exaggerated. Viewers pick up on performance quickly, and a story that doesn't match their experience of you damages trust. A true, specific account told by the people involved is much safer than a polished fiction, and a documentary approach keeps you on solid ground.

items.title: What is data storytelling in marketing? A plain guide
items.excerpt: What data storytelling in marketing means, how it differs from reporting numbers, a six step method to build one, and how to carry a number in a brand film.
items.coverAlt: Two people looking over the Thames and the City skyline from a rooftop at golden hour, one holding a tablet
items.body:
Data storytelling in marketing is the practice of turning numbers into a clear message by combining three things: the data itself, a narrative that explains what it means, and a visual that makes it easy to see. A table of figures informs. A data story tells the reader what changed, why it matters and what to do about it.

This post covers what data storytelling is, how it differs from simply reporting numbers, a method for building one, the pitfalls that make people distrust charts, and how a number can be carried by a person on film rather than a slide. It's the numbers angle only. For stories built from people and pictures see visual storytelling in marketing, and for the wider idea, what brand storytelling is in marketing.

What is the difference between data and a data story?

Take a made-up example. Data is "sales rose 18% in the second quarter". A data story is "sales rose 18% in the second quarter, almost all of it from customers who'd watched our film before they enquired, so we're moving budget from cold ads to more films". The first tells you what happened. The second tells you what it means and what happens next.

The idea is not new. Florence Nightingale used a polar area chart, now often called her rose diagram, to show officials in the 1850s that most soldiers in the Crimean War died from preventable disease rather than battle wounds. The data was grim, but it was the picture and the argument built around it that changed minds. In more recent times, Hans Rosling's talks and his BBC Joy of Stats programme made population and health figures gripping by animating them and narrating them like a sports commentary.

Those two examples show the three parts that make a data story work: true numbers, a clear point and a way of seeing it quickly.

Why does data storytelling matter in marketing?

Because most marketing teams have more data than they can use, and most audiences can't or won't read it. The gap is real. A Canva report on data storytelling, covering more than 2,400 professionals in eight countries including the UK, found that 77% said they felt confident with data, but only 44% kept that confidence on data-heavy tasks. Some 88% said visualising data boosts credibility.

That matches what I see around clients. People collect statistics and then freeze when asked to explain them to a customer, a board or a journalist. A data story is the translation layer. It takes the number and puts it into language and a picture that someone who isn't an analyst can use.

It matters externally too. A well-chosen statistic makes a claim believable, gives journalists a reason to quote you and gives a customer a reason to move. Used badly, it makes you look like you're hiding behind figures.

A number on its own is a fact. A number with a person attached is a reason.

How do you build a data story?

1. Start with a question, not a spreadsheet

The most common mistake is to open the data and look for something interesting. Start instead with something your audience wants to know. "Is it worth replacing the old system now or waiting a year?" "Why does the same job cost more in London?" Then go to the data for the answer.

2. Find the one number that answers it

You may have forty figures. The audience needs one, maybe two. Choose the number that changes the way someone thinks, and put the rest in a footnote or a download. Everything else is supporting evidence.

3. Give it a comparison

Numbers mean nothing without something to measure them against. "Fourteen days" is only a story if the usual figure is thirty, or if the competitor's is forty. Compare with last year, with the average, with what people expect or with what they'd pay without it.

4. Put a human in it

People care about numbers when they can picture who they affect. "Four in ten adults" is abstract. "Think of four people in a waiting room. Two of them have this problem" is easier to hold. In a film, the best way is to have someone explain what the number means to them in their own words.

5. Choose the simplest visual that shows it

A bar chart for comparing, a line for change over time, a single large figure for a standout number. Avoid 3D effects, too many colours and legends that need decoding. If the reader has to work out how to read the chart, the story is lost.

6. Say what to do

The last step is the one that makes it marketing. What should the reader think, choose or do now? A story without a conclusion is just a presentation.

What does good data storytelling look like in practice?

Spotify's Wrapped is the best known consumer example. Each user gets their own listening data presented as a series of short, shareable, personal moments: your top artist, your minutes listened, how you compare. The numbers are the same kind a dashboard would hold, but they're about you, framed as a story, and designed to be shared. People post them because they're personal and visual.

At a smaller scale, it's the case study that opens with a result and then explains how it happened, the pricing page that shows what the figures mean in plain pounds, or the annual report that begins with three numbers and a paragraph rather than forty pages of tables.

If your chart needs a legend, a key and a sit-down, it isn't a story. It's homework.

How do you tell a data story on camera?

This is where documentary-style film helps. Slides with charts are the weakest way to carry a number. A person saying something specific is the strongest. Look at how our case studies describe the work: "210 steps and six months a pair" for a bespoke shoemaker, "343 edited photographs and a video for each" for a day of competition coverage, "thirty three years of cheese" for a business that began in a garden shed. Each of those is a figure, and each works because it's attached to real work and a real person.

The way we approach it on shoots is practical:

  • Find the figure in conversation. We ask people about their work and listen for the number they volunteer. "We've done this for thirty years" is more natural than a statistic read from a card.
  • Let the person say it. A founder who says "we've never had a job go more than a week late" in their own voice is more convincing than the same figure in a graphic.
  • Show it, don't just say it. If the number is about volume, show the volume: the shelves, the stack, the queue. The picture makes the number real.
  • Use on-screen graphics sparingly. One clean figure on a plain background, held long enough to read, then gone. Never a cluttered chart.
  • Source it. If it's a statistic from outside the business, name where it came from, on screen or in the description.

For examples of how the people carry the story, see Carréducker and La Fromagerie, and for the thinking behind it, a documentary brand film example.

What goes wrong with data storytelling?

Cherry-picking

Showing only the figures that flatter you is the quickest way to lose trust, and it's easy to be caught. If the full picture is less impressive, tell the full picture and explain it. People respect honesty about the hard parts.

Misleading charts

Truncated axes that make a small change look huge, areas that exaggerate size, or comparing things that aren't comparable. These tricks work briefly and then damage your credibility with anyone who spots them.

Too many numbers

Three statistics in a sentence is a blur. Give each number room, and a sentence to itself.

Old or unsourced figures

A statistic from ten years ago presented as current, or a number with no source, invites doubt. Prefer recent, UK-based data from sources people recognise, such as the Office for National Statistics, Ofcom or government surveys, and link to them.

Making up the story afterwards

If the data says one thing, the story can't say another. Check that what you're claiming follows from what you measured. Correlation isn't cause, and a film shouldn't pretend otherwise.

How can a small business use data storytelling without an analyst?

You don't need a dashboard. Look for numbers you already have and are proud of: how long customers have stayed, how many jobs you've completed, how quickly you answer, how many hours go into one product, how your prices compare in plain terms. Turn each into one sentence that includes a comparison and a person.

Then use external data to set the context. If you sell to schools, a recent government figure on school budgets gives your message weight. If you work in homes, a UK figure on energy costs or housing helps. The numbers in the boxes on our own posts are an example of the same idea: one clear figure, from a named source, with a plain sentence about what it means for you.

Keep a simple file of your best figures and where they came from, and update it each quarter. When a journalist, a customer or a film crew asks for a number, you'll have it ready and checked.

Where should you use data stories?

Anywhere a claim needs backing. A few places they earn their keep:

  • Case studies. Open with the outcome, in one figure, then tell the story of how it happened. Readers who only skim still get the point.
  • Sales conversations. A single well-chosen comparison, such as how long a job normally takes against how long it took with you, can shift a quote discussion from price to value.
  • Press and PR. Journalists look for a fresh number with a human angle. Original figures from your own work, properly sourced, are far more likely to be picked up than a generic claim.
  • Social posts and carousels. One number per slide, one idea per post. A big figure on a clean background, with a line that says what it means, travels well.
  • Films. A figure spoken by the person it affects, then supported by a single clean graphic if it needs one.

A useful habit is to ask of every number, "so what?" until you reach an answer a customer would care about. If you can't, drop it. Numbers that survive that test are the ones worth building a story around.

How does data storytelling fit with brand storytelling?

It's a supporting character. Brand stories get people to care. Data stories give them a reason to believe and a reason to act. The strongest marketing uses both: a human story that makes someone feel, backed by a number that proves it's not just a nice tale.

That's the balance documentary-style brand films aim for. Real people tell the story, and the specific facts of the work, the years, the hours, the results, give it weight. The complete guide to brand storytelling shows where it sits in the bigger picture, and how effective storytelling is in marketing looks at what the evidence actually says. You can see the finished films on our films page, and if you'd like help turning what you know about your business into a story people believe, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What are the three elements of data storytelling?
faqs.a: Data, narrative and visuals. The data is the accurate foundation. The narrative explains what the numbers mean and why someone should care. The visual makes the pattern quick to see. Remove any one and the story weakens: data with no narrative is a report, narrative with no data is opinion, and either without a clear visual is hard work to read.

faqs.q: What is an example of data storytelling?
faqs.a: Florence Nightingale's rose diagram is the classic: she showed that most Crimean War deaths came from preventable disease, in a chart simple enough to persuade the people who could act. A modern consumer example is Spotify Wrapped, which turns each person's listening figures into a personal, shareable story. A business case study that opens with a result and explains how it happened does the same job.

faqs.q: Do you need a data analyst to do data storytelling?
faqs.a: Not to start. Many small businesses already hold useful figures, such as customer retention, jobs completed or response times. The skill is choosing one number, giving it a comparison and explaining what it means in plain language. For anything complex or high stakes, a second pair of eyes to check the figures is wise, but the storytelling is a writing and editing job.

faqs.q: How do you use statistics in a brand film?
faqs.a: Let a person say the number in their own words, and show something that makes it real. Use an on-screen graphic only for one clean figure held long enough to read. Avoid piling up statistics, and name the source if it's from outside the business. A number attached to real work is more convincing than a chart on its own.

items.title: What is digital storytelling in marketing? How it works
items.excerpt: What digital storytelling in marketing means, how it differs from traditional storytelling, which channels carry which story, and how to make stories findable.
items.coverAlt: A small film crew on a canal towpath at blue hour filming a narrowboat owner
items.body:
Digital storytelling in marketing is telling your brand's story through online channels and formats, such as your website, video, social media, email, search and podcasts, and shaping it to suit how people use each one. The story stays the same. What changes is the length, the first few seconds, how it's found and where it leads next.

This post is about the digital part specifically: how online behaviour changes the way a story has to be told, which channels do what, how to make a story findable and accessible, and how to use the feedback that digital gives you. It sits alongside visual storytelling in marketing, which is about the picture craft, and storytelling in social media marketing, which goes deep on social.

What does digital storytelling mean?

There are two meanings, and it's worth separating them. The older one comes from community and education work, where "digital storytelling" means a person making a short personal film from photos, voice and music. It's a lovely discipline, started in California in the 1990s, but it isn't what marketers mean.

In marketing it simply means story-led communication that lives online. A founder film on a homepage. A five part series on Instagram. A customer story in an email. An interactive article that unfolds as you scroll. The common feature is that the audience is in control. They can leave, skip, scroll, search or share at any moment, and they usually do.

How is digital storytelling different from traditional storytelling?

Four things change when the story goes online.

The audience can leave at any second

In a cinema nobody walks out in the first ten seconds. Online they do, constantly. So the opening of a digital story has to earn the next ten seconds, which is why we think hard about the first frame and the first sentence of every film we cut.

The story is rarely seen in one go

Someone might see a clip on Tuesday, a post on Friday and your homepage the week after. Digital stories work like a series of encounters. Each piece needs to make sense alone and also add to the picture.

It needs to be found

A TV advert arrives. A digital story often has to be searched for. That brings in titles, descriptions, transcripts and links, the unglamorous work that decides whether a good film is watched by hundreds or by nobody.

It gives you data

You can see where people stopped watching, which clip got shared and which email was opened. That feedback loop is the great advantage of digital, and the thing most businesses don't use.

Which digital channels carry which kind of story?

Each channel has a job. Matching the story to the job is more useful than being everywhere.

  • Website. Your home base and the place people check you out before enquiring. It should hold your fullest story: an about page that's honest about how you began, case studies, and at least one proper film. A page built around real people is easier to believe than one built around claims.
  • YouTube. A search engine as much as a video site. Stories that answer a question or show a process can be found for years after they're published.
  • Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and LinkedIn. Where strangers meet you. Short clips, carousels and stills. The story has to work in a moment and nudge people towards the longer version.
  • Email. A direct line to people who've already shown interest. A story gives you something worth sending that isn't a sales push.
  • Podcasts and audio. Good for founders and experts who talk well. Slow-burning trust.
  • Interactive and long-form web pieces. The New York Times's Snow Fall in 2012 became the reference point: a long article with video, graphics and moving images that responded as you scrolled. Few businesses need that scale, but a simple version, like a case study page that reveals a project in stages, borrows the idea.

We've seen what a connected set looks like with Plug In Stations, where a regular schedule of installation days, product videos and company events keeps a YouTube channel fed, each piece feeding the same wider story of an installer that knows its stuff. It's a good illustration that digital storytelling is often less about one big film and more about a steady stream built on a clear idea.

On the internet the story doesn't end when the film does. It ends when the viewer has somewhere to go next.

How do you make the story work for the way people actually watch?

Hook early, but honestly

Open with the most interesting true thing you have, not a logo sting. That might be a line from the interview, a striking detail or the problem itself. Then deliver on it. A hook that promises something the film doesn't give just trains people to leave sooner next time.

Plan for sound off

A large share of social viewing happens muted, in queues, on trains, in meetings. Captions are essential, and subtitled versions help more people than you'd expect. Accessibility matters here too, not just for deaf and hard of hearing viewers but for anyone watching somewhere noisy. For one client we also delivered an audio described version of a film, so that blind and partially sighted viewers could follow it.

Frame for the screen

A film that works on a laptop can feel tiny on a phone, and vertical video needs different framing from landscape. If we know where something will be shown, we frame for it on the day rather than trying to crop it afterwards.

Cut it for each place

One interview can be a three minute website film, a ninety second YouTube cut, a thirty second teaser and three vertical clips. That's the principle behind turning one brand film into a year of content, and it's how a small team keeps a presence going without constantly inventing new stories.

How do you make a digital story easy to find?

Most businesses skip this step, and it costs them. A few basics make a large difference.

  • Write the title for a person and for search. Include the words someone would type, such as "bespoke shoemaking London", rather than a clever name nobody's looking for.
  • Add a transcript or written summary on the page, so search engines and people who prefer reading can follow the story.
  • Use a good thumbnail, a real face in good light, rather than a logo on a plain background.
  • Link between pieces. The short clip points to the long film, which points to the case study, which points to a way of contacting you.
  • Put the film where decisions are made, not just on a video page. Our guidance on this is in where to use your brand film.

A film called "Brand Video Final v3" has never once been found by anyone typing a question into Google.

What does a real example look like?

Our film for char.gy explaining their B Corp certification is a good illustration of digital thinking. It's an interview-led film that explains something complicated in plain language. It was cut eleven ways for different places, and delivered with an audio described version, and it became the most watched thing on their channel. The story was true and useful, the formats fit the channels, and the accessibility was built in. You can see the details in the char.gy B Corp case study.

Another is the single day we spent filming one drainage job for Super Efficient. It became a longform YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels. Each piece suits its place, but the story is the same: real people doing a real job well. The full story is in the Super Efficient case study.

How do you use the data without letting it take over?

Digital gives you a lot of numbers, and the temptation is to chase them. A clip that gets a high number of views isn't necessarily the one that brings you good customers. Treat the data as a set of clues.

  • If many people stop watching at the same point, that part probably drags. Cut it next time.
  • If a clip about one theme gets shared much more than others, you've found what people care about.
  • If people watch to the end but don't click anywhere, the route onward isn't clear.
  • If enquiries mention a particular film, make more like it.

Use these to refine the story, not to replace it. A story that chases whatever got the most likes last week ends up with no shape. For how to judge overall results, see how effective storytelling is in marketing.

How do you start if you've got a small team and no time?

Start with one story and one place to put it. Pick the story that answers your buyers' biggest doubt, film it properly once, and put the long version on your website with a clear way of getting in touch. Then cut two or three short clips for the social channel where your customers already spend time, and send the film to the next few people who ask for a quote.

That's a complete digital story with a beginning, a middle and a route onward, and it doesn't need a content team. Once it's working, add the next story rather than adding more channels. A small, consistent presence that people can trust beats a sprawling one that nobody has time to keep up.

It's also worth keeping the tone consistent across places. The way you'd talk to someone in the workshop should be the way the film sounds, the way the caption reads and the way the email opens. When the voice shifts between channels, the story starts to feel like several different companies.

What mistakes should you avoid?

Treating every channel the same

Posting the same landscape film everywhere makes it feel wrong almost everywhere. Native cuts for each place take a little longer and perform better.

Starting a series you can't sustain

A weekly show is a promise. If you can't keep it, make something smaller and finish it. Consistency beats ambition on the internet.

Hiding the story behind a form

Gating your best film behind an email address means almost nobody sees it. Put the story where people can reach it, and ask for contact details further down the line.

Neglecting the basics of the page

A great film on a slow, confusing page loses people before it starts. Speed, clarity and a visible next step still count.

All of this is easier when the story itself is strong. Documentary-style brand films give you that: real people and real work, shot once and used everywhere. The complete guide to brand storytelling shows how the rest fits together, and our films page shows the finished thing. If you'd like to talk about how a story could work online for your business, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is an example of digital storytelling in marketing?
faqs.a: The New York Times's Snow Fall (2012) is the classic: a long article that combined text, video and graphics that moved as you scrolled. At a business scale, a brand film cut into a website version, a YouTube film and vertical social clips is digital storytelling too. The point is a single story shaped to suit each online channel.

faqs.q: Is digital storytelling the same as content marketing?
faqs.a: They overlap but aren't identical. Content marketing is the wider practice of creating useful material to attract customers, and it can be purely informational. Digital storytelling is a way of making that content, using narrative, people and emotion. A how-to guide is content marketing. A film about the person who learned the trade by doing it is digital storytelling.

faqs.q: What platforms are best for digital storytelling?
faqs.a: It depends where your customers are. For most UK businesses, a strong website plus YouTube for longer films, and Instagram or LinkedIn for short clips, covers it. Email is underrated for existing contacts. Choose two or three you can keep up properly, rather than spreading a thin presence across everything.

faqs.q: How long should a digital story be?
faqs.a: It depends on the place. Social clips work best at under a minute and often much less. A website film can run two to four minutes, and a YouTube documentary can go longer if the story holds. Make the story as long as it needs to be, then cut a shorter version for each place people first meet you.
