items.title: How video actually makes a business money
items.excerpt: The real routes from a brand film to revenue, from trust before the first call to faster sales and hiring, how to measure it simply, and what video can't do.
items.coverAlt: Visitors talking on a busy exhibition stand
items.body:
Video mostly makes a business money indirectly. It builds trust before the first call, shortens the time between someone finding you and deciding, lifts conversion on the pages where people make up their minds, helps you hire, gives the press and partners something to run, and keeps feeding your channels for months. It's rare for someone to watch a film and buy on the spot. The way to know it's working is to pick one of those routes before you make the film, and measure one number against it.

I'd rather be straight about this than sell you on magic. A film is a tool for a sales process you already have. Used well, it makes that process quicker and easier. Left on a homepage on its own, it mostly makes you feel good.

How does a film actually turn into revenue?

Through a handful of routes, and most good films work on two or three at once.

Trust before the first call

If a prospect has already watched your founder talk, seen your team at work and heard a customer describe the job, the first call starts further along. You spend less time proving you're real and more time talking about their problem. For higher priced services, where people research before they ever get in touch, that's where a film does its heaviest lifting.

Shorter sales cycles

Most business decisions involve more than one person, and some of them never meet you. A film you can send after a meeting goes to the finance director, the partner, the board member who'll make the call without ever speaking to you. Fewer meetings to get everyone comfortable means a quicker yes or a quicker no, and both save you money.

Higher conversion on the pages that matter

The pages that make you money are usually a few service pages and the contact page. A short, relevant film on those pages gives someone who's nearly convinced the last bit of reassurance. That works far better than a general film on the homepage that's trying to talk to everyone.

Recruitment

Good people check you out the same way buyers do. A film that shows the real work and the real people helps the right candidates apply and the wrong ones rule themselves out, which saves money on every hire.

PR and partnerships

Journalists, event organisers and partners need something to show. A well made film gives a partner something to post on their own channels and gives a story a visual to run with.

Repurposing

One shoot becomes a main film, a short cut, vertical clips and stills. That's months of content that would otherwise cost time or money to produce. We cover how in turning one brand film into a year of content.

Super Efficient are a good example of the trust route. Almost all of their work came from recommendation, which is a good problem and a fragile one. The brief was to turn the work they already do into something a stranger can watch, judge them on and call them about, without adding a single day to their diary. One day on one job became a longform film, shorts and carousels aimed at two different buyers.

How do you measure whether a video is making money?

Simply. Fancy attribution models tend to give confident answers to questions they can't really answer. A few honest measures beat a dashboard nobody trusts.

  1. Decide the route first. Is this film meant to help sales calls, a specific service page or hiring? That's the whole argument of why a brand film needs a business goal.
  2. Take a baseline. Enquiries per month from that page, how long deals take to close, how many applicants a typical job ad gets. Write it down before the film goes live.
  3. Ask people. Add "did you watch our film?" to your enquiry form or first call. It's crude, and it's also the most reliable signal a small business has.
  4. Track the sends. If the film's for sales, count how often it's sent and how those deals go compared with the ones where it wasn't.
  5. Check the watching. YouTube and most hosting tools show how much of a film people watch. If everyone leaves at thirty seconds, the film's job is being done by the first thirty seconds.

Then give it time, which is the hard part.

How long before a video pays for itself?

About as long as your sales cycle, and usually a bit longer. If customers take a week to decide, you'll get a feel within a couple of months. If deals take six months and involve a committee, the first film sent in a sales conversation might not show up in revenue for half a year.

That's why I'm wary of anyone who promises a return figure up front. The honest answer depends on your prices, your margins and how many people are already looking at you. Our film budget calculator can help with the cost side, and how to set a video budget works backwards from what a new customer is worth.

Which film should you make first if money's the goal?

The one closest to the sale. For most businesses that's a customer story about the service you most want to sell, told by a customer whose situation looks like the people you want more of. It goes straight into sales conversations and onto the page where that service is sold. A founder story or a broader brand film earns its place too, but it usually works further from the moment someone decides. There's more on making the customer version land in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.

What can't video do for a business?

Quite a lot, and it's better to know before you spend.

  • It can't fix an offer people don't want or a price that's wrong for the market.
  • It can't make up for slow replies. If enquiries sit for three days, a better film just means more people waiting.
  • It can't reach people on its own. A film nobody's sent, posted or put behind ads does nothing. See where to put your brand film.
  • It won't usually produce a sale you can trace neatly from one view to one invoice. Most of its value shows up as things going a bit easier.

A film can get someone to pick up the phone. It can't make you answer it.

A film is a tool for a sales process you already have. On its own, it mostly makes you feel good.

If you've got a process that works and you'd like it to work faster, that's exactly when a film is worth making. See how we make them, or tell us where your sales get stuck and we'll tell you honestly whether a film would help.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a single video really increase sales?
faqs.a: It can, but usually by helping a sale that was already possible go more smoothly, rather than creating one from nothing. A film that answers the questions buyers ask, sent at the right moment, tends to shorten decisions and reduce drop-off. It works best alongside a decent offer, quick replies and a sales process people can actually follow.

faqs.q: What metrics should we report on a brand film?
faqs.a: Pick the ones linked to the film's job. For sales, track how often it's sent and how those deals close. For a service page, track enquiries from that page against a baseline. For hiring, track applicant numbers and quality. Views and likes are worth glancing at, but they rarely tell you whether the film is earning its keep.

faqs.q: Is a cheaper video a better return than an expensive film?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A modest video that answers one common question can pay back quickly. A bigger film earns its cost when trust is what's being bought, prices are high and people research hard before committing. The right spend depends on what a new customer is worth to you, so work out that number before deciding how much to put into the film.

faqs.q: Should we put ad spend behind our film to get a return?
faqs.a: Often behind the short cuts, yes, especially shown to people who've already visited your site. A full length film rarely works as a cold ad to strangers. Before spending, make sure your licence and the music licence cover paid advertising on every platform you'll use, and set a clear goal for the campaign so you can tell if it worked.

items.title: What is visual storytelling in marketing? A practical guide
items.excerpt: What visual storytelling in marketing means in practice: the building blocks, formats, brand examples, how to plan a visual story, and the mistakes to avoid.
items.coverAlt: An artist in a pink top stands with a hand on her hip in front of large black and white portrait posters
items.body:
Visual storytelling in marketing means telling your story mainly through what people see, such as film, photography, design and the way a scene is framed and lit, rather than through what they read. A good visual story shows the work, the people and the place so clearly that the words only have to add what the pictures can't.

This post covers what visual storytelling is in practice: the building blocks (people, place, detail, light, movement), the formats that carry it, how to plan it before anyone picks up a camera, and what goes wrong. It's the visual-craft angle only. For the wider idea of a brand telling stories see what brand storytelling is in marketing, and for the online channel side see digital storytelling in marketing.

What counts as visual storytelling?

Anything where the images are doing the telling. Video is the obvious one, but it also covers still photography, illustration, motion graphics, packaging, a well-designed carousel and the look of a shopfront. If you remove the words and the viewer can still tell what's happening and why it matters, it's visual storytelling. If you remove the words and you're left with a stock photo of a smiling person, it isn't.

The idea is older than marketing. Silent film told whole stories without a spoken line, and a good documentary photographer can do the same in a single frame. What has changed is the audience. People scroll through hundreds of images a day, so an image has a fraction of a second to say "this is a person, doing something, and it's interesting".

What are the building blocks of a visual story?

A person we can look at

Faces and hands carry most of the emotion in any image. An interview shot at the right distance, with the person looking slightly off the lens as if talking to someone across a table, feels like a conversation. A person doing their job, absorbed in it, can tell you more about their skill in ten seconds than a paragraph of copy. That's the thinking in our film about the signwriter, a trade that is nearly all hand and eye, where the hands and the brush do most of the talking.

A place that feels real

Where something happens tells you what kind of business it is. A cluttered workshop, a clean showroom, a kitchen table. Real places carry detail that can't be faked: worn tools, handwritten labels, light from a particular window. It's why we shoot where the work actually happens rather than building a set.

Detail shots, or cutaways

The close-up of stitching, the steam off a cup, the sound and sight of a tool. Film makers call these cutaways or b-roll, and they're the visual equivalent of specifics. Without them an interview is just a talking head. With them it becomes a story about a craft.

Light and colour

Light sets mood before anyone speaks. Warm, soft window light says careful and personal. Hard, flat overhead light says institutional. Colour grading, the final colour treatment of a film, pulls a set of shots into one consistent look. We explain what grading actually does in colour grading explained.

Movement and pace

Slow, steady camera work suggests patience and craft. Quick cuts suggest energy. A story about a bespoke maker shouldn't be cut like a gym advert. Matching the rhythm of the pictures to the nature of the subject is a large part of what makes a film feel right without anyone being able to say why.

If the picture says it, don't write it again underneath.

What does "show, don't tell" mean in marketing?

It means proving a claim visually instead of stating it. "Handmade with care" is a phrase. A maker spending the morning on one seam is proof. "Fast, reliable service" is a phrase. A van arriving, a job finished and a customer happy is proof.

The best films we make start from this rule. Instead of asking someone to describe their quality, we find the moment where quality is visible. The film on the bespoke shoemakers, Carréducker, builds around the steps of making a shoe, and the viewer works out for themselves how much skill is involved. The same is true of our film on the jeweller Catherine Marche, built around how she works rather than the pieces in the case.

It doesn't mean never speaking. In a documentary-style brand film the best lines come from the people involved, and the pictures are chosen to support them. It means words and pictures shouldn't repeat each other. If the interviewee says she melts down old gold, the picture should be the gold melting, not her still talking.

Why does the visual side matter so much for small businesses?

Because it's the quickest way to close the trust gap. A potential customer who's never met you decides in seconds whether you look like the real thing. Text can claim anything. Footage of your people doing the work, in the place they do it, is much harder to fake and much easier to believe. For a small business competing with bigger names, that believability is often the whole advantage.

It also compounds. A day of well-planned filming gives you moving pictures for the website, stills for press and social, and clips for months of posts. The same visual identity running through all of it makes you easier to recognise, which is the real job of branding.

Which formats carry visual storytelling?

  • Brand and documentary films. The richest format. Several minutes, people, places, and room for the story to breathe.
  • Short vertical video. Single moments cut from a longer shoot, aimed at social feeds. They have to land in a second or two, so they lean on a striking image and a clear action.
  • Photography. Portraits and behind-the-scenes stills for websites, press and social. A well-made portrait of a founder does more than a headshot in front of a grey wall.
  • Carousels and slide sequences. A way to tell a mini story in swipeable frames, usually built from stills and short text.
  • Motion graphics and animation. Useful for explaining something that can't be filmed, like a process inside a machine. They sit alongside live action rather than replacing it. See VFX and motion graphics for brand video.
  • Infographics and data visuals. Good when the story is a number. That's a separate craft, covered in data storytelling in marketing.

Which brands are known for strong visual storytelling?

A few UK and global examples show what the idea looks like at scale. Cadbury's Gorilla advert from 2007 told almost nothing in words. A man in a gorilla suit sits at a drum kit and plays the drum solo from Phil Collins's "In the Air Tonight". There's no voiceover explaining joy. You feel it, and the brand arrives at the end.

Apple's long running Shot on iPhone campaign, which began in 2015, makes its case through the photographs and films themselves, taken by ordinary users. The product is proven by the pictures it produces. Always's #LikeAGirl campaign in 2014 used simple visuals of people being asked to run and throw "like a girl" to shift how a phrase was understood, the images making the argument.

None of these needs a huge budget to learn from. What they share is an idea that could be understood without sound, and images chosen to carry it.

A drone shot of the building tells me where you live. It doesn't tell me why I should care.

How do you plan a visual story before the shoot?

The planning is where most of it is won or lost. A few questions I'd answer before booking anyone:

  1. What's the one thing a viewer should feel or understand? Visual stories are bad at carrying five messages. Pick one.
  2. What can we show that proves it? List the visible moments: the hands at work, the finished piece, the before and after, the reaction of the customer.
  3. Where does it happen, and when is it at its best? A workshop in morning light looks different from the same room at four in the afternoon. Choose the time on purpose.
  4. Who will be in it, and are they comfortable? People relax when they know what to expect. Briefing your team before a shoot makes a visible difference to how natural they look.
  5. Where will it be used? A film for a website needs wide, composed shots. A cut for social needs to work vertically, so we frame for both on the day.

Then leave room for what you didn't plan. The best frame of the day is often something nobody expected, like someone laughing at a joke, or a tool being put down in just the right light. That's the advantage of shooting documentary style: you watch the work and catch it.

How do words and pictures work together?

Visual storytelling doesn't mean silent. The strongest pieces pair a real voice with pictures that add something the voice doesn't. In an interview-led film, the person speaks and the picture shows what they're describing, or reacts to it, or simply lets us watch their face while they find the words. Those pauses are often the most honest part of a film.

On the page and in the feed, the same principle holds. A caption shouldn't describe the photo. It should say what the photo can't: what happened before, why it mattered, what the person was thinking. And a headline over an image works best when the two make a small tension, like a bold claim above a quiet picture of someone doing the work.

If you're unsure whether a piece is balanced, mute it and watch. Then read the words without the pictures. Each should make some sense alone, and together they should be better than either.

How much does visual quality matter?

Less than most people think, and more than some people think. A phone can capture a strong moment. A good camera and a skilled operator will capture it with more depth, cleaner sound and better light, and sound is half of the picture. We cover what phones can and can't do in phone video for business content.

What matters most isn't resolution, it's intent. A shaky phone clip of a real moment beats a perfect shot of nothing. But when the story is the reason people will trust you with a large decision, having it shot properly, with consistent light, clear sound and careful editing, signals the same care you'd bring to their job.

What mistakes do businesses make with visual storytelling?

Relying on stock footage

Stock can fill a gap, but a story made from it belongs to no one. Viewers can tell, even if they can't say why.

Over-producing

Too many gimmicks, transitions and effects take attention from the people. If a viewer is thinking about the editing, they're not thinking about the story.

Ignoring sound

Bad audio kills a visual story faster than a bad picture. The sound of the work is also part of the story, and sometimes better left untouched by music.

Forgetting captions

Many people watch with the sound off, so a visual story still needs readable subtitles. We make a subtitled version of every cut as standard.

Treating it as decoration

If the images are added at the end to brighten a written message, it isn't visual storytelling. It starts with the picture.

To see the thinking applied to real businesses, browse our films, and for the full picture of how visuals fit within storytelling, the complete guide to brand storytelling is the place to go. If you've got a business with something worth showing, get in touch and we'll talk it through.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the difference between visual storytelling and video marketing?
faqs.a: Video marketing is a channel. Visual storytelling is a way of using images, in video or photography, to tell a story. You can make video that tells no story, such as a product spec reel, and you can tell a strong visual story with a handful of photographs. The two overlap when a film is built around people and a clear narrative.

faqs.q: Do you need professional equipment for visual storytelling?
faqs.a: Not to start. A modern phone with good light and clean sound can capture a real moment well. Professional kit and a skilled crew add control over light, depth, sound and consistency, which matters when the film has to build trust with a large decision. Intent beats equipment: know what you want people to feel before you press record.

faqs.q: What makes a visual story memorable?
faqs.a: A clear single idea, a human face or pair of hands, specific detail and an image people can describe afterwards. Memorable visual stories usually have a moment that could be explained in one sentence, such as a man in a gorilla suit playing drums. Repetition helps too, so use the same visual ideas across channels.

faqs.q: Is visual storytelling only for consumer brands?
faqs.a: No. B2B and trade businesses often benefit most, because their work is hard to explain in words and easy to show. A film of how an installation is done, how a part is made or how a team solves a problem builds trust faster than a brochure. Buyers of expensive, complex services want to see competence before they speak to anyone.

items.title: How effective is storytelling in marketing? The evidence
items.excerpt: What the evidence says about storytelling in marketing: UK research, marketer survey data, why results are hard to measure, and when stories fail.
items.coverAlt: Shoppers queuing at a cheese stall in a covered London food market on a grey morning
items.body:
Storytelling in marketing is effective when it's specific, believable and shown to the right people more than once, and it's much less effective when it's a vague brand narrative nobody can measure. The best UK evidence says emotional, story-led work tends to build more business over time than purely rational messages, but it's slow, hard to attribute and easy to do badly.

This post is the honest look at the evidence. What the research actually shows, where the claims you see online fall apart, what the numbers look like from the marketers using video, and how to judge for yourself whether a story is earning its place. If you want the how-to, that's in how to use storytelling in marketing, and the reasons it works at all are in why storytelling works in marketing.

What does the research actually say about storytelling?

The most respected UK work on this isn't about stories as such. It's about emotion versus rational persuasion, and stories are the main way emotion gets into advertising. In The Long and the Short of It, published by the IPA in 2013, Les Binet and Peter Field analysed hundreds of campaigns entered into the IPA Effectiveness Awards. Their finding was that campaigns built mainly on emotional appeal tended to produce larger and longer lasting business effects than campaigns built on rational messages, particularly over the long term.

It's worth being precise about what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't say every story sells. It says that brands who make people feel something about them, and keep doing it, build a mental shortcut that makes them easier to choose later. A story is a very good way to build that, because people remember a scene or a person far better than a claim.

There's also a body of academic work on narrative and persuasion showing that people who are absorbed in a story tend to resist counter-arguing as much, which is part of why a good story lands where a sales pitch bounces off. I'd treat the more dramatic claims you'll see repeated, such as "stories are 22 times more memorable than facts", with caution. They get passed around without anyone pointing to a study you can read, and I'd rather give you a smaller claim I can stand behind.

What do marketers who use video say about results?

Video is the format where most business storytelling ends up, so the best large survey data we have is on video. The IPA's Binet and Field analysis of effectiveness case studies found that, in campaigns running three years or more, 43% of emotional campaigns reported very large profit effects against 23% of rational ones. That's a strong signal for stories, and the timescale is worth reading carefully.

More businesses are making video, and a lot of it is made without much thought about what it's for. The marketers who are less happy are, in my experience, often the ones who made something generic and expected it to do the work. A film without a clear story, a clear audience and a plan for where it goes will disappoint, however well it's lit.

When everyone's film looks the same, the average result slips.

I read that dip as good news for anyone willing to do it properly. When everybody's making the same polished, empty film, a specific one stands out more.

Why is the effect of storytelling so hard to measure?

Because a story rarely closes a sale on its own. Somebody sees a short film on Instagram in March, reads a case study in May, gets a recommendation from a colleague in July and fills in your form in September. Your analytics will credit the form fill, or perhaps Google. The film that made them trust you won't show up.

This is the problem every brand storyteller has, and it's why a lot of the claims you'll read are either overblown or quietly unfalsifiable. There are three honest ways around it.

Ask people how they found you

A simple "how did you hear about us?" box, with a free text option, is the cheapest tool in marketing. If people write "I watched your film" or "I saw your video about the shoemakers", you've learned more than from any dashboard.

Look at sales conversations

Do prospects arrive already knowing what you do? Do they quote something from a film back to you? Does the first call start further down the line than it used to? Salespeople notice these things before the data does.

Compare like with like

If you send a film to some quote requests and not others, or add it to the pages that matter most, you can see whether those enquiries convert differently. It's not a laboratory test, but it's better than guessing.

Attribution software says the sale came from a Google search. The film that made them trust you is sulking in the corner.

When does storytelling work well in marketing?

From what I've seen on shoots, and from the campaigns that tend to get written up, a story does its job when a few conditions are met.

  • It's specific. A named person doing a particular thing in a particular place. "Our passionate team" isn't a story.
  • It's believable. People can tell when they're being sold to. The more it comes from the people involved, in their own words, the more it's trusted.
  • It's relevant to a decision. It deals with a doubt or a question the buyer has, rather than being entertaining for its own sake.
  • It's seen more than once. One viewing rarely sticks. A story that appears as a film, a clip, a case study and a mention in a sales call builds up.
  • It's tied to the real business. The story has to be true of how you actually work, or the first contact with you undoes it.

The big brand examples show the same pattern. John Lewis built a reputation for its Christmas adverts over many years, and they work as a long investment in a feeling about the brand, not as a one-off promotion. Dove's Real Beauty campaign, which began in 2004, stayed on one idea for years and let women tell parts of it. Neither is a template for a small business budget, but the principle scales down: pick a story that's true, tell it consistently, and give it time.

For smaller examples that sit closer to the work we do, see the La Fromagerie film, which tells a business's story through the founder and the people who run it, and the longer discussion of why that film is built the way it is.

When does it not work?

Stories fail in predictable ways, and it's worth knowing them before you spend money.

When it's invented

Fake customer stories, dramatised founder myths and stock-photo "real people" are noticed and punished. The cost isn't just a flop, it's lost trust in everything else you say.

When it's all about you

A film that's only the company talking about its own greatness is an advert. It can work as one, but it's not storytelling and shouldn't be measured as if it were.

When there's nowhere for it to go

I've seen lovely films sit on a YouTube channel with no links, no mention in sales emails and no place on the website. Nobody saw it, so it didn't work. That's a distribution problem, not a story problem. We deal with this in where to use your brand film.

When you expect it to behave like an ad

A direct response ad is judged on clicks this week. A story is judged on whether people choose you over the next year. Judging one by the other's rules is how businesses abandon a good approach after a month.

When the product doesn't back it up

No story can rescue a bad experience. If the story says you're careful and the delivery is late, the story becomes evidence against you.

How effective is it for a small business in particular?

I'd argue it matters more for a small business than for a big one, because you can't outspend anyone. A large brand can buy repetition. A small one has to buy belief, and belief is made of specifics.

A good example of how this plays out is our film for char.gy about their B Corp certification. It's an interview-led film that explains the certification in plain language, and it was cut eleven ways and delivered with an audio described version. It became the most watched thing on their channel, which tells me something I see repeatedly: a clear, honest explanation told by the people involved often outperforms the slicker, more obvious content around it. You can read the details in the char.gy B Corp case study.

That's one client's result, and I wouldn't promise it to anyone else. What I'd say is that when a story is clear, true and re-used across formats, it's reasonable to expect it to outperform a generic brand video, and that's what the evidence from the wider industry also leans towards.

Is the effect different for B2B and consumer brands?

The mechanism is the same, but the timescale isn't. A consumer buying a sofa might decide in a week. A facilities manager choosing a contractor, or a school choosing a supplier, may take months and involve several people who never meet you. In that world the story has to travel without you. Someone watches your film, forwards it to a colleague with a line like "this is the sort of firm I mean", and the colleague arrives at the meeting already half convinced.

That's why I tend to recommend one strong, longer film for B2B work, with a few short pieces around it. The long film is what gets forwarded. The short pieces are how people first meet you. Both come from the same story, which keeps your message consistent no matter who's looking.

How should you judge your own results?

Set the question before you start. Decide what you want the story to change, whether that's the quality of enquiries, the length of sales conversations, the number of people finding you by name or the win rate against competitors. Pick one or two, write down where they are now, and look again after three to six months.

Then separate the story from the delivery. If a film gets watched but doesn't lead anywhere, fix the route. If it doesn't get watched, look at the opening and the title. If it's watched to the end and nobody enquires, the story might be entertaining but not answering a real doubt. Each of those has a different fix.

If you want to see how the structure of a story affects this, which storytelling structure is most effective goes into it, and the complete guide to brand storytelling puts the pieces together.

Documentary-style brand films are built on this idea: real people and real work give you something specific and believable that you can use for a long time. You can see examples on our films page, and if you'd like to talk about whether it would suit your business, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Does storytelling increase sales?
faqs.a: It can, but rarely in a direct, trackable way. Research from the IPA suggests emotional, story-led campaigns tend to build more business over the long term than rational ones. For most companies the effect shows up as better quality enquiries, shorter sales conversations and more people choosing you by name, rather than a spike the day after a post.

faqs.q: How long does it take for storytelling to work?
faqs.a: Plan on three to six months before judging it, and longer for brand effects to build. A single film won't change how people see you overnight. A small set of consistent stories used across your website, social channels and sales conversations will compound over time, and you'll often hear about it from customers before you see it in the data.

faqs.q: Is storytelling better than traditional advertising?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. Direct response ads are good at catching people already looking to buy. Stories are good at making you the business people already trust when they start looking. Most healthy marketing uses both. If you can only afford one, a small business with no brand awareness usually gains more from trust than from clicks.

faqs.q: What is the biggest mistake that makes storytelling ineffective?
faqs.a: Making it generic. A story that could belong to any company in your sector doesn't build any preference for yours. The second most common mistake is making a good film and then not using it, leaving it on a channel nobody visits. Specific stories, told by real people and placed where decisions are made, avoid both.

stat.title: Very large profit effects from campaigns that ran for three years or more
stat.takeaway: Over three years or more, emotional campaigns were nearly twice as likely as rational ones to report very large profit gains.

source.name: IPA, Binet and Field, The Long and the Short of It

items.title: How to use storytelling in marketing, step by step
items.excerpt: A practical guide to using storytelling in marketing: where to find your stories, which channels suit them, how to repurpose, and how to tell if it's working.
items.coverAlt: A drainage engineer talks to camera in a garden beside a CCTV monitor on a stand, red barriers behind him
items.body:
To use storytelling in marketing, pick one real story from inside your business, tell it through a person rather than a product, and then put it in front of customers at the point where they're deciding. The story is the raw material. The marketing is where it goes, in what shape, and what you ask people to do next.

This post is the practical one. I'm not defining storytelling or explaining the psychology, because that's covered in what brand storytelling is in marketing and why storytelling works. Here it's about the working method: where to find your stories, which channel gets which story, how to repurpose, and how to tell whether it's doing anything.

Where do you find stories worth telling in your business?

Most businesses say they have no stories, and then you sit in a room with the owner for forty minutes and there are six. The trouble is that people hear the word "story" and think of a big narrative with a villain and a happy ending. In practice the material is smaller and much more ordinary, and it's already sitting in your business.

These are the places I look first when I'm working with a new client:

  • The founding moment. Why did this business start, and what was the person doing the day before? The answer is rarely "we spotted a gap in the market". It's usually a frustration, a job loss, a hobby that got out of hand or a customer who asked for something nobody sold.
  • A customer's before and after. Not a testimonial line, but what their life or work was like before, what changed, and what's different now.
  • The work itself. What actually happens between an order arriving and a product leaving. People are fascinated by process when it's shown properly.
  • The people who do it. A longstanding member of staff, a trainee, the person who fixes things when they go wrong.
  • A decision you made that cost you something. Choosing a better supplier, turning down a job, or doing something the slow way for a good reason.

The test I use is simple. Could a competitor tell this story with their name on it? If yes, it's too generic. If the story only works because it happened to your people in your workshop, it's usable.

Which story should you tell first?

Start with the story that answers the biggest doubt your buyers have. Every business has one. A solicitor's prospective client wonders whether they'll be treated like a case number. A homeowner hiring a builder worries about whether the job will drag on. A buyer of handmade goods wonders whether the price is justified.

Work out that doubt by listening to your own sales calls and reading your own reviews, then find the story that deals with it without ever mentioning it. A shoemaker who spends six months on one pair doesn't need a line saying "we're worth the money". The process, shown honestly, does it. That's the approach in our film Carréducker, which follows two makers through the work rather than listing their credentials.

A good story answers the objection without ever naming it.

How do you match a story to the stage someone is at?

This is where most marketing storytelling goes wrong. A business makes one big story, puts it on the homepage and expects it to do everything. A person who's never heard of you needs something different from a person who's got a quote from you and from two other firms.

People who don't know you yet

They need a reason to stop scrolling and a human they can connect with. This is where short, personal stories do best: a maker's hands, a founder explaining why they started, a surprising detail about the work. Keep these light on branding. The aim is for someone to remember a person and a place, not a logo.

People who are comparing you

They want proof and reassurance. A customer story fits here, and so does a longer film that shows how you work. They're already interested, so they'll give you three or four minutes if it's useful. This is the stage where a documentary-style film earns its keep, because it shows how you behave when nobody's selling.

People who are about to buy

They want the final doubt removed. A short clip of a real customer, a walk through what happens after they say yes, a quick answer to the question they're about to email you. It's a smaller story than the earlier ones, but it's the one that gets the enquiry over the line.

People who've already bought

Stories matter after the sale too. Showing new customers what to expect, introducing the team who'll look after them or celebrating their results turns a one-off job into something they talk about. We cover this side in more detail in customer onboarding and customer service videos.

Which channels suit storytelling best?

All of them, with a different shape of the same story for each. Don't think of it as picking a platform. Think of it as one story, cut different ways.

  • Your website. The place for the long version. An about page that tells the real founding story, a work page with proper case studies, and a film people can press play on and stay with.
  • YouTube. Longer films that people find by searching. A search for "how is bespoke jewellery made" is a story waiting for an answer.
  • Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn. Short, vertical cuts and carousels that give a single moment from the story, aimed at people who haven't met you. I go into how this works in storytelling in social media marketing.
  • Email. A story is a good reason to write to your list that isn't a discount. One customer, one problem, one link.
  • Sales conversations and tenders. The most underused place of all. A two minute film sent after a first call does more than a PDF of credentials.
  • Press and PR. Journalists want a human angle. A story you've already got on film is much easier to pitch.

It helps to be honest about what each place is for. Social media earns attention. Your website earns trust. Email earns repeat business. A film on its own page can do all three if you plan it that way.

How do you turn one story into lots of content?

Film the story once, properly, and plan the cut-downs before you shoot. That's the single biggest saving in storytelling, in money and in time, and it's the way we work. On a single shoot day we'll often capture a long interview, the work itself in detail and plenty of small moments, then edit the same material into a main film, short vertical clips, stills and a few quotes for carousels.

Our drainage client is a good example. One day on one job became a longform YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels, all from the same people telling the same story. You can read how that came together in the Super Efficient case study, and the thinking behind it in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

The thing to avoid is the opposite approach, where you make a dozen unrelated bits of content that each say something different. Audiences remember a consistent story. They don't remember a scatter of tips.

If your story needs a stock photo of a handshake, it isn't a story yet.

How do you tell the story if you're not comfortable on camera?

You don't have to be the star. Plenty of owners are better off letting a customer, a long-serving employee or a maker speak, because the audience believes people who are talking about the work rather than the business. If you do have to appear, the best thing you can do is stop performing. People forgive a stumble much faster than they forgive a script.

It helps to prepare in advance. Know the three things you want to say, not a speech. Our guides to preparing for a brand film interview and speaking on camera are written for people who'd rather be doing anything else.

What should the call to action be?

Smaller than you think. After a story, people aren't ready to hand over money. Ask them to do the next small thing: watch the longer film, read the case study, look at the work, or get in touch if they've got a similar project. A story that finishes by shouting an offer feels like a trick, and the trust you've just built leaks away.

It also helps to be consistent about where the story leads. If a short clip on social goes to a longer film on your website, and the film leads to a clear way of getting in touch, you've built a route. Without the route, even a great story just ends.

How do you know if storytelling is working?

Don't expect a straight line from a film to a sale, because that isn't how people buy. What you can measure is whether the right things are moving. Look at:

  • Watch time and completion, which tell you whether the story held people.
  • Enquiry quality, meaning whether people arrive already knowing what you do and who you do it for.
  • Sales conversations, and how often someone mentions having seen a film or a post.
  • Win rate on quotes, especially against competitors where price was similar.
  • Branded searches, as more people look for your name specifically.

The honest answer is that storytelling is a slow build. The evidence on how well it performs is covered separately in how effective storytelling is in marketing. What I can say from shoot days is that the clients who treat a film as something to use across the year, rather than something to launch once, are the ones who get the most from it.

What mistakes do businesses make when they start?

Telling the company story instead of the customer story

"We were founded in 1998" is a fact, not a story. Start with the person in front of you and what they need, then bring your history in where it helps.

Making it about the product

A specification list isn't a story, however nicely it's filmed. If the product is the hero, the film becomes an advert. If a person using or making it is the hero, it becomes something people watch.

Polishing out the honest bits

The hard day, the thing that went wrong, the compromise. Those are the parts people believe. A film made entirely of triumph feels like a brochure.

Giving up after one post

One story won't change how your market sees you. A handful of well chosen ones, told consistently over a few months, will start to.

Done well, this is what documentary-style brand films are for: real people, real work, shot in a way that gives you a story you can use in a dozen places. If you want to see how the pieces fit into a wider plan, the complete guide to brand storytelling pulls the whole subject together, and our films page shows what a finished project looks like.

If you've got a story in your business and you're not sure how to use it, get in touch and we'll talk it through.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is an example of storytelling in marketing?
faqs.a: John Lewis's Christmas adverts are the best known UK example. They tell a short emotional story, often about a child, a pet or a gift, and the product barely appears. On a smaller scale, a film that follows a shoemaker through six months of work does the same thing: the story builds belief in the craft, and the business benefits without having to shout.

faqs.q: How often should a small business publish stories?
faqs.a: Consistency matters more than volume. One strong story told well, then cut into shorter pieces, will keep a small business's channels fed for weeks. Aim for a regular rhythm you can keep up, such as one new story a month, rather than a burst of posts followed by silence. The quality of the underlying story decides how far it travels.

faqs.q: Do you need video to use storytelling in marketing?
faqs.a: No. Written case studies, photography, podcasts and email can all carry a story. Video is simply the closest thing to meeting the person, which is why it works so well when trust matters. If budget is tight, start with the format you can do properly, and add film for the one or two stories that matter most.

faqs.q: How do you measure whether storytelling is working?
faqs.a: Look for movement in the things that follow trust: longer watch times, better quality enquiries, more people mentioning your content in sales calls, a higher quote win rate and more searches for your name. Sales figures matter, but they lag behind. Track the leading signs monthly and judge over a quarter rather than a week.

stat.title: UK adults who trust each group to tell the truth, 2025

bars.label: The ordinary man or woman in the street

stat.takeaway: People believe ordinary people far more than they believe anyone selling, so the best marketing stories are told by customers and staff, not by the brand.

items.title: Who is a brand storyteller, and do you need one?
items.excerpt: A brand storyteller finds, shapes and tells a business's true story. Here's what they do, the skills to look for, and whether to hire one or go it alone.
items.coverAlt: A man sits cross-legged on grey mats inside a cage-style gym while a crew member with a camera sets up
items.body:
A brand storyteller is the person who finds the true story of a business and tells it well across the places customers meet you. They interview the people involved, decide what matters, shape it into a clear account and make sure it's told consistently, on film, on the page and in conversation. It can be a founder, a hire, or an outside studio.

This post is about the person rather than the practice. I'll cover what a brand storyteller does all day, the skills that matter, the three realistic ways to get one, and how to choose. If you want the practice itself, what brand storytelling is and how to tell a brand story come first.

What does a brand storyteller actually do?

The job title sounds airy. The work's practical. On a normal project, a brand storyteller does most of these:

  • **Listens.** Interviews founders, staff, customers and partners, and pays more attention to what's said in passing than to the prepared answer.
  • **Finds the real story.** Works out why the business exists, what it believes and what makes it different, in plain language.
  • **Decides what to leave out.** Most of the job is cutting. A business has twenty good stories, and the storyteller picks the one or two that do the work.
  • **Shapes it.** Turns what they've found into a clear account with a beginning, a turn and a result.
  • **Chooses the medium.** Decides whether a story's best told on film, in writing, in photographs or in a sign on the door.
  • **Keeps it consistent.** Makes sure the website, the sales deck, the emails and the team's own words all tell the same account.

That last one's the part people forget. Telling a story once is a project. Keeping it consistent for three years is a role.

Who counts as a brand storyteller?

Anyone doing that work, whatever their job title. Some of the best I've met were never called one. The title belongs as much to a documentary maker, a copywriter, a journalist turned marketer or a founder who's got a knack for it as it does to someone with "Brand Storyteller" on their LinkedIn.

What they share is a way of working. They're curious about people, patient enough to ask the second and third question, and honest enough to say when a story isn't there yet. They're also usually suspicious of polish. A brand storyteller's instinct is to make a business look like itself, not like a better-funded version of someone else.

What skills does a good brand storyteller have?

If you're hiring or choosing, these are what I'd look for.

Interviewing

The ability to get a nervous person to say something true. This is the biggest one, and it's undervalued. Most people don't speak well about their own business until someone asks the right question in the right way. A good interviewer builds trust in the first ten minutes, then waits.

Editorial judgement

Knowing which of ten true things is the story. This comes from experience, and you can't fake it. If someone shows you a portfolio, look at what they left out as much as what's in.

Writing, and a feel for pictures

Even a filmmaker needs to write, because every film starts with a plan, questions and a way of cutting the interview down. Equally, a writer who understands what the camera does will produce better scripts and captions. The best are comfortable in both.

Craft in at least one medium

Storytelling's an idea, but delivery's craft. Someone who can only talk about narrative arcs and can't produce a finished film, article or page isn't much use. Ask to see finished work and ask what their part in it was.

Consistency and patience

A story needs maintaining. A good storyteller keeps the thread across many pieces and many months, and doesn't get bored of the message before the audience's started to notice it.

Who are the real options? Founder, in-house or studio?

Three routes, each with a place.

The founder or owner

Often the best storyteller a business has, because it's their story. The upside is authenticity and cost. The downside is that founders are usually too close to see which parts are interesting, and they're busy. If you're going this way, it helps to have someone interview you, so you're talking to a person rather than writing into the void.

An in-house hire

Makes sense when you've got a steady stream of content and a team to feed. They learn the business deeply, they're there for the quick turnarounds and they own consistency. The catch is cost, and the fact that one person can rarely do everything. A writer might not be able to shoot, and a videographer might not have the editorial eye. Plan what you'll buy in.

A studio or freelancer

Makes sense when you need craft you can't hold in-house, such as a proper film, or when you need an outside eye. Someone who doesn't work for you will ask the questions your own team has stopped asking. It's also the lowest-commitment way to get a high-quality piece of storytelling done once and then use it for a long time.

This is where we sit. We make documentary-style brand films, which means we spend most of our time doing the listening, finding and shaping parts of the job, with the camera as the tool. You can see how that works in our film with La Fromagerie, where the founder, the cheesemongers and the wholesale side each tell a part of the same business.

If their portfolio is all drone shots and slow-motion pours, ask who they actually interviewed.

Why does it matter that the storyteller's a real person?

Because the audience can tell. Optimizely surveyed 1,000 UK consumers and 100 UK marketers and published the results in September 2026. It found 62% of the consumers said they trust marketing content less since brands adopted AI, 57% said they can usually spot AI-generated content and 72% said they're more likely to engage with content that feels human. Fieldwork details weren't given, and it's a vendor survey, so treat it as an indication rather than gospel. But it matches what I see on shoots.

A brand's story is a claim that real people did real things for real reasons. That's very hard to deliver without a real person, on camera or on the page, vouching for it. Tools can help with the admin, such as transcribing interviews and sorting footage, and we've written about where AI belongs in AI and brand video in 2026 and why real people on camera still matter. But the storytelling, the judgement about what's true and what matters, is still human work.

What does a good brand storyteller ask you?

Here's a quick test of someone you're thinking of working with. In the first conversation they should ask you things like:

  • Why did you start this, in the first place?
  • Who's the customer you most enjoyed working with, and why?
  • What do you do differently that you've stopped noticing?
  • What's gone wrong, and what did you learn?
  • What would you like people to say about you when you're not in the room?

If instead the first question's "what's your budget and what style do you like?", they're selling production. That's fine, as long as it's what you want. But it's not storytelling.

How should you brief a brand storyteller?

Keep it plain. Tell them who you want to reach, what you want those people to do afterwards and who they'll need to talk to. Give them access, because the story lives in the people, and let them have the conversations. Don't hand them a script. A good brief's covered in how to write a video brief, and the part people most often skip is the business goal, which I go into in why a brand film needs a business goal.

Then trust the process. The best films we've made came from clients who let us ask awkward questions and didn't edit their own answers in advance.

What does a brand storyteller's day look like on a shoot?

Mostly conversation. On a documentary-style shoot the camera's set up quickly, and the real work starts when someone sits down and gets talking. I'll spend the first few minutes on small talk, because a person who's relaxed says things a nervous one won't. Then come the questions, which I mostly build from what they've just said rather than from a list.

The telling moments are often small. Someone mentions the first customer they ever had, or how they nearly packed it in, or what their dad used to say about the trade. Those are the lines that end up in the film, and they rarely come from the questions you'd planned. A good storyteller notices when one's landed and stays quiet for a beat so the person carries on.

Afterwards it's the edit, which is where the shaping happens. Hours of conversation get cut to minutes, and the decision of what stays is the storytelling in its clearest form.

What mistakes do people make when choosing one?

A few, and I've seen all of them:

  • **Hiring for the look rather than the listening.** A beautiful showreel says nothing about whether someone can get a real answer out of a nervous person.
  • **Handing over a finished script.** If the story's already written, you don't need a storyteller, you need a crew, and the film will sound like an advert.
  • **Expecting a story to be invented.** A good storyteller finds what's true. If a business has nothing it believes in, no one can make that up convincingly.
  • **Treating it as a one-off.** The film's the start. Someone has to keep the thread going afterwards, whether that's you or us.

Do you need one at all?

Not always. If your business is new, your story's still forming and you've got little to show, spend the money on the work and tell it simply in your own words. If you've been going for years, you've got a team with something worth saying and people ask "how do you do that?", a storyteller will get you more than you'd expect, because the story's already there and nobody's told it properly.

You also don't have to choose permanently. Many of the businesses we work with start with one film made by us, then keep the story alive themselves with a phone and the bank of moments they've collected. Long relationships tend to work better than one-offs, which is something I wrote about in relationships over transactions.

The job is mostly listening, and the skill is knowing which part of what you heard to keep.

Where to go next

For the practical side of putting a story to work, see how a brand story should be used in content creation, and for who's doing it well, what brands use storytelling. The whole subject's in the complete guide to brand storytelling.

If you'd like to talk about whether your business has a story worth filming, get in touch. If it isn't ready yet, I'll tell you that too.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What's the difference between a brand storyteller and a copywriter?
faqs.a: A copywriter writes persuasive words for a given purpose, such as an ad or a landing page. A brand storyteller works earlier and wider: finding the real story, deciding what matters and making sure it's told consistently across film, writing and conversation. Plenty of copywriters do both, and the titles overlap, so judge people by the work they've shown.

faqs.q: Can a founder be their own brand storyteller?
faqs.a: Yes, and often they're the strongest voice a business has, because it's their story. The risks are being too close to see what's interesting and not having time. Many founders do best when someone else interviews them, so they're talking to a person rather than staring at a blank page, then they carry on telling the story themselves.

faqs.q: How much does a brand storyteller cost?
faqs.a: It depends on the route. A founder doing it costs time, an in-house hire is a salary, and a studio or freelancer is a project fee. For a documentary-style brand film, the films page on our site shows what's included and the starting price. Ask any storyteller for finished examples and what their part in each one was.

faqs.q: Do I need a brand storyteller if I use AI tools?
faqs.a: AI tools can speed up the admin, such as transcribing interviews or tidying a draft, but they can't know what's true about your business or which moment matters. The story depends on real people and real judgement. Surveys suggest audiences trust human-feeling content more, so the storyteller's role is, if anything, more valuable as machine-made content grows.
