items.title: What to wear on camera for an interview
items.excerpt: What to wear on camera: colours that film well, why stripes shimmer, logos, fit, mic-friendly layers, glasses, jewellery, make-up and what to pack as a backup.
items.coverAlt: A man in a plain green jumper being interviewed in a living room
items.body:
For a filmed interview, wear solid, mid-tone clothes that fit you sitting down, in fabrics that don't rustle, with a collar or a proper waistband so the mic has somewhere to go. Skip fine patterns, other brands' logos and anything that jangles. Bring a second top in a different colour, some blotting paper or powder for shine, and the glasses you always wear.

I've covered the basics in how to prepare for being filmed. This is the longer version, for people who want to know why the rules exist and what to do when their wardrobe doesn't fit them neatly.

What colours look best on camera?

Mid tones. Navy, slate, olive, rust, mustard, a dusty blue or a soft green. They hold their detail, they sit well against most backgrounds, and they don't fight with the face for attention.

The colours that cause trouble are the extremes. Bright white sits at the very top of what a camera can record, so the person exposing the shot has a choice: keep detail in the shirt and let the face go a bit dark, or expose for the face and let the shirt glow. That gets harder the darker your skin is, because the gap between shirt and face is bigger. Solid black has the opposite problem, and it can turn into a flat shape with no folds in it. Neither is banned. They just make the job harder, and an off-white or a charcoal does nearly everything the extremes do without the fuss.

The thing people forget is the background. If you're being filmed against a navy wall and you turn up in navy, you'll disappear into it. You don't need to know the exact set, so just ask the crew what's behind you. A quick message the week before saves a change of shirt on the day.

Why do stripes and checks shimmer on camera?

The effect is called moiré. A camera sensor is a grid of tiny pixels, and a fine, regular pattern is also a grid. When the two grids nearly line up, they interfere with each other and you get rippling bands of colour that crawl across the fabric every time you move. Your eyes see a perfectly nice shirt. The camera sees a television that's lost its signal.

The usual offenders are pinstripes, narrow stripes, small checks, herringbone, houndstooth, fine corduroy and some knitted textures. The problem is that it depends on the camera, the lens and how wide the shot is, so the same shirt can be fine in a close-up and wobble in a wide.

Every office has one person whose favourite shirt is a fine check. Ask them, gently, to bring a second one.

A quick test at home: film yourself on your phone from a few feet away and zoom in slightly. If the pattern starts dancing, it'll probably dance on the day. Moiré is very hard to remove in the edit, so it's one to settle before you leave the house.

Can I wear a logo or branded clothing?

Your own company's branding is usually fine, and sometimes it's exactly right. Check with whoever's making the film, because some brand films deliberately keep logos out so the people feel less like a corporate video.

Other brands' logos are a different matter. A big sportswear logo on your chest pulls focus, and if the film ends up in paid advertising, a visible third-party brand can cause headaches nobody wants.

How should clothes fit when you're sitting down?

Most interviews are filmed seated, and clothes behave differently in a chair. Jackets ride up at the back and bunch at the collar. Shirts pull and gape between the buttons. Trousers rise, and suddenly the wide shot is all shin and sock.

Do the sit test. Put the outfit on, sit in a chair in front of a mirror, lean forward a little the way people do when they're talking, and look. If anything pulls, gapes or bunches, change it.

For the filmed work, the bits of you doing your job, wear what you'd actually wear to do it. If you're up a ladder or at a bench, your normal work clothes look right, and anything else looks like a costume.

Our film about Signwriting Jack is shot in the workshop and out on the shopfronts. In a film like that the clothes are part of the place, and anything smarter than the work would look odd up a ladder.

What should I wear so the mic is easy to fit?

This is where layers help. The interview mic is usually a small lavalier clipped to the chest, with a cable running down to a transmitter pack on the waistband or belt. I've explained how it all works in lav mics explained, but from a wardrobe point of view, you want three things:

  • Somewhere to clip it. A shirt placket, a collar, the edge of a jacket. A plain crew-neck t-shirt works too, though the mic sits a bit more exposed.
  • A route for the cable. A buttoned shirt or a jacket lets the cable run inside out of sight.
  • Somewhere for the pack. A belt or a firm waistband. A dress with no waistband means the pack goes on a thigh strap or clipped somewhere at the back, which is fine but worth knowing about in advance.

Fabric matters as much as the cut. Cotton and wool are quiet. Silk, stiff new shirts, synthetics and waterproofs rustle against the mic every time you breathe. A chunky knit muffles the voice if the mic has to go underneath it. If you're torn between two outfits, wear the cotton one.

Will my glasses reflect on camera?

They can, but wear them anyway if you normally wear them. You'll look like yourself, and squinting is worse than any reflection.

Reflections come from lights and windows bouncing off the lenses. Moving a light higher or wider usually fixes it, and I've explained where those lights sit in interview lighting explained. Lifting the arms of the glasses very slightly off the ears angles the lenses down, which is an old trick that works more often than it should. An anti-reflective coating helps a lot.

The one pair to leave at home is lenses that darken in daylight. Near a window or outside, they'll slowly turn to sunglasses mid-interview, and the edit can't fix that.

What jewellery should I avoid on camera?

Anything that moves and makes a noise. Bangles and chunky bracelets clink against the table and the chair. Long necklaces swing into the mic. Big hoop earrings can tap a collar mic. Lanyards and ID badges knock against everything, and they often carry a name and a photo you might not want in a film. A watch is fine until you rest your wrist on a hard table, then every gesture becomes a tap.

Your eyes see a perfectly nice shirt. The camera sees a television that's lost its signal.

Rings, studs and a simple necklace that sits close to the neck are usually fine. If a piece matters to you, keep it on and tell the sound person, and they'll work around it.

Do I need make-up for a filmed interview?

Most people don't need much, men included. The main enemy is shine. Interview lighting picks up oil on the forehead, the nose and the top of the head, and a shiny patch reads as sweat even when you're calm.

  • For everyone: a translucent powder or blotting papers for shine, lip balm, and moisturiser that's had time to sink in.
  • If you don't usually wear make-up: powder is enough. If you shave, do it a few hours before rather than right before, so any redness settles. Bald heads shine more than you'd think, so powder there too.
  • If you do usually wear make-up: wear your everyday look, slightly more defined if anything. Go easy on shimmer and highlighter, which turn into hot spots under lights, and match foundation carefully at the jaw so there's no line.

What should I bring as a backup?

A small bag that saves a lot of trouble:

  • A second top in a different colour, in case the first clashes with the background or shimmers.
  • A plain t-shirt or vest to wear under a shirt, which helps the mic and hides it.
  • Blotting papers or powder, lip balm, a comb or brush.
  • Your glasses case, and contact lens kit if you use one.
  • A lint roller, because dark fabric shows every hair under good light.

If you're organising the shoot for other people, forward them this a week before rather than the night before. And if you want the whole planning side in one place, our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, covers it. When you're ready to talk about a film, tell us about the business.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can I wear a white shirt on camera?
faqs.a: Yes, but an off-white or pale blue is easier. Bright white sits at the top of what a camera can record, so the crew has to choose between detail in the shirt and a well-exposed face. Under a jacket or jumper it's much less of a problem, because there's less of it in the frame.

faqs.q: Should I wear the same outfit on both days of a shoot?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the interview might carry on into the second day or the editor might cut between the two. Changing clothes mid-story breaks continuity and makes the edit harder. If the days are clearly separate, say an interview one day and filming the work the next, check with the crew first and they'll tell you what matters.

faqs.q: Is it fine to wear a hat or cap in an interview?
faqs.a: If it's what you always wear for work, often yes, though a peak can throw a shadow across your eyes under interview lighting. The crew can usually light around it or ask you to tip it back slightly. Avoid caps with large logos, and bear in mind a hat you take off halfway through can cause continuity problems in the edit.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring my own make-up to a shoot?
faqs.a: Bring whatever you'd use on a normal day, plus blotting papers or translucent powder for shine. Plenty of brand film shoots don't have a make-up artist, so check in advance whether it's down to you. Keep it simple and close to how you usually look, because the aim is for you to look like yourself on a good day.

items.title: What does a brand story look like? Real forms and examples
items.excerpt: A brand story isn't one document. Here's what it looks like on a website, in a film, on a label and in conversation, with real UK-friendly examples.
items.coverAlt: Rings and bangles laid on wooden display stands and ring cones inside a glass jewellery cabinet
items.body:
A brand story looks like a short, specific account of why a business exists, told by a real person, and repeated in different forms: a paragraph on the About page, a film, a line on the packaging, the answer your team gives when someone asks what you do. It's rarely a single document, and more often the same story turning up in several places.

This post is about what you'd actually see. I'll go through the common forms, from written to filmed to physical, with real examples of each, and then show what separates a story that looks real from one that looks like it came out of a template. If you want a single worked example taken apart line by line, that's in what a brand story example looks like, and for the skeleton underneath, see how a brand story should be structured.

What are the main forms a brand story takes?

Think of a brand story as a thing that has a core and several outfits. The core is the same: who you started for, why, what you believe and what good looks like. The outfits change with the place. These are the ones you'll see most.

  • **The About page.** The most common form, and the most often done badly.
  • **The origin story.** How and why it started, usually a single moment.
  • **The founder's voice.** In a film, a letter, an email or on stage.
  • **The customer story.** The same story, told from the side of someone you helped.
  • **The product or process story.** How something's made, and why it's made that way.
  • **The physical story.** Packaging, signs, a note in the box, the way the shop looks.
  • **The spoken story.** What your people say when someone asks.

You don't need all of them. Most good brands have three or four done well. Let's look at each.

What does a brand story look like on an About page?

At its best, it's short and it's about someone. The first thing a visitor sees is a human reason, not a corporate timeline. "Founded in 2009 and growing steadily ever since" tells you nothing. "I spent eleven years fitting kitchens for people who'd been let down by the last firm, and I got tired of arriving at jobs that were already a mess" tells you a lot (that's an invented line, but you can hear the difference).

A good About page usually has a few things in order: the person or people, the moment or frustration that started it, what you do differently because of it, and what a customer can expect. It's got a photograph of actual humans, not a stock team. It reads like somebody talking. And it's honest about size. If you're four people in a unit, say so, because it's a strength, not an embarrassment.

What it doesn't have is a mission statement written by committee, a list of values like "integrity, excellence, innovation" or a paragraph that could be pasted onto any competitor's site. If you could swap the logo and keep the text, it's not a story.

What does an origin story look like?

An origin story is a moment. The most famous UK example I can think of is Innocent, the smoothie company. In 1999 its three founders sold their first smoothies at a London music festival and put up a sign asking people whether they should give up their jobs to make them, with two bins for the empty bottles, one marked yes and one marked no. By the end, the yes bin was full, and they resigned the next day. It's a small, funny, concrete scene with a clear before and after, and that's why it's repeated.

You'll notice what made it work. It's a single scene. It involves real people taking a real risk. There's a bit of humour. It also tells you something about the brand: a bit cheeky, quite honest, not corporate. The story and the tone are doing the same job.

Not every business has a scene like that, and you shouldn't invent one. But most have a moment they've told friends a dozen times, and it's usually better than whatever's currently on the website. If you can't find yours, ask whoever's been there longest what they remember about the first customer.

What does a brand story look like on film?

On film it looks like people talking, with the business happening around them. That's the honest answer, and it's why I think film's the best medium for it. A paragraph can tell you a founder cares about their craft. A film can show you their hands.

Take our film with Catherine Marche. She's been making bespoke jewellery in London for around twenty-five years and works only in recycled metal, with the packaging held to the same rule. The film skips the tour of the collection and has her at the bench explaining why she works that way, with the camera close on the hand work at the speed it actually happens. That's what a brand story on film looks like: a person, a reason and the craft, with nothing between you and them.

Or take Carréducker, two makers who trained under the same master at John Lobb and set up on their own. Their story includes the fact that they'd documented all 210 steps of a pair of shoes publicly, one post at a time. The film's built around the two of them talking as one conversation. A viewer gets the whole story in a few minutes: the training, the patience, the standard.

Documentary-style brand films have a particular look. There are real locations rather than sets, natural light where it's possible, people who aren't reading a script, and silence left in. If you want to know how this differs from a standard company video, brand documentary versus corporate video goes through it.

If the film opens with a drone shot of the building, the story's on its way out.

What does a customer story look like?

A customer story is your brand story with the camera pointed the other way. The customer does the talking, you're the thing that helped them, and what the viewer sees is a real person like themselves who ended up somewhere good.

Our film for a couple who renovated a period house in Tooting is a clear example. It's told by the people who paid for it, filmed after they'd moved back in. Most renovation films are made from the builder's side, which a prospective client discounts straight away. This one's the account of someone who's been where they are. If you're thinking about this form, customer testimonial videos goes into how to do it well.

A customer story tends to follow a simple pattern: where they were, what went wrong or what they wanted, what happened and where they are now. It looks like a conversation, and it works best when the customer's allowed to be a bit critical, because a story with no friction doesn't feel true.

What does a product or process story look like?

It looks like showing how something's made and why it's made like that. The best ones put a person in front of the process and let them explain the choices. Why recycled metal? Why 210 steps? Why that timber? Those "why" questions are where the brand lives.

It might be a short film at the workbench, a photograph with a caption, a page on the site that follows one product from raw material to doorstep, or a label that says where it came from. The test's whether a customer comes away knowing something they didn't, and caring about it.

Patagonia's habit of publishing the story behind its products and running a repair service is a well-known case of this form working as a brand. The facts are on the page, the actions match them, and customers can see that.

What does a physical brand story look like?

The most overlooked form. It's the note in the parcel, the wording on the box, the signwriting on the shopfront, the way the person behind the counter says hello. These small things carry the story when no one's reading anything.

I notice this most in craft businesses, where the physical object is the story. A hand-painted sign on a shopfront tells you something about the business before you've read a word. It's the reason our film about traditional hand-painted signwriting spends so long on the brush loading and the single unbroken line. The work itself is the story, and the film's job is to get out of its way.

How can you tell a real brand story from a fake one?

A few quick checks:

  • **Specifics.** Does it have names, places, numbers, a moment? Real stories do. Fake ones have adjectives.
  • **A person.** Can you picture someone saying it? If it reads like it was written by nobody, it probably was.
  • **A cost.** Did it cost something, such as a risk, a sacrifice or a hard decision? Stories where nothing was ever at stake feel like adverts.
  • **Consistency.** Do the film, the packaging and the way the phone's answered all agree? A story only the About page tells isn't believed.
  • **Something you'd repeat.** Could a customer tell a friend in one sentence?

Emplifi's 2026 survey of more than 1,600 consumers in the UK and US found 93% say authentic engagement builds trust in a brand, and 85% say they'd pay more for brands they see as authentic. It's a mixed UK and US sample, but it fits with everything above.

A real brand story has a person in it, a reason behind it and something you could repeat to a friend.

Does a brand story look different for a small business?

It usually looks better, because it's closer to the truth. A small business can name the person, show the workshop and say what went wrong on the first job. A large company has to work harder to sound that human, and often ends up with something smoother and less memorable.

The practical difference is production. A small business doesn't need a campaign. It needs one honest page, one good film with the real people in it and a team who can say the same thing in conversation. That's a manageable job, and it tends to look the part precisely because it hasn't been over-produced. The jeweller and the shoemakers above are tiny businesses, and their films carry as much weight as anything a big brand makes.

How long is a brand story, visually?

On a page, it's usually a few short paragraphs and a photograph. On film, it's typically a few minutes, and then cut into shorter pieces. How long to make it is a question with a proper answer in how long a brand story should be.

Where should you start?

With the version you can do this week. Write the page: who, why, what you believe, what good looks like. Put it on your About page in your own voice. Then decide where it deserves a better outfit. For most businesses that's a short film with the real people in it, because it's the one form that lets a stranger see and hear you before they've met you.

If you're comparing forms and want the full picture, the complete guide to brand storytelling collects everything in one place. And if you'd like to talk about what yours could look like on film, get in touch.

faqs.q: Is a brand story just an About Us page?
faqs.a: No, the About page is one place it appears. A brand story is the underlying account of why you exist and what you stand for, and it should also show up in your films, packaging, emails, sales conversations and the way your team talks. If it only lives on the About page, it's a paragraph rather than a story.

faqs.q: Does a brand story have to be a film?
faqs.a: No. Many good brand stories are written, and some are physical, like a label or a shopfront. Film is the strongest form for most businesses because viewers see and hear real people, which builds trust fast. It also gives you material to cut into shorter pieces, but it isn't the only option and a good written story beats a weak film.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a brand story and an origin story?
faqs.a: An origin story is one part of a brand story: the moment or reason the business began. A brand story is wider. It includes who you serve, what you believe, how you work and what customers can expect. Many brands lead with the origin story because it's concrete and easy to remember, then build out from it.

faqs.q: How do I know if my brand story is good?
faqs.a: Check for specifics, a real person, a cost or risk, and consistency across your channels. Then test whether a customer could repeat it in one sentence. If your About page could be pasted onto a competitor's site without anyone noticing, it isn't distinctive enough yet. Asking three recent customers what they think you stand for is a quick, honest test.

items.title: How a brand story helps you create content faster
items.excerpt: What a brand story does for the people making your content: faster ideas, fewer rewrites, easier approvals and a consistent voice, even with a tiny team.
items.coverAlt: A creative team pinning photographs to a long studio wall at dusk, with the London skyline in the window
items.body:
A brand story benefits content creation by taking away the hardest questions before anyone sits down to make anything. You already know who it's for, what it should sound like and what it's trying to say, so ideas arrive faster, drafts need fewer rewrites, approvals are quicker and different people end up sounding like the same business.

This post is about the maker's side of it: what changes for the person who has to produce the content, week in, week out. How to build that system is in how a brand story should be used in content creation, and the wider effect on results is in how a brand story enhances marketing. Here I want to stay on the day-to-day benefits, and be honest about where they stop.

Why does content creation feel so hard without a brand story?

Because every piece starts with the same three decisions. What are we saying? Who's it for? How should it sound? Without a brand story, you make those decisions again every time, usually in a hurry, often alone, and sometimes differently depending on who's holding the pen that week.

That's why so many small businesses burn out on content. Making a video or a post isn't the hard bit. Every single one being a fresh argument is. Then the approvals start: someone says it doesn't feel right, nobody can say why, and it goes round again.

Most UK businesses are tiny, which makes it worse. The government's Business Population Estimates put the number of private sector businesses at 5.69 million at the start of 2025, and 4.3 million of them had no employees apart from the owners. For a huge share of the economy, the person making the content is the same person doing the job, and every hour spent agonising over tone is an hour not billed. A story that settles those decisions in advance is worth more to them than any editing tool.

Does a brand story really make content faster?

Yes, and it's the benefit people notice first. The speed doesn't come from typing faster. It comes from not having to decide the basics.

When you can see, on one page, that your audience is homeowners who've been burnt by a builder before, that you're the plain-speaking option and that your belief is "we show you the price before we start", a lot of ideas generate themselves. You know a post about a hidden-cost horror story belongs. You know a glossy stock-photo montage doesn't. You can say yes or no in seconds.

On shoots, the effect is the same. If we've agreed what the story is before the camera comes out, we know what to ask, which moments to wait for and which shots we can skip. It's the difference between coming home with a day's footage that's about something and a day's footage that's about everything. The second one takes far longer to edit.

What does it do for ideas?

It gives you a way to find them. Without a story, "what should we post?" has no edges. With one, the question narrows to "what's a moment that shows our belief about X?", and that's much easier to answer.

A story also tells you where to look. Your best ideas tend to live in the places where your belief meets real life: a customer's reaction, a mistake you fixed, a thing a team member does without being asked. If your belief is that you build things to last, a repair job from fifteen years ago is a story. A routine delivery isn't.

You'll also stop worrying about originality. Most subjects have been covered. What can't be copied is your reasons, your people and the way you do it, and the story puts those front and centre. That's why our work with Catherine Marche centres on her recycled-metal rule rather than on the jewellery, because lots of people make earrings and very few hold their packaging to the same standard as the metal.

How does it make approvals easier?

This one's underrated. Most approval pain comes from disagreement about taste, and taste is hard to argue with. A brand story swaps "I don't like it" for "does this fit the story?". That's a question with an answer.

If you've got a boss, a client, a partner or a board who signs things off, giving them the story up front changes the conversation. They've agreed what you're trying to say, so the feedback is about whether the piece says it, not about their personal preference for blue. It's also much easier to push back politely on a late suggestion, because you can point to the page.

I'd go further. A shared story is the cheapest way I know to reduce rounds of revisions. On a film, every round of changes costs time on both sides, and a clear story at the start means most of the notes are about trimming, not about direction. For more on how briefing affects the edit, how to write a video brief covers the film side.

Most feedback rounds are people discovering what they wanted by seeing what they didn't.

Does it help when more than one person makes content?

It's one of the biggest benefits. The moment a second person, a freelancer or an agency touches your content, your voice starts to drift. They're doing their best, they just don't have what's in your head.

A brand story is how you get what's in your head onto paper. A new freelancer reads it, watches your main film, and within an hour they've got a decent grip on the tone. A new starter does the same. You spend less time correcting and more time reviewing.

It also helps with people inside the business who aren't "the marketing person". If an engineer wants to write a post about a job, or an installer wants to film something on their phone, the story gives them guard rails. They don't have to ask what's allowed. For more on getting non-specialists comfortable on film, how to prepare for being filmed is worth sharing around.

What does it do for the quality of the raw material?

If you plan to film, the story improves what you capture. People who know what the story is tend to say better things on camera, because they understand what the film's trying to do and can speak to it. Interviews with someone who's never been told the point tend to wander, and you end up cutting around the vagueness.

It also changes who you ask to appear. When the story's about a family business that's lasted three generations, you want the person who's been there thirty years, not just the most confident person on the team. Our film with Carréducker is built around two founders who trained at the same bench, and that's why it's filmed as one conversation rather than two separate interviews. The story told us how to shoot it.

Documentary-style brand film is particularly well suited to this, because it starts with real people and real answers. You can read more on how that differs from a standard promo in brand documentary versus corporate video.

Can it help you say no?

Yes, and it'll save you more time than any scheduling tool. Every business gets offered content ideas that don't fit: a trend someone's seen, a competitor's format, a suggestion from a well-meaning relative. Without a story, you either do it and dilute the brand, or you say no and feel guilty.

With one, you can check it against the page and decline. "It's a good idea, it just isn't us." Over a year, that discipline is the difference between content that adds up and a feed that looks like six different companies took turns.

Content gets easier the moment you're allowed to say no to most of the ideas.

What does it change week to week?

The honest answer is that it makes the work calmer. Monday morning stops being a scramble for something to post. You open the story, look at what you've got in the bank of real moments, and pick. The person making the content stops feeling like they're guessing, and that's worth a lot, because guessing is what wears people out.

It also changes how you review old content. Instead of asking "did that get likes?", you can ask "did that sound like us?" Both questions matter, but the second one's the only one you fully control. Over a few months you'll see which pieces felt most like the business, and which ones were off. Usually the off ones were made in a rush with no story to hand.

Does it help the creative side, or just the admin?

Both, and the creative benefit surprises people. A tight brief is good for creativity. Give a filmmaker a clear story and they can spend their energy on how to show it, such as where to put the camera, what to wait for and when to leave a silence. Give them a vague one and they spend that energy guessing what you want.

The same applies to anyone writing, designing or editing for you. Constraints give them something to push against. The best creative work I've seen on a shoot has usually come from a very clear idea of what the film was for, followed by a lot of freedom in how it got there.

What are the limits? Where won't a brand story help?

I'd be doing you a disservice if I made it sound magical. A few honest limits:

  • **It won't make poor content good.** A clear story told badly is still a bad video. Craft still matters.
  • **It won't replace knowing your audience.** The story says what you stand for. You still need to learn what your customers actually ask, search for and worry about.
  • **It won't save a story that isn't true.** If the founder never really believed the thing the story says, the content will feel hollow. People can tell.
  • **It needs maintaining.** Businesses change. Review it once or twice a year, and update it on purpose.

None of that cancels the benefit. It just means the story's the foundation, not the building.

How do you get these benefits without spending a fortune?

Start with the page. One side of A4, in plain words, covering who you're for, why you exist, what you believe and what good looks like. If you're stuck, what makes a good brand story is a useful checklist to test it against. Share it with everyone who makes or approves content. Use it for a month and see how many decisions it settles.

Then give it a face. A single short film in which the founder, or whoever really holds the story, tells it in their own words, is the thing a freelancer, a new hire or a prospect can watch to get it in three minutes. That's where we come in. Our brand films are built from real conversations with the people in the business, and they work as both the story and the raw material for everything after.

For the wider picture, the complete guide to brand storytelling has everything in one place. And if you'd like to talk about getting yours on film, get in touch.

faqs.q: Does a brand story save time on content creation?
faqs.a: Yes. It settles the questions you'd otherwise answer afresh every time: who it's for, what to say and how it should sound. That cuts the time spent on ideas, drafts and approval rounds. The saving shows up most when several people make content or when you're filming, because everyone knows what the piece is trying to do before work starts.

faqs.q: Can a brand story help if I'm a one-person business?
faqs.a: It helps a lot, because you're making every decision yourself and there's nobody to check against. Roughly 4.3 million UK businesses have no employees beyond the owner, so most are in that position. A one-page story gives you a quick test for every idea, and a short film of you telling it gives you something to share.

faqs.q: Will a brand story make my content more original?
faqs.a: It makes it more distinctive, which matters more. Most topics have been covered by someone, but nobody else has your reasons, your people or your way of working. The story points you at those, so your content shows things competitors can't copy. That's a better route to standing out than chasing an unusual topic.

faqs.q: How often should I update my brand story?
faqs.a: Review it once or twice a year and whenever the business changes in a meaningful way, such as a new service, a new audience or a change of ownership. Update it on purpose rather than letting it drift. Don't change it just because you're tired of it, because the people you're reaching have usually only just started to notice.

items.title: How to use your brand story in content creation
items.excerpt: Turn a brand story into a working content system: story pillars, a story bank, format rules and a simple weekly routine that keeps everything on message.
items.coverAlt: A baker filming dough with a phone on a clamp in a railway arch bakery at dawn
items.body:
Use your brand story as the brief behind everything you publish, not as a piece of content in itself. Break it into a handful of recurring themes, collect real moments that prove each one, then decide what each format should do with them. Every post, film and email then starts from the story rather than from a blank page.

This post is the working method. It covers how to split a story into content pillars, how to build a store of material to draw from, what rules to set for each format, and a simple routine to keep it running. The advantages of doing it this way are in how a brand story benefits content creation, so I'll keep this one practical.

What's the first step in using a brand story for content?

Get the story into a form a busy person can use. A three-page narrative is lovely, but nobody's going to open it on a Tuesday when they need a caption. I'd boil it down to one page with four things on it:

  • **Who you're for.** The specific person you help, described in a sentence.
  • **Why you exist.** The real reason you started, in the words you'd use to a friend.
  • **What you believe.** Two or three opinions about your work that others in your sector might disagree with.
  • **What good looks like.** The change a customer sees when it goes well.

If you haven't written those yet, how to write a brand story takes you through it, and what a brand story should include lists the parts. Once you've got the page, print it and keep it next to whoever makes your content. That person, whether it's you, a colleague or a freelancer, should be able to hold any idea up against it and see in ten seconds whether it belongs.

How do you split a story into content pillars?

A story is one thing. Content needs to be many. Pillars are how you get from one to the other, and the trick is to take them from the story rather than from a list of topics you think people want.

Take the four parts above and turn each into a recurring theme. Say you run a family joinery firm that started because the founder was fed up with throwaway kitchens. Your pillars might be:

  • **The people.** Who's at the bench, how they got there.
  • **The belief.** Why you build things to be repaired, not replaced.
  • **The work.** One job from start to finish, with the awkward bits left in.
  • **The result.** What a customer says a year later.

Four pillars is plenty. Three is fine. Eight means nobody remembers them, and you'll end up posting about whatever's convenient. Each pillar should be able to produce content for years, because it's a theme and not a topic. "The people" never runs dry. "How to choose a hinge" does.

You'll also notice what's missing: a pillar for "promotions" or "company news". Those still happen, but they're not what the story's about. They sit on top, and you'd tag them to a pillar so they don't feel like a different business is speaking.

What's a story bank and why do you need one?

A story bank is a single document, spreadsheet or folder where you drop real moments as they happen, each tagged to a pillar. A customer's message. A photo from site. A line someone said that made the room laugh. A mistake that taught you something. A before and after.

This is the part that makes the biggest practical difference. Most businesses don't lack stories, they lack a place to put them, so they're forgotten by the time anyone sits down to write a post. If you've ever shot a day's filming, you know the best material isn't scripted. It's the offhand thing said at the end of a take, or what someone does when they think the camera's off. A bank catches that sort of thing before it's lost.

Keep entries short. A line or two, a date, a pillar tag and where the raw material lives. Ten minutes a week is enough. If you've got a few months of entries, you'll never face a blank page again.

What rules should each format follow?

The same story behaves differently in each format, and it helps to decide the rules once. Here's roughly how I'd set them for a small business.

Long-form film

This is where the whole story lives and where you get to take your time. One film, built on real people talking about why they do the work, gives you the raw material for nearly everything else. It's how a brand story video does its job, and our guide to how long a brand story should be covers length. Film first, because every short piece can come out of it. Doing it the other way round costs more.

Short video and social

Short-form takes one moment from the story and does nothing else with it. One idea, one person, one reason to keep watching. Don't try to tell the whole story in thirty seconds. Tell one beat and let the viewer chase the rest. Our post on turning one brand film into a year of content goes through how the cutting works.

Website and landing pages

These carry the story in its most compressed form. The homepage says who you're for and why you exist. The About page gives the longer account. Case study pages show the "what good looks like" part with a real customer. They should all use the same wording, because that's what makes a visitor feel they've arrived somewhere coherent.

Email and written pieces

Email is where you can be more personal, and where the "what you believe" part of the story shines. Opinions make good emails. Articles can go deeper on one pillar, and each one should link back to the film or the About page so a reader who's curious has somewhere to go.

Sales material

Decks, proposals and quotes are content too, and they're the ones most likely to drift off-story because someone's in a hurry. Give your sales team the one-page version and a short film to send out before a call.

How do you keep the story from sounding repetitive?

This worry comes up every time, and it's mostly unfounded. You're not repeating the story, you're returning to it from a different angle. A pillar looks different in a film, a caption, a customer case study and a founder's email. People who've seen it four times in four forms don't feel nagged. They feel they know you.

What does help is rotating the proof. Don't tell the "why we started" story every month. Tell it properly once, then show smaller moments that demonstrate it. If your belief is that kitchens should be repairable, show a repair. If it's that you answer your own phone, show the phone being answered.

If you've worked out your story and the first thing you post is a stock photo of a handshake, the story's lost already.

What does a simple weekly routine look like?

Here's one that works for a small team and doesn't eat a day a week:

  • **Monday, ten minutes.** Look at the story bank. Pick the strongest two or three entries, each from a different pillar.
  • **Midweek, one hour.** Turn them into the week's pieces, checking each against your one-page story.
  • **Friday, ten minutes.** Drop new moments into the bank from the week that's just gone.

Once a quarter, review. Which pillars are getting the most attention? Which are going quiet? Have you got enough footage or photographs, or is it time to book another shoot? The quarterly check is also the time to ask whether the story itself needs adjusting, because businesses change and it's better to update it on purpose than let it drift.

If you're stuck on what to film, the answer is nearly always the bank. Look for the pillars with the thinnest evidence and shoot for those.

How do you stay consistent when more than one person makes content?

Write down three things the story can't say, three phrases you do use and a couple of sample posts that get it right. That's a style guide, and it fits on one side of paper. People who haven't been inside the business for years pick up the tone from examples far faster than from rules.

It also helps to have one person own the story, with the authority to say "that's not us". They don't need to be senior. They need to know the business and care about it, and I've written about what that role actually involves in who a brand storyteller is.

What mistakes do people make when they put a story into content?

The commonest one is treating the story as a slogan. They pull out a tagline, stick it on every post and call it done. A tagline isn't a story, and repeating it doesn't give anyone a reason to care. Show a moment that proves it instead.

The second is making everything about the founder's journey. The origin matters, but customers are mostly asking what's in it for them. Use your origin to explain why you do the work, then move to what the customer gets.

The third is skipping the bank and relying on memory. Within a month you're posting whatever's closest to hand, and the story's gone quiet without anyone deciding it should.

The last is leaving it too late to film. Written content can be knocked out in an afternoon, but good footage of real people takes planning, and it's the thing you'll wish you had more of in six months.

Where do people actually watch all this content?

It's worth knowing, because it shapes where the story shows up. YouGov's 2026 UK media consumption research found 57% of adults watch short-form video daily and 37% watch long-form, and 57% of long-form viewers say they're likely to watch all the way through. That's why I usually recommend the long film lives on YouTube and the website, with shorter cuts going out to wherever your customers are.

Pillars come from the story, proof comes from the bank, and the format decides how much of it you can say.

A worked example

Take a cabling manufacturer, an unglamorous business if ever there was one. Suppose its story is built on one belief: that the cheapest cable's rarely the cheapest job. The pillars could be the people who make it, the belief about quality, a customer job where cheap cable caused trouble, and the result.

The film is a documentary with two or three people from the shop floor and a customer, filmed on site. From it you'd cut a short on the people, a short on the belief, a case study page for the customer, an email to the mailing list, and a clip for sales to send before calls. It's all the same story. It just keeps turning up in a different place.

That's essentially how a single day on a drainage job became an eight minute film, a run of vertical shorts and carousels for us. One shoot, one set of real moments, cut for different audiences.

For the broader picture of how this connects to your marketing, how to use storytelling in marketing sits alongside this one, and the complete guide to brand storytelling ties the whole subject together.

If you've got a story and you want help getting it on film so you've got material for a year, tell us a bit about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How often should I post content based on my brand story?
faqs.a: Consistency matters more than volume. For most small businesses that's one proper piece a week, such as a short video, an article or a case study, plus lighter posts around it. If you've got a story bank to draw from, it's easy to keep up. Posting twice a week for a month and then disappearing does more harm than a steady rhythm you can sustain.

faqs.q: What are content pillars and how many do I need?
faqs.a: Content pillars are the three or four recurring themes your content returns to, taken from your brand story rather than from a list of popular topics. Typical ones are the people, the belief behind the work, the work itself and the result for customers. More than four tends to blur, and nobody, including your own team, can remember them.

faqs.q: Should every piece of content tell the whole brand story?
faqs.a: No. Tell the whole story properly once, in a long film or a good About page, then let each piece of content show one moment or belief from it. Short formats can't carry the lot, and trying to makes them dull. A viewer who sees four small, consistent pieces builds up the full picture themselves.

faqs.q: How do I keep other people's content on-brand?
faqs.a: Give them a one-page version of the story, three phrases you do use and three things you'd never say, and a couple of examples that get the tone right. Add one person with authority to say 'that's not us'. Examples work better than rules, because people absorb tone quickly from seeing it done well.

stat.title: UK adults who watch each kind of video daily, May 2026
stat.takeaway: Short-form wins on daily reach, but most people who start a long-form video say they'll watch it to the end.

items.title: Never burn a bridge: how to close the file kindly
items.excerpt: How to end a sales conversation that's gone quiet so the door stays open: the close-the-file email, why people come back later, and how to take a no.
items.coverAlt: People chatting with drinks at an outdoor work event
items.body:
If a conversation with a prospect has gone quiet, the kindest thing you can do is close it yourself. Send one short, warm email saying you've not heard back, that you're taking it as the timing not being right, and that you'll stop there. Leave one door open, tied to something real in their world. People remember being let go gracefully, and a good number of them come back when things change.

Most advice on follow-up is about squeezing a reply out of someone. Chase on day three, day seven, day fourteen, then a "breakup email" written to guilt them into answering. I understand why it exists. I just don't think it suits a business where the work depends on people liking you enough to let you into their building with a camera.

Why does it matter how a conversation ends?

Because the ending is the part people remember. Someone might forget the details of your proposal within a week. They won't forget whether you made them feel hassled.

In creative work especially, a no is rarely a verdict on you. It's usually timing. A budget that hasn't been signed off, a board that hasn't met, a person who's left, a launch that's slipped to next year. None of that's permanent. If the last thing they had from you was polite and easy, you're still a name they'd be glad to see when those things change. If the last thing was the fifth "just bumping this up", you've turned a not yet into a never.

There's a practical side too. The people we'd most like to work with tend to know each other. Marketing leads move jobs, founders sit on the same panels, charity directors compare notes. A heavy-handed chase doesn't stay between you and one inbox.

How many times should you follow up before stopping?

For us it's usually twice, then a close. One email to start, one follow-up a week or so later with something genuinely useful in it, and then a short note saying we'll leave it there. Three touches, spread out, each one easy to ignore without feeling guilty.

The number matters less than the reason behind each email. A follow-up has to earn its place. If you've nothing new to say, saying it again won't help. "Did you get my last email?" is the clearest example. They did. They're busy, or it isn't right for them, and either answer is fine.

And if they've actually told you no, you don't follow up at all. You say thanks, you mean it, and you wish them well with whatever's on their plate.

What does a good "close the file" email say?

Not much, which is the point. It does four things:

  • Says what's happened, plainly. You've written twice and not heard back, or the quote went out and it's gone quiet.
  • Gives them the generous reading. You're assuming it's timing rather than anything else, and that's completely fair.
  • Says you'll stop, so they don't have to manage you.
  • Leaves one specific door open, linked to something they're actually doing, rather than a vague "let me know if anything changes".

Something like: "I've not heard back, which usually means the timing isn't right, and that's completely fair. I'll stop there rather than keep turning up in your inbox. If the new site goes ahead and a film would help, I'd be glad to pick it up then. Shall I close the file?"

That last question does a lot of work. It can be answered in one word, it hands them the decision, and it's the easiest email in the whole sequence to reply to. Some people will say yes, close it, thanks for asking. Some will say sorry, it's been chaos here, can we talk in the spring. Both are better than silence, and both leave you on good terms.

Nobody has ever read a fifth chaser and felt warmer about the sender. They've just got quicker at the delete key.

Why do people come back months later?

Because their situation changes and yours hasn't. The budget lands in a new financial year. The person who was blocking it moves on. A launch finally gets a date. When that happens they think of whoever left the cleanest impression, and that's rarely the person who chased hardest.

A closed file also takes the awkwardness away. There's no pile of unanswered emails for them to apologise for before they can say hello again. You've cleared the slate for them, which makes getting back in touch easy.

A no is usually about timing, and timing changes. How you took it doesn't.

How do you take a no without it stinging?

It does sting a bit, especially when you've put time into a proposal or a treatment you were proud of. I don't think pretending otherwise helps anyone. What helps is having a way of handling it that you don't have to think about.

Reply the same day if you can. Thank them for letting you know, because plenty of people never do, and a clear no is a courtesy. If they've gone with someone else, wish the project well and mean it. If it turns out to be a good film, that's good for everyone who makes this kind of work.

Then, if it feels right, ask one useful question. Not "why didn't you pick us", which puts them on the spot. Something that helps you next time, like who usually holds the budget for this kind of work, or whether there's a better time of year to talk. Most people are happy to answer one small question from someone who's taken the news well.

What you don't do is argue, knock the price down on the spot, or send a revised proposal nobody asked for. That tells them your first number wasn't real. There's more on that in why we don't undercut on price.

Isn't closing the file just giving up?

I see it as choosing where your energy goes. Every hour spent chasing someone who's gone quiet is an hour taken from the people who do want to talk, or from the work itself. A small studio can't keep twenty half-open conversations alive on hope.

It's also more honest. Keeping someone in a follow-up sequence they never asked to join is a way of avoiding their answer. Closing the file means accepting it, and it makes the rest of your week a lot lighter.

How do you keep the door open without pestering?

Leave it alone for a good while, then only come back with a reason that's about them. A film you've made that's close to what they do. Some news in their world you genuinely noticed. A check in that asks for nothing. If you've nothing to say, don't write. I've gone into this more in why the best work comes from people who already trust you.

Keep a note of the closed files somewhere you'll actually see it. Not to chase anyone, just so that when their name turns up again you remember the context and can pick it up properly, without asking them to repeat everything.

And if you're on the other side of this, with a film in mind and no rush at all, that's completely fine by us. Get in touch whenever it suits, or read our free guide first so you know what to expect before the camera comes out.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long should I wait before sending a closing email?
faqs.a: Two to three weeks after your last follow-up is about right. That's long enough that they've clearly seen your earlier emails and chosen not to reply yet, and short enough that the conversation is still fresh. Waiting months and then closing it can read oddly, as if you'd forgotten about them and suddenly remembered.

faqs.q: Should I send a closing email if they've already said no?
faqs.a: No. If someone has given you a clear answer, the closing email is the thank you you send in reply. Thank them for letting you know, wish the project well, and leave it there. Sending a separate close-the-file note after a no just makes them deal with you twice, which is the opposite of what you're trying to do.

faqs.q: Is it pushy to ask who holds the budget after a no?
faqs.a: Not if you ask once, politely, and make it easy to ignore. It's a reasonable question that helps you approach the right person next time, and most people don't mind answering it. What makes it pushy is asking it straight after a hard sell, or following it up when they don't reply. One question, then you're done.

faqs.q: What if they reply to the closing email saying they're still interested?
faqs.a: Then you pick it up as if nothing happened, with no hint of 'finally'. Ask what's changed and what timing would suit them, and let them set the pace. People often reply to a closing email because it took the pressure off, so carrying that same easy tone forward is what keeps the conversation going.

items.title: How a brand story makes your marketing work harder
items.excerpt: A brand story gives every ad, email, post and sales call the same source to draw from. Here's how it improves marketing, and what stops it working.
items.coverAlt: A shelf of finished black and brown leather shoes in a showroom with two framed photos of shoemaking hands above
items.body:
A brand story enhances marketing by giving every channel the same reason to exist. Ads, your website, sales calls, emails and posts stop competing with each other and start adding up, because they all draw on one account of who you are, who you help and why it matters. People remember a consistent story far more readily than a list of features.

This post goes through where that actually shows up: advertising, your site, sales, email, social, PR and hiring. I'll also cover how to tell whether it's working, what to do on a small budget, and the habits that quietly stop a brand story doing its job. If you want the basics first, start with what brand storytelling is.

Why does a brand story improve marketing at all?

Most marketing is produced by several people at different times, for different channels, often under pressure. Without a shared story, each piece answers the question "what should we say?" from scratch. The ad agency says one thing, the person running Instagram says another, and the sales team has their own pitch that's been evolving for years. A customer meeting all three sees three slightly different companies.

A brand story fixes that by sitting underneath everything. It's the answer to "what do we say?" that was decided once, properly, so it doesn't get reinvented every Monday morning. That makes your marketing recognisable. Recognisable marketing gets remembered, and remembered marketing is cheaper to run, because you aren't re-introducing yourself every time.

There's a trust side to it as well. Censuswide surveyed 2,004 UK adults in October 2023 and found that 42% agreed brands who make their mission and values visible are more trustworthy, and 40% said they'd be likely to buy after seeing a piece of content showing a brand's values lined up with their own. Only 35% thought brands were doing a good job of making those values visible. That gap is where a clear story earns its keep.

What does a brand story do for advertising?

It gives the ads a point of view, which is the thing most ads are missing. A product-led ad can say what you sell. A story-led ad says why you sell it, and that's the part a person can repeat to a friend.

Patagonia's "Don't Buy This Jacket" advert, run as a full page in the New York Times on Black Friday 2011, is the one everyone cites, and it's worth citing because it only works if the company means it. The ad asked people to think before buying, and it landed because the rest of the brand, the repair service and the environmental positioning, already said the same thing. The ad was one piece of a story that existed before it. A clever line without that foundation reads as a stunt.

On a smaller budget the lesson holds. If you're running paid ads, the story tells you which proof points to lead with and which to drop. You stop testing twenty random angles and test three that all belong to the same brand.

How does it help your website and sales conversations?

Your website is usually where the story gets tested first, because it's where a stranger decides in a few seconds if you're worth another minute. A homepage built on features and service lists looks like every other homepage in your sector. One built on a clear story, who you started for, what you believe about the work, what it looks like when it goes well, gives the visitor something to react to.

Sales is the same. Anyone who's sat through enough pitches knows the ones that stick are the ones where the person tells you something true about why they do the job. A brand story gives your whole team that material. It means the person who joined last month can explain the business as well as the founder, because the story's written down and they've watched it on film.

This is where video earns its place. A brand story video does the explaining in the founder's own voice, and a sales team can send it ahead of a meeting so the first conversation starts further along. If you want to see how that works with real people, our film for La Fromagerie carries the account of a business through four voices rather than one.

What about email, social and PR?

Email is where a brand story quietly pays off, because email is a relationship channel. Subject lines and offers get opens. The sense of who's writing keeps people from unsubscribing. If your emails sound like the same person who made the film and wrote the About page, they build on each other.

Social is hungry. It needs something to say several times a week, and a brand story is a supply of material. Each part of the story, the origin, the way you work, a customer's before and after, a thing you believe that others in your sector don't, can become a dozen posts. Our guide to turning one brand film into a year of content goes into how.

PR works the same way. Journalists and podcast hosts don't want a press release about your product. They want a reason to talk to you, and a story with a real person and a real stake in it is exactly that. It's far easier to pitch "here's why this plumber started filming every job" than "here's a plumbing company".

Nobody has ever shared a features list with a friend and said "you've got to see this".

Can a brand story help with hiring and partners too?

Yes, and it's one of the most overlooked effects. The people deciding whether to apply to you, or whether to put you forward to their own clients, are using the same cues customers do. A clear story tells a candidate what the place is like before they've set foot in it, which means the people who apply already half agree with you.

For partnerships and referrals the effect's even stronger. If a supplier or an existing client can describe what you do and why in two sentences, they'll recommend you more often, and to the right people. If they can't, they'll say "they're good, I think, they do something with websites?" Your brand story is what they'll quote.

What does it look like in practice when it's working?

You'll notice a few things, usually in this order:

  • The marketing gets easier to produce, because you know what's on-brand without a meeting about it.
  • Different channels start to feel like the same business. People who've seen an ad and a post say "oh, it's you" when they land on your site.
  • Sales calls begin further in. The prospect has watched the film or read the story and already has a view.
  • You say no to more ideas. That sounds like a loss, but it's the sign a story is doing its work, because ideas that don't fit stop getting through.

I'd be careful about promising a measurable lift in any single number. Brand effects are slow and tangled up with everything else you're doing, and anyone who tells you a story will deliver a guaranteed percentage is guessing. What you can track honestly is direction: more enquiries that mention the film, shorter sales cycles, better-fit leads, people quoting your language back to you.

How do you start if the budget is small?

Start by writing the story down in plain words before spending anything on production. A page covering who you help, what you saw that made you start, what you do differently and what a good result looks like. Our piece on what a brand story should include lays out the parts. Then check every channel you already run against it. You'll find posts that don't fit, an About page that says something else, and a pitch deck that's out of date.

After that, pick one place to tell it properly. For most businesses I'd pick a single film, because it does the human part that text can't, and it can be cut into pieces for everything else. That's the logic behind a documentary approach: you film the real people, ask real questions, and the story comes from what they say rather than from a script. It also connects to something I wrote about in why a brand film needs a business goal. A story with no job to do just drifts.

You don't have to start with the expensive version. A tidy, honest story told on the website and in sales conversations beats a polished film built on nothing.

What stops a brand story enhancing your marketing?

Four things come up again and again:

  • **It's invented in a workshop and never believed.** If the team can't say it in their own words, it won't survive contact with a customer.
  • **It lives in one place.** A story that's on the About page and nowhere else is a paragraph, not a brand story.
  • **It's all about the company.** The best ones keep the customer at the centre and show your business as the thing that helped them.
  • **It changes every year.** A consistent story needs repetition. By the time you're bored of it, people are only just starting to notice.

The other one is quieter: treating the story as the marketing instead of the foundation for it. A story doesn't replace the offer, the pricing or a decent follow-up. It makes all of those easier to understand and easier to trust.

A brand story decides what your marketing is allowed to say, and that's most of the battle.

Which brands do this well?

The usual examples are big names, and they're useful because the effect's easy to see. For a wider look at who's using story deliberately, see which brands use storytelling, and for a worked case there's a brand story example broken down line by line.

What I'd add from the other side of the camera is that the businesses who get the most out of it are rarely the famous ones. They're the shoemaker, the jeweller, the cheesemonger and the drainage firm who know exactly why they do the work and have been asked to say so on camera. The story was always there. Our work with Carréducker is a good example, two makers who'd already documented every one of the 210 steps in a pair of shoes. They didn't need a story invented for them. They needed someone to film it properly.

Where does this fit with the rest of your strategy?

A brand story is one part of a larger job, and the full picture is in our complete guide to brand storytelling. If you're weighing up where to put effort first, how to use storytelling in marketing is the practical follow-on to this one.

If you'd like to talk about telling yours on film, get in touch. If we don't think a film's the right next step for you, I'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Does a brand story really improve marketing results?
faqs.a: It improves the conditions your marketing works in. A clear story makes ads more recognisable, sales calls start further along and content easier to produce. What it can't do is guarantee a particular number, because brand effects build slowly and mix with everything else you do. Track direction instead: better-fit enquiries, shorter sales cycles and customers quoting your language back to you.

faqs.q: How long does it take for a brand story to make a difference?
faqs.a: You'll feel the internal benefits within weeks, because decisions about what to say get faster once the story's written down. Outside the business it takes longer. People need to meet the same story several times across different channels before it sticks, so think in months rather than days, and resist changing it just because you've got bored of it.

faqs.q: Can a small business benefit from a brand story, or is it just for big brands?
faqs.a: Small businesses often benefit most, because the founder's reason for starting is usually specific and genuine, and that's hard for a larger competitor to copy. You don't need a big budget. Write the story down, check your channels against it, and tell it properly in one place, ideally on film, before spreading it everywhere.

faqs.q: What's the first marketing channel to apply a brand story to?
faqs.a: Your website and your sales conversations, because that's where people decide whether to trust you. Fix the homepage and About page so they tell one clear story, then give your sales team the same account in their own words. Once those are consistent, extend it to email, social and ads, which will all be easier to write.
