items.title: Why is storytelling important in business?
items.excerpt: Why storytelling matters for sales, hiring, funding, pricing and leadership, not just marketing, and how a small UK firm can start without a big budget.
items.coverAlt: A drainage engineer in a black t-shirt stands in a garden behind a cable reel drum for a CCTV drain camera
items.body:
Storytelling is important in business because most of the decisions that matter, who buys from you, who joins you, who backs you and who stays, are made by people who can't check everything and go on a sense of who you are. A clear, true story gives them that sense quickly, and it works inside the company as well as outside it.

This post looks at storytelling as a business skill rather than a marketing tactic: how it helps with sales, hiring, funding, leadership and price, and what happens to businesses that can't explain themselves. If you're after the brand and marketing angle, that's in why brand storytelling is important and how a brand story can enhance marketing. I'm going wider here, and I'll try to keep it practical.

Why is storytelling important in business, and not only in marketing?

Because every business has to explain itself to someone every day. A new hire wants to know what they've joined. A customer wants to know if you're the right choice. A bank, an investor or a landlord wants to know if you'll still be here in three years. A journalist wants a reason to write about you. Each is asking some version of the same question: what's this business actually about?

Without a story, the answer comes out differently every time, depending on who's asked and how tired they are. With one, the whole organisation says roughly the same thing, and it sounds like a real company rather than a list of services. That consistency is worth more than most owners realise. It's what lets a business scale beyond the founder, because the founder can't be in every conversation.

There's an uncomfortable truth underneath this. In the UK most businesses are tiny. Government figures show that at the start of 2025 there were an estimated 5.7 million private sector businesses, and about 4.27 million of them had no employees at all, so roughly three in four are one-person operations. If you're competing in a market that crowded, being competent isn't enough to be noticed. Being understood is.

How does storytelling help you win customers?

It shortens the distance between "I've heard of you" and "I trust you". Most buying decisions in business happen when the buyer can't fully judge the quality of what they're getting. They can't inspect the plumbing, audit the accounting or assess the film before it's shot. So they look for signals about the people and the way they work.

A story is one of the strongest signals available. A founder who can explain, simply and honestly, why they do the work, what went wrong once and what they learned, sounds like someone who can be trusted with a job. A business that lists its credentials sounds like every other business that lists its credentials.

It also changes the sales conversation. When a prospect has already watched a film or read a page that tells your story, they arrive with context. You spend less time introducing yourself and more time on their problem. Sales teams tell me the difference is obvious: the calls where the person already feels they know you are the ones that move fastest. The channels for this are covered in what brand storytelling in marketing looks like, and there's a look at customer proof in customer testimonial videos.

Why does storytelling matter for hiring and keeping people?

People choose where to work partly on what the business stands for and what working there would be like. A salary and a job spec don't tell them that. A story does.

Candidates check you out. They read your site, watch what you've published and look at who's in the pictures. A business that shows its real people talking about the real work gives them something to picture themselves in. One that shows stock images and a list of benefits gives them nothing to hold on to.

It matters after they've joined, too. New starters who know where the business came from and why it makes the decisions it does find their feet faster. They don't have to guess what's acceptable and what isn't. The story becomes the quiet rulebook: "We don't cut corners on a job like that, because of what happened on the first one." That sort of thing passed on in conversation holds a team together far better than a values poster, and I've seen it written down far less often than it should be. I've dug into the recruitment side in recruitment and employer brand videos.

A story is how a business remembers why it does things, and how new people learn it without a manual.

How does storytelling help with investors, funders and partners?

The numbers get you through the door, but a story is what people remember afterwards. Anyone who's sat on the other side of a pitch knows the feeling of seeing a dozen decks with the same slides in the same order. The ones that stick are the ones where you understand the person and why they're the right one to do it.

For smaller businesses, this extends to lenders, landlords, suppliers and potential partners. They're all asking if you're reliable and if you'll be around. A founder who can tell a short, clear and true account of the business, how it started, what it's learned and where it's heading, reads as someone in control. It doesn't replace the accounts. It makes the accounts easier to believe.

The same applies to charities and community organisations trying to win funding, where the story has to carry evidence of change. I've written about that in brand films for charities.

I've never heard anyone say, "I really backed that business because the slide with the logo wall was so convincing."

Can storytelling help you charge more?

It can, and this is one of the least talked about benefits. When a business is hard to tell apart from the next one, the only thing left to compete on is price. When a customer understands why you do it the way you do, and has a feeling about who you are, they compare you on different terms.

I've watched this happen with craft businesses in particular. A pair of hand-made shoes that takes six months is expensive. A film that shows the 210 steps, as we made for Carreducker, makes the price make sense, because the viewer now knows what they're paying for. Nothing's been discounted and nobody's been persuaded with a trick. They've simply been shown the work. That's the thinking behind why we don't undercut on price, and it applies to any business with something real behind it.

I'd add a note of caution. A story can support a price, but it can't justify one that the work doesn't deserve. If the product isn't good, a story only makes people notice that faster.

What does storytelling do for leadership and internal communication?

Quite a lot, and it's usually neglected. A leader who's explaining a change, a hard year or a new direction can give a list of reasons or tell people what's happening in a way they can follow. The second works better. People remember a story and repeat it, and the more often it's repeated accurately, the less room there is for rumour.

It's also how the business holds on to what it knows. Founders carry a huge amount in their heads: why a supplier was chosen, why a service was dropped, what the first big client taught them. When that stays unspoken, it's lost the moment someone leaves. Capturing it in stories, on paper or on film, is a kind of insurance. Filming a founder talking through the early years is one way to keep it, so the next generation of staff can see it.

What happens to businesses that don't tell their story?

Usually nothing dramatic. They just get compared on price, and they get forgotten. The work might be excellent, but nobody outside the existing customers knows it, because the business has never explained what makes it different. They rely on referrals, which is fine until a good source dries up, and they struggle to hire because candidates can't see what they're signing up to.

Some of this comes from modesty, which I respect. Plenty of the best tradespeople and makers I've met feel awkward talking about themselves. The way round it is not to make them perform. It's to ask questions and film the answers. People are much better at telling their story when someone's curious about it than when they're asked to write it from scratch, and that's where documentary-style film comes in. It captures the real thing, awkward pauses and all, and it reads as honest because it is.

Is storytelling just spin?

It's a fair worry, and the answer depends on what you mean by story. If it means inventing a tale to make an ordinary business sound grand, then yes, and it tends to unravel. If it means choosing which true things to tell and telling them well, it's closer to good communication. Every business already tells a story. The only choice is whether it's one you've shaped or one that forms by accident from your invoices, your emails and what customers say about you.

The test I use is whether the person in the story would recognise it. If the founder reads it and thinks, "that's what happened", it's fine. If they wince, it's spin. That's another reason I like film for this. It's hard to spin a person talking for twenty minutes, and viewers can feel the difference.

How do you start using storytelling in your business?

You don't need to overhaul anything. A sensible order is:

  1. Collect the true stories you already have. The first customer, the near miss, the job you're proudest of, the reason you started. Ask your longest-serving person for theirs too.
  2. Find the thread. Look for what they have in common: the value that keeps showing up. That's the heart of your story. If you're stuck, who a brand storyteller is explains who in a business is usually best placed to find it.
  3. Say it simply. Two or three sentences you could say out loud to a stranger.
  4. Put it to work in more than one place. Your site, your sales conversations, your hiring and your induction. One story used four ways does more than four stories used once.
  5. Get it on film if you can. A single documentary-style film carries a story better than almost any other format, and it can be cut up and used for years. See how video makes a business money for the business case.

Keep it honest throughout. A story people can disprove in a week isn't worth telling. If you'd like more on whether it's right for you, is storytelling a marketing strategy weighs the claim up, and the complete guide to brand storytelling collects the whole subject in one place. When you want to see what a story told on film looks like, our films are a good place to start, and if you've a business with a story worth telling, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Why is storytelling important in business?
faqs.a: Because people decide who to buy from, work for, fund or partner with on limited information, and a clear true story gives them a quick sense of who you are. It helps with sales, hiring, funding, pricing and internal culture. Without one, a business gets compared on price and described differently by every person in it.

faqs.q: How does storytelling help a small business?
faqs.a: A small business usually has real, specific stories close to hand: the founder, the first customer, the way the work is done. Telling them well makes you easier to remember and trust than a larger competitor with a generic message. It costs far less than advertising, and a single film or written story can be reused for years.

faqs.q: Is storytelling only useful for sales and marketing?
faqs.a: No. It matters for hiring, because candidates look for a sense of what working there is like. It helps in funding conversations, where a clear account of the business is easier to back. And it's useful internally, where shared stories explain how decisions get made. Marketing is the most visible use, but it's not the only one.

faqs.q: What's the best way to tell a business story?
faqs.a: Keep it true, specific and short enough to say out loud. Start with a real moment rather than a company history, and use real people. Video is often the strongest format, because viewers can see and hear who's behind the business. Then use the same story across your website, sales conversations, hiring and induction, so it's consistent.

stat.takeaway: A business's story affects who applies, who accepts and who stays.

items.title: How should brand storytelling always begin?
items.excerpt: The best way to open a brand story: start with a person in a moment, not your company history. Five openings that work, six to avoid, and a ten minute exercise.
items.coverAlt: A signwriter in a work vest pencils out a lettering layout on a paper template taped to a white painted wall
items.body:
Brand storytelling should always begin with a person in a specific moment, usually your customer, and something that's at stake for them. It shouldn't begin with your company's history, your mission statement or your name. Open on a human being with a problem or a question, and the viewer has a reason to keep going before they've been asked to care about you.

This post is about that opening and nothing else: the first line of a written story, the first ten seconds of a film, the first thirty seconds of a pitch. I'll cover why beginnings matter so much, five openings that work, the ones to avoid, and a quick rewrite you can try on your own About page. For the whole shape of a story, see how a brand story should be structured. For the writing itself, see how to write a brand story.

Why does the beginning matter so much in brand storytelling?

Because nobody owes you their attention. A film or a page doesn't get a patient audience that sits through the warm-up. It gets someone with a thumb, a lot of tabs open and about three seconds of goodwill. The Advertising Association's 2025 trust research found only 40% of UK adults trust ads, 25% actively distrust them, and enjoyment is the number one driver of trust. Whatever you've made is being judged by people who expect to be bored or sold to, and the judging happens at the start.

The beginning also sets a contract. The first thing you show tells the viewer what kind of story this is: a sales pitch, a corporate update, or something about a real person. Once they've decided it's a sales pitch, you've lost the benefit of the doubt. Once they've decided it's about a person, they'll forgive a lot.

I've sat in edit suites watching a client's first reaction to a rough cut, and it's almost always the same. If the opening works, they lean in and stay there. If it opens on a logo and a drone shot, their attention wanders before the interview starts. The same footage can be rescued by moving one line to the front.

So how should brand storytelling always begin?

With a human moment that has tension in it. That's the rule I'd give anyone, and it comes in a few forms. Each one has a person, a place and something unresolved, and none of them requires a big budget.

1. Start in the middle of something

Open with a person already doing the thing, not introducing it. A signwriter loading a brush. A cheesemonger cutting into a wheel. A mechanic with the bonnet up and a worried customer beside him. You haven't explained anything, and that's the point. A viewer who sees action wants to know what's going on, and curiosity does the work for you. It's the documentary instinct: show the scene first, give the context after.

2. Start with the problem your customer actually has

Not "we offer a full range of services", but the sentence they'd say to a friend. "I'd been putting off sorting the website for two years." "We'd had three quotes and none of them made sense." If your opening line is something your customer has genuinely said, they'll recognise themselves in it straight away. This is the quickest way to make a stranger feel understood.

3. Start with a small, odd, true detail

The wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed. A market stall at Camden Lock. An eighty pound a week shop in Highbury. These come from the La Fromagerie story, and they're better openings than any mission statement because they're specific and slightly surprising. A true oddity makes people curious and also makes them trust you, since you couldn't have made it up.

4. Start with a question your audience is already asking

A good one is honest and narrow, such as "What does a hand-made shoe cost, and why?". It works because the viewer has probably wondered, and you're about to answer it. A weak one is a rhetorical flourish that only exists to sound like an opening. If the question isn't one a real customer has typed into Google, drop it.

5. Start with the end, then rewind

Show the result first: the finished house, the first customer through the door, the signed contract. Then go back and show how it happened. This works when the outcome is striking and the journey is what you want to talk about. It's a standard documentary move, and it keeps people watching for the how.

Open on the person, not the organisation. The company can introduce itself once someone cares.

What should a brand story never open with?

A few openings are so common they've become invisible. If your first line is one of these, your story has already started on the back foot.

  • "Founded in 1998..." A date is a fact, not a hook. If the date matters, put it in the third paragraph, after something has happened.
  • "At [Company], we're passionate about..." Everyone's passionate. It tells the reader nothing.
  • The logo sting. Five seconds of animated logo at the front of a film is five seconds in which viewers can leave.
  • The drone shot with swelling music. It looks expensive and says nothing. If it doesn't serve the story, it goes.
  • The list of services. That belongs on a services page, where someone is looking for it.
  • "In an increasingly crowded market..." Any opening that could be stuck on the front of a hundred other businesses' pages.

The common thread is that they all put the company first. The test is simple: could this opening belong to a competitor with the name swapped? If so, it's not a beginning, it's a placeholder.

If your film opens on a drone shot of your own building, the building is the main character. It's rarely a good actor.

How does this change for different formats?

On a website

The top of your About page or homepage is your first line. Resist the mission statement. Open on the customer's situation or on a small true moment from your own story, and leave the credentials for later. Visitors scroll quickly, so the first screen has to give them a reason to scroll again.

In a film

The first ten seconds decide most of the drop-off. Cold open on a person speaking, or on the work happening, and bring in titles and the logo afterwards. For a documentary-style brand film, I like to start on the most human sentence in the interview, the one where the person says something unguarded, and then build the context around it. That's an edit decision, which is another reason to film more than you think you need. If you want to see how a good opening sits within a whole film, how to make a brand video people watch covers the rest of it.

In a sales conversation

Your first thirty seconds with a prospect are a story opening too. "We're a London-based agency that..." is the logo sting of speech. Try opening with a customer situation you recognise from their business, and let them say, "Yes, that's us."

On social

The opening is the first line of the caption and the first frame of the clip, and both have to earn the next second. Start mid-action, put a plain-spoken line on screen, and don't wait for the point. Social is where the principle is most ruthless.

Can you try this on your own About page?

Yes, and it takes about ten minutes. Here's a quick exercise I'd suggest.

  1. Read the first sentence of your About page. Does it mention a person, a place or a moment? If it names only the company, that's your problem.
  2. Ask the founder or the longest-serving person: "What was the moment you knew this was going to be a business?" Write down their answer exactly, without tidying it.
  3. Look for the line with the most surprise or specificity in it. It's usually not the first thing they said.
  4. Put that line at the top. Keep the company name out of the first paragraph if you can.
  5. Read the rest and cut anything that explains rather than shows.

The before and after is often startling. "We are a family-run heating company established in 2004" becomes "Our first van had no heating. Dad fixed everyone else's boilers while we drove round in our coats." The second is a story. It tells you more about the business than the first, and nobody could have copied it.

Who should the opening be about?

The question I get most from founders is whether the story should open on them. My answer is: only if you're the most useful way into the customer's problem. Often you aren't. Often it's the customer, or a member of your team, or a place.

The reason is simple. A viewer identifies with someone in a situation they recognise. If you're a plumber, the useful opening isn't your apprenticeship, it's a homeowner standing in a kitchen with water coming through the ceiling. If you run a care service, it's the daughter who's just realised her mother can't manage alone. They're moments the viewer has lived or dreads, and your business becomes the answer to a feeling they already have.

That said, the founder can be a brilliant opening when their moment is also the customer's. The tradesperson who started the company after a bad experience as a customer himself has a beginning that does both jobs. Ask yourself whose moment the audience will feel more, and open there.

And be careful with testimonials as openings. A customer saying "they were brilliant" is praise, not a moment. A customer describing what the house looked like the day before the work started is a moment. Ask for the second one, and expect to have to prompt it with a question or two. It's what interview technique is for, and it's why we spend more time on the questions than on the kit.

What if your story doesn't have a dramatic beginning?

Most don't, and that's fine. You're not looking for drama, you're looking for something true and particular. A craftsperson's first bad piece. The day the first customer rang. The customer who almost didn't call. Real stories usually begin small, and small is more believable than an invented epic.

One thing worth knowing from filming: the person who thinks their story is boring usually has the best material, because they haven't polished it. We filmed a trade where the business was built on hand work, a signwriter whose entire craft is the wrist, in the Signwriting Jack film. The film works because it's built around the work, at the speed it's done, and trusts it. You can do the same with whatever your business does best.

If you want to see how an opening fits into a bigger story, how to tell a brand story takes it from first line to last, and what makes a good brand story explains why some work and others don't. The whole subject is gathered in the complete guide to brand storytelling. If you'd like help finding your own opening, and filming it, have a look at our films or get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How should a brand story begin?
faqs.a: With a specific person in a specific moment where something is at stake, usually your customer, rather than with your company's history or mission. A strong opening puts the viewer in the middle of something, names a real problem, or offers a small, true, surprising detail. Once they care about the person, they'll care about the brand that helps them.

faqs.q: Should a brand story start with the founder?
faqs.a: Only if the founder's moment is the most interesting thing you have. Starting with their title or biography rarely works. Starting with a real incident, like the day the business nearly failed or the first customer called, can work well. The test is whether a stranger would want to hear what happens next, not whether it's important to you.

faqs.q: How long should the opening of a brand film be?
faqs.a: Short. The first five to ten seconds decide most of the drop-off, so get to a person and a reason to watch immediately. Skip long logo animations and slow drone shots, and bring titles in afterwards. Open on the most human line in your interview or on the work happening, then build the context around it.

faqs.q: What's the worst way to start a brand story?
faqs.a: With a date, a claim of passion or a list of services. Lines like 'Founded in 1998' or 'We're passionate about quality' are interchangeable with any competitor's, so they tell the reader nothing. The giveaway is that you could swap the company name and nobody would notice. Open on something only your business could say.

items.title: What is Nike's brand story? How it was built
items.excerpt: How Nike's brand story was built, from a car boot in 1964 to Just Do It, what the story gets right, and what a smaller UK business can honestly borrow from it.
items.coverAlt: A boxer shadow boxes with taped white hands in a dim gym with a ring and punch bags in the background
items.body:
Nike's brand story is that sport belongs to everyone, and that effort is the thing worth celebrating. It began in 1964 with a runner, Phil Knight, and his Oregon coach, Bill Bowerman, selling shoes out of a car at track meets. Over decades it grew into a story about the athlete inside anyone who's willing to try, summed up in "Just Do It".

This post walks through how that story was built, from the founders to the slogan to the 2018 campaign that split opinion, and then asks the useful question for anyone running a smaller business: what can you actually borrow from it? For other brands and their stories, there's a wider list in which brands use storytelling, and some worked examples in what a brand story example looks like.

How did Nike start?

The origin is the first half of the brand story, and it's a good one because it's true and a bit scrappy. Phil Knight ran middle distance at the University of Oregon under Bill Bowerman. After business school he and Bowerman founded Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964 to import running shoes from Japan, selling them at track meets from the back of Knight's car. Nothing about it looked like a future global brand. It was two men who cared about runners and thought the shoes could be better.

That's the foundation of everything that follows. The company didn't start from a marketing idea. It started from people in sport solving problems for people in sport. Bowerman tinkered with shoes constantly, and the most repeated tale is that he poured rubber into his wife's waffle iron to make a lighter sole with better grip. It became the waffle sole in the early 1970s. Whether or not every detail is polished by retelling, it works as story because it's concrete: a coach, a kitchen, a gadget, a better shoe.

By 1971 the company had a name and a logo. Nike is the Greek goddess of victory. The Swoosh was drawn by Carolyn Davidson, a graphic design student at Portland State, who was paid $35 for it. Knight's reported first reaction was a lukewarm "I don't love it, but maybe it will grow on me". The story of the logo has been told so often precisely because it's the opposite of the corporate branding exercise: a student, a small fee, a shrug.

What is Nike's brand story today?

The company states its mission as bringing inspiration and innovation to every athlete in the world, with a footnote that has become the most important line in the whole story: "If you have a body, you are an athlete." The line is attributed to Bowerman. It does two things at once. It keeps the founding link to sport and performance, and it widens the idea of "athlete" to include every customer.

That widening is the clever bit. The brand isn't selling to elite runners only. It's telling someone jogging round the park, or trying a first gym class, that they belong in the same story as the people on the podium. The hero isn't Nike, and it isn't even the famous athlete. It's the person pulling their trainers on.

Nike's story isn't about shoes. It's about what you're willing to do in them.

It's worth separating the pieces, because they do different jobs:

  • The origin (runners helping runners) gives it credibility.
  • The mission (every athlete, and everybody is one) gives it breadth.
  • The slogan (Just Do It) gives it a single instruction to remember.
  • The athletes (from Michael Jordan to Serena Williams and others) give it faces and proof.

Where did "Just Do It" come from?

The slogan came out of the agency Wieden+Kennedy in 1988, working with Nike. Nike's sales weren't as strong as they wanted in the late 1980s, partly because aerobics and fitness had pushed Reebok ahead in the US. The brand needed something that spoke to a wider public than serious sport. Dan Wieden, the agency's co-founder, is generally credited with the line.

What's smart about it is how little it says. "Just Do It" is an instruction anyone can apply to anything: starting a run, quitting a job, getting off the sofa. It doesn't mention shoes. It offers no features. It leaves a gap that the customer fills with their own situation, which is the reason it has lasted decades.

Notice that this is also a story-telling technique in miniature. The campaign didn't tell people what Nike made. It showed people, often ordinary and older athletes as well as stars, doing the hard thing, and left the logo to appear at the end. If you want to see how that restraint works on a small scale, I've talked about it in how brand storytelling should begin.

How does Nike use athletes to tell the story?

Athletes are the characters. Michael Jordan signed in 1984 and the Air Jordan line launched the following year, turning a single player into a whole sub-brand. Later campaigns have put Serena Williams, Eliud Kipchoge and many others at the centre, and increasingly the people on screen are ordinary runners and young players, not just champions.

Look at what the films tend to show: the training, the failure, the early mornings, the doubt. Nike's strongest work lingers on the effort rather than the trophy. That's the same instinct as good documentary. The interesting part of a story is usually the struggle before the result, and that's why the brand comes across as being on the athlete's side.

It's the same idea we use in our own work with athletes. Look at the content we made with boxer Isaac Chamberlain in the Boxraw training sessions, or the seminar film at London Fight Factory. The training and the process are the story. Nobody needs a slogan when you can see the person doing the work.

Nike's budget is not the lesson. The lesson is that they filmed the sweaty bit.

What happened with the Colin Kaepernick campaign?

In September 2018 Nike made Colin Kaepernick, the American football quarterback who'd knelt during the national anthem to protest racial injustice, the face of its thirtieth anniversary Just Do It campaign. The line was "Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything." It divided people sharply, some of them burning their shoes online, and it also brought considerable attention.

I mention it for one reason: it shows a brand story being tested under pressure. A story that only works when everyone agrees isn't much of a position. Nike chose to say something, accepted that some customers would object, and stuck with it. You don't have to agree with the stance, or with Nike, to see that a story needs a point of view to carry weight.

It's also worth being honest that Nike's story hasn't gone unchallenged. The company faced serious scrutiny over factory conditions in its supply chain in the 1990s and has had to answer to that publicly since. A brand story is tested by the business behind it, and that's true at every size.

Why has Nike's story lasted so long?

Consistency, mostly, and a story that was always bigger than the product. Shoes change every season. Fashions come and go. A belief like "everyone's an athlete" doesn't date, so each new campaign, whatever the athlete or the year, adds to the same story instead of replacing it.

It's also flexible in a way most brand stories aren't. The same idea can sit behind a marathon runner, a teenager playing football on a car park or a school PE lesson. That flexibility comes from the brand story being about a feeling and a belief rather than a product category. If you can state yours in a way that stretches across everything you do, you've got something that will last.

And it has a tone. Nike is direct, confident and slightly impatient, which suits the subject. You hear it in the copy, see it in the cutting and feel it in how athletes are filmed. A brand story is as much how it's told as what it says, which is why two companies with similar histories can feel completely different. I'd encourage anyone writing their own to read it aloud. If it sounds like a person you'd want to meet, you're close.

The cost of that discipline is saying no. Any brand that holds one belief for decades has to turn down ideas that are perfectly good but don't fit it. Smaller businesses find this the hardest part, because every opportunity feels precious. A story gets stronger the more often you decline things that don't belong in it.

Does a famous brand story guarantee business results?

No, and the numbers say so. Nike's revenue for fiscal 2025 was $46.3 billion, down 10 percent from $51.4 billion the year before, according to the company's own results. One of the most recognised brand stories in the world still saw sales fall, because stories don't replace good products, pricing, distribution and timing. They make you easier to choose and harder to forget, but they don't excuse everything else.

That matters for smaller businesses, because it's tempting to treat a brand story as the answer to a sales problem. It's one part of the answer. I'd always rather say that honestly than promise a result I can't guarantee.

What can a smaller brand learn from Nike's story?

You don't have Nike's money, but you don't need it for the lessons that matter.

Start with the true beginning

Nike's early years are interesting because they're ordinary and specific: a car boot, a waffle iron, a $35 logo. Most businesses have something comparable. The founding detail you're slightly embarrassed by is often the best part. I make the same point in how to write a brand story.

Make the customer the hero

Nike doesn't say it's great. It says you could be. For a plumber, a physio or a food business, the same move applies: tell the story of the person you help and what changes for them, with your business as the guide.

Show the effort

People trust visible work. Whether it's a shoemaker's 210 steps, a signwriter's brush or a coach in a gym, the process is a story most customers never get to see. Film it. A documentary approach is built for this.

Have a line people can repeat

Not a slogan for the sake of it, but a short statement of what you believe that your team and customers can say back. If it's only on a wall, it's decoration.

Match the story to the behaviour

The strongest brand stories are ones the business can keep. Promise less and deliver it all the way down the chain, because that's where stories get tested.

For the principles behind these points, what makes a good brand story goes through them in order, and the complete guide to brand storytelling puts the whole subject in one place. If you'd like a story of your own told on film, have a look at our films and get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is Nike's brand story in simple terms?
faqs.a: Nike's brand story is that sport is for everyone and effort is worth celebrating. It started with a coach and a runner in Oregon in 1964, and it grew into a message that anyone with a body is an athlete. Just Do It, launched in 1988, turns that into a single instruction. The hero of the story is the customer rather than the company.

faqs.q: Who created Nike's Just Do It slogan?
faqs.a: The slogan came from the advertising agency Wieden+Kennedy in 1988, and co-founder Dan Wieden is generally credited with the line. It was created to speak to a broader audience than serious sport. Its power comes from how little it says: it gives an instruction anyone can apply to their own situation, without mentioning a single product feature.

faqs.q: Why does Nike's storytelling work so well?
faqs.a: It uses a true origin, a clear belief and real athletes as characters. The films show effort, doubt and training rather than only wins, which feels honest. The customer is invited into the story as the hero. It also holds a consistent point of view over decades, so every campaign feels like it comes from the same place.

faqs.q: Can a small business tell a story like Nike's?
faqs.a: Yes, in scale if not in budget. The ingredients are a true beginning, a belief you can state in a sentence, and the customer as the hero. A short documentary-style film that shows your real people and how the work is done does the same job. You don't need a global campaign, just a story that's honest and consistent.

stat.title: NIKE, Inc. full-year revenues
stat.takeaway: Even one of the strongest brand stories in the world doesn't make sales automatic, so a story works best alongside a good product, price and service.

source.name: NIKE, Inc., Fiscal 2025 fourth quarter and full year results (SEC filing)

items.title: Colour grading explained: how films get their mood
items.excerpt: What colour grading is, how it differs from correction, what LUTs do, and how The Matrix, O Brother and Fury Road use colour to tell the story.
items.coverAlt: A black and white frame of boxers training on the bags
items.body:
Colour grading is the stage at the end of the edit where the colour, contrast and brightness of every shot are set, so the film looks the way it's meant to feel. It's how a director makes one world feel sickly and another feel cold, or makes a summer field look like an old postcard. Done well, you never notice it. You just feel it.

I covered the basics briefly in what cinematography means. This goes further: what a grade is actually doing, why it isn't the same as fixing the colour, and a few famous films where the colour was doing a lot more of the storytelling than most people realise.

What's the difference between colour correction and colour grading?

Correction is technical. Grading is creative. They happen in that order, and people mix the two words up all the time.

Correction makes the footage accurate and consistent. White balance so a white wall reads white. Exposure evened out so one shot isn't a stop darker than the next. Two cameras matched so a cut between them doesn't jump. The aim is a neutral, honest starting point where every shot in a scene looks like it was filmed in the same place at the same time.

Grading is what you do with that neutral image. Pushing the shadows cooler, warming the highlights, pulling saturation out of everything except one colour, crushing the blacks or lifting them so the image goes soft and milky.

On a documentary shoot you can't control most of what's in front of you, so correction does a lot of heavy lifting. A morning interview by a window and an afternoon shot under strip lights need to sit next to each other without the viewer feeling the join. There's more on why mixed light causes so much trouble in interview lighting explained simply.

How does colour create mood?

Mostly through association. We've spent our whole lives seeing warm light at sunset, by a fire, in a kitchen at night. Cool, blue light is overcast mornings, hospitals and the hour before dawn. A grade borrows those associations and points them at a scene.

A few of the levers a colourist actually pulls:

  • Temperature. Warmer reads as comfortable, nostalgic or intimate. Cooler reads as detached, clinical or lonely.
  • Saturation. Rich colour feels alive and heightened. Muted colour feels serious, tired or documentary-real.
  • Contrast. Deep blacks and bright highlights feel punchy and dramatic. Lower contrast feels gentle and soft.
  • Separation. Different colours in the shadows and the highlights, which is where most stylised looks live.

None of these mean anything on their own. Cool and desaturated can feel calm in one film and grim in another. The grade only works when it agrees with what the story's already saying.

Why is The Matrix green?

Because the computers made it. The Matrix is probably the best-known example of colour being used as a map. Scenes inside the simulation carry a green tint. Scenes in the real world, aboard the ship and in the ruins, are cool and blue, with almost no green in them at all.

The film's cinematographer, Bill Pope, explained the thinking in an interview for the film's official website. The Matrix is a decaying world created by machines, so it got a green hue, and it was meant to make you feel slightly sick. The real world got a colder, bluer look, because in that future the sun's been blotted out and there's no natural warmth left.

Once you've noticed it, you always know where you are.

What is the teal and orange look?

It's the look of a huge number of action films from the 2000s onwards: skin pushed warm towards orange, and shadows, skies and backgrounds pushed cool towards teal. Watch almost any big blockbuster trailer and you'll see it.

It caught on for a sound reason. Orange and teal sit roughly opposite each other on the colour wheel, so they contrast strongly, and most skin tones fall in the orange range. As Adobe's guide to the look puts it, pushing blues into the shadows helps those skin tones stand out. It also mimics golden hour, warm sun on a face against a blue sky, which people already find beautiful.

The trouble is that it got used everywhere, whether the story asked for it or not. When every film has the same look, the look stops meaning anything, and it starts to feel like a preset rather than a decision.

Which other films use colour to tell the story?

O Brother, Where Art Thou?

The Coen brothers wanted a dry, dusty, faded postcard look. The problem was that they were shooting in Mississippi in summer, where everything was lush and green. Roger Deakins, the cinematographer, told Filmmaker Magazine that they didn't want anything to be green, and couldn't find a way to turn the greens into browns and yellows with traditional film processing. So they scanned the film and graded it digitally. It's widely credited as the first Hollywood feature to be colour graded digitally from start to finish, which makes it a quiet turning point.

Mad Max: Fury Road

Fury Road went the opposite way to most post-apocalyptic films. Its colourist, Eric Whipp, told FilmLight that George Miller had noticed thirty years of the genre using the same desaturated, bleached look, and was adamant this one should be saturated, sharp and graphic. Whipp built rich skies against warm sand and characters, and the night scenes were shot in bright sun, then darkened and pushed blue in the grade. He worked on it for about a year.

The official trailer above shows that saturated orange and blue at full volume. Miller has since said he thinks the black and white version, released as the Black & Chrome edition, is the best version of the film, as /Film reported. Same footage, completely different grade, and the director's favourite.

Same footage, completely different grade, and a different film.

What is a LUT, and is it the same as a grade?

A LUT, short for look-up table, is a file that maps one set of colours to another. Feed it a pixel of one colour and it hands back a different one. That's all it is.

There are two kinds worth knowing about. A technical LUT converts footage from one colour space to another, most often turning the flat, grey log footage a cinema camera records into a normal-looking image. A creative LUT applies a look, like a filter on your phone.

Treat a LUT as a starting point. It treats every shot exactly the same way, and no two shots are exactly the same. A look built for a bright exterior can turn a dim interior muddy and push skin somewhere strange. A proper grade still goes shot by shot, adjusting each one so the look holds across the whole film.

Half the LUT packs online promise a Hollywood look. The other half promise a vintage film look. Very few of them promise your skin will still look like skin.

Why do skin tones matter so much in a grade?

Because people notice faces before anything else, and they're very good at knowing when one looks wrong. A wall can go teal and nobody minds. A face goes grey, green or orange and the viewer feels something's off straight away, even if they can't say what.

Colourists usually protect skin first, isolating it so it stays natural while the rest of the image is pushed around it. There's a scope for this called a vectorscope, which has a line marking roughly where healthy skin of every complexion tends to sit. The real skill is lighting and grading darker and lighter skin in the same frame so both look right, which was handled badly for a long time and still is on plenty of corporate video.

What does grading mean for a brand film?

Most brand films don't need a dramatic look. They need to look like the place on a good day and to feel consistent from start to finish. A workshop should feel warm and lived in, a shop should look like the shop, and the founder should look like themselves. If the grade gets noticed, it's probably gone too far.

Where it does earn its keep is in mood and in continuity. A documentary is shot over different days, rooms and weather, and the grade is what makes it feel like one film. It can also carry a story, the way The Matrix does.

On our films the grade is done by a specialist colourist, after the edit is locked, because it's one of the clearest differences between a film that looks expensive and one that looks like a video. You can see how that fits into the rest of the process on the films page, and if you're working out what a film should cost, the film budget calculator is a decent place to start.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long does colour grading take?
faqs.a: It depends on the length of the film and how stylised the look is. A short brand film might take a day or two of a colourist's time, while a feature can take weeks. Most of the time goes on matching shots and adjusting skin, not on building the look itself. Documentary footage shot across different rooms and days usually needs more matching than something filmed in one controlled space.

faqs.q: Can grading fix footage that was badly shot?
faqs.a: Only partly. A grade can rescue white balance, lift a slightly dark shot and match cameras, but it can't add detail that was never recorded. Blown out windows stay blown out, and heavily underexposed shots get noisy when they're brightened. Log footage gives the colourist more room to work, but the best grades start from footage that was lit and exposed properly on the day.

faqs.q: What software do colourists use?
faqs.a: DaVinci Resolve is the most widely used grading software, from freelancers up to feature films, and it has a capable free version. Baselight, made by FilmLight, is common on high-end features and television. Most editing software, including Premiere Pro and Final Cut, has colour tools too, which are fine for correction and simple looks but less suited to detailed shot by shot work.

faqs.q: Should our brand film have a distinctive colour look?
faqs.a: Only if the story calls for it. Most brand films are better served by a natural, consistent grade that makes your place and people look their best on a good day. A strong stylised look can date quickly and can make real people look less real. If there's a reason for it, like a change in time or mood across the film, a deliberate look can help tell the story.

items.title: What is a brand story example? Five worked examples
items.excerpt: Worked brand story examples from Dove, Hovis, Patagonia, John Lewis and Airbnb, plus a small London business, and what they share that you can use.
items.coverAlt: A couple on a grey sofa look wide-eyed off camera while being interviewed in their renovated living room
items.body:
A good brand story example is Dove's Real Beauty Sketches: a forensic artist drew women twice, once from their own description and once from a stranger's, and the gap between the two drawings made the point about self-image without a single product claim. Hovis, Patagonia and John Lewis tell stories in different ways, and a small London cheese business can do it too.

This post is a set of worked examples, picked apart so you can see what each one actually does. I'll go through five from the wider world, one from our own work, and then pull out the pattern they share. I'm not covering how to write your own, which is in how to write a brand story, or Nike, which gets its own post in what Nike's brand story is.

What counts as a brand story example?

Anything where a brand tells you who it is by showing something happen, rather than listing what it sells. It might be a film, an advert, a page on a website, a founder's talk or a product launch. What makes it a story rather than a slogan is that there's a person, a tension and a change, even if the whole thing lasts ninety seconds.

A quick test I use: could you retell it to a friend at the pub without looking anything up? If you can, it's a story. If all you remember is the logo, it was an advert. The examples below pass that test, which is why they're still talked about years later.

Which brand story examples are worth studying?

Dove: Real Beauty Sketches (2013)

Dove had been running its Real Beauty campaign since 2004. In 2013 it made a film with Ogilvy Brazil in which a forensic sketch artist, Gil Zamora, drew each woman twice. First from how she described herself without being seen, then from how someone else, who'd just met her, described her. The two portraits hung side by side. The stranger's version was kinder, and more accurate.

Why it works: the product is never mentioned until the end card, and the story belongs entirely to the women. The idea does the persuading. It won the Titanium Grand Prix at Cannes Lions that year, and Guinness World Records verified it as the most viewed online video advert at the time, with 124.9 million views by November 2013.

The lesson for a smaller brand isn't to hire a forensic artist. It's that the strongest stories are built around a human truth your customers already feel, with the brand as the one who noticed it.

Hovis: Boy on the Bike (1973)

A boy pushes a loaf of bread uphill on an old-fashioned bike, delivers it, and freewheels back down a cobbled hill to the sound of Dvořák's New World Symphony. Ridley Scott directed it, in Shaftesbury in Dorset. It's a British classic, and I'd argue it's still one of the best brand story examples because it sells an emotion, wholesome and traditional, rather than a loaf.

Why it works: it's one scene, one character, and a place. It takes a plain product and ties it to a feeling people already have about Britain's past. A caution, though. That kind of nostalgia only works if it's true to the brand, which is why it's tricky to copy.

Patagonia: Don't Buy This Jacket (2011)

On Black Friday 2011, Patagonia ran a full-page ad in the New York Times with a picture of one of its fleeces and the words "Don't Buy This Jacket". The text explained the environmental cost of making it and asked customers to think before buying. A brand telling people to buy less sounds like a joke, but it was consistent with a story the company had been telling since its founding by Yvon Chouinard, and later it was backed up in 2022 when ownership passed to a trust and a non-profit to protect the planet.

Why it works: the story isn't a campaign, it's the behaviour. The advert was believable because the company had already acted that way for years. If a brand story doesn't match what the business does, people spot the gap fast.

John Lewis: the Christmas films

Every year the department store releases a Christmas film that gets talked about in the pub and written about in the papers. In 2014 it was Monty the Penguin, a boy's lonely imaginary friend who gets a companion on Christmas morning. The product is a toy penguin in the shops. The story is about giving.

Why it works: it's a short film with one emotional beat, made for the moment people are thinking about presents. It turns an annual retail event into something people look forward to, which is the real prize.

The best brand stories are about the customer's life, with the brand turning up as a helpful extra.

Airbnb and the host stories

Airbnb has built much of its marketing around real hosts and guests telling what happened: the person who rents out a spare room and ends up making a friend, the family who travel to meet relatives. These are small and specific, and the brand barely appears. They show what the platform is for.

Why it works: it uses real people rather than actors, in their own words, and the stories are different enough to feel true. That's a useful pointer for any business that has customers worth hearing from.

What does a brand story example look like for a small business?

Most of the famous examples come with enormous budgets, which makes them look out of reach. They're not the only model. Some of the best brand stories I've seen are small, local and shot on a couple of days.

Take La Fromagerie, the London cheese business. The story is a real one: it started with a market stall at Camden Lock and a shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week, and thirty three years later it's three shops with walk-in cheese rooms and a wholesale side supplying restaurants across London. The founder tells it, and the cheesemongers and the wholesale team fill in what the business is now. We filmed it during trading hours, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark.

Look at what it has in common with the big names. There's a person. There's a beginning that's small and a bit unlikely. There's a change over time. And there's nothing invented. The reason it works as a brand story is that someone who watches it knows what it would be like to walk into that shop and talk to those people.

A craft example is Carreducker, two shoemakers at the Oxo Tower who trained at John Lobb. The story sits in the numbers they've always been open about: 210 steps, six months a pair. And the film we made for Signwriting Jack is built around the hand, the brush loading, a single unbroken line. Neither needs a voiceover telling you the brand is passionate. You can see it.

Nobody has ever watched a brand film and thought, "that's convinced me, they said 'passionate' four times."

What do these brand story examples have in common?

Put them side by side and the same handful of things keeps turning up. This is the pattern, and it's more useful than any single example.

  • A real person or a real place. Nobody's moved by a company. They're moved by a boy on a bike, a woman describing her face, a founder in a shed.
  • A tension. Something is at stake or something is wrong: self-image, a hill, a lonely penguin, a planet. Without it you've got a brochure.
  • The product comes last. In nearly all of them the thing being sold barely appears, or appears at the end.
  • It matches the business. Patagonia could tell its story because it behaves that way. The ones that fail are the ones where the story and the company don't line up.
  • It's specific. Eighty pounds a week. 210 steps. A wheel of Beaufort. Specific details make a story believable and make it stick.

If you're wondering how this fits into the wider picture, the examples sit at the "what does good look like" end of the subject. The principles behind them are in what makes a good brand story, and there are more brands to look at in which brands use storytelling.

What can you take from these examples without a big budget?

Three things, in order.

First, find the true beginning. Most businesses have one that's more interesting than their "About us" suggests: the first customer, the odd decision, the thing that nearly didn't happen. Ask the founder how it started and write down what they say before they tidy it up.

Second, put a real person on camera. Documentary-style film exists for exactly this. You don't script it, you ask good questions and keep the answers that sound like a human being. I've written about how that differs from a corporate video, and there's a longer look at one project in the La Fromagerie film.

Third, leave things out. A good story is mostly editing. Strip out the awards, the list of services and the mission statement. Keep the part somebody would retell.

What does a weak brand story example look like?

It helps to know the failures too, because you'll see far more of them. The commonest is the founder's-vision page: "Our passion for excellence began in 2009, and we've been delivering innovative solutions ever since." Nothing happens in it. There's no person, no moment and no detail you could repeat. It's a CV for a company.

The second is the story that doesn't match the business. A brand that talks about care and then takes three weeks to answer an email has told a story the customer can disprove in a day. The third is the borrowed story, a copy of something that worked for somebody else, with the names swapped. On shoots I often meet a founder who's worried their own story is too ordinary. It almost never is. The ordinary details, the first shop, the rent, the person who helped, are exactly what a viewer finds believable.

So when you look at any brand story example, ask what's real in it, what's specific, and what you could still repeat a week later. If the answer is "not much", it's an advert dressed up as a story.

What's the difference between a brand story example and a brand story?

An example is a finished piece someone else made. Your own brand story is the raw material those pieces are built from: a short statement of where you came from, what you're for and who you help. Studying examples is useful for taste, but copying one is a mistake. Dove's idea works because it's Dove's. Yours has to come from the facts of your own business.

When you're ready to build yours, the complete guide to brand storytelling sets the whole subject out in order, and what a brand story looks like covers the written version on a website. If a film would carry your own story best, take a look at our films and get in touch when you want to talk it over.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the best example of a brand story?
faqs.a: There's no single best, but Dove's Real Beauty Sketches is one of the clearest. It tells a human story, women seeing themselves more kindly through a stranger's eyes, and the product barely appears. Patagonia's Don't Buy This Jacket is another, because the story matches the company's behaviour. The best example for you is the one closest to your own audience and facts.

faqs.q: Can a small business have a brand story as strong as a big brand's?
faqs.a: Yes, and often a more believable one. Small businesses have real founders, real origins and real customers within reach, which is exactly what stories need. The big brands spend on production. You don't need their budget to tell a true, specific story well, and a short documentary-style film shot on location can carry it.

faqs.q: What makes a brand story example memorable?
faqs.a: A real person or place, a tension that creates interest, and specific detail. The product usually comes last, and the story matches how the business actually behaves. Think of a boy pushing a loaf up a hill, or a founder starting with a wheel of cheese in a shed. People retell stories like that. They don't retell slogans or lists of services.

faqs.q: Should I copy a famous brand story for my own business?
faqs.a: No. Copying a format is fine for inspiration, but the story itself has to come from your own business. Dove's idea works because it fits Dove, and Patagonia's works because of how Patagonia operates. Borrow the structure of a person, a tension and a change, then fill it with your own facts. Anything else tends to sound borrowed, because it is.

items.title: What is brand storytelling in marketing? A practical guide
items.excerpt: How brand storytelling works in marketing: where it sits in the mix, what it does at each stage of the customer journey, and how a small UK firm can measure it.
items.coverAlt: A homeowner in a green sweatshirt sits on a sofa and explains his renovation with open hands, a lamp glowing behind him
items.body:
Brand storytelling in marketing means using real narrative, people, a problem and a change, as the thread running through your marketing, so customers remember who you are and why you exist instead of just reading a list of features. It's less a single campaign and more a way of deciding what goes on your website, in your sales calls, on social and in your films.

This post is about the marketing side of it: where storytelling sits in the mix, what job it does at each stage of a customer's decision, which channels carry it, and how a small UK business can tell whether it's working. If you want the plain definition first, start with what brand storytelling is. Everything below assumes you've got that and want to know what to do with it.

How is brand storytelling different from advertising and content marketing?

Advertising buys attention. Content marketing earns it by being useful. Brand storytelling is the thing underneath both that decides what they say. You can run a paid ad with a story in it, or a blog post with none. The story is the point of view that makes your advertising sound like it came from one place rather than from whichever freelancer wrote the last batch.

I find it helps to think of three layers. At the top there's the campaign, which comes and goes. In the middle there's content, which keeps the shelves stocked. At the bottom there's the story, which is slow to change and decides how the other two layers sound. A business with strong campaigns and no story ends up with a lot of good-looking one-offs that don't add up to anyone remembering it.

That's also why storytelling in marketing isn't the same as a brand story. A brand story is a document, usually a page on your site. Storytelling in marketing is what you do with it every week. I've covered the page itself in what a brand story should include, and whether the approach counts as a proper strategy in is storytelling a marketing strategy.

Why does marketing need stories at all?

Because attention is the scarce thing, and everyone is paying for it. The Advertising Association and WARC put UK advertising investment at £11.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026, up 9.3% on a year earlier, with social media spend up 17.7%. When that much money is chasing the same few seconds of someone's eye, what you say once you've got it is what counts.

A feature list loses that contest almost every time. A person doing something interesting, with something at stake, wins it more often. That's not a mystical claim about the human brain, it's just what happens on a shoot when we play back a rough cut to the client: they sit forward when a human being starts talking about why they do the work, and they reach for their phone during the spec section.

The deeper reason it works, and I'd rather not oversell this, is that stories are how people explain things to each other. When a customer recommends you to a friend, they don't recite your service list. They tell a bit of a story: "they came out the same week, the bloke explained it all, and he was honest about the price." Brand storytelling in marketing is the act of giving them a better story to pass on. I go into the mechanics in why storytelling works in marketing.

What job does storytelling do at each stage of the customer journey?

This is the part most guides skip. Stories aren't only for the top of the funnel. They do a different job at each stage, and it helps to know which one you're asking of a given piece.

Awareness: being worth remembering

At the first meeting, nobody cares about your company. The job here is to be interesting enough that they'd recognise you next time. A short, human film or a sharp piece of social content about the people behind the business does this far better than a logo and a tagline. You're not trying to sell. You're trying to leave a trace.

Consideration: showing how you think

When someone's comparing three suppliers who all look much the same, the story is what separates them. This is where the longer pieces earn their keep: the founder talking honestly about why the business started, a customer describing what changed, a look at how the work is done. It's the stage where a documentary-style film does its best work, because it answers the question buyers can't ask out loud: "Are these people the real thing?"

Decision: lowering the risk

Late in the process, buyers aren't looking for excitement. They want to feel safe. Customer stories, case studies and testimonials that sound like a person rather than a press release do the job here. They show the outcome and the manner of working together, which is what someone worried about being let down wants to see.

After the sale: giving people something to repeat

Existing customers are the most overlooked audience in marketing. A story they recognise themselves in gets forwarded, referenced in meetings and used by your own team when they onboard someone new. Retention and referral are quiet storytelling jobs.

The story isn't the campaign. It's the reason every campaign sounds like it came from the same people.

Which marketing channels carry a brand story?

All of them, which is exactly the problem. If the story lives only on the About page, it's not doing marketing work. A few places it needs to show up:

  • Your website. The homepage headline, the About page, the case studies. Visitors decide in seconds whether you sound like a real business with a point of view.
  • Video. The strongest carrier, because people can see and hear the person. A single documentary-style film can sit at the top of the site and be cut into shorter pieces for social. I've written about how to turn one brand film into a year of content.
  • Social media. Not a different story, but a different dose. Small fragments of the same one, posted consistently. More in storytelling in social media marketing.
  • Sales conversations. The founder or salesperson who can tell the origin and a customer outcome in two minutes beats the one reading from a deck. This is storytelling too, and it costs nothing but preparation.
  • Email and PR. Newsletters that tell what happened this month rather than what's on offer, and press pitches that lead with a human angle.
  • Recruitment. Your story is half of your employer brand. Candidates check. See recruitment and employer brand videos.

The consistency matters more than the volume. I'd take one clear story told in five places over five different stories told everywhere.

What does brand storytelling in marketing actually look like in practice?

It looks less grand than the famous examples suggest. Take a small London food business. The marketing-friendly version of its story is "premium, artisan, passionate about quality". The storytelling version is the founder explaining how it began with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, then a market stall at Camden Lock, then a shop in Highbury. That's what we filmed for La Fromagerie, and the point is that the facts did the work. Nothing was dressed up.

Or take a craft business like Carreducker, where two makers who trained at John Lobb now run their own bench at the Oxo Tower. The story isn't "bespoke shoes". It's two people who finish each other's sentences describing 210 steps and six months a pair. The marketing implication is that every channel can pull from that one source: the website, the Instagram, the sales conversation, the film.

If you want more worked examples from brands you'll know, I've set a few out in what a brand story example looks like, and there's a longer list in which brands use storytelling.

If your brand story could be swapped with a competitor's and nobody noticed, it's a tagline with a nice font.

How do you measure whether storytelling is working in marketing?

Honestly, indirectly, and you shouldn't expect a single number. Storytelling works on memory and preference, and those don't show up in a click report. I'd be wary of anyone who promises you an exact return on a brand story. I've never seen one that held up.

What you can watch is a set of signs that move together over a few months:

  • Branded search. More people typing your name into Google is one of the cleaner signals that you're being remembered.
  • Direct and referral traffic. People who turn up on their own, rather than from an ad.
  • Sales conversations. Prospects arriving already knowing what you stand for, and fewer arguments about price. Ask your sales lead what the first five minutes of calls feel like now.
  • Watch time on video. Whether people stay for the human parts, and where they drop off.
  • What customers repeat back. If they quote your own language to you, the story has landed.

Give it a decent window. Short campaigns can be judged in weeks. A brand story needs a few quarters of consistent showing up before you can read anything useful from it. For the evidence side, I've pulled together what's known in how effective storytelling is in marketing.

What mistakes do businesses make when they bring storytelling into their marketing?

Telling the company's history instead of the customer's change

"Founded in 1998 by two friends" is a fact. It's not a story until something happens. The most useful stories in marketing are about what changes for the customer, with your business as the guide rather than the hero. The opening of the story matters more than most people think.

Treating it as a one-off project

A brand film that's launched once, posted on the homepage and never mentioned again is a waste of a decent film. The story has to show up in the sales deck, the emails, the cut-downs and the way your team talks.

Making it up

Invented personas and polished origin tales get found out. People can tell when a story was workshopped in a meeting room rather than lived. The reason documentary-style film works so well for this is that it captures the real thing, awkward pauses included, and that reads as honest.

Skipping the proof

A story without evidence is just a claim. Pair it with specifics: what was made, for whom, how long it took, what changed. Even a small number does more than an adjective.

How much does a small business need to do?

Less than you'd think. You don't need a campaign. You need one clear story, one proper piece of video that carries it, and the habit of using the same language everywhere. A single well-made documentary-style brand film, cut into a long version for the website and a handful of short ones for social, covers more ground than a year of scattered posts.

The order I'd go in: get the story straight on paper, film the real people telling it, put it where buyers look first, then repeat the best fragments consistently. If you want the full picture of how this fits together, the complete guide to brand storytelling is the place to go next, and how to use storytelling in marketing covers the practical rollout in more detail. For a sense of what a film can do on a real site, have a look at our films, or read why a brand film needs a business goal before you commission anything.

If you're working out how storytelling could fit your own marketing, get in touch and we'll talk it through.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the difference between brand storytelling and content marketing?
faqs.a: Content marketing is the output: blog posts, videos, emails and social posts. Brand storytelling is the point of view that decides what those pieces say and how they sound. You can do content marketing without a story, but it tends to read as generic. With a clear story underneath, every piece feels like it comes from the same people, which makes it easier to remember.

faqs.q: Is brand storytelling only for big brands with big budgets?
faqs.a: No. Small businesses often have the advantage because the story is real and close to hand: the founder, the first customer, the workshop. A single well-made film and consistent use of the same language across your website, sales calls and social costs far less than a national campaign, and it usually feels more believable at a smaller scale.

faqs.q: How long does it take for brand storytelling to show results in marketing?
faqs.a: Expect a few quarters rather than a few weeks. Storytelling builds memory and preference, which show up slowly as more branded searches, warmer sales calls and customers repeating your language back to you. Short campaigns can be judged quickly, but a brand story needs consistent repetition before you can read anything reliable from it, and nobody can honestly guarantee a result.

faqs.q: Which format is best for telling a brand story in marketing?
faqs.a: Video is usually the strongest, because people can see and hear a real person, and one film can be cut into many short pieces. Written stories on your site and in your sales material matter too. The best approach is one story told consistently across formats, with a documentary-style film as the anchor and everything else drawing from it.
