items.title: What brands use storytelling? UK examples
items.excerpt: From Dove and Patagonia to small UK makers and trades, here are the brands that use storytelling, what they actually do, and what any business can learn from them.
items.coverAlt: A corner cheese shop with a dark green frontage and awning on a London street, a customer walking in through the open door
items.body:
Brands that use storytelling include Dove, Patagonia, Innocent, John Lewis and Hovis among the household names, and thousands of small UK businesses such as craft makers, family firms and independent shops. What they share isn't size or budget. Each has a clear reason for existing and tells it through real people, places or moments rather than a list of features.

This post looks at who does it well, what they actually do, and what a smaller business can take from them. I'm not covering Nike, which has its own post in what Nike's brand story is, or a full walkthrough of one example, which is in a brand story example. Think of this as a tour of the field.

Which big brands are known for storytelling?

A few have become reference points, and it's worth knowing what each one really did.

Dove. The Campaign for Real Beauty launched in 2004 and put ordinary women, not models, at the front of its advertising. In 2013 the brand followed it with Real Beauty Sketches, a film in which a forensic artist drew women from their own descriptions and then from a stranger's. The story was about how people see themselves, and the product barely appeared in it.

Patagonia. The outdoor clothing company ran a Black Friday advert in the New York Times in November 2011 under the headline "Don't Buy This Jacket", asking customers to consider the environmental cost of what they bought. In 2022 its founder, Yvon Chouinard, moved ownership of the company into a trust and a non-profit so that profits go toward tackling climate change. The story and the actions point in the same direction, which is why it holds.

John Lewis. The retailer's annual Christmas advert has become something people look forward to and talk about in the UK. Each one is a short narrative, often with a small emotional turn, and the products are almost incidental. The feeling ends up attached to the shop.

Innocent. The smoothie company began in 1999 when three friends sold their drinks at a London music festival and put out two bins, one marked yes and one marked no, under a sign asking whether they should give up their jobs to make smoothies. The yes bin filled up. That story has been told in the brand's voice ever since.

Hovis. The 2008 "Boy on the Bike" advert, directed by Ridley Scott, followed a boy pushing a delivery bike up a hill through a century of British history. It sold nostalgia and heritage rather than bread, and it's still one of the best known UK adverts.

All five are very different, and none of them is about the product's features. They're about a feeling, a belief or a place, and the product is how you join in.

Do small UK businesses use storytelling too?

Constantly, though many don't call it that. Anyone who explains how they started, shows how the work is done or lets customers speak is telling a story.

The ones I've filmed are a good cross-section. La Fromagerie tells thirty three years of a cheese business, starting from a garden shed. Carreducker makes bespoke shoes by hand in the Oxo Tower, and the film is about the six months and 210 steps behind each pair. Catherine Marche is a goldsmith who works only in recycled metal, and her film is built around the way she works rather than the pieces in the case. And a hand painted signwriting trade is shown in the workshop and out on the shopfronts.

None of those businesses has a huge advertising budget. They have a way of working that other people find interesting, and a film that lets them show it. That's all storytelling needs as a starting point.

You don't need a Christmas ad budget. You need one person who can explain the work and a camera that's pointing at them.

What kinds of business use storytelling most?

Any business where trust, craft or character matters. Looking across the films and brands I know, some sectors turn up more than others.

  • Craft and heritage businesses. Makers, food producers and traditional trades, where the process is the product. There's more in filming craft and heritage businesses.
  • Charities. Where people give because they believe in the cause. See brand films for charities.
  • Professional services. Lawyers, accountants, architects, where the client is buying a person as much as a service.
  • Trades and installers. Businesses people have to let into their homes, where seeing the team on camera takes away the fear of the unknown.
  • Founder-led businesses of every kind. Anywhere the owner is still part of the picture.

Businesses that sell on price alone use it least, and they tend to struggle when the next cheaper supplier arrives.

Which formats do these brands tell their stories in?

Rarely just one. The big names run films, adverts, packaging copy, social posts and the way their staff answer the phone, all from the same story. Smaller brands do the same on a smaller scale.

  • Film. The most direct way to put a real person in front of an audience. Documentary-style films suit makers and service businesses best.
  • Written pages. The About page, the product description, the email newsletter.
  • Social. Short clips and photographs, each carrying one piece of the story. See storytelling in social media marketing.
  • Packaging and physical things. Innocent's labels talk in the founders' voice, and a tradesman's van can tell you plenty before they get out.
  • Events and conversations. What people say at the trade stand or on the doorstep.

Can a business with a serious message still use storytelling?

Yes, and often it's where storytelling is most useful. A serious or technical subject is easier to follow when a person explains it. Our work for char.gy is a good case: an interview-led film explaining its B Corp certification in plain language, which went on to become the most watched thing on its channel. The subject was a certification, which most people would call dry. A clear human voice made it watchable.

The same applies to charities, healthcare, finance and energy. The more complicated or sensitive the subject, the more a real person helps. It gives people a way in.

What can a small business take from the big names?

Four things, none of which need a big budget.

Pick one idea and keep returning to it. Dove has returned to the same idea about real beauty for twenty years. A small business should be able to say in a sentence what its story is and check every new piece against it.

Back the words with actions. Patagonia's story carries weight because of how the company is run. Your story should be something your customers could verify if they came to see you.

Use real faces. Innocent's early success owed a lot to three real people the audience could picture. Your own team is your most distinctive asset, and nobody else has it.

Be patient. Brand stories build up over years. John Lewis didn't earn its Christmas slot with one advert. Make the first film, then keep adding to it.

Why do these brands bother?

Because stories move people, though less than the hype suggests. A 2016 meta-analysis by Kurt Braddock and James Dillard, published in Communication Monographs, pooled studies of narrative persuasion. It found positive links between exposure to a story and story-consistent beliefs (37 studies, 7,376 people), attitudes (40 studies, 7,132 people), intentions (28 studies, 5,211 people) and behaviours (5 studies, 978 people). The correlations were small, between .17 and .23. That's research on stories in general rather than any one brand's film, so treat it as a reason the big names keep telling them, not a promise of what yours will earn.

The logic is plain enough. When a brand is remembered for who it is, it gets chosen without a fight. People will pay a bit more, wait a bit longer and recommend you without being asked. If all you've done is describe your features, you're one of several options in a comparison table.

For the wider case, why brand storytelling is important goes through the reasons in more depth.

What do brands that tell good stories have in common?

Looking across all of the above, the pattern is surprisingly consistent.

They stand for something specific. Dove for how women see themselves, Patagonia for protecting the planet, Carreducker for slow, handmade work. You could describe each in one sentence.

They show it rather than say it. Patagonia backed its message with its ownership. Carreducker shows the 210 steps. The proof is visible.

They use real people. Actual customers, makers and founders, not stock footage. This is the biggest thing a small business can copy, because it costs nothing extra to be authentic.

They're consistent. The story appears on the website, in the packaging, on social and in the way staff talk. It isn't a one-off campaign.

The brands people remember aren't the loudest. They're the ones whose story stays the same wherever you meet them.

Can any business use storytelling, or does it need a famous name?

Any business can, and small ones often do it better, because the founder and the team are right there to be filmed. A multinational has to build a story from research and committee. A family firm just has to turn a camera on someone who knows what they're talking about.

What you need is a reason, a person and the willingness to be specific. If you can say why the business exists and who does the work, you've got enough to begin. The rest is shaping it, which is what how to tell a brand story goes through step by step.

A word of caution about copying the famous examples. Dove and Patagonia worked because they were true to the brands behind them. A business borrowing a cause it doesn't hold will be spotted straight away. Choose the story that's yours, even if it seems small. The quietest story told honestly beats a loud one that doesn't fit.

It also helps to remember that none of these brands began as famous. Innocent was three friends and a stall. Patagonia began as a small business making climbing equipment. The stories got bigger because the brands kept telling them, the same way, to the same kind of people, long before there was an audience worth the name.

That patience is the part smaller businesses find hardest. A film that goes out this month won't change your quarter. Ten pieces of honest work over two years will change how people talk about you, and you can start with one afternoon.

How do you find the story in your own business?

Start by asking the people who've been there longest what they'd tell a friend about the place. Then ask a few customers why they chose you and why they stayed. The overlap between those answers is usually the story. It's often something the owner takes for granted, which is why an outsider with a camera and a list of questions can find it in an afternoon.

For a longer example of that process, there's a full breakdown in the story behind the La Fromagerie film. The complete guide to brand storytelling collects every part of the subject in one place. If you'd like help finding yours, see our brand films or get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Which UK brands are best known for storytelling?
faqs.a: John Lewis with its Christmas adverts, Innocent with its friendly founder voice, and Hovis with its 2008 Boy on the Bike film are three that most UK audiences will recognise. Dove, though global, has run a long-running story about how women see themselves. Among smaller businesses, makers and family firms with strong founder stories tend to do it best.

faqs.q: Do B2B companies use storytelling?
faqs.a: Yes, and often with good results, because B2B purchases involve more people and a longer decision. A film that explains how a supplier works, shown through real clients and staff, helps a buying committee trust a company they haven't used before. The tone is usually more practical, with more proof, but the same ingredients of origin, belief and people apply.

faqs.q: Is storytelling only for big budgets?
faqs.a: No. The famous examples are large because large brands get written about, but a good story depends on specifics and honesty, not spend. A small business with a clear reason for existing and someone who can explain it on camera has everything it needs. The budget affects how polished the film is, not whether the story is any good.

faqs.q: What's the difference between storytelling and advertising?
faqs.a: Advertising asks you to do something, usually buy. Storytelling gives you a reason to remember and trust a business, so you're more likely to choose it later. Many brands use both: a story to build the relationship and adverts to prompt the sale. A good story makes the advertising work harder because people already know who you are.

stat.title: How strongly stories are linked to story-consistent views and actions
stat.takeaway: Stories nudge what people believe and do, consistently but modestly, which is why brands use them as one tool among several.

source.name: Braddock and Dillard, Communication Monographs (2016), meta-analysis of narrative persuasion

items.title: Testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials
items.excerpt: How to make a customer testimonial video people believe: let the customer tell their own story, film once the result is real, and ask about them, not you.
items.coverAlt: The homeowner in the finished front room at Nimrod Road
items.body:
A testimonial video stops sounding like a testimonial when the customer tells the story of what happened to them, in their own words, instead of praising the business. You film them once the result is real, ask about their situation rather than about you, and cut it as their account. The praise is then implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Most testimonial videos are a customer on a sofa saying they were really professional and they'd definitely recommend them. It's sincere, and it doesn't land, because every business has one and they all sound the same.

Why do most testimonial videos sound the same?

Because the questions are about the business. Ask someone what it was like working with you and you get adjectives. Professional, friendly, on time, tidy. Lovely to hear and almost impossible to believe, because the viewer knows the business picked its happiest customer and pointed a camera at them.

There's a scripting problem too. When a customer's been handed lines, or asked to say that again but mention the price this time, it shows. People can hear the difference between someone remembering and someone performing.

And trust in second hand praise is wearing thin. In a Which? survey of 2,000 UK adults, 41% said they find it difficult to tell whether an online review is genuine or fake, and only 17% said they find it easy. Generic praise gets discounted in any format. Specific stories still get through.

What makes a customer story believable?

Specifics, stakes and a bit of friction. What the person needed, what was at risk, what was hard, and what they've got now. A story with a worry in it is more convincing than one that's all praise, because real projects have worries.

The Nimrod Road film works because of its stakes. A Victorian house in Tooting that had sat empty after the previous owners died. A couple who wanted the period features kept and the ground floor opened up. A project that started in September, with a baby due at the end of November. The work was finished in eight weeks, two weeks inside the estimate. Both homeowners tell it as their account, and anyone weighing up the same decision hears it from people in their own position.

The praise is implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Who should tell the story, the customer or the business?

The customer, almost always. A business talking about its own quality is the one voice a prospective customer discounts straight away, because it's the voice being paid.

That was the thinking behind Barry Road, a full house renovation in East Dulwich. Every contractor says the same things about themselves: quality, on time, on budget. So the film is the homeowner giving their own account of the job, what they wanted, what it was like to live through, and what they ended up with. We handed the film to them and let them say whatever they were going to say.

The business can still appear, briefly and doing the work. Just don't let it narrate its own reputation.

Which customer should you film?

Not automatically the happiest one. Pick the customer whose situation looks most like the people you want more of. If your best jobs are period houses with tight deadlines, film the family with the period house and the tight deadline. Someone weighing you up should watch it and recognise their own situation.

Look for someone who had something at stake and can talk about it naturally. A worry, a deadline, a previous bad experience with someone else. They don't need to be polished, and the ones who are a bit unsure on camera often come across as the most honest. Most of all, they need to want to do it. A customer doing you a reluctant favour sounds exactly like one.

When should you film a testimonial?

Once the result is real, and ideally while it's still fresh. Both of those renovation films were made after the family had moved back in, so the customer is talking about a home they live in rather than a promise.

The downside of waiting is that the before has gone. At Nimrod Road the before only exists in the original listing photos, so those were cut against the finished rooms. At Barry Road, before and after floorplans were cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. If there's any chance you'll want a customer film, photograph the start of the job properly. It costs almost nothing, and you can't get it back later.

The best time to plan a testimonial is before the customer has anything to testify about. Annoying, but true.

What should you ask in a testimonial interview?

Ask about them, not you. Questions that tend to open people up:

  • What was going on before you got in touch?
  • What were you most worried about?
  • What was it like day to day while the work was happening?
  • Was there a moment you weren't sure it would work out?
  • What's different now?
  • What would you tell someone in the position you were in?

Then listen, and follow whatever's interesting rather than ticking through the list. Never feed them the answer. If a customer says something in a way that's a bit clunky but true, keep it. The odd stumble is part of why it sounds real. There's more on this in how to make a brand video people actually watch.

How do you get the most from a customer story film?

Use it in the sales conversation, which is where it earns its money. Both renovation films were made as edits a contractor can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. That's a precise job, and it decided how they were cut.

Beyond that, put the full film on the relevant service page, cut a short version for the top of the site, and pull vertical clips for social, where one honest line can carry a post. Ask the customer's permission for every use up front, paid ads included, so you're not chasing them six months later.

If you've got customers whose stories would sell your work better than you can, see the films we've made or tell us about them.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should customers be paid to appear in a testimonial video?
faqs.a: Generally no, and it's worth avoiding anything that looks like payment for praise. A small thank you for their time is fine, but the value of a testimonial comes from it being freely given. If a customer is paid or given something significant, viewers would reasonably want to know, so be open about it. Choosing customers who genuinely had a good experience makes the question mostly irrelevant.

faqs.q: How long should a customer testimonial video be?
faqs.a: Long enough to tell one story properly, which is usually two to five minutes for the main film. That's what you send in a sales conversation or put on a service page. From the same interview you can cut a sixty to ninety second version for the top of your site and short vertical clips for social, where a single honest line from the customer can work on its own.

faqs.q: What if a customer gets nervous on camera?
faqs.a: Most people do at first, and it usually passes within ten minutes. Run it as a conversation, with no lines to learn and no autocue, and start with easy questions about their situation before anything that matters. Film them somewhere familiar, ideally the place the work was done. If they stumble, carry on rather than restarting, because those natural moments are often what makes it believable.

faqs.q: Do we need a customer's written permission to use their video?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent that covers where the film will appear and for how long, including your website, social media and any paid advertising. It protects you and it's fair to them. Agree up front what happens if they later want it taken down, and keep their personal details, like a full address, out of the film unless they're happy for them to be shown.

stat.title: How easy UK adults find it to tell a genuine online review from a fake
stat.takeaway: Generic praise is being discounted, so a specific customer story told on camera carries more weight than another five star line.

source.name: Which?, survey of 2,000 UK adults, September 2021

items.title: What is a brand story video? A plain guide
items.excerpt: A brand story video tells your business's story through real people on camera. Here's how it differs from adverts and corporate videos, the types, and how one is made.
items.coverAlt: Extreme close-up of a bearded man looking down in concentration, face half out of frame
items.body:
A brand story video is a film that tells a business's story through the people who run it, rather than selling a product or service directly. It covers where the business came from, what it believes and what it's like to deal with, usually in the words of real people on camera. It's closer to a short documentary than an advert.

This post is about the format itself: what a brand story video is, how it differs from the other kinds of business video, the types you can make, and what goes into one. For the written version of the story, see how to write a brand story, and for length see how long a brand story should be.

What makes a video a brand story video?

Three things have to be true. It's about the business itself, not just one product. It's told by people connected to the business, in their own voices. And it's trying to make you understand and trust the business, not to push you toward an immediate purchase.

That last point matters. An advert asks for something now. A brand story video asks for your attention for a few minutes and gives you a reason to remember the name later. It does the slow work of building recognition and trust, which is why it's usually the first film a business should make, with the sharper, shorter promotional pieces coming afterwards.

The look usually follows from the purpose. Natural light, real locations, people talking about work they actually do. If it feels like watching a short documentary about a business you'd like to know better, that's the target.

How is a brand story video different from other business videos?

Business video terms get thrown around loosely, so it helps to line them up. The differences come down to who's speaking and what the film wants from the viewer.

  • Brand story video: people from the business explain who they are and why. It builds trust.
  • Promotional video: pushes an offer, a launch or a service. It drives action. Covered in promotional videos.
  • Corporate video: usually a formal presentation of the company, often with a voiceover and stock footage. See corporate videos.
  • Explainer video: teaches how something works, often animated.
  • Testimonial: a customer says the business did a good job. It's one voice, one angle.

A brand story video can borrow from all of these, but its centre of gravity is different. It's one of the main reasons we talk about brand documentary vs corporate video as a real choice, because the two make people feel quite different things about the same company.

If the film opens with a drone shot of your building and a voiceover saying "since 1998", I'm afraid we've made a corporate video.

What types of brand story video are there?

There are a handful of useful shapes. Most businesses end up with two or three of them.

The founder story. Where it started and why. La Fromagerie is built on this: a cheese business that began in a garden shed, told by its founder and the people who now run it. It works when the founder has a story worth hearing and the business is still shaped by them.

The craft or process story. The work itself, shown properly. The Carreducker film follows two shoemakers through the steps of making a bespoke pair, and the signwriting film shows a hand painted trade in a workshop and out on shopfronts. These suit any business where the work is the proof.

The customer story. The business seen through someone it's helped. Our film on a live supermarket site is a version of this. It's more convincing than a testimonial because it shows the job and not just the verdict.

The partnership or team story. Two organisations or a team explaining how they work together. Good for B2B businesses, where the relationship is the product.

The purpose or values story. A statement of what the business stands for, backed by evidence. This is the hardest to get right because it can slide into slogans, so it needs real examples to hold it up.

Who appears in a brand story video?

Real people who know the business well. That usually means the founder or owner, one or two members of staff who do the work, and sometimes a customer or supplier. We choose them for how they talk about the work, not for their job title.

This is where a lot of businesses get nervous. Most people haven't been filmed before, and they assume they'll be stiff. In my experience the nerves drop away within a few minutes of a real conversation, because we're asking about things they know inside out. If you're one of the people being asked, how to prepare for being filmed covers what to expect.

One thing I'd say strongly: don't replace real people with a presenter, an actor or generated footage if your story is meant to be true. Audiences notice. Getty Images' 2024 VisualGPS research, covering more than 30,000 adults in 25 countries including the UK, found 98% agree that authentic images and videos are pivotal to establishing trust. It's a global survey, so take it as a direction and not a verdict, but it matches what I see on shoots.

The camera doesn't make people trustworthy. It just shows whether they are.

What goes into making one?

The process is simpler than people expect. Here's how it generally runs.

  1. A conversation. We talk about the business, the audience and what the film needs to do. Nothing gets written yet.
  2. Finding the story. We work out who should appear and what the key moments are. Sometimes this means a short call with each person.
  3. The shoot. Usually one day, sometimes two. Interviews, the work being done, the place itself. What a day looks like is covered in what a brand film shoot day in London looks like.
  4. The edit. We shape the interviews into the story, add the footage that illustrates it, choose licensed music and grade the picture.
  5. Feedback and delivery. You review it, we adjust, and you receive the final film in the formats you need.

Nobody writes a script in the normal sense. The words come from the interviews, so the preparation is about asking good questions rather than writing lines. That's why it sounds like people, not copy.

What makes a brand story video good?

The sound, first. People will put up with an average picture but not with muffled or echoey audio. A clean voice, recorded close, is the single biggest quality marker, and it's why we always mic the person being interviewed directly.

Second, pace. A good one lets people finish their thoughts. There's room for a pause, for a hand doing something while a voice carries on over the top. Rushed cutting makes everything feel like an advert.

Third, specificity. The best lines in these films are always small and concrete: the name of a tool, the number of steps, the story of the first customer. Anyone can say "quality matters to us". Only the person who's done the work can tell you what it looks like at seven in the morning.

Finally, restraint. A story told simply and well doesn't need many effects. Most of the time the best move is to leave the camera on someone who's good at explaining what they do.

What do businesses get wrong with brand story videos?

The usual mistakes are about ambition, not skill.

Trying to say everything. A film that covers every service, every founder and every award ends up memorable for none of them. Pick one story and tell it well. The rest can go into other pieces.

Over-scripting the people. Handing someone a prepared answer takes the life out of it. It's much better to give them the questions in advance and let them answer in their own words.

Hiding the problems. Stories need a bit of difficulty. A business that's honest about what was hard is more believable than one that sounds flawless.

Making it a one-off. A single film posted once and forgotten wastes most of its value. Plan where it will live, and what shorter pieces will be cut from it, before the shoot, not after.

What do you receive at the end?

Typically the main film, a shorter version for the homepage, and a set of vertical cuts for social. You also want captions, since many people watch with the sound off, and a licence for the music that covers every platform you'll use. We cover why that last point matters in music licensing for brand videos.

On our films, the licence covers everything indefinitely on every platform, which is worth checking with whoever you hire. It's covered in more detail in who owns the footage when you commission a film.

Why do people respond to this kind of film?

Because they get to see who they'd be dealing with before they pick up the phone. For most small and mid-sized businesses, the biggest hurdle is that a stranger has to take a chance on you. A film where the owner explains the work, and someone who does it every day shows how it's done, closes some of that distance before the first conversation.

It also gives the people who already like you something to share. A customer who'd happily recommend you can send a link to a four minute film far more easily than they can explain what makes you different. The film does the explaining for them, in your words, with the right tone.

Where do you use a brand story video?

Anywhere that someone is deciding whether to trust you. The homepage and About page are the obvious places. After that: the top of your proposals, your LinkedIn page, email signatures, recruitment pages, trade show screens and the start of sales calls.

The best use is as a master film that feeds shorter pieces. One day of filming gives you the main film and months of social clips, which is covered in where to use your brand film and turning one film into a year of content.

Does a brand story video work for any business?

For any business that has people and a reason to exist, yes, but it suits some better than others. It works especially well where trust matters, where the purchase is considered rather than impulsive, and where the owner or team is the difference. Trades, professional firms, craft businesses, charities, manufacturers and independent shops tend to get the most from it.

It works less well when there's no real story to tell yet, for example a business that opened last month with no track record. In that case a simpler introduction film is better, and the fuller one can come once there's something to show.

If you want to see what a finished one looks like, a brand story example goes through one in detail, and the complete guide to brand storytelling sets the format in context. Our brand films page explains how we make them, and if you've got a business you think deserves one, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is a brand story video the same as a brand film?
faqs.a: The terms overlap heavily. A brand film is the broader label for a film that represents a business, and a brand story video is a brand film whose main job is telling the story of the business. In practice, people use them interchangeably. What matters is the approach: real people, real places and a clear point, not the name on the file.

faqs.q: Do you need a script for a brand story video?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. In a documentary-style film, the words come from interviews with real people, guided by a set of questions and a planned structure. A script would make it sound rehearsed. What you do need is a plan: who appears, what each person covers and what the film needs the viewer to think at the end.

faqs.q: How many people should be in a brand story video?
faqs.a: Between one and four is typical. One person gives a focused story but can feel like a talking head. Two to four voices give variety and let people answer each other. More than that tends to dilute it unless the film is longer. Choose people for what they can say about the work, not for seniority.

faqs.q: Can a brand story video be shot on a phone?
faqs.a: It can, and for some short social pieces it's the right call. For a main film, a proper camera, sound and lighting make a visible difference, particularly to the audio, which people forgive least. Our phone video post covers where a phone is enough. A phone is fine for supporting clips around a well-shot core film.

stat.title: Consumers who say authentic images and videos are pivotal to trust

bars.label: Agree authentic images and videos are pivotal to trust

stat.takeaway: Almost everyone says it matters, which is a good reason to put real people on camera.

items.title: How long should a brand story be?
items.excerpt: A brand story needs different lengths in different places: 30 seconds spoken, 300 to 500 words on a page, 60 to 90 seconds on a homepage, four to ten minutes as a film.
items.coverAlt: A lone commuter walking a long wet railway platform beside a row of Victorian arches
items.body:
A brand story should be as long as the place it's told in allows: about 100 words spoken in 30 seconds, 300 to 500 words on a web page, 60 to 90 seconds as a short film for your homepage, and four to ten minutes as a full documentary-style film. The right length depends on the format and the audience, and it shouldn't be padded to fill it.

Length is the question owners ask me most after "what should it say?" Below I'll go through the length of a brand story in each place it appears: spoken, written, on film and on social. I'm not covering what goes in it, which is in what a brand story should include, or the order, which is in how a brand story should be structured.

Is there one right length for a brand story?

No, and anyone who gives you a single number is guessing. A brand story isn't one piece of content. It's a story you tell in several sizes, depending on where you are and how much of the audience's time you've got.

The sensible way to think about it is as a set. You want a version you can say in a sentence or two, a version you can say in half a minute, a written version, a short film and a longer film. They all tell the same story. Each one is simply cut to fit the room.

That's also why a business that has only ever written one "About us" page often struggles when someone asks for something shorter or longer. The story hasn't been built in layers, so there's nothing to take from.

How long is a spoken brand story?

The short spoken version is your answer when someone at a networking event asks what you do and why. Aim for 30 seconds, which is roughly 75 to 100 words at a normal speaking pace. It needs the origin, the problem and the point for the customer, and nothing else.

The longer spoken version, a minute to two minutes, is for a pitch, a podcast or a meeting. That's room for a belief and one piece of proof as well. Past two minutes, a spoken story needs to be properly interesting, because the listener can't skim.

Practise them out loud, not on paper. Words that look fine on a page often trip up when spoken. If you stumble on a phrase, nobody else will believe it either, so change it.

How long should a written brand story be?

For a web page, somewhere between 300 and 500 words is a good working range. That's enough for an origin, a problem, a belief and a line of proof, with a couple of subheadings so people can skim. It reads in about two minutes.

Go longer if you've got a genuinely strong story and good photographs to carry it. A founder's page that runs to 800 words is fine if every paragraph moves the story on. Go shorter if the page is one of several that a visitor sees, such as a product page that includes a short "why we make this" panel.

Whatever the length, the same test applies: cover the bottom half of the page and see whether you'd miss it. If you wouldn't, cut it. The first paragraph and the last paragraph do most of the work, so make those sharp before you worry about anything in between.

Nobody has ever finished an About page and wished it had been longer.

If you're about to write one, how to write a brand story goes through the process from the first notes to the final draft.

How long should a brand story video be?

This depends on the job the film is doing. I split it into three.

  • The homepage film: 60 to 90 seconds. A visitor lands, gets a feel for who you are, and decides whether to keep looking. It carries the strongest moments of the story and nothing else.
  • The main film: four to ten minutes. This is the full documentary-style version. It has room for people to speak at their own pace, for the work to be seen properly, and for the middle of the story to breathe.
  • The short cuts: 15 to 60 seconds. Vertical clips for social, each built around one moment or one line.

We cover the main film in detail in how long a brand film should be, and what the format actually is in what a brand story video is. A good example of range is La Fromagerie, where four people tell thirty three years of a business and the film needs the extra room.

A story should be the length of what it has to say, and no longer.

Do people really watch long videos?

They do, if the video is worth it, but short videos get far higher engagement on average. Wistia analysed more than 13 million videos on its platform for its 2026 State of Video report and found that videos under a minute average a 52 per cent engagement rate. Customer testimonial videos came in at 46 per cent and product videos at 50 per cent. Past 30 minutes, it reports engagement dropping off by 11 per cent.

Those numbers are for engagement, meaning how much of the video gets watched, and shorter films finish more often almost by definition. A one minute film that 52 per cent of people engage with isn't automatically better than a six minute film that fewer people finish but that the right people watch to the end and then call you about.

That's the trade-off. Short is for reach, and it's the sensible choice at the top of the funnel. Long is for conviction, and it works on people who already have a reason to be there: someone who's been sent your website, someone comparing three suppliers, someone you've just met who wants to know who they're dealing with. Make both.

What's the right length on social media?

Shorter than you think, and told in pieces. On social platforms, you're competing with everything else in someone's feed, and the first two seconds decide if you're watched. Most brand story clips I'd cut for social land between 15 and 45 seconds.

The mistake is trying to squeeze the whole story into a single clip. It's much better to take one beat, such as the shed where it began or the moment the first order arrived, and give that its own short piece. A run of six of those across a few weeks tells the story more effectively than one rushed minute.

For more on how story works on those platforms, see what storytelling in social media marketing is.

Can you build all the lengths from one master version?

Yes, and it's the most practical way to do it. Write or film the longest version first, then cut downwards. Going the other way, from a tagline up to a full story, tends to produce padding.

Start with the full story at its natural length. From that, pull the two or three moments that carry the most weight. Those become the homepage film and the 300 word page. From those, pull one line and one image each, and you've got your social posts and your spoken version. Everything is connected, so nothing contradicts anything else.

The reverse problem is common. A business writes a punchy 100 word blurb, then tries to turn it into a two minute film and finds there's nothing underneath. The blurb was a summary of a story that was never told in full. If that sounds familiar, go back to the people and ask them for the long version first. The short ones will be better for it.

Does the audience change how long a story should be?

It changes how much they'll tolerate and what they're looking for. A prospective customer wants reassurance and will watch a few minutes if the film is helping them decide. A potential employee is often more patient, because they're looking for what working there is like. A journalist or partner wants the facts fast, so they need the short written version with the proof up top.

This is why it pays to know who the story is for before choosing a length. A film for a trade audience that already understands your product can start in the middle of things. A film for a general audience has to set the scene first, and that takes a little longer.

How do you decide how long yours should be?

Work backwards from three questions.

Who is watching or reading, and how much do they already care? Someone who's never heard of you will give you thirty seconds. Someone who's on your site comparing quotes will give you five minutes if you've earned it.

Where will they meet it? A homepage, a pitch deck, a trade show screen, a social feed and an email all have different tolerances. Match the piece to the place.

How much story have you actually got? This is the honest one. If you only have an origin and one good proof point, you've got ninety seconds of material, and stretching it to five minutes will leave it thin. Sometimes the right answer is to go and find more story, by talking to more of your people, before deciding on length.

When I'm planning a film I'd rather shoot generously and cut hard. Material that doesn't make the main film often becomes the short cuts, which is how one day of filming turns into months of content. The one brand film into a year of content post covers how that works in practice.

What happens when a brand story runs too long?

You lose the audience at the point where it stops adding anything new. Usually that's the same place in every overlong story: after the origin and the main proof, the piece begins repeating itself. A second testimonial that says what the first one did. A third paragraph about values. A closing montage that lasts a minute.

The fix is nearly always cutting, and cutting is easier with a colleague or a film maker who isn't attached to any of it. Founders find it hard to lose a line they remember saying. I get it. But people remember the whole piece by how it felt, not by which sentences were in it.

And what happens when it runs too short? Less often, it feels like a slogan. The audience gets a claim without a reason to believe it. If you've got a 30 second piece that doesn't carry any proof or any person, it may be a good tagline and not yet a story.

Get the lengths right and you end up with a story you can use everywhere, in whatever size the moment needs. The complete guide to brand storytelling covers the rest of the subject. To see how we cut the same story into long and short versions, look at our brand films, or get in touch if you'd like to talk about yours.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How many words is a 60 second brand story?
faqs.a: Around 150 words if it's spoken at a natural pace, though most good films say less and leave room for pictures and pauses. A 60 second brand film with an interview in it often carries only 100 to 130 words. Write it, then read it aloud against a timer, because words on a page always run shorter than they sound.

faqs.q: Should the About page and the brand film tell the same story?
faqs.a: Yes, in the same order with the same core facts. They suit different audiences, so the film can show what the page has to describe and the page can hold detail the film leaves out. Make sure the origin, the belief and the main proof match, so a visitor who sees both gets a consistent picture of the business.

faqs.q: Is a one minute brand video too short?
faqs.a: Not if it has one clear job. A one minute film works well on a homepage or in an email as a first introduction. It can't carry a full story with a middle, so it should point to a longer film or page. Use it as the opening of the story, not as the whole of it.

faqs.q: How long does it take to make a brand story video?
faqs.a: A typical documentary-style brand film takes a few weeks from first conversation to delivery: planning, a shoot day or two, and editing with a round or two of feedback. Longer or multi-location films take longer. The timeline depends mostly on how quickly feedback comes back, so agree who signs off before you start.

stat.title: Average engagement rate for videos under a minute
stat.takeaway: Shorter videos hold more of their audience, which is why a brand story needs short cuts as well as a full film.

source.name: Wistia, 2026 State of Video Report (over 13 million videos)

items.title: How should a brand story be structured?
items.excerpt: A brand story needs a clear beginning, a middle with some struggle in it and an ending that shows what changed. Here's the order that works and the mistakes to avoid.
items.coverAlt: Two men at a table in a meadow watch a tall rocket standing at the water's edge in golden light
items.body:
A brand story works best structured in three parts: a beginning that sets up where the business came from and what was wrong, a middle where something gets tested or goes against it, and an end that shows what changed and what it means for the customer. Put the problem before the solution and the person before the product, and the rest tends to fall into place.

This post is about order: what comes first, what comes last, and where the tension sits in between. The list of ingredients is in what a brand story should include, and the length question is in how long a brand story should be. Below I'll cover the shapes that work, how documentary-style films build theirs, and the order mistakes I see most.

Why does the structure of a brand story matter?

Because the same facts in a different order make a completely different story. "We've been trading for thirty years and we're family run" is a fact sheet. "A man loses his job, borrows a van, and thirty years later his daughter is still driving it" is a story, and it contains the same two facts.

Structure gives the audience a reason to keep going. Each part raises a small question that the next part answers. Take that out and people can still follow it, but they have no pull. They watch the first thirty seconds, decide they know where it's going, and leave.

There's also research on why this matters. Researchers at the University of Illinois, Stanford and the University of Texas studied TV ads and found that a "repetition-break" structure, where a pattern is set up and then broken with a surprise, is used in only 4% of them. Those ads were more likely to be singled out by industry judges, more likely to be shared on YouTube, and better at improving people's opinion of the brand. A list of facts gets forgotten by the car park. The same facts held in a shape tend to stick.

What's the simplest structure for a brand story?

Beginning, middle, end. It sounds too basic to be useful, but most weak brand stories fail here because the middle is missing. They go straight from "we started" to "we're great now" with nothing in between.

  1. Beginning: the situation and the problem. Where things stood, who was involved, what was missing or broken.
  2. Middle: the effort. What the business tried, what was hard, what nearly didn't work.
  3. End: the change. What's different now, and what that means for the person watching.

The middle is where trust gets built. Audiences believe a business that admits it was difficult. A story with no struggle in it sounds like a brochure, because no real business has ever had it that easy.

Keep each part proportionate. On a five minute film I'll often aim for a beginning of about a minute, a middle of about two and a half, and an ending of about a minute and a half. Those aren't rules. They're a starting sketch you adjust once you hear what the people say.

What does the origin, conflict, change shape look like?

This is the beginning, middle, end shape with the labels changed to suit a business. It's the one I reach for most.

Origin. Open on a specific moment, not on a mission statement. The first customer, the first workshop, the day the idea arrived. La Fromagerie begins in a garden shed with a wheel of Beaufort, and that single image sets up everything that follows.

Conflict. This is whatever pushed against the business. It could be money, a rival, a bad decision, or simply the long slog of getting good at something. The conflict doesn't have to be dramatic. For a craft business it's often time itself: in the Carreducker shoemakers film, a pair of shoes takes six months and 210 steps, and the patience that takes is the tension.

Change. Close on where things are now and what that gives the customer. The change can be small. A business that survived, a product that got better, a customer who's still coming back after twenty years.

Every founder wants to skip the middle. It's also the only bit anyone remembers.

What if the customer is the hero?

Some brand stories put the customer at the centre instead of the founder. The business plays the guide: it notices what the customer is struggling with, offers a way through, and steps back while they get on with it. Author Donald Miller built a whole marketing method on this idea in his book Building a StoryBrand, and it's well known among marketers.

It's a useful corrective for businesses that talk about themselves too much. The Easee brand films work in this spirit, starting from the moments when a person decides they need a charger, like moving house, passing their test, or being a landlord with a property to look after. The company is in the background and the person's situation is up front.

The risk is that it can feel generic. If every beat is "customer has a problem, we solve it", it ends up sounding like an advert for any business. Fix that by putting a real person from your side into the story as well, someone with a name and a way of talking. The guide has to have a face.

Does the hero's journey work for a brand?

Joseph Campbell described the hero's journey in 1949, in The Hero with a Thousand Faces, as a pattern running through myths: someone leaves the familiar, faces trials, and comes back changed. Film makers have borrowed it ever since.

For a brand it can work if you keep it small. A founder leaves a job, struggles through the first year, finds the thing that works and comes back with something to offer. But a full twelve stage version is too much for a five minute film about a plumber. Take the shape, leave out the myth. Someone had a reason to start, faced something hard, and came out with something worth sharing.

If you're trying to decide between these shapes for a campaign, the comparison is covered in which storytelling structure is most effective in marketing. Here I'm more interested in how you build the one you pick.

How do documentary-style films structure a brand story?

Differently from a scripted piece, because we don't write the lines first. In an interview-led documentary the structure comes out of the material. We shoot long conversations, listen back for the moments that carry the story, and then arrange them.

In practice that means the first edit isn't a story, it's a pile of good answers. We sort them by theme (where it started, what was hard, what the work involves, why it matters) and then build the order. The strongest answer often ends up near the end, not the start, even if it came first in the interview.

A few habits help:

  • Open on something visual and specific. A pair of hands, a workshop door, a tool in use. It sets place before anyone speaks.
  • Let two voices answer each other. When one person raises a point and another responds, the film has a conversation in it.
  • Hold the strongest line for the turn. The best moment shouldn't be in the first thirty seconds. Give the audience a reason to arrive at it.
  • Finish on a person, not a logo. The last thing people see is the last thing they feel.

If you want to see how this looks across different brands, what a brand story looks like shows several in practice, and brand documentary vs corporate video covers why we shoot this way.

One more thing about the middle: it's the best place for proof. Instead of dropping a testimonial or a number in a separate box, let it arrive as part of the struggle. A customer who stayed through the difficult year says more about the business than a quote on a banner ever will, because it's attached to something that happened.

Does the structure change for a web page, a film and a social clip?

The skeleton stays put and the proportions shift. A written About page has room for all three parts, and readers can skim, so it helps to make each part a clear block with a plain heading. The reader controls the pace, which means your opening has to earn the scroll.

A film controls the pace for them. That's a strength, because you can hold a pause or let someone finish a thought, but it also means a slow start costs you viewers you can't win back. Cut the first ten seconds harder than feels comfortable.

A short social clip usually carries only one beat of the story: the origin moment, or the turn, or the change. Treat it as a single scene from the larger structure rather than a squashed copy of the whole thing. When a main film is cut into shorter pieces, each piece should still have its own small beginning and end, even if it's only fifteen seconds long.

This is one reason we plan the structure of the main film first. If the bones are sound, the cut-downs come easily, because every strong moment already sits in a place that makes sense.

What order mistakes do brand stories make?

The same four, again and again.

Starting with the company. "Founded in 1998, we are a leading provider of..." is where most About pages open, and it's the point where most readers stop. Start with a person or a moment.

Burying the problem. If the audience doesn't know what was wrong in the first thirty seconds, they don't know why to care about the fix. Put the problem early and keep it clear.

Skipping the middle. Covered above, but it's the most common by a distance. The jump from "we started" to "we're brilliant" has no struggle in it, so there's nothing to believe.

Ending on a sales pitch. A story builds feeling, and a list of services at the end undoes it. Finish on the change, then give a single, quiet next step.

Say what was wrong before you say what you do about it.

How do you test the structure before you commit?

Write it as six lines on a single page, one for the situation, the problem, the effort, the hard part, the change and the point for the customer. Then read it aloud to someone who doesn't know the business. If they can tell you the story back in their own words, the structure holds. If they say "so what do you actually do?" before you reach the end, the order needs work.

Another check is to cover the last line and ask whether the story already feels finished. If it does, the ending is repeating itself. If it feels unfinished, you're missing the change. Either way you'll know before anyone picks up a camera, which is the cheapest moment to find out.

Once the shape is right, writing it down is a separate job, covered in how to write a brand story. And the whole subject sits inside the complete guide to brand storytelling. If you'd like a second opinion on yours, or want to see how we'd build it into a film, have a look at our brand films or get in touch.

faqs.q: Should a brand story start with the founder or the customer?
faqs.a: Start with whoever the audience will care about most in the first thirty seconds. For a craft or family business that's usually the founder, because the person is the draw. For a service business the customer's situation can be a stronger hook. Either way, bring the other one in by the middle so the story has both sides.

faqs.q: Does every brand story need a conflict?
faqs.a: Yes, though it can be small. Conflict is just whatever the business had to push against: money, time, a hard skill, a sceptical market. Without it, the story has no middle and nothing for the audience to believe. Quiet conflict, like six months of patient work on a pair of shoes, is often more convincing than a dramatic crisis.

faqs.q: Can the structure change between a film and a written story?
faqs.a: The shape can stay the same, but the pace changes. A film leans on pictures and pauses, so it can say less and linger more. A written piece has to carry that setting in words, so the opening often needs a sharper, more specific image. Test both by reading the written version aloud and watching a rough cut.

faqs.q: How do you structure a brand story with several people in it?
faqs.a: Treat each person as a voice that answers a different question. One covers where it started, another what the work involves, another why it matters. Cut between them so they respond to each other rather than each telling a full mini story. Keep one person as the thread that opens and closes the film.

items.title: What should a brand story include? Six essentials
items.excerpt: A brand story needs an origin, a problem, a belief, proof, real people and a point for the customer. Here's what each one does and what to leave out.
items.coverAlt: Gold lettering names on a dark wooden honours board with a hand holding a brush at the bottom corner
items.body:
A brand story should include who started the business and why, the problem it exists to solve, what it believes that others in its market don't, proof that it delivers, the real people behind it, and what all of that means for the customer. Leave any of those out and the story starts to sound like every other company's About page.

This post is a checklist of ingredients, not a method. If you want the order they go in, that's covered in how a brand story should be structured, and the question of how much room it all gets is in how long a brand story should be. Here we're just looking at what has to be on the table before you write or film a single thing.

What are the essential parts of a brand story?

After enough shoots you start to notice that the stories that land all carry the same handful of things, whatever the business sells. Here they are in the form I use when I'm planning a film:

  • An origin. Where the business came from, in a specific place and time.
  • A problem. The thing that was wrong or missing that made the business worth starting.
  • A belief. A view the business holds that someone could disagree with.
  • Proof. Evidence that the belief turns into something real.
  • People. Named humans who do the work, in their own words.
  • A point for the customer. What the story means for the person watching or reading.

You don't need to give every one the same weight. A business with a dramatic founding story can spend most of its time there. A business that's been quietly good for forty years might lean on proof and people instead. But if one of the six is missing completely, the audience can feel the gap even when they can't name it.

If you're starting from zero and want the basics first, what brand storytelling is is the place to begin. Everything below assumes you know why you'd want one.

Why does the origin matter?

Because an origin is the only part of your story that nobody else can copy. Competitors can match your prices, your services and your website copy. They can't have started in your garden shed in the year you started.

Good origins are small and physical. La Fromagerie is the clearest example I've filmed: a London cheese business that began with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, and thirty three years later the story is still hanging off that image. Nobody has to be told it's a business with real roots. The shed does it.

When I ask a founder how they started, the first answer is nearly always the polished one: "We saw a gap in the market." It's accurate and it tells you nothing. The better answer comes about ten minutes later, usually after they've forgotten the camera is there. It's the job they hated, the conversation in a kitchen, the first customer who paid cash. That second answer is the origin. The skill is in getting to it.

Keep it specific. A date, a place, a first customer, a first mistake. Vague origins ("we've been serving the community for years") read as filler, because they are.

What problem does your business solve?

Every business that has lasted exists because somebody was fed up with something. The problem is the reason the origin matters. A cheese shop started in a shed is just a quaint detail until you know that good, properly aged cheese was hard to find and the founder wanted to fix that.

State the problem from the customer's side, in the words a customer would use. Not "fragmented supply chains" but "you couldn't buy it anywhere near here." If your customers wouldn't recognise the sentence, it belongs in an investor deck, not a brand story.

This is also where a lot of businesses go wrong with a founding story that's all about them. It's lovely that you left corporate life to follow your passion. Your customer wants to know what that did for them. The problem is the bridge between your story and theirs.

If the sentence "we're passionate about quality" could sit on a competitor's website without anyone noticing, it can't be in your story.

What do you believe that your competitors don't?

A belief is a position. It's something a reasonable person in your market could say no to. "We care about our customers" isn't one, because nobody says they don't. "A pair of shoes should take six months and 210 steps, and we won't speed that up" is one, because plenty of makers would look for a shortcut. The Carreducker shoemakers film runs on exactly that kind of commitment, a pair of shoes that takes 210 steps and six months, and it carries weight because it asks something of the maker.

Patagonia is the famous example. In November 2011 it ran a Black Friday advert in the New York Times under the headline "Don't Buy This Jacket", asking people to think before buying. A brand has to hold a belief pretty firmly to put it in print on the busiest shopping day of the year. Most businesses don't need to go that far. They do need one belief they'd defend in an argument.

Here's a quick test. Write down your belief, then try to write the opposite. If the opposite is something no sane business would ever say, you haven't found a belief yet. Keep digging.

What proof does a brand story need?

Proof is what separates a story from a slogan. Anyone can say they're trustworthy. A story earns it by showing something that would be hard to fake: years in business, a particular piece of work, a customer in their own words, a process you can watch happening.

This matters more than it used to. People are wary of what businesses say about themselves. YouGov's research found 71% of UK shoppers check reviews or ratings to decide whether an online store is legit, and only 26% look at the seller's own website. So a large share of the people who find your brand story are starting out unsure.

The best proof on film is often the dullest-sounding thing: a process shown at the speed it really happens, in full. On the drainage job we filmed, there was no need for a voiceover claiming the team was skilled. You watch them do the job. Proof is something the audience sees, not something you tell them.

Numbers help if they're yours and they're true. Years in business, jobs completed, repeat customers. Don't borrow a statistic from an industry report and present it as your own result, and never round a number up because it sounds better. That's the quickest way to lose the trust you were building.

Who should be in the story?

Real people, named, saying things in their own voice. This is the part I care most about, because it's the part that most separates a documentary-style film from a corporate one. You can read more about that split in brand documentary vs corporate video.

A brand story needs at least one person who isn't the founder. A founder telling you the company is great is a founder doing their job. A colleague, a customer or a supplier telling you the same thing, unprompted, is evidence. On the La Fromagerie film the story is carried by the founder and by the people who run the business with them, and the difference between those voices is a big part of why it feels true.

Pick people who talk about the work, not about the brand. Somebody who says "it took us three attempts to get that rind right" is more convincing than somebody who says "we're passionate about our product". Ask about the work and the brand takes care of itself.

People believe the person who describes the work. They stop listening to the person who describes the brand.

What does the story mean for the customer?

The last ingredient is the one that gets skipped most. A story that's entirely about the business is a memoir. A brand story ends by pointing back at the person reading it, and says, in effect, here's why this matters to you.

You don't need a hard sell. It can be as light as a closing line: this is why every order gets checked by hand, which is why you can trust what turns up. The point is that the audience leaves knowing what they get from all of this.

The Easee brand films are built this way. Each starts from a moment in the customer's life, like moving house or passing a driving test, rather than from the company.

Do these ingredients change for a small business?

The list stays the same. What changes is where you find the material. A large company has archives, old adverts and a long line of people to ask. A small one has the owner, a couple of staff and a few customers who've been around from the start, and that's plenty.

Smaller businesses often have the advantage on people and origin, because the founder is still there and can be filmed. Larger ones tend to be stronger on proof, with years of work to point at. Play to whichever you've got. Trying to sound bigger than you are is one of the commonest mistakes I see, and it strips out the very detail that would have made the story worth telling.

If you can only gather three of the six today, make them the origin, the people and the proof. The belief and the customer point can be sharpened in the edit, once you can hear how everyone actually talks about the work.

What should you leave out of a brand story?

Almost everything that isn't one of the six. A few things show up in first drafts again and again and can usually go:

  • A full list of services. That's what the services page is for.
  • Awards and logos in bulk. One that matters is plenty.
  • Corporate vocabulary: solutions, synergies, "world class".
  • Every founder's career history. Keep the bit that explains the business.
  • Anything you wouldn't say out loud to a customer across a table.

Cutting is the hardest part, and it's where people who aren't used to editing struggle. Every extra detail feels like it's earning its place. It isn't. A story with six clear ingredients is easier to remember, and easier for someone else to repeat, which is how stories really spread.

How do you check your brand story is complete?

Before anything is written or filmed, try saying the story out loud in about two minutes to someone who doesn't work for you. If you hit all six without notes, you've got the material. If you keep reaching for adjectives where a fact should be, that's the part missing.

Then ask the other person one thing: what would you tell someone else about us? Their answer is your real brand story, because it's what survives. Compare it to what you meant to say. The gap between the two is your editing brief.

If you want to see how the finished thing looks, a brand story example walks through a full one, and the complete guide to brand storytelling ties the whole subject together. When you're ready to turn the material into a film, our brand films page shows how we work, and if you'd like to talk it through, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the most important part of a brand story?
faqs.a: The belief. Origin and proof matter, but a belief is what makes a business distinct, because it's a position some people will disagree with. A brand that stands for something specific is easier to remember, easier to recommend and harder to compare on price. If you're stuck, start by writing down what you'd defend in an argument.

faqs.q: Does every brand story need a founder?
faqs.a: No. A founder is a handy source of origin, but plenty of strong stories are carried by a team, a craft or a place. If the founder has left or the business was inherited, use the people doing the work now. What matters is that someone real and named speaks for the business, not that it's the person whose name is on the door.

faqs.q: How many of the ingredients should a short brand story cover?
faqs.a: Even a 90 second version should touch all six, lightly. A line on where it began, the problem, the belief, one piece of proof, a person and a closing point for the customer. You won't give each room to breathe, but dropping one entirely tends to show. Longer pieces can spend more time on the ones that are strongest.

faqs.q: Can a brand story include customer reviews?
faqs.a: Yes, as proof. A customer describing what changed for them works better than a star rating. Use reviews that name something specific, and get the person's permission if you're quoting them on film. Keep the review in the customer's own words rather than polishing it. A slightly rough quote reads as more honest than a perfect one.

stat.takeaway: Shoppers trust other people's words over yours, so show proof in your story, not only claims.

items.title: Why real people on camera matter more now
items.excerpt: As AI content floods feeds, real people on camera become proof. What the 2026 trust research says, and why documentary films built on real voices land.
items.coverAlt: A competitor with his hand raised after a match, surrounded by his team
items.body:
Real people on camera matter more as AI content floods feeds because they're proof. A generated face can say anything, so it carries no weight. A real founder, a real member of staff or a real customer, filmed where the work actually happens, is evidence that the business exists and stands behind what it says. Research from The Harris Poll UK, published in April 2026, found seven in ten consumers trust adverts made entirely by humans, and that drops to two in ten when an advert is generated by AI alone.

I've believed this for a long time, but the gap is getting wider. The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more a viewer's first question becomes whether it is.

Why do people trust a brand more when they see real people?

Because a person on camera is putting their face to it. They can be recognised, called, held to what they said. That's a risk a business takes on deliberately, and viewers read it as confidence. A stock presenter or a generated spokesperson costs the business nothing to put in front of you, so it proves nothing.

It's also about who's speaking. People have always believed customers and staff more than the company talking about itself. We wrote about why in brand documentary vs corporate video, and it's the same instinct here. Someone in your position, describing what happened to them, is the version people believe.

What happens to trust when AI is involved?

It falls, and it falls further the more of the work AI does. The Harris Poll UK found trust in an advert drops from seven in ten when it's made entirely by humans, to four in ten when AI tools are used, to two in ten when it's generated by AI alone. Six in ten said a person should always be involved in making advertising that uses AI.

The same research picked out what makes people suspicious. Images that look too perfect, scenes that feel unrealistic and small inconsistencies were the most common giveaways. That's an interesting turn. For years, polish was how a brand showed it had spent money. Now flawless can read as fake.

The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more people want to know whether it is.

Does it have to be the founder on camera?

No, and often it's better when it isn't only the founder. The most convincing person in a film is usually the one with the least reason to flatter the business.

On Barry Road it's the homeowner describing a full renovation in their own words, once the family had moved back in. On the Car Planet film for Plug In Stations, the whole thing is the customer talking. The installer never makes the claim about themselves, which is exactly what makes it usable in a sales conversation.

And La Fromagerie carries four people's accounts of the same business. The founder tells how it started, with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, and the cheesemongers and the wholesale side fill in what it is now. Four voices that don't sound rehearsed are harder to doubt than one polished one.

What if you or your team hate being on camera?

Most people do, at first. The good news is that documentary filming doesn't ask anyone to perform. Nothing's read off an autocue, and nobody's asked to do it again with more energy. The interviews are conversations, and the people who are most nervous at the start often give the best answers an hour in, once they've stopped noticing the camera.

Nobody has ever been more relaxed because someone said “just act natural”. A decent conversation does the job far better.

We've written a practical guide to preparing to be filmed for a brand film, and the short version is that you don't need to be good on camera. You need to know your subject, which you already do.

How do documentary films use real people differently?

They let the story come from the people instead of handing them a script. We spend time with a business before filming, work out what the story actually is, and then go and film conversations in the places the business really lives. La Fromagerie was filmed during trading hours, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. That's harder work. It also looks exactly like the shop you'd walk into, and no prompt can give you that.

The other difference is time. A documentary leaves room for the pause before someone answers and the work happening at the speed it really happens. Those are the moments that make a viewer feel they're seeing something true, and they're the hardest thing to fake.

Isn't AI content just cheaper to make?

Per piece, yes, and that's exactly the problem with it. When anyone can produce a polished video in an afternoon, polish stops telling the viewer anything about you. Feeds fill up with it, and it all starts to look the same. What can't be produced in an afternoon is access: the people in your business, the place they work and the things they've been through.

A smaller business usually has more of that than it thinks. The owner answers the phone. The person on camera is the person who'll turn up. That's something a big brand with a generated spokesperson can't buy, and it's worth putting on screen while it still stands out.

Is polished production a bad thing now?

No. Craft still matters. A badly lit, badly recorded film of real people tells the viewer you didn't care enough to do it properly. The point of a proper grade, proper sound and a patient edit is to show real people clearly. Smooth them into something that looks generated and you've thrown away the reason they were there.

Where I'd draw the line is anything that makes the person look less like themselves. Heavy retouching, a script they'd never say in real life, a set that looks nothing like where they work. Keep the people real and spend the budget on showing them well. If there's someone in your business people should hear from, tell us about them, or see more of the films we've made on our films page.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do we need professional actors for a brand film?
faqs.a: No, and for a documentary-style film you'd usually avoid them. The people who actually run the business, work in it or buy from it carry far more weight than anyone hired to play them, because viewers can tell. Actors make sense for scripted adverts and dramatised scenes. For a film meant to build trust, real people with real stories are the stronger choice.

faqs.q: Can we use customers in our brand film?
faqs.a: Yes, and they're often the most convincing people in it. Ask customers who had a genuinely good experience and are happy to talk about it, and film once the result is real. Keep it a conversation rather than a script, and get their written consent to appear and to the footage being used. A customer's own account is the version prospective buyers believe.

faqs.q: How many people should appear in a brand film?
faqs.a: As many as the story needs, which is usually fewer than people expect. One strong voice can carry a short film. A longer documentary often works best with two to four, each adding something the others can't, like the founder's history alongside the people doing the work now. Every extra person needs time on screen, so more voices usually means a longer film.

faqs.q: Is AI ever fine to use in a film about real people?
faqs.a: Yes, behind the scenes. Transcribing interviews, cleaning up audio, drafting captions and reframing clips for social don't change what anyone said or did. The line is making a real person appear to say or do something they didn't, or generating scenes presented as real. That undermines the whole point of filming real people, and platforms like YouTube ask you to label it.

stat.title: How many consumers trust an advert, by who made it
stat.takeaway: Trust drops sharply as AI takes over the work, so a film that shows real people doing real things has more to offer than ever.
