items.title: How to write a brand story: a step-by-step process
items.excerpt: How to write a brand story step by step: gather the raw material by talking, draft, find the voice, cut hard, and check it works for a page or a film.
items.coverAlt: A signwriter in a white shirt paints gold lettering with a fine brush onto a dark honours board of past names
items.body:
To write a brand story, talk first and write second. Record yourself or the founder answering a handful of plain questions, pull out the moments that are specific and true, put them in order, and then edit hard until it sounds like a person speaking. The best brand copy starts as speech, because that's where the honest detail lives.

This post is the writing process, step by step: how to gather the raw material, draft, find the voice, edit, and test the result, for a page on your site or the script for a film. What to put in it is covered in what a brand story should include, the order is in how a brand story should be structured, and the length question has its own post: how long a brand story should be.

Where do you start writing a brand story?

Not at a blank page. Writing a brand story from nothing is how you end up with "founded with a passion for excellence". Start by collecting what's already there, spoken out loud.

Sit down with whoever knows the business best and ask these, recording the answers on a phone:

  • What did you do before this, and what made you stop?
  • What was the first job, the first customer or the first thing you made?
  • What went wrong in the first year, and what did you do about it?
  • What do customers thank you for that you never advertised?
  • What would you refuse to do, even if it cost you the work?
  • Why does this matter to you more than it should?

Transcribe it, or use the phone's transcript. You're not writing yet. You're getting twenty minutes of material you'd never have produced by sitting and thinking.

How do you pick what goes in?

Read the transcript with a highlighter and mark everything that is specific, surprising or slightly awkward. Ignore anything abstract. "We always put the customer first" is out. "I drove to Kent at midnight because I'd promised her on the phone" is in.

Then choose a spine. Most brand stories have one thread running through them: a founder who left a job to do it properly, a craft that takes longer than anyone would choose, a mistake that shaped the business. Pick the thread with the most feeling and the most evidence behind it. The rest of the highlighted material either supports it or waits for another day.

The first draft is allowed to be terrible. The transcript isn't.

How do you draft it?

Write the rough version quickly, in the order things happened, in short sentences. Don't worry about elegance. A workable first draft has four parts:

  • A person, doing something. One or two sentences, in a real place.
  • The reason. Why they started or why they work this way.
  • The difficulty. What got in the way, and what they did.
  • What it means now. What changed, and what the reader gets from it.

If the structure feels wooden, you can reorder it later, using the options in the structure post. At this stage just get the pieces onto the page using your own words and the actual quotes from the recording. Quotes are gold. A good line from a transcript is better than anything you'd come up with.

Should it be in first person or third?

First person usually wins for a small business. "I started this in a garden shed" has more weight than "the founder started the business in a garden shed". If there are several founders or the story is about the team, "we" can work, but make sure a particular person is still visible. Third person suits a larger organisation, or a story about someone else, such as a customer.

How do you make it sound like a person?

This is where most brand copy falls over, so it's worth spending time on. The test I use is simple. Read it aloud. If you'd feel silly saying a sentence to a friend in a pub, change it.

Some specific habits help:

  • Use contractions. "We're", "it's" and "didn't" are how people talk.
  • Short sentences, then a longer one. Mix them. A run of the same length reads like a machine.
  • Plain words. "Use" not "utilise". "Help" not "facilitate". "Start" not "commence".
  • Name things. The shop's real name, the real street, the real material.
  • Say it once. If the point has landed, move on.
  • Cut the adjectives. Most of them can go. Keep the ones that tell you something.

Spoken language is also what makes a script work on camera. A line written for the eye, such as "we strive for excellence in all that we do", sounds odd in a person's mouth. Lines drawn from the transcript sound like them, because they are.

If you wouldn't say it out loud to a customer, don't write it in their story.

What should you cut?

More than feels comfortable. Here's a quick edit list:

  • The opening sentence, if it's a general statement about the industry.
  • Any line that begins "At [company name], we..."
  • Every use of passionate, innovative, bespoke (unless you really are, and say how), cutting-edge, leading, solutions, journey, or world-class.
  • Dates that don't change anything about the story.
  • A second example when the first already did the job.
  • The final paragraph, if it only repeats what you've already said.

Read what's left. If something is missing, put it back, but in the plain version. A story that's half as long and twice as specific almost always improves.

How do you write it for a film rather than a page?

Differently, because you're writing for ears and for pictures. The words on a page are for reading. The words for a film are mostly the person's own, so what you write is the structure and the questions, not the lines.

For a documentary brand film, I wouldn't script the interview. I'd write a short outline of the beats, the questions that draw each one out, and a list of what the camera needs to see while they talk. Then I'd record the person and build the final story from what they say. It means the words are theirs, and it avoids the stiff, recited feel of a script.

If you're writing a voiceover instead, keep it short, leave plenty of gaps for the pictures, and never describe what the viewer can already see. For a worked version of this in practice, our Nimrod Road film is the couple's own account of the renovation. It wasn't scripted and it reads better for it. For help turning a story into a brief a production company can work from, see how to write a video brief.

What does a rewrite look like?

Here's an invented before and after, to show the moves. The business is a small joinery firm.

Before: "Established in 2009, Hartley Joinery is a passionate team of craftspeople dedicated to delivering bespoke solutions of the highest quality to clients across the region."

After: "I left a site manager job in 2009 with a van, a bandsaw and a customer who wanted a staircase that didn't creak. It took three attempts to get right. She still sends a Christmas card."

The second version has a person, a place in time, a difficulty and a result, and it's shorter. Nothing in it is clever. Every detail came from a conversation, which is why it works. The first was written. The second was said.

Notice what the rewrite leaves out as well: the word quality, the region, the team and the mission. They're not wrong, they're just not the story. They can sit lower on the page, or in a different piece.

Is there a template you can copy?

A skeleton is useful as long as you treat it as scaffolding rather than a form to fill in. This one has served me well on both pages and film outlines:

  • One line that puts us somewhere. A person, a place, a moment.
  • One line on why it matters to them. The real reason.
  • Two or three lines on the hard part. What happened and what they did.
  • One line on what changed. For them or for the customer.
  • One line on what that means for you. What the reader can expect.

Keep the whole thing to a few short paragraphs for a page. If you want to know what else a fuller story might hold, look at the checklist in what should a brand story include.

What mistakes do people make when writing one?

  • Writing before listening. Without the transcript you get slogans.
  • Writing for the boss. The reader is a stranger with a problem. Write for them.
  • Packing in every achievement. Awards and accreditations belong in a list, not in the story.
  • Using the same words as everyone else. If it appears on a competitor's site, change it.
  • Over-editing the life out. After the third round of changes, check whether the odd, human detail is still there. If not, put it back.
  • Leaving it unfinished. A story half written sits on the site for years. Set a date, finish it, then improve it.

How do you check that it works?

Run three checks before you call it done.

  • The read-aloud test. Does every sentence sound like something a person would say?
  • The retell test. Ask someone to read it once, then tell you what it said. What they remember is what's working.
  • The swap test. Replace your company name with a competitor's. If the story still makes sense, it's too vague.

For a deeper set of tests, see what makes a good brand story.

How long does it take to write one?

Less than you'd think, once you've got the raw material. An hour of recorded conversation, an hour or two to transcribe and highlight, and a couple of hours to draft and edit. Most of the delay is waiting for people's time and for approvals. If a story has to pass through five reviewers, it will lose most of its character on the way, so I'd keep sign-off to the person whose story it is plus one other.

What if you're not a writer?

You don't need to be. This approach suits people who aren't, because the work is listening and cutting, not composing. If you can hold a conversation and tell which bits are interesting, you can write a brand story. And if the thought of it still makes you freeze, talk to someone who'll ask the questions for you.

Once you have the story, how to tell a brand story covers what to do with it: who tells it, in what format and where it goes. The whole series sits together in the complete guide to brand storytelling. And if you'd like help drawing your story out, on the page or on camera, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How do you write a brand story from scratch?
faqs.a: Record a conversation first. Ask the founder plain questions about the start, the first customer, what went wrong and what they refuse to compromise on. Highlight the specific, surprising moments, choose one thread to follow, and draft in short sentences using their own words. Then cut hard and read it aloud until it sounds like a person.

faqs.q: What should the first line of a brand story be?
faqs.a: Start with a person doing something in a real place rather than a statement about your industry or your mission. A specific image or moment gives the reader a reason to keep going. Avoid opening with the company name or a founding date unless it is the surprising part of the story.

faqs.q: Should a brand story be written in first or third person?
faqs.a: For a small business, first person usually works best because it sounds honest and puts a real person on the page. Use we if the story is about a team, and keep a named individual visible. Third person suits larger organisations or stories about customers, where the writer is not the subject.

faqs.q: Can AI write a brand story for me?
faqs.a: It can tidy a draft or suggest structure, but it can't supply the true, specific moments that make a story worth reading, because it doesn't know your business. Those come from real conversations. If you use AI, feed it your transcript and check every claim, then rewrite until it sounds like you.

items.title: How to tell a brand story: who, which format, and where
items.excerpt: How to tell a brand story: who should tell it, which format suits it, how to draw it out of people, and where to show it so your customers see it.
items.coverAlt: An artist in a pink top talks to someone off camera with open hands in front of framed manga-style artworks
items.body:
To tell a brand story, find the true moment that explains your business, pick the person who lived it, choose a format that lets them tell it in their own words, and put it where your customers already look. Then keep telling it, in different lengths, across your site, sales conversations and social channels. Telling is a process, not a single post.

This post is the delivery side: who tells the story, in which format, in what order, and where it goes. It isn't about the words on the page, which is covered in how to write a brand story, or the shape of the story, which is in how a brand story should be structured. The first line of a story gets its own post too: how brand storytelling should begin.

What's the first step in telling a brand story?

Decide what it's for. A story told to win tenders looks different from one told to attract staff, and both look different from one told to make a cold lead warm. If you start with "we should have a brand story", you'll make something pleasant that does no job.

Write one sentence: "This story should make [who] feel or understand [what], so they [do what]." For example, "make a procurement manager understand we're a stable, careful supplier, so they invite us to tender." It sounds obvious, and hardly anyone does it. It's the same discipline I describe in why a brand film needs a business goal.

Who should tell the story?

The person who lived it, in their own words. That's the whole principle, and it's the difference between a documentary brand film and a promo. A voiceover reading a script tells people about you. A founder talking at the counter of their own shop shows them.

Some practical points from the shoots I've done:

  • Choose one lead voice. Usually the founder, though not always. Add one or two others who give a different angle, such as the person who runs the daily work or a customer.
  • Pick people who like talking about it. Enthusiasm for the subject matters far more than camera confidence.
  • Don't use the person with the best title. Use the one with the best stories.
  • Let them speak in their own register. If they swear a bit when they're excited, or go quiet before the important bit, keep it. That's what makes it theirs.

If your lead is nervous, how to prepare for being filmed will take the edge off. And it helps to know what actually happens on the day, which I cover in what a brand film shoot day in London looks like.

Which format should you tell it in?

There are four formats I'd consider, in rough order of impact.

  • A documentary film. The person tells it on camera, with the work shown over their words. Best when trust is the main thing you're selling.
  • A written story with photographs. Cheaper and quicker, and it works well for About pages and press. Less effective at showing character.
  • Short social video. One clip, one idea. Good for reaching new people, poor at telling the whole story.
  • Live or in-person. Pitches, open days and events. Powerful, but it doesn't scale unless you record it.

My own bias is clear, but it isn't only bias. A film is the one format that lets a stranger see your face, your premises and how you talk, all in about four minutes. If you do only one, it's usually the film, with the other three cut or written from it. The comparison between a brand documentary and a conventional video is in brand documentary vs corporate video, and the format itself is explained in what a brand story video is.

Pick the format that lets the right person say the right thing in their own voice.

How do you draw the story out of someone?

You don't ask them for "the story". People freeze on that question. You ask about the smaller things and the story turns up by itself.

On a shoot, I'd usually start with something easy, such as how a normal day begins. Then I move towards what they remember: the first customer, the worst week, the moment they nearly stopped. I ask for an example every time somebody says a general thing like "we care about quality". "Tell me about a time" gets a story. "What are your values?" gets a slogan.

I also leave silences. Most people fill a pause with the real answer. It's the most useful interview habit I've got and it costs nothing.

For a long founder story, such as our La Fromagerie documentary, the structure arrives in the edit. Several people, including the founder, the cheesemongers and the wholesale side, each give their account of the same business. We cut between them. None of them was told what to say. They were asked good questions and given time.

In what order should you tell it?

You'll find a fuller treatment in the structure post, but a delivery rule of thumb is to start with a person doing something, move to why it matters, show the difficulty, then show what changed. End on something the viewer can carry away rather than a call to action and a logo.

For multiple pieces, plan a hierarchy:

  • The main film, three to five minutes, tells the whole thread.
  • Short cuts of 30 to 90 seconds, each carrying one idea.
  • Vertical clips of a single strong sentence with captions.
  • Written and photographic versions for your site and press.

All of it comes from the same shoot. Deciding the cuts before you film is cheaper than asking for them afterwards, which I explain in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

Where should you tell it?

Where your customers already are, which is almost certainly more places than one. A useful split:

  • Your website. The home page, About page and key service pages. This is where people go to check you out before getting in touch.
  • Your sales conversations. Send the film before a first call. It does the introduction so the call can start in a better place.
  • YouTube and social. Where new people find you. The long film lives on YouTube. Short cuts go to Instagram, LinkedIn and TikTok.
  • Email and proposals. A link in a signature or a tender document puts a human in front of the reader.

The choice depends on who you're talking to. Where to use your brand film goes through each place in more detail.

Does where people watch change how you tell it?

Yes. Ofcom's Media Nations 2025 found UK viewers spent an average of 39 minutes a day on YouTube in 2024, and 16 of those minutes were on the household TV set. The same film might be watched on a phone in a queue or on the big screen at home, so one story often needs two different cuts, and it's worth knowing which audience you're talking to before you decide where to put it. The viewing habits of your audience decide where a film should live. If your customers are younger, the film belongs on YouTube and social. If they're older and higher up in a company, it belongs on your site, in your proposals and in your emails.

Screens matter as well. A film watched on a phone on a train has to work with the sound off and in a vertical crop, so captions and framing are decided at the shoot, not afterwards.

The most common reason a good story fails is that it was sent to the wrong place.

How often should you tell it?

More than you think. A story you tell once is an announcement. Told repeatedly, in different lengths and from different angles, it becomes what people know you for. You don't need to reshoot it. You need to keep re-telling it as you add new evidence: a new customer, a new product, a milestone.

Our Nimrod Road film is a good example of working with what you have. It was filmed after the renovation, with the family already back in the house, so the "before" came from the original listing photos. The couple told it as their own account. It didn't need a time machine, only a decision about how to use what was available.

What does the process look like from idea to published?

In rough order, and with timings that vary a lot by project:

  • Conversation. An hour or so with the founder to find the thread and the job it needs to do. Cheap, and the most valuable hour of the process.
  • Plan. Who's on camera, where, what the work looks like at its best, and which cuts you want at the end. This is where the brief gets written, and how to write a video brief will help.
  • Shoot. Usually a day, sometimes two. Interviews first while people are fresh, then the work and the place.
  • Edit. The story is built here, from what people said. Expect a first cut, one round of changes and a final.
  • Release. Site, YouTube, social, email, proposals. Plan this before you film, so the files are the right shape.
  • Review. After a few months, look at what you said you wanted. Did sales calls change? Are the enquiries better?

Most of the waiting is on the client side. Approvals, availability and finding the right day for everyone. A story told by three busy people takes longer to schedule than to film.

What mistakes should you avoid when telling it?

  • Telling it once. A single launch post is gone by the weekend. Keep it in circulation.
  • Reading from a script. People who recite sound like they're reciting. Use questions and a rough list of topics instead.
  • Over-polishing. Take out the stumbles and you take out the person. Clean up the sound, keep the character.
  • Telling too many stories at once. One thread per piece. If you have three good ones, make three pieces.
  • Hiding the ending. Some brands spend three minutes talking and never get to what they do. Say what you do, plainly, before the end.
  • Forgetting the viewer's next step. A soft, clear line telling people how to get in touch, and nothing pushier.

What does it cost to get wrong?

Mostly time and credibility. A story told in the wrong format, to the wrong audience or in a voice that isn't the speaker's feels off even if no one can say why. The fix is rarely a bigger budget. It's going back to the basics: one clear job, one true person, one format that suits the telling.

If you'd like all the strands in one place, the complete guide to brand storytelling links to every post in this series. And if you've got a story and you're not sure how to tell it, get in touch and we'll work out the best way.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What's the best way to tell a brand story?
faqs.a: Let the person who lived it tell it in their own words, ideally on camera, with the work shown alongside. A documentary-style film does this well because viewers see a real face and hear a real voice. Then cut shorter versions from the same material for your site, social channels and sales conversations.

faqs.q: How do you tell a brand story without a big budget?
faqs.a: Start with one person, good sound and a quiet place. A phone and a clip-on microphone can capture an honest interview, and a written version with a few photographs costs even less. Spend the effort on the questions and the editing. A simple, true story told well beats an expensive, empty one.

faqs.q: Where should a brand story be published first?
faqs.a: Your own website, usually the About page or home page, because that's where people check you out before getting in touch. After that, put the long version on YouTube and the shorter cuts on the social channels your customers use. Send the link in proposals and before first calls.

faqs.q: How often should you retell your brand story?
faqs.a: Regularly. A single post is an announcement, but a story repeated in different lengths and from fresh angles becomes your reputation. Update it with new evidence such as customers, milestones or projects, and keep the core thread consistent so people recognise it each time they meet it.

items.title: What makes a good brand story? Seven tests to run
items.excerpt: What makes a good brand story: seven practical tests, warning signs of a weak one, and real examples of specific, true storytelling that people actually repeat.
items.coverAlt: A jeweller in a black jumper and pearl necklace looks off camera during an interview in front of a glass display cabinet
items.body:
A good brand story is specific, true and about a person. It has a clear difficulty and a change, it shows its proof instead of claiming it, and it leaves the viewer knowing something they couldn't have guessed about you. If it could be swapped onto a competitor's website without anyone noticing, it isn't good yet.

This post is the quality check. Rather than defining the thing or walking through how to write one, it gives you seven tests to run on a story, the warning signs of a weak one, and examples of the difference. The basics are in what brand storytelling is, the checklist of parts is in what a brand story should include, and the drafting process is in how to write a brand story.

What are the tests of a good brand story?

I use seven. A story that passes five or six is in good shape. One that passes two or three needs another go.

Is it specific?

"We care about quality" fails. "We make each pair in 210 steps and it takes six months" passes. Specifics are what a viewer remembers and what a competitor can't borrow. If you can swap a number, a name or a place in your story for another without it changing anything, it was vague.

Is it true?

Obvious, but it's where many stories fail quietly. A founder polishes the origin story until it sounds like a pitch, and it loses the one slightly awkward detail that made it real. Customers can't always say what's off, but they can feel it. Keep the odd bits in.

Is it about a person?

People connect to people. A story about "our team" is a story about nobody. Pick one face. A founder, a maker, a customer. The viewer should be able to describe them to a friend afterwards.

Is there a difficulty?

Without something in the way, there's nothing to resolve. It doesn't need to be dramatic. A renovation that had to be finished in eight weeks with a baby due. A shoemaker whose order takes six months from first measurement to delivery. The obstacle is what gives the audience something to lean towards.

Is there a change?

By the end, something has to be different. The business grew, the customer's problem went away, the maker passed the skill to someone else. If a viewer reaches the end and thinks "so what happened?", the change is missing.

Does it show its proof?

Anyone can say they're the best. A good story shows the workshop, the work, the customer, the result. In film terms, it's the difference between a person saying "we're meticulous" over a shot of a logo and the camera staying on a hand as it does the work at the speed it really happens.

Would someone repeat it?

The final test is the one I find most useful. After watching or reading, could somebody retell it in two sentences to a friend? If yes, it's working. If they'd have to say "it was a nice film, I can't quite remember what it was about", it isn't.

If nobody can retell it in two sentences, it's a mood, not a story.

What does a good brand story look like in practice?

Our signwriting film is a handy illustration, because the subject is a trade that's almost entirely hand and eye. The film doesn't explain signwriting. It watches the brush load, the single unbroken line and the finished sign on the street. A viewer comes away understanding why it's hard, without anyone telling them. That's proof doing the work that a claim would normally try to do.

The Catherine Marche film takes a different route. It's built around why she works only in recycled metal, told by her at the bench. The reason is the story. The jewellery is the evidence.

Beyond our own work, two campaigns are worth studying for their craft. Dove's Real Beauty Sketches (2013) is built on a single surprising moment, and Patagonia's "Don't Buy This Jacket" Black Friday advert (2011) works because a clothing brand told customers to buy less, which was a real position it then had to live up to. Neither relies on a slogan. Both rely on something that happened or something the brand actually did.

What are the warning signs of a weak brand story?

  • Everyone says the same word. "Passion", "innovation" and "solutions" crop up in a hundred other brands' stories. If you can predict the vocabulary, it's weak.
  • It's told from the company's side. "We're proud to announce" is a press release. The viewer is the hero, or at least a person they recognise is.
  • No proof on screen. A lot of talking over generic stock footage and drone shots.
  • Too many people. Eight voices in four minutes means no voice. One or two, deep, beats six on the surface.
  • It never mentions a problem. Smooth is suspicious.
  • It's long on history, short on now. Founding dates are fine, but the viewer needs to know what you do for people today.

If the script includes the phrase "passionate team of experts", the experts have left the building.

What does weak turned into strong look like?

Here's a made up example, so nobody gets embarrassed. A plumbing firm's About page says: "We're a family business with over twenty years of experience, committed to delivering the highest standards of service." It's not untrue. It just isn't anything.

Now sit with the owner for twenty minutes and ask what a bad week looked like. He tells you about the winter the boilers all failed on the same cold weekend, and how he and his brother drove around the borough until two in the morning because they'd told one elderly customer they'd be there. That's the story. It has a person, a difficulty, a promise kept and a reason the business works the way it does.

Nothing about the facts changed. The first version is a description. The second is something that happened. That move, from description to event, is the single biggest upgrade you can make to any brand story, and it almost always starts with a conversation rather than a writing session.

How should a good story handle the difficult parts?

Include them, proportionately. A difficulty isn't a confession. It's the part of the story that proves the business is real. Nobody believes a company that has never had a bad day.

The rule I use is to show the problem, show what was done about it and show who did it. Leave out blame, drama for its own sake, and anything that would embarrass a customer or colleague. And if a part of the story is still raw for the person telling it, check they're comfortable with it being public before it goes anywhere. A story that costs the storyteller something they didn't agree to give is a bad story, however well it plays.

What's the biggest mistake you see?

Starting with the logo and the mission. Most films I'm asked to fix open on the company name over a sweeping drone shot, then a voiceover saying what the company believes. Within ten seconds the viewer knows it's an advert. Start instead on a person doing something or saying something unexpected, and the viewer stays long enough to find out why.

The runner-up is trying to cover everything. A brand story isn't the whole company in four minutes. It's one true thread that makes a viewer curious enough to ask about the rest. Pick the thread with the most feeling in it and let the rest wait.

Who should judge your brand story?

Not only you. You're too close to it, and so is everyone in your office. Ask two people who fit your ideal customer, plus one person who knows nothing about your industry. Show it to them cold, and ask what they'd say about the business afterwards. Their answers beat any internal review, because they're hearing it for the first time, which is exactly how your future customers will.

Be careful with feedback from people who'd prefer to see themselves in it. Everyone wants a line, a logo or a thank you. Politely keep to the thread that passes the tests.

Do good brand stories need a big budget?

No. The tests above cost nothing to run. Whether a story is good depends on the thinking and the honesty, not the kit. A phone, decent sound and a founder who talks easily can produce something far better than a glossy production with nothing to say.

A bigger budget buys you things around the story: better light, sound that's easier to listen to, more coverage of the work and careful editing. It doesn't buy the story itself. I've written more on the difference between a polished video and one people actually watch in how to make a brand video people watch.

Does a good story have to be emotional?

It has to be felt, which isn't the same as being sad or sentimental. A dry, funny founder explaining something they've obsessed about for twenty years is an emotional experience. A cheese shop owner describing a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed is emotional because it's tender and a bit absurd.

Trying to force a tear usually backfires. Viewers are sceptical of manufactured emotion, and the sensible approach is to let the person be themselves and trust the audience to feel what they feel. If someone cries in an interview, that's theirs, and the decision on whether it stays in is a joint one with them.

Why does consistency make a story better?

A brand story isn't one film. It's what comes through across your site, your sales calls, your social posts and your packaging. The most memorable brands tell the same true story a hundred ways. Familiarity matters too. Feefo's 2026 research with 3,000 UK consumers found 63% are concerned about fake reviews. People are wary of what brands say about themselves. A good story, told consistently and visibly true, is how you become believable.

That's the reason I like documentary-style brand films. One shoot gives you enough real material to cut a long film, short clips and quotes that all say the same thing in the same voice. It also means a sales team and a social team aren't inventing different versions of who you are. The difference between this approach and a conventional promo is set out in brand documentary vs corporate video.

How do you test yours before you spend anything?

Here's a cheap exercise. Tell your story out loud to someone who doesn't work in your industry, with no slides. Watch their face. Where do they lean in? Where do they glance at their phone? Those are the parts to keep and the parts to cut. Then ask them to repeat it to you afterwards. What they remember is your real story. What they forget was filler.

Do that, then work through the seven tests, and you'll have a version worth putting in front of a camera. The wider picture is in the complete guide to brand storytelling, and if you'd like a second pair of eyes on your story, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the most important part of a good brand story?
faqs.a: Specificity. A story full of real names, places, numbers and moments is memorable and can't be borrowed by a competitor. Vague claims such as passion and quality could belong to anyone. If you can change a detail in your story without it making any difference, that part isn't doing any work and needs replacing with something true and particular.

faqs.q: Can a boring business have a good brand story?
faqs.a: Yes. The story rarely comes from the product. It comes from the person who cares about it, the odd detail that shows it and the problem they solved. Trades, manufacturers and professional firms often have the most distinctive stories because nobody has told them before. The work is finding the real detail and filming it honestly.

faqs.q: How long should a good brand story be?
faqs.a: As long as it takes to pass the tests, and no longer. For film, that usually means one main piece of a few minutes with shorter cuts drawn from it. A story told with specifics tends to be shorter than a vague one, because every line is doing a job. There is a dedicated post on length in this series.

faqs.q: Do good brand stories need to be dramatic?
faqs.a: No. Drama can help, but a quiet story about a craft, a family business or a changed process is often more convincing. What matters is a real person, a real difficulty and a real change. Manufactured drama tends to feel false. Honest, small and specific almost always beats big and generic.

items.title: What we keep hearing from businesses about video
items.excerpt: No faces on the website, stock passed off as content, a decision maker who isn't in the room, missed timing and camera nerves. What we hear, and how to fix it.
items.coverAlt: An engineer in hi-vis smiling on camera on site
items.body:
When businesses talk to us about video, the same handful of things come up again and again, whatever the sector. The work's excellent but there isn't one real face on the website. The content they've got turns out to be stock. The person keen on a film isn't the person who signs it off. The moment that would have made the story has already gone. And nobody wants to be on camera. Every one of these is fixable, usually without spending more.

I'm keeping this general and anonymised. These are patterns, and if you recognise your own business in one, you're in very good company.

Why does great work end up with no faces on the website?

Because the people doing the best work are usually too busy doing it to think about how it looks. You get a site with brilliant project photos, a logo, a phone number and nobody. Or a team page with a row of grey silhouettes.

The trouble is that buyers choose people. For anything expensive or personal, someone wants to know who's turning up, who they'll be dealing with and whether they seem trustworthy. A business with no faces on its site is asking a stranger to trust it blind, and a competitor with a slightly weaker portfolio and a friendly face on the homepage will often win that one.

The fix is smaller than people expect. Proper photos of the team at work, a short film of the founder explaining why they started, and one or two customers talking about the result. That's often a single day. Our Spotlight shoot exists for exactly this.

What's wrong with "we've already got content"?

Often, nothing. But sometimes, when you look properly, the content is stock footage, AI images and a few phone clips from years ago. Stock fills space, but it can't prove anything about you, because the same handshake and the same smiling team in the same glass office appear on hundreds of other sites. People have learned to scroll straight past it.

The test I use is simple. If you swapped your logo for a competitor's, would the content still make sense? If it would, it's doing no work for you. Footage of your actual people, premises and jobs can only belong to you, and that's why people believe it.

The Super Efficient drainage film shows real content made without much fuss. One day on a live job in Enfield, filmed start to finish with no reshoots, became an eight minute YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels. Nothing staged, and nothing that could belong to any other company.

Why do video projects stall when someone else decides?

Because the person who gets in touch is often a marketing lead, an office manager or a founder's right hand, and the decision sits with a director, a board or a partner who wasn't on the call. The enthusiasm doesn't travel up the chain. What reaches the decision maker is a line on a spreadsheet with a number next to it.

It's common enough that Wyzowl's annual survey lists being unable to convince key decision makers as one of the reasons marketers give for not using video at all. If that's where you are, give the person deciding something to react to besides a price: the job the film will do, everything that comes out of one shoot, and an example from a similar business. Our free 56-page guide, Before the camera comes out, was written partly for this. Send it upwards.

Better still, get the person who signs it off into a conversation early. Twenty minutes with them saves weeks of relaying questions back and forth.

Somewhere in the UK right now, a brilliant video idea is sitting in the inbox of someone who's on holiday until the 14th.

What happens when the timing window closes?

Lots of stories have a moment, and once it's gone you can't film it again. A building going up. A project finishing. An anniversary. A team that's about to change. A customer in the first weeks after the work's done, while they're still delighted with it.

We see it with renovation films. On Nimrod Road, the family had already moved back in by the time we filmed, so the before only exists in the original listing photos. It still works, because the couple tell it well and the listing photos are cut against the finished rooms. But it shows how easily the most visual part of a story disappears while a business is still deciding.

So when someone says "let's do it next year", I'd ask what will have changed by then. Sometimes nothing, and waiting's fine. Often the scaffolding's down, the event's over or the people involved have moved on. A film takes six to ten weeks from the first conversation, so if there's a date that matters, count backwards from it.

What if nobody wants to be on camera?

Almost nobody does at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal. People worry about how they'll look, what they'll say and whether colleagues will take the mickey afterwards.

Almost nobody wants to be on camera at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal.

A few things make a real difference. Interviews run as conversations, with nothing to learn. No autocue. Filming people doing the job they're good at, which relaxes them because they're on their own ground. And time. The good material tends to arrive once people stop noticing the camera, which is one reason our films take two to three shoot days rather than an hour.

It doesn't have to be the boss, either. Sometimes the best person in the film is the engineer who explains things clearly, a long serving member of the team, or a customer. If you're the one going on camera and you're dreading it, read how to prepare for being filmed. It's less painful than you're expecting.

Is any of this a reason not to make a film?

Not really. Each of these comes down to planning and permission. The businesses that end up with a film they're proud of tend to decide early what it's for, get the decision maker involved, pick their moment and let real people speak. Budget matters, but less than any of that.

If one of these sounds like your business, tell us where you're stuck. If a film isn't the right spend yet, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we make a brand film if the boss won't appear in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The founder or MD doesn't have to be the face of the film, and sometimes someone else tells the story better. An engineer who explains the work clearly, a long serving member of staff or a customer talking about the result can carry a film well. It's worth the boss appearing briefly if they can, because buyers like to know who's in charge, but it isn't essential.

faqs.q: Is stock footage ever fine to use in a business video?
faqs.a: It's fine for small jobs like filling a gap in an explainer or illustrating something you genuinely can't film, such as a general street scene. It shouldn't carry the story. Anything meant to build trust, like who you are, what your work looks like and what customers say, needs real footage of your own people and jobs, because stock can't prove anything about your business specifically.

faqs.q: How do I pitch a video budget to a director or board?
faqs.a: Lead with the job the film will do and the business problem it's tied to, then the price. Show everything that comes from one shoot, such as the main film, short cuts, vertical clips and photography, so the cost reads per use rather than as one video. An example from a similar business helps. Better still, get the decision maker on an early call so questions don't get lost in relay.

faqs.q: What if the best moment for our film has already passed?
faqs.a: You can often still make a strong film. Existing photos, plans and the people who were there can rebuild the before, and a customer talking about a finished result is very convincing. What you lose is the footage of the moment itself. For the future, photograph the start of important projects properly as a habit, even if you're not sure a film will follow.

stat.title: Why marketers who don't use video say they don't
stat.takeaway: Most of the reasons businesses hold off on video are about doubt, time and planning, which can usually be talked through before anything is spent.

items.title: Why is brand storytelling important for a business?
items.excerpt: Why brand storytelling matters for UK businesses: it builds trust, makes you memorable, supports price, helps hiring, and what it costs you to skip it.
items.coverAlt: Two shoemaking cofounders sit side by side at a wooden bench in front of shelves of wooden shoe lasts, the woman glancing
items.body:
Brand storytelling is important because people buy from businesses they understand and trust, and a story is the quickest honest way to earn both. It makes you memorable, gives customers a reason to choose you beyond price, and gives staff, partners and the press something true to repeat. It matters most when your competitors all look the same.

This post is the business case: the practical reasons a UK company should bother, what the evidence does and doesn't back up, and what it costs you to skip it. For the psychology of why stories stick, see why storytelling works in marketing. For hard numbers on results, how effective storytelling is in marketing goes further.

Why do customers choose a business with a story?

Because most businesses in a given market look and sound the same. Open ten websites for electricians, accountants, gyms or marketing agencies in the same postcode and count how many say "friendly, professional, reliable". Every one of them. When the claims are identical, the buyer falls back on the one thing that's easy to compare, which is price.

A story breaks that deadlock. It gives somebody a reason to pick you that isn't a number. They know who started it, why, what you won't compromise on and what working with you feels like. None of that is on a price list, and none of it can be copied by a competitor with a cheaper quote.

I've seen this on shoots many times. The film isn't what changes the business, the clarity is. When a founder has said out loud, on camera, why they do things the way they do, they can say it in sales calls, on tenders and to new hires. The film just makes it travel.

Does it really build trust?

Trust is the bit I'd put first, because it's getting harder to come by. Ofcom research from late 2024 found four in ten UK adults had come across misinformation or deepfake content in the previous four weeks, and most of them had seen it online. People are on their guard, and they're right to be.

In that climate, polished claims carry less weight than they used to. What carries more is evidence that real people are behind the business: a face, a voice, a workshop that exists, a customer who says something specific. A brand story done properly is a pile of that evidence in one place.

The more people doubt what they see online, the more a real person in a real room is worth.

It also helps that stories are hard to fake convincingly. Anyone can write "passionate about quality". Very few can spend four minutes explaining the 210 steps in a hand-sewn shoe, as the two makers in our Carreducker film do, without the detail giving them away one way or the other.

Why does a story make you memorable?

Nobody remembers a feature list. They remember a moment, a person or something that surprised them. If someone watches your film on a Tuesday and brings it up on a Friday, the story is what they repeat, not the services page.

That matters because most purchases in B2B and in high-value consumer decisions aren't made on the day someone first hears of you. There's a gap, often weeks or months, between first contact and the decision. A story is what survives the gap. When your name comes up in a meeting, somebody says "oh, they're the ones who..." and finishes the sentence with your story.

That's the practical test of whether your brand storytelling is working. Can a customer finish the sentence "they're the ones who..." without looking at your website?

Does storytelling help with price?

It does, indirectly. When a customer understands why you do something the way you do, the price makes more sense. It's the difference between "£X for a pair of shoes" and "£X for a pair that takes two people six months to make by hand". Nothing about the shoes changed. The customer's understanding of what they're paying for did.

I'd never promise that a film will let you put your prices up, because it depends on the business and the market. But I've seen over and over that businesses with a clear story get fewer "can you do it cheaper?" conversations, because the people who come to them already know what they're buying.

That's connected to why a film should have a job to do. I've written about that in why a brand film needs a business goal.

What does it do for hiring and staff?

More than most owners expect. A story tells potential employees what it's like to work somewhere and what the business stands for, and it tells existing staff what they're part of. The people in the film become the best recruitment material you've got, because candidates see how they speak about the job when nobody's selling.

There's a quieter effect too. The staff who appear in your film tend to stand a bit taller afterwards. They've been asked to explain what they do and why it matters, and most don't get asked that very often. If you're building the case for this side of it, take a look at recruitment and employer brand videos.

I've yet to hear a candidate say "I applied because of your mission statement".

Does it matter for B2B as well as consumer brands?

Yes, possibly more. In B2B, several people have to agree before anything is bought, and none of them has time to read everything. A short film that explains who you are lets one champion inside the buyer's business pass your story to the others without having to retell it badly.

Our char.gy work is a good example. Being certified as a B Corp is hard to earn and dull to explain, so we let the people who'd done the work explain it in plain language. The film is now the most viewed video on their YouTube channel. Complex, serious subjects don't need to be told in a complicated way, and they often land best when told through the people who lived them.

What does the evidence actually say?

I'd rather be straight about this. There's plenty of research on video and on trust, but very little that cleanly proves "story X produced Y extra pounds". Be wary of anyone quoting a precise multiple for what a story does to sales. Most of those figures come from marketing surveys that ask people what they think works, which isn't the same as measuring it.

What I'd rest the case on is simpler and easier to check against your own business. Do customers mention your story unprompted? Do enquiries arrive already warm? Do you spend less time explaining who you are in the first call? Those are the signs I look for with clients, and they show up in sales conversations long before they show up on a dashboard.

The Ofcom figures above are a good example of the kind of evidence worth trusting. They don't claim stories sell more. They show the environment you're talking into, one where people are more guarded about what they see online. How a business responds to that is a judgement call, and mine is that showing real people is the best response going.

What if my business seems boring?

Almost nobody thinks their business is interesting, and almost every business is. The cabling manufacturer, the drainage firm, the accountant who's been in the same building for thirty years. What makes it interesting isn't the product. It's the person who cares about it more than seems reasonable, and the specific, slightly odd detail that shows it.

You don't have to be glamorous. A day on a drainage job in Enfield turned into a longform YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels for one client of ours, because the work and the people were real and nobody tried to dress it up. Ordinary trades are often easier to film well than polished ones, because there's nothing to hide.

If you're in a regulated sector, such as finance, law or healthcare, you can still tell a story. It just needs to stay inside what you're allowed to claim. Stick to the people, the process and the reasons, and leave outcome promises out.

How do you know if it's working?

Pick one or two things before you start, and look at them after a few months. Some options:

  • Sales calls. Do prospects mention the film or the story without being asked?
  • Enquiry quality. Are the people getting in touch closer to your ideal customer than before?
  • Win rate on tenders and pitches. Does the film travel with your proposals, and what happens when it does?
  • Hiring. Do candidates mention it, and are they a better fit?
  • Watch figures. Views matter less than whether people watch to the end, but they tell you where the film is landing.

None of these needs special software. It needs somebody to keep notes. If you want help picking the right measure for your goal, our post on how video makes a business money is a sensible companion.

What does it cost you not to have one?

Three things, in my experience.

  • You compete on price. When there's nothing to tell, the only difference left is the number at the bottom of the quote.
  • You're forgettable. Customers can't recommend you in a sentence, so they don't, or they describe you generically.
  • Other people tell your story for you. Reviews, competitors and search results fill in the gaps, and you don't control what they say.

None of those are dramatic. They're a slow drag on enquiries, referrals and margin that you'll never see as a line on a report, which is why it's easy to put off.

Is it worth it for a small business?

I'd argue small businesses benefit most. A large company has a recognised name and a marketing budget to push it. A sole trader or a ten person firm has the owner, the work and the people, and those are exactly the ingredients of a good story. You can't outspend a national brand, but you can be more real than one.

The caution I'd add is that a story only works if it's true and you actually deliver on it. If the film says you care about service and your phone goes unanswered for days, the gap shows. That's why I like to film the business as it is, rather than as it wishes it were.

What should you do first?

Before you think about cameras, get clear on what the story is. If you're not sure where to start, what makes a good brand story gives you the tests to apply, and the plain definition is in what brand storytelling is.

Then decide what you want the story to do: win tenders, attract better customers, hire, or support sales calls. A story with a job is far easier to make and far easier to measure than one made because everyone else has one. Our guide to how video makes a business money goes through the ways that plays out.

You can see how all the pieces fit together in the complete guide to brand storytelling. And if you'd like to talk about whether a film is right for your business, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Why is brand storytelling important for small businesses?
faqs.a: Small businesses can't outspend bigger rivals, but they can be more real. The owner, the work and the team are the ingredients of a strong story, and customers can meet the person behind the business. A clear story gives people a reason to choose you beyond price and something specific to say when they recommend you.

faqs.q: Does brand storytelling increase sales?
faqs.a: It can support sales by building trust and giving buyers a reason to choose you, but I wouldn't promise a number. A story works on the stage before the sale, when people are deciding who to trust. Results depend on whether the story is true, where it's shown and how well your enquiries are handled afterwards.

faqs.q: How long does it take for brand storytelling to pay off?
faqs.a: It's rarely instant. A film can start helping straight away on sales calls and tenders, but the wider effect of being remembered and recommended builds over months. That's why I'd plan to use the same story across your website, social channels and sales material for a long period, rather than treating it as a single campaign.

faqs.q: Can brand storytelling backfire?
faqs.a: Yes, if the story isn't true or the business doesn't deliver what it promises. Customers notice the gap between a warm film and a poor experience quickly. Keep it honest, include the real difficulties, and tell the version you can live up to every day. Invented or exaggerated stories do more harm than having none.

items.title: Brand storytelling: the complete guide for UK business
items.excerpt: A complete guide to brand storytelling for UK businesses: what it is, why it works, how to build and structure a story, put it on video and use it in marketing.
items.coverAlt: The founder gestures with both hands as she talks over a coffee cup, shelves of jars and a basket of walnuts behind her
items.body:
Brand storytelling is the practice of explaining who you are, what you do and why it matters through a real story with people in it, rather than a list of features. Done well, it makes a business easier to remember, easier to trust and easier to choose. The short version is in what brand storytelling is, and this guide covers the rest.

I make documentary brand films for a living, so I've watched a lot of businesses find their story on camera, and a lot more fail to find it on paper. This guide walks through the whole subject in the order a UK business owner tends to need it: what it is, why it works, how to build a story, how to structure it, how to put it on video, how to use it in your marketing, and what good looks like. Every section links to a deeper answer on the questions that come up most, so you can read it straight through or jump to the part you're stuck on.

What is brand storytelling, and who does it?

Strip the jargon away and it's this: a business tells people where it came from, what it believes, who it helps and what changed because of it, in a way a stranger can follow. That's the plain version of the answer in what is brand storytelling. It isn't a slogan or a mission statement. It's the account of events behind them.

The marketing definition is narrower, and it's worth knowing the difference. Brand storytelling in marketing means using that account deliberately, across your website, your sales conversations, your social posts and your films, so each piece adds to the same picture instead of starting from scratch. A founder telling the origin story at a networking event is storytelling. Doing it on purpose, in the same shape, everywhere a customer might meet you, is the marketing version.

It's also not a job for one department. Most businesses already have someone doing it without the title, and who a brand storyteller is often turns out to be the founder, the longest serving member of staff or the customer who tells it better than anyone. Sometimes it's an outsider whose job is to ask the questions you've stopped asking yourself. On shoots, that's usually what I end up doing: asking the obvious questions that insiders no longer notice are interesting.

The practice isn't limited to household names either. If you want to see which brands use storytelling, the list runs from the very large to a three shop cheese business in London, and the small ones often do it better because they've got a real person to put at the front.

Why does storytelling work, and does it actually pay?

People don't remember bullet points, they remember what happened to someone. That's the simple reason behind why storytelling works in marketing: a story gives the listener a person to follow, a problem to care about and an outcome to wait for. A list of benefits gives them nothing to hold on to. When I cut an interview, the lines that make the final film are almost never the polished claims. They're the bit where somebody says what went wrong before it went right.

There's a wider argument for it too, which I've covered in why brand storytelling matters and why storytelling is important in business. The first is about the customer: what a story does to their trust and memory. The second is about the business itself, because a company that can tell its own story clearly usually knows what it's for, which makes hiring, pricing and sales conversations easier.

Then there's the question every sensible owner asks, which is whether it pays for itself. How effective storytelling is in marketing depends on how you measure it, and I'm wary of anyone who promises a figure. What I can say is that money is following video. The IPA's Bellwether Report for the second quarter of 2026 found video was the only main media area where UK companies raised budgets, with a net balance of +8.2%, while main media as a whole managed +1.5%. Marketers are putting their money where they expect people to watch.

None of that means every business needs a film tomorrow. It means the audience for a well told story on screen is already there and already used to watching it.

One more thing before moving on. Storytelling isn't a tactic you bolt on, and whether storytelling is a marketing strategy comes down to where it sits. As a one off campaign it's a tactic. As the thread that decides what you say, to whom, and in what order, it starts to behave like a strategy. I'd treat it as the second, even if you only ever start small.

What makes a good brand story?

A good brand story is specific, honest and about someone other than the brand. That's the short answer to what makes a good brand story, and the third part is where people struggle. Most business stories are written in the first person plural: we are passionate, we are committed, we are proud. The ones that land are written around a customer, a craftsperson or a founder at a particular moment, with something at stake.

Honesty matters more than it sounds. A story with no difficulty in it reads as an advert, because nobody's life goes that smoothly. The shoemaking film we made for Carreducker works because it doesn't hide that a pair takes six months and 210 steps by hand. The slowness is the story.

If your brand story could be swapped with a competitor's and nobody noticed, it isn't a story yet. It's a paragraph.

It also needs to be clear what's in it. What a brand story should include is a short list: where you started, the problem you saw, what you did about it, who you do it for and what you stand for now. Leave any of those out and people fill the gap themselves, usually with something less flattering. Put all of them in at full length and you've written a company history, which is a different document.

If you're wondering what the finished thing looks like, what a brand story looks like might be a page on your website, a three minute film, a founder's talk or a pinned set of posts. The format isn't the story. The story is the account underneath that can be told in any of them.

How do you tell and write a brand story?

Start by gathering, not writing. How to tell a brand story begins with conversations: your founder, your longest serving staff, three customers who've stayed with you for years and one who nearly didn't. Record them, or at least take proper notes. The best lines are in what people say off the cuff, and almost none of them will survive a meeting called to brainstorm the brand narrative.

Then comes the page. How to write a brand story is mostly a matter of cutting. You'll have far more material than you can use, so pick one person, one turning point and one idea you want a stranger to leave with. Write it the way you'd tell it to a friend, then take out every sentence that sounds like a company wrote it.

People also ask how brand storytelling should always begin. My answer is with a moment, not a mission. Open on something that happened: the market stall, the first order, the phone call that changed the plan. It gets the listener into the story before they've had time to decide whether they're interested in a brand.

A word on length, since it trips people up. How long a brand story should be depends on where it lives. A website about page can carry 300 to 500 words, a film often runs somewhere between two and five minutes, and a social cut might be under a minute. If you're planning a film, I've written about running time in how long a brand film should be.

How should a brand story be structured?

Structure is what stops a good pile of material from rambling. How a brand story should be structured is, at heart, a sequence: a situation, a problem, a turning point, a change and what it means for the person watching. You'll recognise it from every film you've enjoyed, because it's how people have told stories for a very long time.

The follow-up question is which shape wins. Which storytelling structure is most effective in marketing doesn't have a single answer, and anyone who names one is selling something. The shapes that tend to do the work are the origin story, the customer transformation and the challenge and resolution. Pick whichever one your real material supports, and don't force a founder's struggle into a hero's journey if what you've actually got is a quiet, well made craft business.

Underneath structure sits narrative in marketing: the larger idea that connects your individual stories. If a story is one film, the narrative is the reason you'd make five. It's the belief your business keeps coming back to, and it's what makes separate pieces feel like they belong together.

A brand story isn't what you say about yourself. It's the account a stranger could repeat to a friend after hearing it once.

How do you put a brand story on video?

Video is where a story stops being something you describe and becomes something people can see and hear. A brand story video is a film built around that account, usually with the founder or customers speaking for themselves, rather than a product advert with a voiceover. It's the format I work in, and it suits stories where the people are the interesting part.

The distinction matters when you're choosing a style. A documentary approach follows real people in their real place of work and lets them speak, while a corporate video tends to script and stage. I've written about the difference in brand documentary versus corporate video, and it's worth reading before you brief anyone.

On the day, the work is less glamorous than people expect. We turn up, set up the interview, and spend most of the time getting someone relaxed enough to talk the way they do in their own kitchen. Then we film the place doing what it normally does, around the people who work there. For La Fromagerie, that meant filming in shops while they were open and trading, which is a different discipline from an empty set. You can watch the result below, and I've written up what went into it in the La Fromagerie film breakdown.

If you're weighing up cost and brief, two earlier posts do the groundwork: how much a brand film costs in the UK and how to write a video brief. A story that's been properly thought through before the shoot is cheaper to film than one found in the edit.

How do you use a brand story in your marketing?

Once you've got the story, the job is to put it to work. How to use storytelling in marketing is mostly about repetition in different clothes. The same account becomes the about page, the opening of a sales call, the first thirty seconds of a film, a run of social posts and the answer you give when someone asks what you do. If each of those tells a different version, you've got five stories and no brand.

The payoff is consistency. How a brand story can enhance your marketing efforts mainly comes down to your ads, emails and posts no longer competing with each other, because they all draw from the same source. People start to recognise you before they've read the small print.

Content is where this gets practical. How a brand story should be used in content creation comes down to treating it as the brief for everything else. Before anyone writes a post or books a shoot, ask which part of the story this piece tells. And the way a brand story benefits content creation shows up quickly: you stop staring at a blank calendar, because the story already supplies the themes, the people and the proof.

A single film can carry a lot of that weight. I've explained how to stretch it in how to turn one brand film into a year of content, and it's the best argument I know for filming the story once and properly. If you're still working out the purpose, why a brand film needs a business goal is the place to start.

Visual, digital, data and social storytelling

The channel changes how a story gets told, though not what it is. Visual storytelling in marketing lets images and footage carry the weight that sentences would otherwise have to. digital storytelling in marketing is the same idea delivered through websites, email, video and apps, where people can interact with it as well as watch.

Data storytelling in marketing is the odd one out, because it starts with numbers instead of people, and the skill is in finding the human point inside them. Use it for reports and case studies where the figures are the proof. And storytelling in social media marketing is the short, fast version: a story told in pieces, over weeks, to people who are scrolling and give you a couple of seconds.

What do brand stories look like in practice?

Examples help, as long as you take the principle and not the polish. A brand story example is easiest to learn from when it's small enough that you can see all the moving parts. A business with one founder, one origin and one clear belief shows the structure far more clearly than a multinational with forty years of campaigns.

Of the big names, Nike's brand story is the one people ask about most. It runs from a runner and his coach, through Just Do It, which arrived in 1988, to campaigns built around athletes who'd taken a risk. What makes it useful isn't the budget. It's that the story keeps coming back to the same belief about effort, whatever the product is.

Others show different strengths. Dove's Real Beauty work, which began in 2004, put ordinary women where models would usually be. Patagonia ran a Black Friday advert in 2011 telling people not to buy a jacket they didn't need, which only worked because the company had been saying the same thing about waste for years. In each case the story could be believed because the business had behaved that way first.

The smaller examples are closer to what most of my readers need. Catherine Marche works only in recycled metal, so the story is the material. Signwriting Jack is about a trade that's nearly all hand and eye. Neither needed a big idea invented for it. They needed someone to point a camera at what was already true.

Where do you start?

Start with one person and one moment. Pick the founder, the customer or the craftsperson who tells it best, write down the turning point in a sentence, and see whether a stranger would care. If they would, you've got the beginning of a story. If they wouldn't, keep asking questions until you find the part that is.

If you'd like help finding it, have a look at the films page to see how we work, and when you're ready, the easiest way to start is getting in touch.

The thirty questions below each have their own deep dive. Pick the one you're stuck on.

faqs.q: What's the difference between brand storytelling and brand messaging?
faqs.a: Messaging is what you say: your claims, tagline and key points. Storytelling is the account that makes those claims believable, with real people and events behind them. Messaging tells someone you're reliable. A story shows a moment you were. Most businesses need both, but the story should come first because it gives the messaging something to stand on.

faqs.q: Do small businesses need brand storytelling?
faqs.a: Small businesses often benefit most, because they've got something big companies can't fake: a real founder, a real place and a real reason for starting. You don't need a large budget. You need a clear account of why you do what you do and the willingness to put a person at the front of it.

faqs.q: How do I know if my brand story is working?
faqs.a: Look for signs that people repeat it back to you. Customers who mention the story on sales calls, staff who tell it the same way, and enquiries that arrive already understanding what you stand for are all good signals. Watch time on your films and time on your about page can help, but I'd trust those conversations first.

faqs.q: Does a brand story have to be a video?
faqs.a: No. A brand story can live on a page, in a talk or across a run of posts. Video suits it well because people and places come across more truthfully when they're seen and heard, and one film can feed a lot of other content. If a film isn't the right next step, start by writing the story down.
