items.title: Why good tripods cost so much
items.excerpt: Why good video tripods cost more: fluid heads vs ball heads, why smooth pans matter, what makes legs stable, counterbalance and what each budget buys you.
items.coverAlt: Two people at a table in a field above a fjord, a steady wide shot from a documentary
items.body:
Good video tripods cost more mainly because of the head. A fluid head uses thick grease inside to dampen movement, so a pan starts and stops smoothly instead of sticking and then lurching, and the legs underneath are stiff enough not to flex or twist. Cheap tripods usually cut corners on both. For stills that barely matters. For video, where the camera moves while it's recording, it's most of the job.

It's also why a tripod is one of the few bits of kit that doesn't really age. A camera from ten years ago looks dated. A good fluid head from ten years ago still does exactly what it did on day one, which tells you where the money went.

What's the difference between a fluid head and a ball head?

A ball head is built for photography. It's a ball in a socket that you loosen, point the camera wherever you want, then lock tight. It's quick, light and great for stills, because the camera doesn't need to move during the shot. Try to pan with one and it either won't move or it flops, because it's designed to be either locked or loose.

A fluid head is built for moving the camera while recording. Inside, sealed chambers of thick fluid or grease resist the movement, a bit like stirring honey. That resistance, called drag, means the camera moves at the speed your hand moves, without jumps. You can usually set how much drag you want for pan and tilt separately: more for slow, controlled moves on a long lens, less for quick reframing.

In between sit friction heads, which you'll find on a lot of cheaper "video" tripods. They use plain friction instead of fluid. They're fine for locking off a static shot. On a pan, they tend to grip, then slip, and the shot jerks at the start and end of every move.

Why do smooth pans matter so much?

Because the viewer's eye goes straight to anything that moves when it shouldn't. A pan that hesitates, jerks or bounces at the end pulls attention away from whatever you were showing and onto the camera. Once someone's noticed the camera, they've stepped out of the film for a second.

Smooth movement is also about control. The start and end of a move are the hardest parts, and a fluid head lets you ease in and ease out, which is what makes a pan feel deliberate rather than accidental. Even when the camera's not moving, a solid head and legs mean a locked-off shot stays perfectly still, which matters more than you'd think on a long interview or a close-up where tiny shakes get magnified.

A cheap tripod is a very reliable way of turning a slow, elegant pan into a short film about an earthquake.

What makes a tripod stable?

Stability is mostly about the legs. A few things make the difference:

  • Stiffness. Good legs resist twisting as well as bending. When you pan, the head pushes against the legs, and flimsy ones wind up and spring back, which shows as a little wobble at the end of the move.
  • Fewer, thicker sections. Every extra joint in a leg is a place for flex. Legs that fold down very small often pay for it in stiffness.
  • Spreaders. A brace that links the legs, either near the ground or halfway up, stops them sliding apart and adds rigidity.
  • No tall centre column. Photo tripods often have a column that winds up the middle. Raised high, it turns a stable tripod into a camera on a stick.
  • A levelling bowl. Video tripods often have a bowl at the top that the head sits in, so you can level the head in seconds without fiddling with each leg. That matters, because a head that isn't level will tilt the horizon as you pan.
  • Material. Carbon fibre is lighter and damps vibration well. Aluminium is heavier and cheaper. Both can be excellent. Weight matters more if you're carrying it all day.

What is counterbalance, and do you need it?

Counterbalance is a spring inside better fluid heads that pushes back against the weight of the camera as you tilt it. With it set correctly, you can tilt the camera up or down, let go, and it stays exactly where you left it. Without it, a heavy camera tilted forward wants to keep going, and you're fighting gravity on every move.

The setting needs to match the weight on top. Every head has a payload range, and it matters at both ends. Too heavy and it can't hold the camera. Too light and the spring pushes the camera back up. When you're working out what to buy, add up the camera, lens, microphone, monitor and anything else you'll mount, and pick a head whose range sits comfortably around that number.

The best camera support is the one nobody watching ever thinks about.

Our film about Signwriting Jack is built on close, patient coverage of the hand work, filmed at the speed it actually happens. That kind of shot lives or dies on the frame staying calm while the hand moves. Any wobble in the picture and your eye goes to the wobble instead of the brush.

What should you look for at different budgets?

I won't name products here, because models change every year and the categories matter more. Roughly, tripods fall into four groups.

  • Photo tripods with a ball head. Fine for static shots and interviews where the camera never moves. Not built for pans.
  • Budget "video" tripods. Usually a friction head and thin legs. They'll hold a phone or a light camera still. Expect sticky pans and some wobble.
  • Entry-level fluid heads on proper video legs. The point where it starts to feel right. Real fluid drag, a levelling bowl, usually a fixed counterbalance, and legs stiff enough for a small camera. For most people filming their own content, this is where I'd spend.
  • Professional systems. Heads with several steps of drag and adjustable counterbalance, larger bowls, twin-tube legs and spreaders. Built for heavier cinema cameras and long days, and built to last for many years.

Because good heads last so long, the second-hand market is worth a look, and hiring for a shoot day is a sensible option if you only need one now and then. What I wouldn't do is spend heavily on a camera and then put it on the cheapest legs going. The tripod is what decides whether the shot holds still.

Do you always need a tripod?

Not always. Handheld camera work has its own feel, closer and more alive, and it suits some moments in a documentary well. Gimbals and other stabilisers do smooth walking shots that a tripod can't. But for interviews, for slow detail shots and for anything where the camera needs to sit quietly and watch, the tripod is still the tool. If you're commissioning a film, this is part of what the day rate covers, and it's one reason a quote for a proper crew looks different to a quote for one person with a camera. There's more on where that money goes in how much a brand film costs in the UK, and on how camera movement shapes the feel of a film in what cinematography actually means.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a photography tripod for video?
faqs.a: For shots where the camera doesn't move, yes. A photo tripod with a ball head will hold a camera still for an interview or a locked-off wide. It won't give you smooth pans or tilts, though, because ball heads are designed to be either locked or loose. If you plan to move the camera during a shot, you need a fluid head.

faqs.q: Is carbon fibre worth it for a tripod?
faqs.a: It's worth it if you carry the tripod a lot. Carbon fibre legs are noticeably lighter than aluminium and absorb vibration well, which helps on long days and location shoots. Aluminium is cheaper, heavier and perfectly stable when well made. If the tripod mostly lives in a studio or the boot of a car, good aluminium legs are a sensible saving.

faqs.q: What does a 75mm or 100mm bowl mean on a tripod?
faqs.a: It's the size of the levelling bowl at the top of video tripod legs, where the head sits. The bowl lets you level the head quickly without adjusting each leg. Smaller bowls usually suit lighter camera setups, and larger bowls are built for heavier cameras and bigger heads. The head and legs need matching bowl sizes, or an adapter.

faqs.q: How long does a good tripod last?
faqs.a: Many years, often well over a decade with basic care. Good fluid heads and legs are built to be serviced rather than replaced, which is why they hold their value and why the second-hand market is busy. Keep the leg locks clean, avoid sand and salt water where you can, and have the head serviced if the drag ever starts to feel uneven.

items.title: What a brand film shoot day in London actually looks like
items.excerpt: From the recce and permits to the interview, the B-roll and the edit: how a documentary brand film shoot day in London really runs, start to finish.
items.coverAlt: A handmade earring being worn, filmed in the shop
items.body:
A shoot day for a documentary brand film in London is usually one long, full day: an early setup, a long interview, then the work filmed as it actually happens, with stills taken alongside. Most of what makes it go well is settled weeks before, in the research, the recce and the permits.

I'll be honest, the day itself is the easy bit. Most people who ask us about a film have never been on a shoot, so here's how one really runs for us, start to finish.

What happens before a brand film shoot day?

By the time a camera comes out, we should already know what the film is about. That comes from research and pre-interviews: time with the people who'll be in it, finding out what they've been through and what nobody outside the business knows. We come back with the story we think it is, and the client tells us whether we've got it right.

Then there's the recce. I want to stand in the space before the shoot, ideally at the time of day we'll be filming. I'm looking at where the light falls at ten in the morning, whether there's a fridge humming in the corner, whether the window behind the obvious interview chair will blow out on camera, and where we can put the kit so it's out of everyone's way. Twenty minutes on a recce saves an hour on the day.

Out of that comes a plan. Who we're interviewing and in what order, the work we need to see happen, where the interview goes, and a rough schedule that leaves room for things to run over. It will change on the day. That's normal.

Do you need a permit to film in London?

Sometimes, yes. If any of the day happens in a public space, the pavement outside, a park, a market, you may well need permission first. Each borough has its own process for filming on its streets, and the Royal Parks and Transport for London run their own. A small crew with handheld kit is often treated more lightly than a full unit with lights, cables and a generator, but the rules vary from place to place, so we check rather than assume.

Every London borough handles filming slightly differently. Nobody quite knows why. Plan for it anyway.

Then there's getting there. Parking near most London locations runs from difficult to impossible, and a car full of cases on a single yellow line is a bad start to anyone's morning. Depending on the location we'll sort a loading bay, a parking suspension if the shoot genuinely needs a vehicle outside, or just travel lighter. The Congestion Charge and ULEZ go into the plan as well, because they affect the call time as much as the cost.

What happens when the crew arrives?

Call time is usually early. The first hour goes on setup, and nobody being filmed needs to watch that happen.

We build the interview first, because it's the spine of the film and the part with the least room for error. The light gets shaped so the room looks like itself on a good day, rather than a studio someone dropped into the corner. Sound gets more attention than picture: a lav mic and a second mic overhead, levels checked, and then we go round switching off whatever we can. Fridges, air con, the radio in the back. And somebody writes a note to switch the fridge back on before we leave.

On a working site, all of this has to fit around the business. We filmed La Fromagerie during trading hours, around customers, including in cheese rooms that are cold, dark and full of people. Nothing stopped for us and nothing should have.

How is the interview filmed?

The interview is a conversation. Nothing read off an autocue, no script handed over the night before. I'll have questions, but the good material nearly always comes from following up on something the person said in passing.

It runs long, often well over an hour. People spend the first stretch giving the answers they think they're supposed to give. Somewhere past that they relax, and they start telling you what actually happened. I ask them to answer in full sentences, folding the question into the answer, because my voice won't be in the finished film and the answer has to make sense on its own.

Some films need a different setup. Deborah Carre and James Ducker of Carreducker are two founders who finish each other's sentences, so we filmed them together as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts, rather than as two separate interviews cut together afterwards.

How do you film the work itself?

After the interview, or sometimes around it, we film the work itself. As it happens, at the speed it happens. For Carreducker that meant close, patient coverage of the hand sewing and the bench work. Every pair goes through 210 steps and takes six months, and the parts that matter most are the slowest to watch, so you have to wait for them.

The interview usually tells you what to shoot next. If someone mentions a tool, a habit, a corner of the workshop, it goes on the list. That's how the pictures end up matching the words in the edit, instead of being generic shots laid over the top.

Some places fight you. Catherine Marche works at the bench and sells from a glass fronted shop, and reflections and mixed lighting fight you the whole way. You deal with it angle by angle. We shoot stills across the same day too, so the film and the photographs look like the same company.

Why use a small crew in London?

We keep crews small on purpose. Most of the places worth filming in London are tight: workshops, back rooms, shop floors, kitchens. A small crew fits, moves quickly, and doesn't block the pavement. It also changes how people behave. Someone being interviewed relaxes a lot faster with two people in the room than with eight, and for documentary that relaxation is the whole thing you're after.

In London, the smallest crew in the room is usually the one that gets the shot.

Then there's the city itself. Sirens, aircraft on the approach, building work starting up next door at the worst possible moment. You stop, wait, and go again. The light through the windows changes across the day too, so the schedule puts the interview where the light holds steadiest and moves the B-roll around it.

What if the work's already finished?

Not every shoot day catches the work in progress. Our renovation films for Nimrod Road in Tooting and Barry Road in East Dulwich were both filmed after the job was finished, with the families already moved back in. At Nimrod Road the before only exists in the original listing photos, so those got cut against the finished rooms. We filmed the street and the neighbourhood as well, because part of that couple's story is why they bought there in the first place.

That kind of shoot day is quieter. The interview carries far more of the weight, and the B-roll is about the finished spaces and the life going on in them.

What happens after the shoot day?

The edit starts with the interviews, not the pictures. Everything gets transcribed and the structure gets built on paper first, then pace, then picture. The client sees a rough cut while changing it is still cheap, and again before it's finished. After that the colour grade and the sound mix go to people who do only that.

Then come the cut-downs. Our main films usually run four to ten minutes, with a sixty to ninety second version for the top of a website and six to ten vertical pieces cut for the feed. For char.gy, one shoot turned into eleven finished exports: the long film, a sixty second cut and a thirty second cut, each in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1, plus an audio described version of the long film and the sixty second cut.

From first conversation to finished film is usually six to ten weeks, and most of that is the bit you can't rush. If you want to see what comes out the other end, the films page has the process and the work side by side.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How many people are in a brand film crew?
faqs.a: For a documentary brand film it's usually a small crew: one camera, proper sound and only the people the day actually needs. We keep it small on purpose. London workshops, shop floors and kitchens are tight, a small crew moves quickly, and people being interviewed relax much faster with two people in the room than with eight. Every extra person adds a day rate without always adding anything to the film.

faqs.q: Do we have to close the business on filming day?
faqs.a: No, and we'd usually rather you didn't. A shop filmed after hours looks empty and a bit lifeless, and the point of a documentary is showing the business as it really runs. La Fromagerie stayed open and trading the whole time we filmed. We work around customers and staff, and only ask for small things, like switching off a noisy fridge during the interview and switching it back on afterwards.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book a brand film?
faqs.a: Allow six to ten weeks from the first conversation to the finished film, and longer if it has to land on a fixed date like a launch or an event. Most of that time goes on research before the shoot and the edit after it. If you need something next week, a documentary film is the wrong purchase. Get in touch early and work back from the date you actually need it.

faqs.q: Does a film crew need insurance to shoot on my premises?
faqs.a: Yes. Any professional crew should carry public liability insurance, and it's fair to ask for a copy of the certificate before the shoot. Plenty of landlords, venues and managed buildings won't let a crew in without it. Insuring the kit is the crew's own job, so that shouldn't land on you. If any filming happens in public space in London, the borough or landowner may also want to see cover before granting permission.

stat.title: UK film and high-end TV production spend
stat.takeaway: The UK's production industry is growing fast, which means London has the crews, kit and know-how to make a small brand film look like it belongs on a big screen.

source.name: BFI, Official BFI statistics 2025 (published 5 February 2026)

items.title: Lav mics explained: microphones for interviews
items.excerpt: Lavalier, shotgun or handheld? How interview microphones differ, where a lav mic goes, how to hide it under clothing and how to fix rustle and wind noise.
items.coverAlt: Clipping a lav mic onto an interviewee before filming
items.body:
Most interviews are recorded on a lavalier mic, the small clip-on one, often with a shotgun mic on a boom pole above the speaker as well. The lav sits on the chest a few inches from the mouth, so it hears the voice clearly even in a noisy room. A boom sounds more natural but needs someone holding it, and a handheld mic is for news, events and vox pops, where nobody minds it being in the shot.

If you're paying for a film, sound is the part you'll notice least when it's right and most when it's wrong. People will sit through a slightly soft shot. They'll click away from a voice that crackles, booms or disappears under traffic.

What types of microphone are used for interviews?

Lavalier mics

A lav is a tiny microphone, about the size of a pea or smaller, on a thin cable that runs to a transmitter pack or a recorder on the belt. Being that close to the mouth means the voice is far louder than the room around it. Most lavs are omnidirectional, so they hear in every direction equally, and the speaker can turn their head without the level dropping away.

The catch is that a lav lives on clothing, so it hears clothing. Every brush of a lapel or tap on the chest goes straight into it.

Shotgun mics on a boom

A shotgun is a long, narrow microphone that mostly hears what it's pointed at and turns down sound from the sides. On an interview it's held on a boom pole just above the top of the frame, angled down at the mouth, by a sound recordist who follows the speaker. Because it sits in the air rather than on the body, it sounds open and natural, closer to how you'd hear the person if you were sat across the table from them.

It needs a reasonably quiet room and someone whose whole job is holding it, and in a small room with hard walls it picks up more echo.

Handheld mics

The one you see on the news. It's tough and good at ignoring background noise, and it's in the shot, which is fine for an event or a reporter stopping people in the street. For a documentary it's usually wrong, because it turns a conversation into a press interview and everyone watching can feel it.

Why use a lav and a boom together?

On a properly crewed interview you'll often see both running at once, recorded to separate tracks. The boom gives the more natural sound, and the lav covers the moments when a bus goes past or the speaker leans out of the boom's sweet spot. Two microphones on one voice is cheap insurance on a recording you can't get back.

If you're filming on your own, a lav on its own is usually the better bet. A shotgun sat on top of the camera is too far from the speaker for a sit-down interview and hears the room as much as the voice.

Where should a lav mic go?

The usual spot is the middle of the chest, on the breastbone, roughly a hand's width below the chin. That's close enough for a strong, clear voice and far enough down that breaths and lip noise don't take over. Go higher, onto a collar, and the voice gets thinner and changes every time the person looks down. Go lower, towards the stomach, and the room starts creeping in.

Two things decide the exact spot:

  • Which way they'll turn. If the interviewer sits to the speaker's left, put the mic a touch left of centre so the voice stays on it when they turn to answer.
  • Jewellery, lanyards and ties. Anything that can swing will tap the mic. Take it off or tape it down.

Visible or hidden is a choice. A small mic clipped neatly to a shirt is completely normal in a documentary, and it usually sounds better than a hidden one. When someone's in their own clothes in their own workshop, I'd rather see a tidy mic than lose half a sentence to rustle.

How do you hide a lav mic under clothing?

Hiding a lav is a small craft of its own, and the aim is always the same. Stop the mic moving against the fabric, and stop the fabric moving against the mic.

  • Tape it down. Sound recordists use double-sided toupee tape, often folded around the mic so there's a layer between the capsule and the cloth, then fixed to the skin or the inside of the shirt.
  • Build a small gap. A soft pad or a purpose-made cover between the mic and the shirt stops the two rubbing directly.
  • Loop the cable. A small loop taped just below the mic soaks up any tug, so a movement at the belt doesn't drag the capsule across the fabric.
  • Keep the front clear. The mic needs to face out through as few layers as possible. Under a thin cotton shirt is fine. Under a heavy jumper the voice goes muffled.

Clothing matters more than people expect. Cotton and wool are quiet. Synthetics, waterproofs, silk and stiff new shirts crackle every time someone breathes. If you're the one being filmed, plain cotton is the easy answer, and there's more on that in how to prepare for being filmed.

Nothing tests a working relationship like asking a managing director if you can tape something to their chest. Ask first, explain why, and offer to let them do it themselves.

Why does my lav mic sound scratchy?

Nearly always it's clothing rustle. It sounds like crackling, scratching or a dull thump, and it lines up with the speaker moving their arms, shifting in the chair or patting their chest to make a point. It's one of the hardest things to clean up afterwards, because the noise sits right on top of the voice.

Before you blame the mic, check these:

  • Is the clip or tape loose, so the mic can slide?
  • Is the cable rubbing on a seam or a button further down?
  • Is a necklace, lanyard or tie touching it?
  • Is the person a hand talker? Some people tap their chest on every point. Move the mic slightly off centre, away from that hand.

If the voice crunches when someone laughs, that's a different problem: the level's set too high and the recording is clipping. Noise reduction in the edit can soften rustle, though push it too far and the voice sounds watery. Fixing it on the day is always better, which is the whole argument for a second mic.

People will sit through a slightly soft shot. They'll click away from a voice that crackles.

How do you stop wind noise on a lav?

Outside, the enemy is wind. Even a light breeze across an uncovered mic causes a low rumble and loud pops that wreck a sentence. The fix is a windshield: a small foam cover for gentle air, and a furry cover, which the industry calls a dead cat, for anything stronger. The fur slows the air down before it reaches the capsule.

A hidden lav has a head start, because the clothing works as a windshield. It's one of the few times hiding the mic actually helps. Beyond that, the easy wins are turning the speaker's back to the wind, using a wall or a doorway as shelter, and recording thirty seconds of the location on its own, called room tone or a wild track, so the editor has something to smooth the gaps with.

If you've ever seen what looks like a small grey animal on a pole at a film shoot, that's a boom in its windshield.

Our film for Carreducker is a good example of why interview sound needs planning. Two founders who finish each other's sentences, filmed as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts. Two voices overlapping in a workshop is a sound problem as much as a picture one, because each person has to come through clearly for the edit to hold together.

What does this mean if you're paying for a film?

Ask who's looking after sound on the day. On a small shoot it might be the camera operator doing both, which can work for one interview in a quiet room. For more than one voice, a noisy location or someone moving about, a dedicated sound recordist earns their day rate quickly. It's worth asking who does the sound mix too. On our films the grade and mix are done by people who only do that, and the films page shows how the rest fits together. If the mic is wireless, there's a second set of things that can go wrong, which I've covered in how wireless audio works for interviews.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a phone with a lav mic for interviews?
faqs.a: Yes, and for someone filming on their own it's one of the cheapest big improvements you can make. A wired lav plugged into a phone puts the mic close to the mouth, which matters far more than the recording device. Check the connector suits your phone, keep the cable out of shot, and do a short test recording with headphones before you start the real interview.

faqs.q: Should a lav mic be visible on camera?
faqs.a: It can be, and in documentary and interview work it usually is. A small mic clipped neatly to the centre of a shirt looks normal to viewers and generally sounds better than a hidden one. Hiding it makes sense for drama, for scenes where the person moves around a lot, or when a visible mic would clash with the look the client wants.

faqs.q: What clothes cause the most microphone noise?
faqs.a: Synthetic fabrics, waterproof jackets, silk, stiff new shirts and anything with a zip or loose buttons near the chest. They crackle and rub against the mic every time the person moves or breathes. Soft cotton and wool are the quietest. Avoid noisy jewellery and lanyards too, because anything that swings will tap the microphone during the interview.

faqs.q: How many microphones does an interview need?
faqs.a: One good microphone close to the speaker is the minimum, and a lav does that job well. A professional crew will often add a boom mic on a second track as a backup and for a more natural sound. With two people talking, each person needs their own mic so the editor can control each voice separately.

items.title: How to make a brand video people actually watch
items.excerpt: A person with something at stake, an interview as the spine, and the nerve to cut what's merely nice. What keeps people watching a brand film to the end.
items.coverAlt: Hand painted signwriting, filmed in the workshop and on the street
items.body:
People watch a brand video to the end when there's a real person in it with something at stake, when it starts where something's already happening, and when whoever edited it had the nerve to cut everything that wasn't needed. It also has to be made for a reason. A lovely film with no job to do gets watched once, mostly by the people who paid for it.

Most brand videos get signed off by people who already care about the company. Everyone in that meeting knows the product, likes the logo and wants it to do well, so the video passes. Then it goes on the website and a stranger gives it a few seconds before they're gone.

The films people finish are made with that stranger in mind from the very first conversation. This is what I think actually makes the difference, from the films we've made and the plenty I've switched off myself.

Who should a brand video be about?

People watch people. Someone telling you about a decision that could have gone badly is a lot harder to leave.

Stakes don't have to be dramatic. In our film about a period house in Tooting, the couple bought a Victorian house that had sat empty since the previous owners died. The renovation started in September and they had a baby due at the end of November. That's all the tension the film needs. You want to know whether they made it, and you keep watching to find out.

Every business has something like that if you look properly. A founder who nearly gave up. A craft that took years to learn. A customer who took a risk on you. The work is finding it before anyone turns up with a camera.

What's the film actually for?

I'll say this plainly, because it's the thing people skip. Filming alone often isn't enough. A great film with nothing planned around it gets a launch post, a few kind comments from people who already know you, and then it sits on the About page.

Filming on its own isn’t enough. A film earns its money when it’s built for a job.

The work lands when the creative is tied to the goal or the campaign it's there to serve. That decision shapes everything: who's in it, how it opens, how long it runs and which cuts come out of it. The Barry Road film was made to be an edit a builder can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. The char.gy film runs as the principal video on two pages of their site. Both had a job before a frame was shot.

So before you talk about cameras or locations, be clear about where the film's going to live and what you want someone to do after watching it. If you can't answer that, you're not ready to shoot yet.

Should you plan the story before filming?

Yes, and properly. Most of what decides whether a film works happens before the shoot. Research, pre-interviews, time spent working out which story is actually the one. The obvious story is usually the product. The one people watch is usually the person behind it, or the part of the process nobody outside ever sees.

How should a brand video start?

In the middle. Don't open with the logo, the company history or someone saying their name and job title. Start where something is already happening. A line from the interview that makes you lean in, or the work half done.

The context can come later. Viewers are surprisingly happy to catch up as long as they've got a reason to. What they won't sit through is a slow warm up before anything interesting has happened.

Should a brand video have a voiceover?

I'd almost always say no. For documentary brand films, the interview carries the story and the pictures follow it. Get the interview right and the edit has something to hang off. Get it wrong and no amount of B-roll will fix it.

That means a real conversation with nothing read off an autocue, and enough time that the person stops performing. In my experience the best line often turns up late, once they've forgotten the camera.

It also means skipping the voice of god. A narrator telling you how good a company is carries no weight, because you know someone paid for those words. When a London builder wanted a film about a full house renovation, we handed it to the homeowner. The only version a prospective client believes is the one from someone who has already handed over the money.

Should you cut fast to keep people watching?

Mostly no. The instinct in an edit is to cut fast so nobody gets bored. Usually it does the opposite. When someone pauses before an answer, or a hand does something difficult, holding on it is what makes people watch.

With Signwriting Jack, the value is the single unbroken line that either works or doesn't. Cut away halfway through and you've thrown out the one moment that proves the skill. Craft films in particular need the patience to show the work at the speed it's actually done.

How much does sound matter?

More than most people think. Viewers will forgive slightly soft footage. They won't sit through bad audio. A clean interview recording is the minimum, and after that, real sound from the place does a lot of quiet work: the brush on the board, the needle through leather, the noise of a shop that's open and trading.

On a drainage job we filmed for Super Efficient, some of the vertical cuts left the jetter and the water alone rather than burying them under music. That sound is the satisfying bit. Covering it would have made the clip worse.

How much music should a brand video have?

Less than you'd expect. Music is the easiest way to make a film feel like an advert. Wall to wall, swelling at all the expected points, it tells the viewer how to feel, and most people can sense that and pull back a little.

If the music’s doing all the emotional work, the film isn’t.

Use it where it earns a place. Under a transition, to lift a moment that's already working, to give the ending some space. Then let it drop out when someone's saying something that matters. Silence in the right place lands harder than any track.

What should you cut?

Anything that's merely nice. This is the hardest part of any edit. You'll have shots you love, a drone pass that cost a morning, an answer that's lovely but goes nowhere. If it doesn't move the story on, it comes out.

I ask the same thing of every scene: would anyone miss it? If the honest answer is no, it goes, however good it looks. A shorter film that holds attention all the way through beats a longer one that loses people at the halfway mark.

How long should a brand video be?

There's no correct length for a brand film. There's only the length the story can carry. Our main films usually run four to ten minutes, because that's the room some stories need, but every one comes with a sixty to ninety second cut for the places where nobody's going to give you ten minutes, and vertical pieces cut for the feed.

What doesn't work is a two minute story stretched to six because someone thought longer looked more premium. People feel the padding and they leave.

What does that look like in a real film?

When char.gy were certified as a B Corp, they had a problem. Certification is a genuinely hard thing to earn and a genuinely dull thing to explain. The easy version puts a score on screen and hopes people are impressed.

We did it the other way round. The char.gy film lets the people who did the work explain why it mattered, from the team who ran the certification to the engineers on the street. It was cut into a long version, a sixty second and a thirty second cut, with an audio described version so people who can't see it can still follow it. It's now the most viewed video on their YouTube channel.

More of our work is on the films page, and if you've got a story you think is worth telling, that's where to start.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should brand videos have subtitles?
faqs.a: Yes, especially anything going on social. Plenty of people scroll with the sound off, so vertical cuts need captions to make sense at all. On the main film, subtitles help anyone watching somewhere they can't play sound, and they're an accessibility basic for viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing. Go further where it fits, like the audio described version we made for char.gy, so people who can't see the screen can follow it too.

faqs.q: Is one long brand film better than lots of short videos?
faqs.a: You don't have to choose if the shoot's planned properly. One shoot can give you the main film, usually four to ten minutes, a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of your site and six to ten vertical pieces for the feed. The long film earns trust with people who are already interested. The short cuts reach the people who'd never give you ten minutes in the first place.

faqs.q: How do you measure whether a brand video worked?
faqs.a: Measure it against the job you gave it before filming. If it was made to help sales, look at whether buyers who watched it move faster or stall less. If it was for hiring, look at the quality of applications. For views, check how far people get as well as how many start, because a film people finish is doing its work. YouTube and social analytics show you retention for free.

faqs.q: Where should I share my brand video once it's finished?
faqs.a: Put it where people are deciding whether to trust you. That's usually your homepage or a key service page, YouTube, sales emails and proposals, recruitment pages and any events you run. The short cut goes at the top of the site, and the vertical pieces go out on social over the following weeks. A single launch post won't do much on its own, so plan where the film keeps working after that.

stat.title: How people most like to learn about a product or service
stat.takeaway: People choose a short video over everything else by a mile, so keep your film tight and make every second earn its place.

items.title: Charity and fundraising films: the complete UK guide
items.excerpt: A complete guide to charity and fundraising films for UK charities: storytelling, making the video, campaigns, appeals, donors, impact reports and legacy giving.
items.coverAlt: A couple on a sofa look off camera during their interview, colourful paintings on the wall behind
items.body:
A charity film or fundraising video works when it shows real people, real need and a clear next step for the viewer, in a few minutes that respect everyone in it. It isn't a sad face and a piano. The practical steps are in how to make a charity video, and this guide covers the wider picture around it.

I make documentary brand films, and a fair number of the people who ask me about charity work aren't asking about film at all. They're asking how to raise money, who to ask, how long to make things and how to keep donors. So this guide walks through the whole subject in the order a UK charity or fundraising team tends to need it: what charity marketing is, how to tell stories properly, how to make the video, where it runs, how to run campaigns and appeals, how to look after donors, and how to report back. Each section links to a deeper answer, so read it straight through or jump to the part you're stuck on.

What is charity marketing, and is a charity a brand?

Charity marketing is everything a charity does to get its cause understood and supported: the website, the posts, the adverts, the appeals, the events, the films. It has the same job as any marketing, which is to get the right people to care and then act. The difference is what they're acting on. What charity marketing is comes down to asking for time, money or attention for a cause, not selling a product, and that changes the tone of nearly everything.

That leads to a question some trustees dislike: is a charity a brand? It is, whether or not anyone calls it that. Donors, volunteers and funders carry a picture of you in their heads, and that picture is built from every film, letter and conversation. The only choice is whether you shape it on purpose. A charity with a clear, consistent identity is easier to recognise, easier to trust and easier to give to.

Brands often have faces too. A charity brand ambassador is someone who speaks for the cause publicly, from a celebrity to a beneficiary or a long serving volunteer. The ones who work are the ones who actually care, and the best ambassador I'd want on camera is rarely the most famous person in the room. Pick someone who can say why it matters in their own words.

How do you tell a charity's story without exploiting anyone?

Nonprofit storytelling means using real accounts of the people you help, and the people who help, to explain your work. It's the heart of everything else here, because every film, appeal and report is a story in some form. The risk is that the person in the story is often at the hardest point of their life, and they're doing you a favour by sharing it.

That's why I treat consent as something built up and rechecked, not a form signed on the day. Explain where the film will go, let people stop at any point, show them the cut before it's published and agree how they can ask for it to come down later. The longer treatment is in brand films for charities: dignity, consent and budget. Where children or adults at risk are involved, your safeguarding policy leads and the crew follows it.

It also means letting people be whole. Show what they're good at and what they're doing now, not only the worst moment. A person with agency on screen is more moving than a person being pitied, and donors have noticed.

If the plan is a sad piano over slow footage of someone crying, ask them first whether they'd choose to be remembered like that.

How do you make a charity or fundraising video?

Start with one person and one ask. Making a charity video is mostly decisions made before anyone picks up a camera: who is the film for, what do you want them to do afterwards, and who is the best person to tell the story. A film for potential donors, a film for a funder and a film for new volunteers are three different films, even if they share footage.

A fundraising video is the same craft with a sharper job. How to make a fundraising video comes down to a clear story, a specific need and a direct request, and the request needs to be somewhere the viewer can't miss it. In the edit, I'd rather lose a lovely shot than bury the ask.

Plan the practical side too. Write a proper video brief, decide who signs it off, and find out early whether the people you support can be filmed at all. Music needs licensing, and music licensing for brand videos is worth a read before you pick a track you can't use. If you want to see what a documentary approach looks like, the Southwick D-Day 80 film is a community story told through the people who made it happen.

A charity film isn't judged on how well it's shot. It's judged on whether the person watching understands what to do next.

What makes a good fundraising video, and how long should it be?

A good fundraising video is specific, human and honest about what a gift does. It has one person at the centre, a problem the viewer can picture, and a result they can believe. The weaker ones lean on statistics and general sadness. The stronger ones let someone explain, in plain words, what changed.

Length is where people overthink. How long a fundraising video should be depends on where it plays: under a minute for social, two to three minutes for a website or an appeal email, and longer only for a room that has chosen to be there, like a gala dinner. I've covered the general version in how long a brand film should be. Make the version you need, then cut it down.

Where do charities advertise, and why?

The honest answer to why charities advertise is that a charity can't help people nobody knows it exists to help. Advertising brings in donors, volunteers, referrals and awareness, and the money it raises usually has to outweigh what it cost. Trustees are right to ask for the numbers.

As for the how, how charities advertise runs from television and radio to paid social, search, direct mail, billboards and partnerships. Most small charities don't need most of those. A well made film, a good website and a steady rhythm of posts will do more than a scattered budget across six channels.

You may have noticed the long ones on television, and why charity adverts are so long has a practical answer: a longer ad has room to tell a story and make a direct ask. If you're wondering what the big screen would cost, how much charity TV adverts cost breaks down the airtime and the production. Most small charities won't go near it, but it's worth knowing what you're not buying.

How do charities use social media?

For most charities, social media is where the story meets the public every day. How charities use social media is a mix of storytelling, campaign updates, thank yous, behind the scenes and calls to action, and the ones doing it well post as people rather than as an institution. A volunteer talking to camera beats a polished graphic.

If you're the one running the account, how to promote a charity on social media is about consistency and clarity: pick the one or two platforms where your supporters are, post regularly, and make every post answer a simple question, namely why should someone care today. One good film can feed a long run of posts, and I've explained how in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

How do you run and promote a fundraising campaign?

A campaign is a fundraising push with a goal, a deadline and a story. How to run a successful fundraising campaign starts with a specific target and a reason it matters now. "Help us this winter" is weak. "Help us fund 40 emergency heating grants before January" gives people something to picture and a finish line to rally round.

Then comes getting it in front of people. How to promote a fundraising campaign means going to the people who already know you first: existing donors, volunteers, trustees, partners and local press. They're your best chance of early momentum, and early momentum persuades everyone else. A short film at the centre gives all of them something to share.

Social media does much of the work after that. Promoting a fundraising campaign on social media works best as a countdown: launch, progress updates, a story or two along the way, thanks as targets are hit, and a final push in the last days. Show the total moving. People give to things that look like they're succeeding.

What are capital campaigns and capital appeals?

Some fundraising isn't about running costs at all. A capital fundraising campaign raises money for something that lasts: a new building, a refurbishment, a piece of equipment or an endowment. It's usually larger, slower and more reliant on major donors than everyday fundraising.

The mechanics are covered in how a capital campaign works. Typically there's a quiet phase where the biggest gifts are secured privately before anything is announced, then a public phase that brings in the wider community. That order matters, since a public launch with nothing already pledged tends to look like a hope rather than a plan.

The word you'll hear is appeal, and capital appeals are the public face of a capital campaign: the film, the brochure, the website and the events that ask for support. For a building project, a film that lets people see the space as it is now, and hear from the people who'd use the new one, does more than a computer render.

How do you write a fundraising appeal?

A written appeal still earns its place alongside video. How to write a fundraising appeal comes down to writing to one person, telling one story and asking for one thing. Open with the individual, say what their situation is, explain what a gift does, and then ask clearly, with a specific amount where you can.

The best appeals read like a letter from someone who cares, not a press release. Read yours aloud, and if it sounds like an organisation talking, rewrite it. The same discipline applies to a film script, and the best appeals I've seen could have been scripts.

Why do donors give, and why do they stop?

Everything above depends on understanding why donors give. The reasons are mostly personal: a connection to the cause, trust that the money will be used well, being asked by someone they know, and feeling that their gift made a difference. Nobody gives because a charity is worthy in general. They give because something specific moved them.

The harder question is why donors stop giving. Often it's not that they lost interest. It's that nobody told them what happened to their money, they were asked too often, or they were thanked late and generically. Looking after the donors you have is cheaper and more reliable than winning new ones, and a short thank you film from a real beneficiary is one of the best retention tools I know of.

For new supporters, how to find donors for nonprofit organisations starts close to home: people who already volunteer, attend, receive help or have a personal link to your cause. Beyond that come local businesses, trusts and foundations, and community groups. Cold audiences are the most expensive place to look.

What is an impact report, and how do you write one?

Donors and funders want to know what changed. An impact report is the document, and increasingly the film, that shows it: what you set out to do, what you did, what difference it made and what's next. It's accountability, but done well it's also your best fundraising tool.

Knowing what an impact report should include keeps you honest: a clear picture of the problem, the work you did, real numbers, a few human stories, what didn't go to plan, and how the money was spent. Leaving out the difficult parts makes it read like marketing, and funders can tell.

On the practical side, how to write an impact report is mostly about choosing less. Pick a handful of measures that matter, show them clearly, and let people's voices carry the rest. A two minute film of someone describing what the charity changed for them will often get watched when the PDF doesn't get read.

How do you talk about and promote legacy giving?

Gifts in wills are among the most valuable and the most sensitive part of fundraising. Why legacy giving is important is simple: for many UK charities it's a major source of income and one that can fund work well into the future. It's also the area where the way you speak matters most.

That is why how to talk about legacy giving deserves care. People don't want to be hurried or made to feel they're being asked to die for your cause. The best conversations are gentle, specific and about the life the person has lived, and the way a supporter's connection started.

On the marketing side, how to promote legacy giving works best through real stories from people who've already left a gift or planned to, told on their terms, with the family's agreement where it applies. This is a place where a quiet, unhurried documentary film beats any advert, because the audience is deciding whether they trust you with something that matters.

Where do you start?

Start with the person and the ask. Pick the one story that best shows why your charity exists, decide the one thing you'd like the viewer to do, and work backwards from there. Everything in this guide, from the film to the appeal to the report, is a different way of telling that same story to a different audience.

If you'd like to see how we work, the films page is the place to look. When you're ready to talk through a charity project, get in touch.

The thirty questions below each have their own deep dive. Pick the one you're stuck on.

faqs.q: Do small charities need a professional film?
faqs.a: Not always. A clear, honest film shot on a good phone can do a lot, especially for social media and internal use. A professional crew earns its fee when the film will carry your main appeal, go in front of funders, or involve people who need sensitive handling. Start with what the film has to achieve, then match the effort to it.

faqs.q: How much should a charity spend on a fundraising video?
faqs.a: There's no standard figure, because it depends on length, crew and how many locations and people are involved. Work out what the film needs to raise or achieve, then set a budget that looks sensible against that. Be open with your production company about the number, so they can suggest what's worth paying for.

faqs.q: Can we film the people we support?
faqs.a: Often yes, but only with proper, informed consent, and never at the cost of their safety or privacy. Explain where the film will be used, let them see it before it's published and agree how they can withdraw. Where children or vulnerable adults are involved, follow your safeguarding policy and get advice from whoever owns it.

faqs.q: How do we know if a charity film has worked?
faqs.a: Decide the measure before you film. It might be donations through a campaign page, sign ups to a mailing list, volunteer enquiries or how many funders mention it. Watch time helps, but I'd trust actions over views. Track what people did after watching, then use it to improve the next one.

items.title: How to make a fundraising video, step by step
items.excerpt: How to make a fundraising video: choose one person and one ask, plan the shoot, film with consent and good sound, and edit it to end on a clear request.
items.coverAlt: The homeowner leans forward on a sofa talking to someone off camera, a warm lamp behind him
items.body:
To make a fundraising video, decide who it's for and what single action you want from them, pick one person whose story carries the work, plan the shoot around that story, film it with consent and good sound, then edit it so it ends on a clear ask. Most of the effort sits before the camera and after the edit.

This is the process I'd follow from a blank page to a finished film, in the order the decisions come up. It's about the making. If you want to know whether the result is any good, that's in what makes a good fundraising video, and how long it should run is covered in how long a fundraising video should be. The wider picture sits in the complete guide to charity and fundraising films.

What do you need to decide before anyone picks up a camera?

Three things, and they take an afternoon rather than a month. Who is watching, what do you want them to do, and where will they be when they watch it.

Who is watching is rarely "the public". It's a regular giver who hasn't heard from you in a year, a local business that might sponsor an event, a trust officer reading your application at their desk, or a stranger who's just seen a clip on their phone. Each of those wants something different from the film. Pick the main one and write their name, or a real person you know who fits, at the top of your plan.

What you want them to do needs to be one thing. Give a monthly amount, sign up for the sponsored walk, come to the open evening, leave a gift in their will. A video that asks for four things gets none of them. If you can't state the ask in one short sentence, the film isn't ready to be shot.

Where they'll watch decides the shape. A film that opens a gala dinner is made for a dark room, a big screen and a captive audience. A film for Instagram is watched on a phone, on mute, by someone with a thumb already moving. You can make both from the same shoot, and I'd always plan for that, but one of them leads.

Whose story should a fundraising video tell?

One person, in most cases. A fundraising video works because a viewer feels something for a single human being and then sees that their gift reaches people like that. Eight stories in two minutes give the viewer nobody to hold on to.

That person might be someone the charity supports, a volunteer, a nurse, a coach or a founder. The test I'd use is whether they can talk about the work without a script, in plain words, and whether they want to. A person who's keen but nervous is fine. A person who's been persuaded to do it for the charity's sake is a risk to them and to the film.

If your person is someone you support, the film has a duty to them that goes beyond a signed form. I've written about consent, dignity and when to leave a face out in brand films for charities, and Bond's guidance, Putting the people in the pictures first, is worth reading before you ask anyone. UK fundraising also has its own rulebook. The Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice has a section on fundraising involving children and people in vulnerable circumstances, and your safeguarding lead needs to see the plan before anyone's booked.

How do you plan the story and the shoot?

Write the story down in five lines before you film a frame. Where does this person start, what's the problem, what does the charity do, what's different now, and what does the viewer's gift make possible. That's your spine. The interview, the footage of the work and the ask all hang off it.

Then list what the camera needs to see. Not "the building", but a particular moment. A tea being made at the start of a session. A hand on a shoulder. Someone arriving nervous and someone else leaving easy. A fundraising video made of people talking, with nothing to look at while they do, is a radio programme with a logo.

Two practical points save the most money. First, work out what you can film in one day, because the day is the expensive part. Second, plan the cuts at the same time: the main film, a short version and some vertical pieces for social media all come out of the same shoot if you shoot for them. Adding them afterwards means going back. I go through how to get a year of material from one shoot in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

A written brief makes all of this easier, when you're hiring someone and when you're doing it yourself. How to write a video brief has the structure I'd use.

If the plan includes the phrase "and then a montage of smiling people", that's the bit nobody will remember.

What happens on the day of the shoot?

Quieter than people expect. A small crew is better for a fundraising film than a big one, because the person on camera is the point and a room full of kit and strangers makes them tight. On most documentary shoots we're a couple of people with a camera, a light or two and a microphone, set up in the space where the person actually does the thing.

Start with the footage of the work, not the interview. People relax once they've been filmed doing something ordinary for twenty minutes, and the camera stops being an event. Then sit down for the conversation, somewhere the person is comfortable, with a window or a lamp for light and a quiet room. Sound gets more fundraising films wrong than picture does. A voice recorded in an echoing hall with the central heating humming sounds distant, and distant doesn't make anyone cry. A clip-on microphone close to the speaker fixes most of it, and I've covered the options in wireless microphones for interviews.

Ask open questions that start with "tell me about" and let silences run. The best line in an interview usually comes after the person thinks they've finished. And be clear before you start that they can stop, skip a question or take something back. That's what makes it possible for them to say something real.

If you're filming alone or on a phone, the same rules hold. Steady the phone, hold it at eye level, film in landscape for the main interview and portrait for anything that's going to social, and put the microphone nearer than you think you need to.

How do you edit a fundraising video so it asks for something?

Start the edit with the best 20 seconds of the interview, the sentence that makes you lean in, and build from there. Most first cuts are too long and too polite. They start with the charity's name, the mission and the history, and the viewer has left by the time a human being appears.

Open on the person. Let them say who they are and what happened, in their own words. Cut away to the footage that shows what they're describing. Bring in the charity's role late and briefly, as the thing that changed their situation, not as a speech. Then move to the ask.

The ask should be specific and sound like a person. "£12 a month covers a weekly session for one family" is better than "please give generously", as long as the figure is true and you can stand behind it. Make sure what you promise matches what the money does. The Code of Fundraising Practice expects fundraising material to be honest, and a figure you can't back up is the quickest way to lose a donor and cause a complaint.

Put the ask on screen as text as well as in a voice. Most people watching on a phone will have the sound off or low, so captions are essential, not decoration. Add them to every version. Use music sparingly, and only music you're licensed to use; music licensing for brand videos explains how that works.

Before you publish, show the cut to the person at the centre of it. I'd say that's non-negotiable. Nobody should see themselves for the first time on a charity's public page.

Why does the way you ask matter so much?

Because supporters remember how a charity made them feel long after they've forgotten the film. The Fundraising Regulator's 2026 survey of 3,018 UK adults found that almost two thirds of people who had experienced charitable fundraising described it as a positive experience, and that people with positive experiences were more inclined to keep supporting charities afterwards. The reverse is also true. A video that guilts, exaggerates or pressures costs you the next gift.

A fundraising video is a conversation with a stranger who owes you nothing. Treat them like a guest.

That's why I lean towards films where the ask arrives after the viewer has been given something, usually a real moment and a clear picture of what happens next. You don't have to shout. You have to be clear.

Where should a fundraising video go once it's finished?

Everywhere your audience already is, and in the right shape for each place. The long film goes on your donation page, at the top of your appeal email, on your YouTube channel and on the screen at your event. The short cut goes on social media with captions burned in, and links to the donation page. Vertical clips of the strongest moment go on Reels, Shorts and TikTok.

The page the viewer lands on after clicking matters as much as the film. If the video ends with "donate now" and the link takes them to a page that asks for six details before showing a button, you've thrown it away. Test the donation journey on a phone before you publish.

Publish it more than once. Charities often make one film, post it on a Tuesday, then wonder why it didn't change much. The audience on any platform sees a small share of what you post. Re-use it across the campaign, and put it back in front of people at the moments that matter, a giving day, a match-funding window or Christmas. Where to use your brand film lists the places I'd start.

How long does it take, and what should you budget?

For a documentary style film, plan on six to ten weeks from the first conversation to the finished edit. A lot of that is waiting on approvals, contributor reviews and diaries rather than anyone working on it. If you have a hard date, such as a gala or a giving day, work backwards from it and leave a fortnight spare.

On cost, a single content day with us starts at £795 plus VAT, and that can produce a short appeal film and a set of social clips if the story is simple. A fuller documentary piece costs more, and what drives it is the number of shoot days, the people involved and how many versions you need. I've broken down where the money goes in how much a brand film costs in the UK.

If you'd rather make it in-house, a phone, a lavalier microphone and an afternoon with a willing volunteer will get you something honest. What you're buying from a production company is the planning, the sound, the ability to handle a delicate interview and the edit. Our films show the sort of documentary approach we'd bring, and the char.gy B Corp film is a good example of an interview-led piece cut into several lengths for different places, including an audio described version.

If you've got a charity story and you're weighing up whether to film it yourselves or bring someone in, tell us what you're planning and we'll give you a straight answer.

faqs.q: What is the first step in making a fundraising video?
faqs.a: Decide who the video is for and the one action you want them to take. Everything else follows from that: whose story you tell, how long the film runs, where it gets published and what the ending says. If you can't write the ask in one short sentence, it isn't ready to film. This usually takes an afternoon of thinking, not weeks of meetings.

faqs.q: Can we make a fundraising video on a phone?
faqs.a: Yes, and plenty of effective ones are made that way. Keep the phone steady, film at eye level, use a clip-on microphone because phone audio is the weak point, and shoot near a window for light. Film landscape for the main interview and portrait for social clips. What matters most is an honest story, a person who wants to tell it and clear sound.

faqs.q: Do we need permission from people who appear in our fundraising video?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent from anyone identifiable, explain where and for how long the film will be used, and show them their part before it goes public. For children or adults at risk, your safeguarding policy leads and the Code of Fundraising Practice applies. Agree up front how someone can ask for the film to come down later.

faqs.q: How many versions of a fundraising video do we need?
faqs.a: Usually three: a main film of two to four minutes for your website, emails and events, a shorter cut of around a minute for social media, and a few short vertical clips for Reels, Shorts and TikTok. Plan all of them before the shoot so you capture the footage once. Adding versions later means going back to the people involved.

items.title: How long should a fundraising video be?
items.excerpt: How long a fundraising video should be for social, email, your website and events, with a simple way to spend the seconds so the ask lands before people leave.
items.coverAlt: Runners and supporters at a charity fun run finish in a south London park on an overcast morning
items.body:
A fundraising video should be as long as it takes to make one person's story land and ask for one thing, which in practice means 60 to 90 seconds for social media, two to three minutes for a website or email appeal, and up to five minutes for an event or a major donor. Under a minute suits a cold audience. Longer only works with an audience that has already said yes.

This post is about length, and about how to spend the seconds you have. How to make the film is in how to make a fundraising video, and what separates a good one from a forgettable one is in what makes a good fundraising video. If you've wondered why some charity adverts run for several minutes, why charity adverts are so long has that. For the general version of this question, I've covered how long a brand film should be.

Is there one right length for a fundraising video?

No, and anyone who gives you a single number is guessing. Length depends on who's watching, where, and how warm they already are towards you. A stranger scrolling past your clip on a phone will give you a couple of seconds, then maybe ten if you've earned them. A trustee, a major donor or someone who's been a volunteer for years will sit through five minutes if the film is honest.

What I'd say instead is that a fundraising video has a shortest sensible length, which is the time it takes to introduce a person, show a problem, show what changed and make the ask. For most stories that's about a minute. Everything over that has to justify itself with something the viewer wants to see.

The mistake I see most is the opposite of what people expect. Charities are often so careful to say everything that they cram a three-minute film into 90 seconds, with six voices and fast cuts, and it ends up feeling longer than a calm three minutes would. Length is felt, not counted. A slow, clear 150 seconds beats a frantic 60.

How long should a fundraising video be for each place you'll use it?

Here's what I'd aim for, and it's a starting point rather than a rule.

  • Social media feed, cold audience: 30 to 60 seconds. Open on a face or a moment, caption everything, and put the ask in the last five seconds or the caption.
  • Reels, Shorts and TikTok: 15 to 45 seconds. One moment, one line, one link. These are trailers for the longer film, not replacements.
  • Website homepage or donation page: 60 to 120 seconds. Someone who has already clicked is interested, so you can afford to say a little more.
  • Email appeal: 90 seconds to three minutes. People who open your emails already know you. A still frame with a play button in the email, linking to a hosted video, usually works better than trying to embed it.
  • Event or gala: three to five minutes, played in a room where people are paying attention and there's a moment to ask straight afterwards.
  • Funder or major donor: three to six minutes, sent with a personal note. These viewers are reading you as evidence, so they'll forgive length if the content is specific.

Notice that none of these is a ten minute documentary. A longer piece has a place, usually as the thing you make for your supporters on YouTube or at your anniversary, but it's not a fundraising video. It's a different job, and it's worth a different plan.

What do the numbers say about how long people watch?

The most useful data I know comes from business video rather than charity video, so it's not a perfect fit, but it points the same way as everything else I've seen on set and in analytics. Vidyard looked at more than 940,000 business videos made across 2024 and found that, on average, 65% of viewers watched a video under 60 seconds all the way through, falling to only 20% for videos longer than 20 minutes.

That drop is gradual, not a cliff. The point isn't that long films fail. It's that every extra minute costs you some of the audience, so each minute needs to earn its place. The honest consequence for a charity is that if the ask comes in the last 20 seconds of a four minute film, a lot of the people who might have given will be gone before they reach it.

There are two ways to deal with that. Either make the film shorter, or move the ask earlier. A soft ask in the first third, such as a name on screen and a link in the description, and a firm ask at the end, catches both the people who leave early and the ones who stay.

Nobody has ever complained that a charity film was two minutes shorter than it needed to be.

How should you spend the time you have?

Whatever the length, I use the same rough proportions. Here's how a 90 second film breaks down, and you can scale it up or down.

The first 10 seconds

A person, a place or a line that makes someone stop. Not a logo, not a slow fade in, and not the charity's name read by a narrator. If the viewer doesn't know within ten seconds that this is about a human being, they've gone.

Seconds 10 to 40

The problem, in the person's own words. What it was like, specifically. Keep the detail concrete: the morning routine that stopped, the stairs they couldn't climb, the number of nights they slept on a sofa. Detail is what makes a story feel true.

Seconds 40 to 70

What the charity did and what changed. This is the part where your work appears, and it should come across through the person, not a mission statement. Show a session, a conversation, a result.

The last 20 seconds

The ask. One action, one amount if you have one, one place to do it. "£12 a month pays for a weekly session for a family like Sam's" works if it's true. Finish on the donate address and a human face rather than a logo wall.

For a three minute film, you get to stay longer in each part, not add more parts. Add a second voice if it adds a new angle, such as a volunteer or a family member, and give the scenes room. Don't add a history of the organisation. If someone needs it, it's on your website.

Is shorter always better for charity video?

No. A short film that doesn't say anything gets watched to the end and does nothing. Completion rate is a decent measure of whether people stayed, and a terrible measure of whether they cared.

Some of the best-performing charity work is long. The television appeal that runs for several minutes does so because it's reaching an audience who've chosen to sit with it, and because it's got room to build a case and make a direct request. Those films work through a different set of rules, which I cover in why charity adverts are so long.

For online fundraising, the question to ask is what your audience will do at the moment they see the film. If they're scrolling, shorter. If they've clicked through from an email to find out more, they've chosen to be there, and they'll give you a couple of minutes. If they're sitting at a table at your annual dinner with a glass in their hand, they'll give you five. The setting decides the length more than any rule from a blog.

Length is felt, not counted. A calm 150 seconds beats a frantic 60.

How do you find out whether your length is right?

Look at the audience retention graph on YouTube or your social platform a week after posting. It shows where people leave. A steep drop in the first five seconds means the opening is wrong, not the length. A steady slide with a cliff near the end means people left when they sensed the ask was coming, so try giving them something first.

Then compare the number of people who watched past the halfway mark with the number who clicked your link. If plenty watched and few clicked, the film moved them but the ask was unclear. If few watched and a fair share of those clicked, you've got a good ask in front of too small an audience. Keep a note of what you changed each time, so the next film starts from evidence rather than opinion. Two or three films in, you'll know your own audience's length better than any benchmark can tell you.

Can you make one film that works at every length?

You can make one shoot that works at every length, and that's the better question. The way to do it is to film with the cuts in mind: a long interview with proper pauses, plenty of footage of the work, and a few self-contained moments that can stand alone as 15 second clips.

In the edit, you build the longest version first, because that's where the story is told in full. Then you pull a 90 second version from it by keeping the strongest through-line, and a 30 second version by keeping one moment and the ask. The vertical clips come last. You can't make a good long film from short clips, but you can make good short clips from a long film.

This is how we handled the char.gy B Corp film: a long form interview film, a 60 second cut and a 30 second cut, each delivered in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1 and with an audio described version, so the same material worked wherever it was posted. It's a commercial client rather than a charity, but the principle is the same. Decide on the set of cuts before you film.

What do you do if the film is too long?

Cut the middle first. Most films that run long have a good beginning, a good end and a middle full of things the team loved filming. Watch the film with someone who's never heard of your charity and notice the moment they look at their phone. That's where it needs trimming.

Then look at how many voices there are. If a film has four people talking, ask what the third and fourth say that the first and second haven't. If it's nothing, they go. Then look for repeated points. A film that tells you twice that the work matters has said it once too often.

Don't squeeze it by speeding up the speech or cutting out all the pauses. The breaths and silences between sentences are where the viewer feels something. A tight edit leaves them in and removes the throat clearing, the preamble and the second example.

If you'd like a second pair of eyes on a cut, or a plan for a film that works at three lengths from one shoot, you can tell us what you're working on. There's more on the whole subject in the complete guide to charity and fundraising films, and you can see the sort of documentary work we make on our films page.
