faqs.q: What is the best length for a fundraising video on social media?
faqs.a: Aim for 30 to 60 seconds for a cold audience in the feed, and 15 to 45 seconds for Reels, Shorts and TikTok. Open on a person, caption everything because most people watch with the sound off, and put the ask in the last few seconds and the caption. Use the short cut to send people to the longer film on your donation page.

faqs.q: How long should an email fundraising video be?
faqs.a: Between 90 seconds and three minutes, because people opening your emails already know you and will give a little more time. Most email platforms don't play video reliably, so use a still frame with a play button that links to a hosted version. Put a clear donate link under it, and keep the film's ask consistent with the email's.

faqs.q: Should a fundraising video be under two minutes?
faqs.a: For cold audiences, usually yes. For people who've chosen to watch, such as supporters on your donation page or guests at an event, two to five minutes can work well if the story is strong. The test is whether every scene earns its place. Cut anything the viewer wouldn't miss, and move the ask earlier if the film runs long.

faqs.q: Can we use the same video at different lengths?
faqs.a: Yes, if you plan for it before the shoot. Film a full interview, plenty of footage of the work and a few self-contained moments. Edit the longest version first, then take a 90 second cut and a 30 second cut from it, and finish with vertical clips. It's far cheaper than going back to reshoot, and every version stays consistent.

stat.title: Share of viewers who watch a business video to the end, by length
stat.takeaway: Every extra minute costs you part of the audience, so keep the film as short as the story allows and don't leave the ask until the last few seconds.

source.name: Vidyard, 2025 Video in Business Benchmark Report (943,305 videos, 2024)

items.title: What makes a good fundraising video?
items.excerpt: What makes a good fundraising video: one real person, specific detail, change you can see, clear sound and an honest ask. A quality checklist from a film maker.
items.coverAlt: A grey-haired founder in glasses and a black shirt looks off camera during an interview inside her cheese shop, shelves of
items.body:
A good fundraising video centres one real person, tells their story in their own words, shows the change rather than describing it, sounds clear, and makes a single honest ask at the end. It treats the viewer as an equal and the person on screen with dignity. Polish matters far less than whether the viewer believes what they're seeing.

This is the quality check, the things I'd look for if you handed me a cut and asked whether it was ready. It isn't the production guide, which is how to make a fundraising video, and it isn't about running time, which is in how long a fundraising video should be. If you want the reasons people give in the first place, why donors give goes into that, and the whole subject is mapped in the complete guide to charity and fundraising films.

Does a good fundraising video start with a person?

Yes, almost always. The viewer needs someone to care about before they can care about the cause. A statistic about how many people are affected is true and forgettable. A woman telling you what her mornings used to be like, and what they're like now, is not.

The best fundraising films I've seen get to a face and a voice within a few seconds. They don't open with the charity's name, a map, a number or a sweep of the building. They open with a human being saying something specific. After that they can bring in the context the viewer needs.

The person has to be the right one. They need to be able to talk about the work in ordinary language, and they need to want to. A reluctant or rehearsed contributor shows up on camera in the first sentence, and no amount of editing hides it. I'd rather film someone who stumbles and means it than someone who delivers a perfect line from a script.

Why does specific detail matter more than a big message?

Because detail is how viewers decide whether something is true. "We help families in crisis" slides off. "She'd been sleeping in the car with the two kids for three weeks when someone told her about us" sticks. The first is a claim, and the second is a scene.

When you review a draft, underline every line that could appear in any charity's film. "We make a real difference." "Every gift counts." "Together we can." Then see what's left. Often the real film is hiding underneath, in the one sentence where the person forgot the camera was there and described the actual kettle, the actual door, the actual phone call.

Specific numbers help in the same way. "£15 buys a week of hot meals for one person" gives the viewer a real unit of change. A round claim like "thousands of lives transformed" doesn't. If you can't back a figure with your own accounts, leave it out.

How do you show change rather than describe it?

With pictures of before and after, or better, of the thing changing. A good fundraising film lets us see the shift: someone arriving unsure and leaving at ease, a child doing something they couldn't last term, a room that was empty and now has people in it. Interview answers carry the meaning. The footage proves it.

This is where plenty of films come up short. They have strong interviews and then cover them with generic shots of buildings, sunsets and hands on keyboards. The covering footage should be there because it shows what the speaker is saying. If someone describes the group at the community centre, show the group at the community centre.

It's also where trustees and funders look. The Charity Commission's research on public trust has found that people trust charities more when they can see that the money makes a real difference to people. A film that shows change is doing trust work as well as fundraising. I've written more about that side of it in brand films for charities.

If a shot could be dropped into any charity's film without anyone noticing, it probably should be.

Why is good sound the difference between a decent video and a moving one?

Because the voice is the emotion. Most viewers will forgive a plain picture, but a muffled or echoey voice makes them tune out without knowing why. On every shoot I'd rather have the right microphone close to the speaker in a quiet room than a better camera in a noisy one.

The common problems are easy to fix if you plan for them. Switch off the fridge, the air conditioning and the radio in the next room. Avoid big, hard-walled halls. Put a clip-on microphone on the person and listen with headphones before you start. Wireless microphones for interviews explains the kit, and interview lighting explained covers the picture side, which also matters more than people think.

Captions are part of sound now. Plenty of people watch with the sound off, so a film that only works with the audio on loses them before it starts. Burn the captions in, check the spelling of names and keep them in step with the speech.

What does a good ask look like?

One action, clearly stated, with a reason that follows from the story. "Give £12 a month" lands better after you've seen what the sessions do than as the opening line. And it should be proportionate. A film about one family's turning point shouldn't ask someone for a £50,000 gift.

The ask also has to be honest. The Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice sets the standard for UK fundraising material, and the simplest way to meet it is to promise only what the money does and to avoid language that pressures or guilts. A viewer who feels manipulated may not give, and may not forgive.

That matters because trust is already thin. The Fundraising Regulator's 2026 survey of 3,018 UK adults found that the share who trust local charities to deliver what they promise fell from 42% to 34% between 2023 and 2026, and for national charities from 32% to 27%. People who only trust some fundraisers say it's because of how funds are used and because it's hard to tell which charities are genuine. A film that's open about what the money does answers both worries. If you're curious why supporters drift away, why donors stop giving is worth a read.

How does a film earn trust from a sceptical viewer?

By showing its working. Viewers have seen enough charity appeals to be wary, and they notice when something has been smoothed over. The films that earn trust are usually the ones that admit what's hard, say plainly what the money does and don't claim more than the charity can deliver.

In practice that means letting a member of staff say what's still difficult, showing the ordinary, unglamorous part of the work and naming a real figure rather than a vague promise. It means a visible, plain-spoken donate page after the film, with the charity number on it. And it means resisting the urge to tidy every rough edge. A pause, a laugh or a sentence that doesn't quite finish tells the viewer a real person is talking.

How do you treat the person on screen well?

That's part of quality, not an add-on. A film that exploits someone's worst moment may raise money once, and it leaves them defined by it. A good fundraising film lets people be whole: skilled, funny, proud, tired, whatever is true. It lets them decide how much to share and shows them the finished cut before anyone else sees it.

Bond's guidance, Putting the people in the pictures first, makes the case clearly, and it applies far beyond international charities. Consent, plain language and the right to change their mind should be built into the plan.

The best fundraising films make you want to meet the person, not pity them.

Dignity also helps with performance. People who feel respected relax, and relaxed people say true things. It's the single most practical reason to do it properly, quite apart from it being the right thing.

Does production quality matter for a fundraising video?

It matters up to a point, and the point is lower than most people fear. Viewers forgive a plain setting, a handheld shot or a modest camera. They don't forgive wobbly sound, a face in shadow or a cut that lands on a half-finished sentence. Those make a film feel careless, and care is what a donor is trying to judge.

The other side of this is over-production. A glossy film with drone shots, a swelling score and a perfect grade can make a small local charity look as though it has money to burn. Funders and supporters notice. Match the finish to the organisation. A clean, warm, honest film with a steady camera and a good voice beats a cinematic one that doesn't look like you.

If you're deciding where to spend a limited budget, put it into planning, sound and the edit, in that order. Camera upgrades come last.

What do bad fundraising videos have in common?

A few things come up again and again, and you can spot most of them in the first thirty seconds.

  • They start with the organisation. A logo, a mission statement, a founding year. The viewer hasn't met anyone yet.
  • They have too many voices. Six talking heads in three minutes means nobody gets room to say anything real.
  • They use stock footage. Viewers can tell, and it tells them the charity didn't have a real picture of its own work.
  • They hide the ask. A film that never says what the viewer can do wastes its own emotion.
  • They run on a slow sad piano. It gets the effect wrong, and music you don't have the licence for causes trouble later. Music licensing for brand videos covers that.

None of these is about money. A well planned film made on a modest budget avoids all of them.

How do you tell whether yours is good enough to publish?

Show it to three people who don't work for you: one who knows your cause, one who doesn't and one who'd never normally watch a charity film. Don't explain anything beforehand. Afterwards, ask them to tell you in their own words what the film was about and what they'd do next. If their answers match your plan, it's working. If they remember the music, the logo or the building, the story isn't strong enough.

Then ask the person in the film. They should recognise themselves and feel comfortable that it's fair. If they hesitate, find out why before you publish.

Finally, ask what you'd say if a funder asked for the one scene that shows what you do. If you can name it, it's probably in the film, and it's probably what you should lead with.

The char.gy B Corp film is a commercial project, but it follows the same approach: the people who did the work explain it in their own words, rather than a score on screen. You can see more of how we film in our films, and if you've got a story you'd like to talk through, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the most important element of a fundraising video?
faqs.a: A real person telling a specific story in their own words. Everything else supports that: footage that shows the change, clear sound, an honest ask and respect for the contributor. Viewers decide within seconds whether they believe what they're watching, and a believable person does more for that than production polish, music or a clever concept.

faqs.q: Do fundraising videos need to be emotional?
faqs.a: They need to be human, which isn't the same as heavy. Warmth, humour and pride move people as much as sadness, and they leave the person on screen with more dignity. Let the story set the tone. If you push for tears you risk a film that feels manipulative, and a supporter who feels manipulated is unlikely to give again.

faqs.q: Should a fundraising video include statistics?
faqs.a: A few, used sparingly and only if you can back them up. One or two specific figures, such as what £15 provides, give the viewer a clear unit of change. Large totals and percentages tend to wash over people. Put the figure after the story, not before, so it lands as proof rather than as the opening.

faqs.q: How much should a fundraising video cost to look professional?
faqs.a: Professional comes from planning, sound and a clear story more than from budget. A phone, a good microphone and a calm interview can look honest and polished. Spend on the things viewers notice: clean audio, steady shots, good light and a careful edit. A production company is worth it when the story is sensitive or you need several cuts.

stat.takeaway: Trust in charities is falling, so a fundraising video has to earn belief by being specific, honest and clear about what the money does.

items.title: How to make a charity video: a guide for UK charities
items.excerpt: How to make a charity video: the kinds of film, who must approve it, in-house or production company, what it costs and how to plan the shoot and where to use it.
items.coverAlt: A filmmaker shooting rails of clothes and books in a busy charity shop from the doorway
items.body:
To make a charity video, pick the one job it has to do, choose whose voice carries it, get consent and sign-off in place before filming, shoot it with a small crew and clean sound, edit it for the places it will be seen, and plan how you'll use it for the next two years. Decide whether to make it in-house or with a production company based on how sensitive the story is and how many versions you need.

This post is the whole-charity view: the different kinds of charity video, who needs to agree to it, who should make it and what it costs in time. If your video is specifically meant to raise money, the step-by-step is in how to make a fundraising video. If you want the thinking behind the stories, read what nonprofit storytelling is. The full map is in the complete guide to charity and fundraising films.

What kinds of charity video are there?

More than people expect, and each has a different job. Picking the wrong one is the commonest reason a charity spends money on a film that doesn't get used.

  • The "what we do" film. A calm introduction for your website, new volunteers, funders and partners. It should last for years, so keep dates and campaign slogans out of it.
  • The impact or thank-you film. It shows what last year's support achieved, usually for donors, funders and your annual report. It's more specific and more evidence-led than the introduction.
  • The appeal film. Built to raise money against a deadline, with one ask.
  • The volunteer or recruitment film. A day in the life, from someone who does the role, answering the questions a nervous newcomer has.
  • The event film. Coverage of a fundraising event, a celebration or a commemoration, edited to thank people and promote the next one.
  • The short social clip. One moment, one message, made for a phone.

Most charities need the first, a version of the second every year, and a steady supply of the last. The mistake is trying to make one film do all six jobs. It ends up too long for social, too vague for funders and too soft for an appeal.

Who has to agree before you film?

More people than you'd think, and getting them in the room early saves weeks. At a small charity that may be two people. At a bigger one it can be a chief executive, a head of fundraising, a safeguarding lead, a data protection officer and a trustee.

Safeguarding comes first. If children, young people or adults at risk are involved, your safeguarding policy decides who can be filmed, who must be present, whether faces can show and where footage is stored. The Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice has a section on fundraising involving children and people in vulnerable circumstances, and it's worth having your lead read it before you plan anything.

Next is consent. Everyone who is identifiable should sign a release that explains where the film will be used, for how long and how they can withdraw. Because the people you support are often relying on the charity, consent needs to feel like a real choice, and I've covered how to do that in brand films for charities. Bond's guidance, Putting the people in the pictures first, is the best short read I know on telling these stories with dignity.

Finally, agree who signs off the finished film and how many rounds of feedback there are. One round of comments from one person is ideal. Five people each sending conflicting notes is how a six week project becomes a six month one.

Should you make a charity video in-house or hire a production company?

It depends on the story, not only the budget. Here's how I'd think about it.

In-house works well when the subject is simple, the contributors are staff or confident volunteers, you need regular short content and you have someone who enjoys doing it. A phone, a clip-on microphone and some patience will get you honest, usable clips. Plenty of effective charity social content is made this way.

A production company earns its fee when the story is sensitive, such as when you're filming people at a vulnerable point in their lives. It also earns it when the film has to work for funders and trustees, when you need several cuts for different places, or when nobody on your team has the time. What you're paying for is judgement: how to interview someone gently, how to get clean sound in a noisy hall, how to cut forty minutes of conversation into three honest ones.

A mixed approach often suits charities best. Commission one properly made flagship film, filmed in a day or two with plenty of extra footage, and let your team make the everyday clips yourselves in the same style.

What does a charity video cost?

The range is wide, from a few hundred pounds for a volunteer-shot clip to many thousands for a documentary piece, and the number depends on shoot days, crew, locations, edit time and how many versions you need. I've set out the main drivers in how much a brand film costs in the UK. For a simple story, a single content day with us starts at £795 plus VAT.

Funding the video is often the harder problem. The Charity Digital Skills Report found that 69% of charities received no funding for digital work in the past year, rising to 73% among small charities, against 53% of large ones. If that's your position, it helps to know that some funders will cover communications or evaluation costs inside a project grant if they're written into the bid from the start. Ask before assuming they won't, and say clearly how the film will be used.

A film costs less than the three meetings spent arguing about its logo placement, if you add up the hours honestly.

How do you plan the shoot?

Start from the story and work out what you need to see and hear. For a charity that usually means one or two people talking about the work, plus footage of the work happening. Book the day around when things are actually going on, not when it's convenient for the office. A Tuesday afternoon session with real people in the room is worth more than a quiet Friday with everyone posing.

Tell everyone what to expect. Contributors should know who is coming, what they'll be asked and roughly how long it takes. Staff should know where the cameras are allowed and where they aren't. A short email the day before saves a lot of nervous energy, and so does this guide to preparing for being filmed, which you can pass on to anyone who's anxious.

A written brief helps whoever is filming, whether that's your colleague or a producer. How to write a video brief sets out the structure. Aim for one page covering the audience, the aim, the people, the places, the length and the versions.

On the day, keep the crew small, start with footage of the work so people relax, record the interview somewhere quiet and ask open questions. Capture plenty of cutaways: hands, rooms, objects and moments that you can use to cover edits and make social clips later. And film more of the ordinary than you think you need.

What should the finished video include?

A person at the start, the work in the middle and a clear next step at the end. Add captions to every version, put your charity number and website at the close, and check every name and figure against your records before it goes out. Credit people the way they asked to be credited.

If you use music, make sure it's licensed for your use and your platforms. Music licensing for brand videos explains the options. And make sure you own the footage, or have a licence that covers what you want to do with it. Who owns copyright in commissioned video is the page to read before you sign anything.

The video doesn't have to say everything about your charity. It has to say one true thing, well.

Keep a log of who has appeared in which version, with the date of their consent. When someone asks for their story to come down in two years, you'll be glad you wrote it down.

Where should a charity video be used?

Everywhere you talk to supporters, and more than once. The main film sits at the top of your website or on a page people reach from a donation link. A short cut goes into email appeals and funding applications. Clips go on social media, and the full version goes on YouTube, where it can be found by search. At events, it plays on a screen at the start. Volunteers can be sent it as part of onboarding, and staff can use it when they talk to partners.

I wrote about the options in where to use your brand film, and in how charities use social media there's more on the channel side. The film should work hard for at least two years, which is another reason to keep it free of dates and fads.

We handle this kind of community material in our own work. For Southwick D-Day 80, a village commemoration where nothing could be repeated, we filmed the arrivals, the ceremony and the full panel talk, and delivered edits the organisers could use to record the anniversary and promote the next one. You can read about it in the Southwick D-Day 80 case study, and the rest of our documentary work is on the films page.

What mistakes do charities make with video?

Three come up most. The first is leaving distribution until the film is finished. By then the energy and budget have gone, and the film sits on a shelf. Plan where it will be seen before you shoot a frame.

The second is making the film about the organisation. Staff love the mission, the structure and the history, and viewers want a person. Put a human being at the front and let the organisation appear as the thing that helped.

The third is skipping the contributor review. Show people their part before it's public. It's good practice, it builds the sort of trust that makes the next film easier, and it avoids the worst outcome, which is someone seeing themselves online for the first time on your page.

A fourth, smaller one is treating the video as a one-off. Charities that get the most from film tend to shoot a little and often: one properly planned day each quarter, with the clips cut to suit the season, the appeal or the report. It spreads the cost, keeps your supporters hearing from real people and means you're never starting from nothing when something urgent comes up.

If you've got a charity story and you're working out how to tell it, tell us what you've got in mind. If we don't think a film is the right spend for you, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How do you make a charity video with no budget?
faqs.a: Use a phone, a clip-on microphone and a willing volunteer or staff member in a quiet room with window light. Film landscape for the main interview, hold the phone at eye level and keep each clip under two minutes. Get written consent from anyone identifiable. Honest, well-lit, clearly heard footage beats a polished video that doesn't sound like your charity.

faqs.q: How long does it take to make a charity video?
faqs.a: For a documentary style film, plan on six to ten weeks from the first conversation to the finished edit, because approvals, contributor reviews and diaries take most of that time. A simple phone-shot clip can be done in a day. If you have a fixed date, such as an event or giving day, work backwards from it and leave spare time.

faqs.q: Do you need consent to film people for a charity video?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent from everyone identifiable, explain where and how long the film will be used, and let them see their part before it's published. For children and adults at risk, your safeguarding policy leads. Agree how someone can ask for the film to come down later, and keep a record of every consent.

faqs.q: What should a charity video include?
faqs.a: A real person at the start, footage of the work, a clear explanation of what changed and one next step at the end, whether that's donating, volunteering or getting in touch. Add captions, your charity number and website, and check every figure. Keep the main film free of dates so it stays useful for a couple of years.

items.title: What is nonprofit storytelling? A UK guide for charities
items.excerpt: What nonprofit storytelling is, what a charity story is made of, whose stories to tell and how to tell them ethically, with consent and dignity, in the UK.
items.coverAlt: A couple sit side by side on a sofa, the man glancing off to the side as the woman speaks to camera
items.body:
Nonprofit storytelling is the practice of using real people's experiences, told honestly and with their consent, to show what a charity or community organisation does and why it matters. It turns programme data into a human account of change, so supporters, funders and volunteers can understand the work and decide whether to back it.

This post is the definition and the thinking: what nonprofit storytelling is, what a nonprofit story is made of, whose stories to tell and what goes wrong. It isn't the production guide. For that, see how to make a charity video. For what separates a strong film from a weak one, there's what makes a good fundraising video, and the whole subject is mapped in the complete guide to charity and fundraising films.

What does nonprofit storytelling actually mean?

In the UK we mostly say charity, voluntary sector or third sector, and "nonprofit" is the American word that tends to turn up in search results. The idea is the same: an organisation that exists to do good, not to make a profit, explaining its work through the experience of the people it touches.

The story can be told in writing, in photographs, in an annual report, on a stage at a gala or in a film. What makes it storytelling, rather than a press release, is that it has a person in it, something happens to them, and the viewer or reader ends up knowing something they didn't before. "We supported 1,200 families last year" is a report. "Priya hadn't left the flat in three weeks when she walked into our Tuesday group" is a story.

It isn't spin. A good nonprofit story is truer than a statistic, not less true, because it shows the particular and the complicated. And it isn't free advertising for the charity's ego. The person at the centre is the point, and the organisation appears as part of their story.

Why do charities tell stories at all?

Because the work is usually hard to see. A charity's output is often invisible: a changed mind, a safer evening, a child who now reads. Numbers capture how many, and stories capture what it's like. Supporters need both, but they decide with the second.

There's also a human reason. NCVO's Time Well Spent survey asked volunteers in 2023 why they started: 40% said they wanted to improve things or help people, and 34% said the cause was important. When asked why they'd carry on, making a difference was the joint top answer, at 46%. People get involved because of what the work changes. A story is the most direct way to show that change, and a glossy brochure rarely does.

And there's a practical reason. Stories get reused. One good account can anchor a funding bid, an annual report, a social post, a trustee meeting and a film. A team that gathers stories well has a stock of material that makes every other bit of communication easier. What is charity marketing looks at where stories fit in the wider picture.

"Impactful journey" appears in a lot of charity stories and in none of the ones people remember.

What is a nonprofit story made of?

Four things, and you can check any story against them.

A person

Someone specific, with a name if they're happy to share it, a voice and an actual life. Not "a beneficiary" and not a composite. Real people can tell you what they ate that morning, and that's the kind of detail that makes a story land.

A problem

What was wrong, in concrete terms. Not "isolation" but the Sunday afternoons with nobody to call. The problem should be something the viewer could picture, and the person shouldn't be reduced to it.

A change

What happened, and what part the charity played. The change doesn't have to be dramatic. It can be small and still true: a first job interview, a first full night's sleep, a reunion. Be honest about what the charity did and what the person did. The best stories give the credit to the person.

A reason to care now

What the viewer or reader can do, and why it matters. This is where the ask sits. In many stories it's quiet, such as a link to volunteer, or a mention of how to give, because the story has already done the persuading.

That structure is the same one that runs through all good storytelling, and I've written about its use for businesses in the brand storytelling guide. The difference for a charity is the weight of responsibility. The person in your story is often more vulnerable than the audience.

Whose stories should a nonprofit tell?

More than just the people you support. Each voice answers a different question for the audience.

  • People you support. They show what the work does. These stories need the most care.
  • Volunteers. They show what it's like to be involved and make it feel possible for a newcomer.
  • Staff. They explain the craft, the hard parts and what still isn't solved.
  • Donors and supporters. They show why someone chooses to give, which is often what another person needs to hear.
  • Founders. They explain why the charity exists. Use them lightly, because supporters mostly want to hear about the people being helped.
  • The community. A neighbour, a local business or a school can show what changes around the work.

Mixing them tends to produce a more rounded picture, and it takes pressure off the people you support to carry every story. Why donors give goes into which stories move supporters to act.

How do you tell these stories ethically?

By putting the person's wellbeing ahead of the story. That's easy to say and takes discipline to do. In practice it means they choose whether to take part, they understand where the story will appear and for how long, they can stop at any point, and they see it before it's published.

It also means avoiding the old shortcut of showing people at their lowest to prompt a reaction. Bond, the UK network for international development organisations, has published guidelines on this called Putting the people in the pictures first. They were written for NGOs, and they put it plainly that images of Black and Brown people suffering and in need of being "saved" have created and perpetuated racism. The principles apply to any organisation telling the story of someone it supports.

The UK fundraising rulebook backs this up. The Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice covers behaviour when fundraising and fundraising involving children and people in vulnerable circumstances. Your safeguarding lead should be part of any storytelling project from the start. I've gone through consent and dignity in more detail in brand films for charities.

A story told with someone is worth more than a story taken from them.

How do you find the stories?

Ask the people on the front line. Support workers, volunteer coordinators and the person who answers the phone know the stories long before the communications team does. Ask them what happened this week that they told someone about on the way home. That's usually your story.

Then make it easy to collect. A short, regular conversation is better than a form, and a recorded call with consent is better than a written summary, because the exact words matter. Keep a simple log with the person's name, the date, what they agreed to and where it can be used. Check the details are accurate, and never combine two people into one to make a neater story.

Pay attention to what people say about their own experience. Often the line you'd never have written is the best one. A woman describing a sewing group as "the only place nobody asks me anything" will do more than your best paragraph.

What goes wrong with nonprofit storytelling?

A few patterns repeat. The first is the saviour story, where the charity is the hero and the person is passive. It flatters the organisation and takes away the person's agency. Flip it so the person is the main character and the charity is a helpful supporting one.

The second is the one-size story. A single powerful account is used for every purpose until the person is tired of it and the audience has seen it. Gather several, and let different stories do different jobs.

The third is data with no person in it, or a person with no data. A story with no evidence behind it invites doubt, and statistics with no human face invite a shrug. The best pairing is one person's account backed by one honest figure showing it isn't a one-off.

The fourth is polish. Beautifully produced stories sometimes lose the thing that made them true. A rough edge, a pause or a laugh is often the sign that a real person is talking.

How do you know whether your stories are working?

Look for behaviour, not praise. A story that works gets used: it's quoted in a bid, repeated by a trustee, shared by a volunteer or mentioned back to you by a donor at an event. Those are better signs than a count of likes.

Then check the plain numbers that sit near the story. Did sign-ups for the volunteer evening rise after the film went out? Did the donation page get more visits on the days the story was posted? Did funders refer to it in their feedback? None of this proves cause and effect, and I wouldn't claim it does, but over a year the pattern tells you which kinds of story earn their place.

Ask the person in the story too. If they feel it was fair and would do it again, you've done it right. If they hesitate, that's the most useful feedback you'll get.

One last point on the word itself. Some small charities hear "storytelling" and picture a marketing department they don't have. You don't need one. A volunteer who writes down what a regular said on Thursday, with permission, is already doing it. The craft lies in noticing, asking well and treating what you hear with respect.

Where does film fit into nonprofit storytelling?

Film is one way of telling the story, and a strong one, because it carries a face, a voice and a place in a single frame. It works when the person is willing to be seen and the story gains from being heard. It doesn't suit every story, and sometimes a photograph, a written case study or a voice recording is the kinder and better choice.

When we film for organisations, we start with the story and the person, then decide the format. Our documentary approach is to let people explain things in their own words, and you can see it in the char.gy B Corp film, where the team who did the work explain it rather than putting a score on screen. If you're thinking about telling your charity's stories on film, get in touch and we'll talk it through.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the difference between nonprofit storytelling and fundraising?
faqs.a: Storytelling is the way you communicate your work through real people's experiences. Fundraising is one purpose it can serve. A story might recruit volunteers, thank donors, support a funding bid or inform trustees without asking for money at all. Fundraising stories add a clear ask. The best fundraising stories are still honest accounts first, with the ask following naturally.

faqs.q: Do charities need permission to tell someone's story?
faqs.a: Yes. Get informed consent from the person, explain where and for how long the story will be used, and let them see it before it's published. For children and adults at risk, your safeguarding policy leads, and the Code of Fundraising Practice applies to fundraising material. Record the consent and agree how someone can ask for their story to be removed.

faqs.q: What makes a nonprofit story effective?
faqs.a: A specific person, a clearly described problem, a believable change and a reason for the audience to care now. It also needs honesty, which means being clear about what the charity did and what the person did. The most effective stories give the person agency and use concrete detail rather than general claims about impact.

faqs.q: How many stories does a charity need?
faqs.a: Enough to cover your main audiences and not rely on one person. A handful of well-collected stories each year, across people you support, volunteers and staff, will feed your website, reports, bids and social media. Refresh them regularly so no individual is asked to carry the organisation's message for years.

items.title: What is charity marketing? A plain UK definition
items.excerpt: A plain-English definition of charity marketing: what it covers, how it differs from marketing a business, who it talks to and the UK rules that apply to it.
items.coverAlt: Students in blue, white and black gis kneel in a circle watching a demonstration on the mat
items.body:
Charity marketing is everything a charity does to get its cause understood and supported: the stories, campaigns, adverts, events, emails and films that bring in donors, volunteers, service users and attention. It's marketing with a different job. The thing being sold isn't a product, it's a change in the world, and the people paying rarely get anything back for it.

This post is the plain definition: what charity marketing includes, how it differs from marketing a business, who it's aimed at and the UK rules around it. How charities use social media, how they advertise and why they do it each get their own posts, and I'll link to them as we go.

What does charity marketing actually include?

The term covers more than most people expect, because a charity has to persuade several different groups of people, often at the same time. In practice it breaks into five jobs.

  • Fundraising communications. Appeals, regular giving campaigns, legacy messages, events and thank-you letters. Anything meant to make someone give.
  • Awareness and campaigning. Getting a subject on the public's mind, or changing a rule. Think of a charity trying to get a law amended or a symptom recognised sooner.
  • Brand and reputation. How the charity looks, sounds and behaves, and whether the public trusts it.
  • Service promotion. Telling the people who need help that it exists. For some charities this is the most important job and the least glamorous.
  • Supporter care. Keeping people who've already given, volunteered or signed up. It costs far less than finding new ones.

In a big charity those jobs sit in separate teams. In a small one, they sit with one person who is also running the volunteer rota. That's worth remembering when you read advice written for national organisations, because most of the sector doesn't look like that.

How is it different from marketing a business?

The techniques are the same ones businesses use: storytelling, targeting, testing, email, video. The differences are in who you're talking to and what you're allowed to say.

The person who pays isn't the person who benefits

A business sells to a customer who gets the product. A charity asks a donor to pay so that someone else benefits. That means the message has to make a stranger care about a person or an animal or a place they may never meet, and it has to do it without a purchase to point at. It's one of the hardest briefs in marketing.

You answer to more people

A charity has donors, trustees, funders, beneficiaries, volunteers, staff and regulators all watching what it says. A line that gets a lot of clicks can still upset the people the charity exists to serve. I think this is the biggest practical difference. Commercial marketing asks "did it work?" Charity marketing has to ask that and "was it fair to the people in it?"

Trust is the main asset

People give because they believe the money will do something. When the Charity Commission asked the public what makes them trust a charity, the top answers were about money going to the cause and a visible difference to people. I've covered that research in more detail in brand films for charities. For marketing, it means a flashy campaign that makes people doubt where the money goes can do more harm than good.

A business can survive a bit of hype. A charity runs on being believed.

Who is charity marketing aimed at?

Most charities talk to at least five audiences, and they want different things. It helps to write them down, because a message that works for one often falls flat with another.

  • Individual donors want to feel their gift matters and to be told what happened to it.
  • Funders and grant makers want evidence, plans and honest reporting.
  • Corporate partners want a cause that fits their business and gives their staff something to get behind.
  • Volunteers want to know what they'd actually be doing, how much time it takes and whether they'll be useful.
  • The people the charity helps want to find the service, understand it and trust it enough to walk in.

That last group gets forgotten. A charity can spend its whole budget persuading donors and still have people who need it who've never heard of it. If you've only got room for one extra thing in a year's plan, make sure those people can find you.

How big is the competition for attention?

Bigger than most people assume. The Charity Commission's figures put the register of charities in England and Wales at 171,112 at the end of March 2026, with a combined annual income of about £107 billion. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own registers on top of that. Every one of those organisations is trying to be remembered by the same public.

Donor numbers have been falling at the same time. The Charities Aid Foundation says the sector has lost around 600,000 donors a year over the last decade. I go into what that means in why charities advertise, but the short version is that a charity can't assume its supporters will still be there next year. Marketing is how it replaces the ones who drift away.

What do the UK rules say?

Charity marketing in the UK sits under several sets of rules, and it's worth knowing the headlines even if someone else handles compliance. This is general information rather than legal advice.

  • The Code of Fundraising Practice from the Fundraising Regulator applies to fundraising in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Its core values are that fundraising must be legal, open, honest and respectful.
  • The ASA's CAP Code covers adverts and promotions, including on social media. A charity ad can't mislead, and claims about impact need to be backed up.
  • Data protection and electronic marketing law (UK GDPR and PECR) govern how you can contact people by email, text and phone. Consent matters a lot more than it did, and charities have been fined for getting it wrong.
  • The Charity Commission's guidance expects trustees to make sure marketing is lawful and a reasonable use of charity money.

Scotland has its own charity regulator, OSCR, and its own fundraising arrangements. If you work across the UK, check which rules apply to you.

What does good charity marketing look like?

When I look at the campaigns that have lasted, they share a few things. They're simple enough to say in a sentence. They give people something to do. And they're built on something true about the cause.

Dogs Trust's line "A dog is for life, not just for Christmas" was coined in 1978, when the charity was still called the National Canine Defence League, and it's still being used. Macmillan's Coffee Morning started as one local committee's idea in 1990 and became a national event, because the ask was easy: put the kettle on, invite some people, give what you'd have spent. Neither relied on a huge media budget to begin with. They had a clear idea and a simple thing for people to do.

The same goes for film. A short documentary can explain a cause far better than a paragraph of copy, because people believe what they see someone say in their own words. If you want to see how I'd approach that, the post on what makes a good fundraising video goes through it, and what nonprofit storytelling is covers the thinking underneath.

Where does video fit into charity marketing?

Video sits across almost all five jobs. One film can go on the website to explain the cause, open a funder presentation, play at an event and be cut into short pieces for social. That's a lot of work out of one shoot, which is why I'd rather charities plan a film as a set of cuts than as a single video.

Marketing a charity is the only job where the product is a better world and the customer still wants a receipt.

It also helps with the trust problem. A film of a real person describing what changed for them is hard to fake, and viewers know it. I've written about turning one film into a year of content, and the same idea works well for charities with limited time. We made a set of cuts from a single interview-led shoot for char.gy, for example, so the same footage worked on the website, on LinkedIn and in short vertical pieces. A charity can do the same with a film about a service or a beneficiary who's happy to be involved.

How do you start if you've never done charity marketing?

Start smaller than you think you should. Pick one audience and one thing you want them to do. Write down the single sentence you'd want them to repeat to a friend. Then choose one or two channels you can actually keep up, rather than five you'll abandon by March.

  1. Decide the audience. Donors, volunteers, funders or the people you help. Just one for now.
  2. Find your proof. A real person, a real number, a real afternoon at the project.
  3. Choose the channel. The one your audience already uses. For many small charities that's Facebook and email.
  4. Make something repeatable. A monthly story beats a huge launch you can't follow up.
  5. Say thank you properly. It's the cheapest marketing there is.

The complete guide to charity and fundraising films pulls the rest of this series together. For the social side, how charities use social media is the next stop, and how charities advertise covers the paid routes.

How do you know if charity marketing is working?

It depends on the job. For fundraising, you can count gifts, regular givers and the cost of getting each one. For awareness, you're looking at reach, searches for your name and whether the right people start asking about you. For service promotion, it's referrals and first contacts. For supporter care, it's how many people are still giving after a year.

The trap is measuring only what's easy. Views and likes are easy, and they tell you very little about whether anyone gave, volunteered or turned up. I'd pick two numbers per audience and look at them monthly, and I'd keep a record of the comments and emails that mention a film or a post, because they often show you what actually landed. Trustees and funders respond well to that kind of plain evidence, and it stops you drifting into activity for its own sake.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Treating it as fundraising only. If the only time you contact people is to ask for money, they notice.
  • Talking about the organisation instead of the person. Nobody cares about your mission statement until they've met someone it helped.
  • Using shock where honesty would do. Distressing images can bring in money once and cost trust for years.
  • Ignoring the people you help. Plenty of charities have more donors than beneficiaries who've heard of them.
  • No plan for the long term. A campaign without a follow-up is a one-night stand.

If you're a charity with a story you'd like filmed properly, get in touch and tell us what you're trying to achieve. If a film isn't the right spend at this stage, we'll tell you.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is charity marketing the same as fundraising?
faqs.a: No. Fundraising is the part that asks for money, and it's one piece of charity marketing. Marketing also covers awareness, campaigning, promoting your services, building the brand and looking after existing supporters. In a small charity one person often does both, which is why they get mixed up, but the goals are different and so are the measures of success.

faqs.q: Does a small charity need a marketing budget?
faqs.a: It needs a plan more than a big budget. Many small charities do well with a few hours a week, a handful of real stories, an email list and one or two social channels. Spend only where you can see a result, and put time into thanking and updating the people who already support you before paying to find new ones.

faqs.q: What are the main rules for charity marketing in the UK?
faqs.a: Fundraising has to follow the Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice, adverts fall under the ASA's CAP Code, and contacting people by email, text or phone is governed by UK GDPR and PECR. The Charity Commission also expects trustees to make sure marketing is lawful and a sensible use of funds. Get specific advice for your organisation.

faqs.q: How is charity marketing different from marketing a business?
faqs.a: The person giving the money doesn't receive the benefit, so the message has to make a stranger care. A charity also answers to donors, funders, trustees, regulators and the people it helps all at once, and its biggest asset is public trust. The channels are the same as a business uses, but the tone and the standards of proof are higher.

items.title: How do charities use social media? What UK charities do
items.excerpt: What UK charities actually do on social media: the types of post, which platforms they use, how they raise money and what separates the accounts that work.
items.coverAlt: A volunteer filming on her phone in a busy church hall community kitchen
items.body:
Charities use social media to tell the stories of the people they help, ask for donations and sign-ups, recruit volunteers, run campaigns, answer questions and give supporters a reason to stay. Most of that happens through a small set of repeatable moves rather than anything clever, and the ones that work best put real people in front of the camera.

This post looks at what charities actually do on social media, platform by platform and post by post, using the latest sector research. It isn't a how-to for your own charity, which is what how to promote a charity on social media is for. This is the picture of what's going on across the sector, so you can see where you fit.

What do charities post on social media?

Nearly everything a charity posts falls into one of six buckets. The mix changes with the size of the charity and the cause, but you'll recognise all of them from your own feed.

  • Stories of the people or animals they help. The staple. A service user explaining what changed, a volunteer on a shift, a rescue and its happy ending.
  • Calls to action. Donate, sign, sign up for an event, share. Usually timed to a campaign or a date in the calendar.
  • Behind the scenes. The kitchen before service, the van being loaded, the team in a meeting. It shows where the money goes without a spreadsheet.
  • Updates and thank-yous. What a campaign raised, what was bought, who took part. Underrated, and one of the most effective ways to keep supporters.
  • Information and advice. Health charities, in particular, publish guidance that people share because it's useful.
  • Events and moments. Awareness days, fundraising events, anniversaries and news hooks.

The sector has noticed that audiences respond better to the first and third of those. The Charity Digital Skills Report 2026 found that more than half of charities (52%) are prioritising storytelling that involves people with lived experience, and 47% want to share more video and informal, co-created content. The stat further down the page shows the whole list.

Which platforms do charities use?

There isn't one answer, because the right platform follows the audience. Here's how it tends to break down in practice.

Facebook

Still the workhorse for UK charities, mostly because of its age range and its tools. Local charities use groups and events to reach the community, and supporters can set up fundraisers for a charity directly. If your donors are over 45, this is probably where most of them are.

Instagram

Good for visual causes and a younger audience. Charities use Reels and Stories for short films, and Stories link stickers for donations. Animal welfare, youth work, the arts and environmental causes do particularly well here.

YouTube

The home for longer films, and it behaves more like a search engine than a feed. People find charity films by searching for the problem, so a clear title matters more than a clever one. It's also where a documentary-style film earns its keep, because viewers who choose to watch have chosen to stay.

LinkedIn

The channel for corporate partnerships, funders, trustees and recruitment. A charity's CEO posting honestly about the work often does better here than the organisation's own page.

TikTok

Increasingly used to reach younger supporters, often through a single person from the team rather than a brand voice. It rewards authentic, unpolished content and punishes anything that looks like an advert.

X and other channels

Mostly for campaigning, news reaction and contact with journalists and politicians. WhatsApp and email newsletters sit behind the scenes for community and supporter groups.

How do charities use social media to raise money?

Directly and indirectly. The direct routes are the donation button or link on a post, platform fundraising tools, and sponsored challenge pages that supporters share with their own friends. Online giving platforms make this easy to set up, and Gift Aid can add 25p for every £1 given by a UK taxpayer when the donor ticks the box, which is why charities mention it so often.

The indirect route is more important. Social media rarely closes a donation on its own. It builds familiarity, so that when someone gets an email, sees an advert or hears about the charity from a friend, they already know it. That's why charities with a steady stream of honest content tend to see better results from their appeals. The people who give via a link are mostly the people who've been quietly watching for months.

Most people don't give the first time they see you. They give the fifth time they notice you were still there.

What else do charities use social media for?

Fundraising gets the attention, but the sector uses social media for plenty more.

  • Recruiting volunteers. Showing what a shift looks like does more than a job description.
  • Reaching service users. Some of the people a charity helps find it first through a post or a friend's share, and they won't read a leaflet.
  • Campaigning. Hashtags, petitions, tagging MPs and organising people around an issue.
  • Running communities. Peer support groups, forums and live Q&As.
  • Building the brand. A consistent tone and look so people recognise the charity before they read the name.
  • Crisis response. Quick updates and corrections when something goes wrong.

It's also a direct line to the person asking a question. Replying to comments promptly and warmly is one of the cheapest ways for a charity to look like what it is: a group of people who care.

What does a good charity social post look like?

I've watched a lot of charity content and made some of it, and the ones that work share a handful of habits.

  1. A real person in the first second. A face, a voice, a hand doing something. Not a logo.
  2. One idea. A post that tries to explain the whole charity explains nothing.
  3. Captions on the video. A lot of people watch with the sound off, and captions help everyone.
  4. A plain ask. Say what you'd like them to do, once.
  5. Honest numbers. "£15 covers one hot meal" is better than a vague promise, as long as it's true.

Dignity matters more on social than almost anywhere, because posts are public, shareable and permanent. I've written about consent and portrayal in brand films for charities, and the same principles apply to a 20 second Reel.

The best charity post of the year is usually someone making tea and saying something true.

How do charities get supporters to do the posting for them?

This is where social media works differently for charities than for most businesses. Supporters are happy to post on a charity's behalf, because it says something about them. A runner sharing their sponsorship page, a school sharing its bake sale photos or a company posting about its volunteering day all reach people the charity could never reach alone.

Smart charities make that easy. They give event participants a ready-made photo frame or hashtag, share the best supporter posts on their own page with permission, and tag partners so the post lands in front of the partner's followers. Some bring in ambassadors, which what a charity brand ambassador is covers properly. The point is that the charity isn't the only voice. When ten different people say the same true thing in ten different ways, it carries far more weight than a polished post from the organisation.

How much of it is organic and how much is paid?

Mostly organic, because most charities don't have the budget to do much else. Paid social tends to be used for a specific campaign: promoting an appeal, an event ticket page or a volunteer recruitment drive to a defined local audience. The results are easier to measure than organic posts, since you can see what each pound brought in, but it needs enough budget and attention to test properly. I look at the paid routes in how charities advertise, so I won't repeat them here.

What I'd say from the production side is that the content you pay to promote should be the content that already worked unpaid. If a film gets a warm response from your own followers, that's the one to put money behind. If a post got no reaction, spending on it won't change that.

How does video change what charities can do on social?

A lot. A written post asks someone to imagine the story. A short film lets them watch a person tell it. Video also travels: the same film gets shared by supporters, played at events and used in funding bids.

The trick is planning it as a set. One shoot with the right interviews can give you a three or four minute film for the website and YouTube, plus half a dozen vertical cuts for Instagram and TikTok, plus stills for Facebook and LinkedIn. We did this for char.gy, where one interview-led film was cut eleven ways, and I explain the idea more fully in turning one brand film into a year of content. For the broader craft of making business video work on each channel, social media videos for business is the one to read.

It's the same principle I use for community events like the Southwick D-Day commemoration: film the real people at the real moment, then work out which cuts suit which channel. Charities with an annual event or a flagship service can do the same. If you're still working out how to make the film itself, how to make a charity video is the step by step.

What are charities getting wrong on social media?

  • Posting only appeals. If every post asks for money, people stop looking. A good rule of thumb is that most of your posts shouldn't ask for anything.
  • No strategy. The same research found that only about a third of charities (36%) say developing their social media strategy is a priority this year, up from 25% last year. A lot of accounts run on whoever has an hour spare.
  • Not measuring. 35% say they want to monitor and evaluate what's working, which suggests plenty are still guessing.
  • Polished but empty. A stock photo and a slogan gets scrolled past. A volunteer who looks slightly nervous and means every word doesn't.
  • Forgetting the people in the film. Consent, safeguarding and the right to withdraw don't stop when the post goes live.

What can a small charity take from all this?

You don't need to be on six platforms. Pick one or two where your supporters already are, post a real story every week or two, thank people in public and answer every comment. Add video when you can get a good interview, and plan the cuts before you shoot. For ideas on a wider plan, the complete guide to charity and fundraising films ties the series together, and what charity marketing is explains where social fits in the whole picture.

If you'd like help turning a story into a film that works across channels, get in touch and tell us what you've got in mind.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Which social media platform is best for a charity?
faqs.a: It depends on who you're trying to reach. Facebook still suits older donors and local communities, Instagram and TikTok suit younger audiences and visual stories, LinkedIn suits funders and corporate partners, and YouTube suits longer films that people search for. Most small charities do better doing one or two properly than spreading thin across five.

faqs.q: How often should a charity post on social media?
faqs.a: Consistency matters more than volume. For a small team, two or three good posts a week on one or two platforms is realistic, and better than a flurry followed by silence. Plan content around real stories and events, batch it when you can, and make sure someone is replying to comments, because that's where relationships actually form.

faqs.q: Can charities fundraise directly on social media?
faqs.a: Yes. Platforms offer donation buttons and fundraising tools, and supporters can set up their own sponsored pages and share them. Charities still need to follow the Fundraising Regulator's code and the ASA's rules, and be clear about what donations are used for. Most giving is influenced by repeated exposure over time, not a single post.

faqs.q: Should a charity use video on social media?
faqs.a: Yes if you can do it well. Video lets people see and hear someone telling their own story, which builds trust faster than text. It doesn't need to be expensive, but it does need consent, clear sound and captions. Plan a longer film with shorter cuts from the same shoot so it works across your channels.

Sharing more video and informal, co-created content
Monitoring and evaluating what is working

stat.takeaway: Charities are putting real people and video first, and many are still building the strategy and measurement behind them.

items.title: How to promote a charity on social media: a practical guide
items.excerpt: A step-by-step guide to promoting a charity on social media: what to decide first, what to post, how to get seen and a simple 30 day plan for a small team.
items.coverAlt: A man in a black t-shirt laughs beside a colourful prize wheel at a summer party in a yard of shipping containers
items.body:
To promote a charity on social media, pick one audience and one action, choose one or two platforms where those people already are, post real stories from the people involved on a steady schedule, make the next step easy, and check once a month what's working. Consistency and honesty beat budget. Most small charities don't need more channels, they need a routine.

This is the how-to for your own charity, step by step, with a simple 30 day plan at the end. If you want the wider picture of what charities across the sector do on social, that's in how charities use social media. And if you're promoting a specific fundraising drive rather than the charity itself, how to promote a fundraising campaign on social media is the closer fit.

What should you decide before you post anything?

Four things, and they take an afternoon. Skipping them is the reason most charity accounts go quiet by spring.

  1. Who you're talking to. Donors, volunteers, local people who need your service, funders. Choose the main one. A post written for everyone lands with no one.
  2. What you want them to do. Give, sign up, turn up, share, get in touch. One action per audience.
  3. What you can sustain. Be realistic about hours. Two posts a week that actually happen beat daily posting that stops in three weeks.
  4. Who's in charge. One named person, with a backup. Everyone else sends them material.

Write the answers on one page and pin it somewhere the team will see it. When someone suggests joining another platform or doing a trend, you can check it against the page.

Which platform should you start with?

Go where your audience already is, not where you wish they were. A few rules of thumb:

  • If your supporters are mostly over 45 or very local, start with Facebook.
  • If your cause is visual, or you want younger supporters, add Instagram.
  • If you're after funders, corporate partners or trustees, LinkedIn.
  • If you'll have films of ten minutes or more, YouTube is where they'll be found by search.

You can ask your existing supporters. A line in your next email or a question at your next event ("where do you see us?") is faster than guessing. Ofcom's research shows nine in 10 adult internet users (89%) use at least one social media platform, so your audience is almost certainly on one. The question is which.

What do people actually do on social media?

Here's the part that changes how you make content. Ofcom found that around half of adult social media users (49%) now actively post, share or comment, down from 61% a year earlier. The rest are watching and scrolling. So most of the people you want to reach won't comment, share or even like. They'll just watch.

That has practical consequences for a charity:

  • Don't judge a post by comments alone. Silence doesn't mean it failed.
  • Make content that works for someone who's half paying attention: a face and a clear first line.
  • Think about the quiet watcher who gives in six months. Your job is to be the charity they remember when they decide.
Most of your audience will never comment. Plenty of them will still remember you.

What should a charity post?

Use a simple rotation so you're never staring at a blank screen. I'd build every month from four kinds of post:

  • A story. One person, one change. This is the anchor.
  • A behind the scenes. A volunteer shift, a delivery, a team meeting. It makes the work feel real.
  • A thank you or an update. What your supporters made possible, with the real result.
  • An ask. Donate, volunteer or come along. One a week at most.

Three out of four posts shouldn't ask for anything. That ratio does a lot of the work. People are far more willing to answer a request from a charity they feel they know.

How do you get stories to post?

Ask for them constantly and make it easy. A short note to frontline staff and volunteers at the end of each week ("send me one moment that made you proud") fills a content bank quickly. Keep a shared folder for photos and clips, with the consent status written next to each one. Then, when you've got a bigger story, plan to film it properly.

What about people with lived experience?

Their stories are the strongest content you have and the ones that need the most care. Ask in plain language, explain where the post will appear and for how long, let them see it first and let them change their minds. I go through this in detail in brand films for charities. A person who feels in control of their own story tells it better, and the audience can feel that.

How do you make posts people actually watch?

Most of what makes a charity video work is simple. I'd put these on a sticky note:

  1. Start with a person talking, not a logo. The first two seconds decide it.
  2. Add captions. Plenty of people watch with the sound off.
  3. Keep it short for social. Fifteen to forty-five seconds for the feed, longer on YouTube for people who've chosen to stay.
  4. Film vertical for Reels, TikTok and Stories. Square or landscape for Facebook and LinkedIn can work too.
  5. Use natural light and clean sound. A window and a cheap lavalier microphone beat a fancy camera with a noisy room.
  6. End with one clear next step.

If you want the fuller version, what makes a good fundraising video goes through what holds attention, and how to make a brand video people watch covers the craft in more detail.

Nobody ever shared a charity post because it had a lovely gradient.

How do you get more people to see it?

Charities have more free reach available than they tend to use.

  • Ask your own people. Staff, trustees and volunteers sharing a post with a line of their own can double its reach. Give them the post and the wording.
  • Tag partners and venues. Funders, local councils, businesses and event hosts like to be thanked, and a tag puts you in front of their followers.
  • Collaborate where the platform allows it. Joint posts and shared Reels show up on both accounts.
  • Join existing conversations. Awareness days, local news and community groups. Add something useful rather than just dropping a link.
  • Use local groups. Neighbourhood and community pages are often where a local charity's best supporters are.
  • Put it everywhere else. Your website, email signature, newsletter and printed material should point to your social accounts.

Paid promotion can help with a specific campaign, usually a small boost on a post that's already working. That's covered in how charities advertise. Check the Fundraising Regulator's code and the ASA's rules on advertising before you spend.

How do you make it easy to give or get involved?

Every post that asks for something needs a route that works on a phone in under a minute. Link directly to the donation page or sign-up form, not the homepage. Test it yourself on your phone. Mention Gift Aid where it applies, because a UK taxpayer's donation can be topped up by 25p for every £1 at no extra cost to them. And thank people immediately, by name where they've agreed to it. That first thank-you is when a one-off giver becomes a regular one.

How do you handle comments, criticism and mistakes?

Someone will eventually leave a comment you don't like, and a charity's reply is public. Reply quickly, politely and in a human voice. If the person has a genuine problem, offer to take it offline and give them a name and an email. If they're simply wrong, correct the fact once, calmly, and leave it. If it's abusive, hide or report it and move on. Have a short written policy so whoever's covering the account isn't deciding in the moment, and make sure it covers anything that touches safeguarding.

If you post something wrong, say so. Correct it, say what you changed and carry on. Supporters forgive honest mistakes much more readily than a charity that goes quiet or deletes everything. That's the same trust issue that sits underneath all charity marketing, and what charity marketing is covers why it matters so much.

Who should run the account?

Ideally someone who's close enough to the work to know what's worth posting and senior enough to say yes to things quickly. In a small charity, that often means a part-time communications person, or a trustee or volunteer with an eye for it. If you use a volunteer, give them a one page guide to your tone, your consent rules and what never to post, and make sure two people have the logins.

Avoid handing the account to whoever happens to be youngest. Social media looks easy and is surprisingly demanding, particularly when a post goes wrong. Treat it as a proper role, with time protected in someone's week. If budget allows, pay for a few hours of help setting up a content calendar and a filming routine, then run it in-house. That tends to be better value than outsourcing the posting.

What does a simple 30 day plan look like?

If you're starting from nothing, this is a plan I'd be happy to follow:

  • Week 1. Set the audience, action and platform. Update bios and links. Collect five stories and photos with consent confirmed.
  • Week 2. Post a story on day one, a behind the scenes on day four. Reply to every comment. Ask supporters to share.
  • Week 3. Post a thank-you or update, plus one soft ask. Try one short video with captions.
  • Week 4. Look at what people watched, shared and clicked. Do more of that. Plan the next month.

After that, repeat. If you want a film to anchor the content, how to make a charity video walks through it, and how to turn one brand film into a year of content shows how a single shoot feeds the whole calendar.

What are the usual mistakes to avoid?

Four come up again and again. Charities set up five accounts and feed none of them. They post only when they want money. They use a stock photo where a real volunteer was available. And they stop in the quiet months, which is when a steady presence matters most because the bigger charities have gone quiet too. Pick fewer channels, ask less often and show more real faces, and you've avoided most of the problems.

How do you tell if it's working?

Pick a few numbers and check them monthly: new followers who match your audience, link clicks, donations or sign-ups from social, and replies that show someone cared. Ignore the vanity numbers. A hundred clicks to a sign-up page beats ten thousand views that went nowhere. Keep a note of what each audience actually did, and show it to your trustees. It makes the next budget conversation much easier.

The complete guide to charity and fundraising films collects the rest of this series. And if you've got a story that deserves a proper film behind it, see how we tell a business story on screen and get in touch.

faqs.q: How can a small charity get followers on social media?
faqs.a: Ask the people closest to you first: staff, trustees, volunteers, service partners and existing donors. Post real stories regularly, tag the people and organisations involved, reply to every comment and mention your accounts in emails, on your website and at events. Followers grow slowly and steadily when people see you're consistent, honest and worth following.

faqs.q: How often should a charity post?
faqs.a: Two or three posts a week on one or two platforms is a realistic target for a small team, and it's better than daily posting that fizzles out. Keep a content bank of stories, photos and clips so you're not scrambling. If something big happens, such as an event or a campaign, post more for that short period and then return to your usual rhythm.

faqs.q: Do charities need to pay for social media promotion?
faqs.a: Not to start. Organic posting, supporter sharing, partner tags and community groups can take a small charity a long way. Paid promotion is useful for a specific campaign, such as an event or appeal, once you know which content works. Always follow the ASA's advertising rules and the Fundraising Regulator's code if you do spend.

faqs.q: What if people we help don't want to appear in posts?
faqs.a: Respect that completely. You can tell their story without showing their face, use a voice with other footage, change names, or let a member of staff or volunteer describe what you see. Never pressure anyone. Get clear written consent from anyone who is identifiable, explain where the post will appear and let them withdraw later.
