items.title: How do charities advertise? The main routes in the UK
items.excerpt: How UK charities advertise: the channels they use, how they pay for them, the rules they follow and how a small charity can start without a big budget.
items.coverAlt: A glowing bus shelter panel on a rainy London high street at dusk with a red bus passing
items.body:
Charities advertise through the same channels as businesses: television, radio, online video, paid social, search, posters and press, plus direct mail and door drops. What's different is the rules they follow, the budgets they have and the partnerships that cut costs. Most also lean on donated media space and search grants, and plenty of the best work starts with a film.

This post walks through the main routes, who uses which and what the rules say. It doesn't cover why charities advertise at all, which is in why charities advertise, or what TV airtime costs, which belongs to how much charity TV adverts cost. Free social posting is a separate subject too, covered in how charities use social media.

What's the difference between advertising and the rest of charity marketing?

Advertising is paid or donated space bought to carry a message. Everything else you do for free, such as a post on your own page, a press release or an event, is promotion. Both sit inside the bigger job described in what charity marketing is, and charities usually need both.

The distinction matters because paid advertising has different controls. You choose who sees it, how often and when. You can measure it more precisely. And it has to follow the advertising rules. That's the trade: more control and more accountability than a post that just goes out to your followers.

What advertising channels do charities use?

A national charity might use all of these in a year. A small local charity might use two. Here they are, roughly in order of how much budget they need.

Television

Still the way big charities reach millions at once, particularly for appeals aimed at regular givers. Some run direct response ads, which ask people to give or text there and then, and others run brand ads that build familiarity. Every TV ad needs to be cleared before broadcast, and the process is run by Clearcast on behalf of the broadcasters. I leave the costs and the format to the sibling posts.

Online video and YouTube

This is where more charities are shifting, because it reaches the same people at a lower entry cost and with more targeting. Ofcom reports that the average person in the UK watched 41 minutes of YouTube a day in 2025, and 19 of those minutes were on a TV set. A film that would have needed a TV slot a few years ago can now be placed in front of a defined audience online for a modest budget.

Paid social

Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn all sell targeted ads. Charities use them to promote appeals, events, volunteer drives and sign-ups, and to reach people who look like their existing supporters. It's also the easiest way to test a film: put a small budget behind two cuts and see which one people watch.

Search advertising

This catches people already looking: for help with a condition, for a charity to give to at Christmas, or for volunteering near them. Google's Ad Grants programme gives eligible charities up to $10,000 a month of search advertising credit, and many UK charities use it. There are conditions on how the account has to be run, so read them before you apply.

Radio and audio

Radio and podcasts work well for local charities and for appeals with a clear call to action. Audio can be cheaper to produce than video, and a good voice telling a short story carries a lot of weight.

Out of home

Posters, bus shelters, digital screens and rail stations. Outdoor companies sometimes donate unsold space to charities, which can make a campaign possible for far less than rate card. It's usually offered at short notice, so have creative ready to go.

Press and magazines

Print adverts have shrunk, but they still work for older donors and for legacy giving, where the audience reads the paper and has time to think. Many local charities use community newspapers and parish magazines because they cost little and everyone reads them.

Direct mail and door drops

Letters, leaflets and inserts through the letterbox. It's one of the oldest charity channels and still brings in a lot of regular and one-off gifts, particularly from older supporters. A story told in a short letter with a photo does the same job as the film, in print.

How do charities pay for advertising?

Sometimes they don't pay full price. The usual routes are:

  • Donated media. Broadcasters, outdoor companies and publishers occasionally give space or airtime to charity campaigns, often through partnerships or at quiet times.
  • Grants and credits. Search credits like Ad Grants and platform schemes for non-profits.
  • Corporate partners. A business pays for or supports the campaign in return for association.
  • Restricted funding. A trust or foundation funds a specific campaign, sometimes including the film.
  • Part of the fundraising budget. Advertising that recruits regular givers is usually seen as an investment, paid back over time.

Trustees care a lot about the last one, because they have to be satisfied that spending money on advertising is a sensible use of charitable funds. A charity that can show what each recruited donor is worth over time has a much easier conversation.

Nobody has ever given to a charity because of a clever transition.

What rules do charity adverts have to follow?

Charities don't get a pass on advertising law. This is general information, not legal advice.

  • The CAP Code and BCAP Code. Enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority, these cover non-broadcast and broadcast ads. They require ads to be legal, decent, honest and truthful, and they have specific rules about charity-linked promotions.
  • The Code of Fundraising Practice. The Fundraising Regulator's code covers fundraising communications and ads, with its core values of being legal, open, honest and respectful.
  • Impact claims need evidence. "£10 provides a meal" is fine if it's true on average. Vague or inflated figures aren't.
  • Vulnerable people and children. There are extra expectations about how they're shown, and you should follow your own safeguarding policy as well.
  • Data and consent. If your ad collects details, UK GDPR and PECR rules apply.

What makes a charity advert work?

The channel matters less than the idea behind it. The adverts that stick are usually built around one person or one clear picture, rather than a list of what the charity does. Dogs Trust has used the same simple line about dogs and Christmas since 1978, and it still works because it's true and it's easy to repeat.

For video ads, the first few seconds carry most of the weight. If a viewer can skip after five seconds, those five seconds need a human face and a reason to keep watching. Beyond that I'd keep to the basics: one message, one person, one call to action. Documentary-style filming suits this because the person is talking in their own words, which makes the advert feel like something you chose to watch rather than something that interrupted you. If you want to see how I approach people on camera, La Fromagerie is a good example of letting someone tell their own story.

An advert gets you noticed once. A true story gets you remembered.

How do charities plan a campaign across several channels?

The bigger charities work backwards from a single moment: a Christmas appeal, an awareness week, an emergency response. They decide the one thing they want people to do, then pick channels to reach different groups. Television or out of home creates awareness, online video explains the story, search catches the people who go looking, and email and direct mail pull in the gifts. Each piece points to the same landing page, with the same look and the same wording, so someone who sees two of them recognises it as one campaign.

Smaller charities can copy the structure at a smaller scale. One film, one landing page, one local radio spot, one boosted post. What matters is that each piece reinforces the others, and that you've decided in advance how you'll measure the result. Set aside a few days after the campaign to look at what came in, what each channel cost and who gave. That review is worth more than the next creative idea, because it tells you what to repeat next year.

How can a small charity advertise on a small budget?

Start with the free and low-cost routes, then add paid only where you can see a result.

  1. Apply for Ad Grants. If you're eligible, it can drive people looking for your cause straight to your site.
  2. Boost your best content. Put £50 behind a post or film that has already done well organically, targeted at your area.
  3. Use local media. Community radio, parish magazines and local news sites are affordable and trusted.
  4. Ask for donated space. Approach local outdoor firms, shops and venues. The worst answer is no.
  5. Test small first. Run two versions for a week with a modest budget before committing.

For the organic side, how to promote a charity on social media sets out a plan you can run alongside.

Should a charity make a film for its advertising?

If you've got a story that people respond to, yes, and I'd plan it as a set. One shoot can give you the longer film for your website, YouTube and funder meetings, plus short cuts of 15 to 30 seconds for paid social, plus stills for print and posters. That's far better value than commissioning each piece separately. I've explained the approach in how to turn one brand film into a year of content, and brand video ads on social and online covers the ad formats from the production side.

The same footage can serve as the heart of a campaign. We've done this for brands, such as the cuts we made for char.gy, and for a charity the thinking is identical: one interview-led shoot, many placements. If you're making your first charity film, how to make a charity video is where I'd start, and brand films for charities covers consent, dignity and budget.

What mistakes do charities make with advertising?

  • Spending before they know the message. A weak idea with a big budget is still a weak idea.
  • Using shock where honesty would work. It might get attention, but it can damage trust and attract complaints.
  • No way to measure. Use a unique web address, phone number or tracking link for each ad, so you know what worked.
  • No follow-up. Someone who donated after seeing an ad should get a warm thank-you within days.
  • Wrong audience. A broad ad aimed at everyone usually reaches nobody who cares.

For the full series on films and campaigns, the complete guide to charity and fundraising films pulls it together. If you have an advert or appeal in mind and you're not sure a film's the right route, get in touch. We'll tell you straight if it isn't.

faqs.q: Do charities pay for adverts?
faqs.a: Often, yes, though not always at full price. Charities sometimes receive donated airtime or poster space, search credits through programmes like Google Ad Grants, or corporate sponsorship of a campaign. Trustees expect any spend to be justified as a sensible use of charity funds, so most track what each pound of advertising brings in over time.

faqs.q: Do charity adverts have to follow advertising rules?
faqs.a: Yes. Charity adverts fall under the same ASA codes as any other advert, so they must be legal, decent, honest and truthful. Fundraising communications also follow the Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice. Claims about impact need to be supportable, and extra care applies when children or vulnerable people appear. Take advice for your own organisation.

faqs.q: What's the cheapest way for a small charity to advertise?
faqs.a: Start with search credits if you qualify for Google Ad Grants, community media, and small paid boosts to posts that have already done well on your own pages. Ask local firms about donated poster space too. Test two versions of an advert on a modest budget before you spend more, and track results with a dedicated link or phone number.

faqs.q: Is video advertising worth it for a charity?
faqs.a: It can be, because it lets people hear a real story rather than read about one. Online video also reaches defined audiences at a lower entry cost than television. It works best when one shoot produces a longer film plus short cuts for paid placements, and when the first seconds put a real person on screen.

items.title: Why do charities advertise? The real reasons, explained
items.excerpt: Why UK charities advertise: replacing lost donors, raising awareness, reaching people who need help, and whether it's a fair use of donated money.
items.coverAlt: A fundraising quiz night in a warm, busy London pub, seen from the bar
items.body:
Charities advertise because supporters drift away, new people have to be found, and the public can't help a cause it has never heard of. Advertising recruits donors and volunteers, tells people in need that help exists, and changes behaviour or opinion. Spending on it is justified when each pound brings back more than a pound over time.

This post gives the reasons, one by one, and then deals with the objection people raise most: "isn't that donation money being wasted on ads?" It sits alongside how charities advertise, which covers the channels, and how much charity TV adverts cost, which covers the price tag.

Why can't a charity just rely on word of mouth?

Some do, and for a small local charity it can be enough. But word of mouth only reaches the people your supporters already know, who tend to be a lot like your supporters. It's slow, it's hard to steer, and it can't be switched on in time for an emergency or a deadline.

It also can't replace the supporters who leave. People move house, change jobs, hit financial trouble, lose interest or die. A charity that never recruits is a charity that's slowly getting smaller. That's the heart of why advertising exists, and the numbers are stark.

How many donors are charities losing?

The Charities Aid Foundation says the UK charity sector has lost around 600,000 donors every year for the last decade, which adds up to almost six million in total. Its analysis puts the income lost over that decade at more than £12 billion, because fewer people are giving.

So a charity isn't just trying to grow. It's trying to stand still, in a world where each year several hundred thousand supporters stop giving. Advertising is one of the few reliable ways to replace them in volume. Why people stop, and what keeps them, is the subject of why donors stop giving, and I'd read it alongside this one.

A charity that stops recruiting isn't saving money. It's shrinking slowly.

What are the main reasons charities advertise?

There are seven, and most charities advertise for several at once. Knowing which one a given advert is for makes it much easier to judge.

1. To find new regular donors

A monthly direct debit is worth much more than a single gift, because it's predictable, and charities can plan staffing and services around it. Recruiting those donors costs money upfront, and the return arrives over years. That's why the big television appeals are usually asking for a small monthly amount.

2. To raise awareness of the cause

Plenty of people haven't heard of a condition, a problem or a charity until they see an advert. Awareness advertising doesn't ask for anything, or only a little. It prepares the ground so the next ask, an email, a collection or a letter, lands with someone who recognises the name.

3. To tell people that help exists

This is the one that's most often forgotten. A helpline, a food bank, a support group or a free legal advice service only works if the people who need it know about it. For those charities, advertising is a service delivery cost, not a marketing luxury. Someone seeing a poster at a bus stop at the right moment can be the difference between asking for help and not.

4. To change behaviour

Many charity campaigns are public information. Think of health charities encouraging people to check symptoms or get screened, road safety charities, or campaigns about safer drinking. The goal is that people act differently, not that they give.

5. To recruit volunteers, fosterers and supporters

Animal charities need foster homes, youth charities need mentors, and hospices need shop volunteers. Advertising finds them, particularly when the ask is specific and local.

6. To drive campaigning and policy change

Advertising can put an issue on the agenda for the public and for politicians, and give campaigners a way to show support is large. Charities have to take care on this one, because charity law limits political campaigning, so trustees should take advice.

7. To support events, legacies and corporate partnerships

Ticket sales for an event, a legacy campaign that plants the idea of leaving a gift in a will, or a business partnership that needs visibility to be worth a company's time all benefit from paid promotion.

Isn't advertising a waste of donated money?

It's a fair question, and trustees ask it constantly. The honest answer is: it can be, if it's done badly. But in most cases the maths works in the opposite direction.

The test is return. If a charity spends £1 on advertising and eventually brings in more than £1 in donations, plus the long-term value of loyal supporters, then the advertising has funded more of the cause than the same money spent on the cause would have. That isn't a trick. It's the reason charities recruit regular givers at a cost they recover over a couple of years.

What matters is transparency. The Charity Commission's research on public trust shows the public cares most that money goes to the cause and that the charity makes a real difference. A charity that explains why it advertises, what it costs and what it brings in is usually on safe ground. A charity that hides it isn't. The Fundraising Regulator's code asks for openness and honesty for the same reason, and the ASA's rules require adverts to be truthful.

If a charity ad made you cry in a car park, the media buyer did their job.

How should a charity judge whether an advert paid off?

By tracking what it brought in. That means a dedicated web address, phone number or donation form per campaign, so the money can be traced to the advert. Then compare what each regular donor recruited cost with what they're expected to give. A charity that can show those numbers to trustees and funders has an answer ready when someone asks.

Why do the adverts look and sound the way they do?

People often find charity adverts uncomfortable: the sad music, the close-ups, the direct ask. They exist in that form because they've been tested and, for a long time, they worked. The sector is now questioning how far to push it. The public is more aware of how people are portrayed, and many charities have moved towards showing people with dignity and agency instead of pity. I go into the thinking in brand films for charities.

A good test: would the person in the advert be happy to see it, and would they feel it showed them fairly? If yes, you're probably on the right side of the line. Why adverts run so long is its own question, answered in why charity adverts are so long.

What happens if charities stop advertising?

The effect is slow, which is what makes it tempting to cut. Income doesn't fall off a cliff in the first month. The pool of supporters just gets a little older and a little smaller each year, until a charity looks up and finds it has half the regular givers it used to. Rebuilding is more expensive than maintaining, because the name has faded as well as the list. That's why careful charities treat a baseline level of recruitment as a running cost, rather than something to switch off when money is tight.

Who decides whether a charity advertises?

In the end, the trustees. They're responsible for making sure charity money is used properly, so a sensible board asks for a proposal, a budget, a target and a review date before approving any campaign. In larger charities the fundraising director brings forward the plan, and it often includes a test phase, a "payback period" (how long until recruited donors have repaid the cost) and a worst case.

In a small charity, it can be one conversation at a trustee meeting. That's fine, as long as it's written down. Trustees who are comfortable with advertising are usually the ones who've seen the numbers, so give them the numbers. A one page summary of what you plan to spend, what you expect back and how you'll check it does more than any amount of persuasion.

What does it look like at the small end?

For a local charity, advertising rarely means television. It's a boosted post to people within five miles, a banner at the school gates, a slot on community radio and an ad in the parish magazine. The reasons are exactly the same as for a national: replace the supporters you lose, tell people you exist, and ask. The difference is scale, and the main skill is knowing your own patch. A small charity with a clear message and a well chosen few hundred pounds can do a surprising amount, particularly if the money goes behind a real story rather than a generic slogan.

What about charities that don't advertise?

Plenty don't, and it's the right call for some. A charity funded mostly by grants and contracts, with a small, well-defined group of beneficiaries, may get little from broad advertising. What it still needs is a way to be found by the right people, and that often means a strong website, local relationships and honest storytelling. Those are the cheaper cousins of advertising and they work for smaller budgets.

For a charity in that position, film can do a lot of the work. A short documentary about the service gives referrers, funders and potential supporters something to watch before they ever call. It can sit on the website, travel through partners and be cut into posts. That's where I come in. We've done similar work in other sectors, like the cuts we made for char.gy, and the approach carries across: a real person, a real place, a clear ask. How that works for a fundraising ask in particular is covered in how to make a fundraising video.

What should a charity do before it decides to advertise?

  1. Name the goal. Donors, awareness, service users, volunteers or behaviour change. One main goal per campaign.
  2. Know the number. What is a new supporter worth over two or three years? That sets how much you can afford to spend finding one.
  3. Fix the basics. A donation page that works on a phone, a thank-you process and a clear message.
  4. Test small. A trial before a full campaign.
  5. Get consent right. Anyone in your advert needs a clear agreement, and you should be able to take it down if they change their mind.
  6. Plan the follow-up. The advert isn't the end. Someone has to welcome the person who responded.

The complete guide to charity and fundraising films pulls the series together, and what charity marketing is explains where advertising sits in the bigger picture. If you've got an appeal and you're wondering whether a film is the right way to carry it, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Why do charities spend money on adverts instead of the cause?
faqs.a: Because advertising can raise more than it costs. A charity that spends £1 recruiting a regular donor can get back several pounds over the following years, which funds more of the cause than that £1 would have done directly. Good charities track the return and are open with trustees and the public about what they spend and what it brings in.

faqs.q: Do charity adverts actually work?
faqs.a: Many do, especially for recruiting regular donors and raising awareness, though results vary a lot by cause, message and channel. The sector loses hundreds of thousands of donors each year, so recruitment advertising is partly about replacing them. The best way to know is to track each advert with its own link or phone number and compare cost with income.

faqs.q: Are charities allowed to advertise?
faqs.a: Yes. Charities can advertise like any other organisation, provided adverts are legal, honest and truthful under the ASA's codes and fundraising follows the Fundraising Regulator's code. Trustees must be satisfied it's a reasonable use of charity funds. Political campaigning is more restricted for charities, so get advice before running anything that argues for a change in law.

faqs.q: Is advertising only about raising money?
faqs.a: No. Many charity adverts exist to tell people about a service, change behaviour, recruit volunteers or foster carers, or raise awareness of a condition. For a helpline or support group, advertising is how the people who need it find out it exists. Fundraising is only one of the reasons, though it's the one most people notice.

items.title: Why are charity adverts so long? What the length is for
items.excerpt: Charity appeals run to 60 or 90 seconds because they have to explain a cause, make you care and ask for action. Here's why length works, and when it doesn't.
items.coverAlt: A camera operator filming two people talking in a hospice day room beside a rainy window
items.body:
Charity adverts run long because they're doing a different job from a product advert. They have to explain a cause most viewers know little about, make someone care, and then ask for something specific, all in one sitting. A 30 second spot rarely has room for all three, so many charity appeals stretch to 60 seconds, 90 seconds or two minutes.

This post is about the reasons behind that, from a film maker's side of the table, and what a smaller charity can take from it. It isn't a guide to buying airtime, which is in how much charity TV adverts cost, or to the wider mix of channels, which is in how charities advertise. If you're deciding how long your own film should be, how long a fundraising video should be is the better starting point.

Are charity adverts really longer than other adverts?

Often, yes, though not always. The standard length of a TV ad in the UK is 30 seconds, and Thinkbox, the TV industry's marketing body, says roughly half of all ads are exactly that. Anything beyond it is a choice, and charities make that choice more than most.

The options are simple. Airtime is sold in multiples of ten seconds, so an ad can be 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60 seconds, and longer formats of 90 seconds or two minutes exist too. Thinkbox describes those longer ones as typically used to launch a campaign before it switches to shorter versions. Charities tend to reach for the longer lengths because they're trying to move someone to act in the moment, not to be remembered at a supermarket shelf three weeks later.

That's the honest first answer. The ad isn't long because the charity is indulgent. It's long because the viewer has to travel a long way in a short time: from not knowing about the problem, to caring about it, to getting their phone out.

Why does a charity ad need more time than a product ad?

A product ad is selling something people already understand. Nobody needs a minute to be told what a sofa is. A charity is usually selling a feeling and an idea, and the viewer has to build the whole picture from scratch.

Think about what has to happen in a typical appeal film:

  • The problem has to become real. "Thousands of children" means nothing. One child, in one place, doing one ordinary thing, means something.
  • The viewer has to feel it before they're asked. If the ask arrives before the feeling does, it lands as a demand.
  • The solution has to be believable. People want to know that a gift of a certain size does something specific, and that takes a few seconds of proof.
  • The ask has to be clear. A donation amount, how to give, what happens next. That alone can take 10 to 15 seconds if it's done properly.

Add those up and you've used a 30 second ad before anyone's been moved. That's the arithmetic behind most long charity ads, and it's the same arithmetic a documentary maker deals with on every project. A story needs room to build, and a story with an ask on the end needs a bit more.

The ad isn't long because the charity is indulgent. It's long because the viewer has to travel a long way in a short time.

Is it about the ask, not just the story?

Partly, yes. A lot of charity television is built to get a response, and a response ad has jobs a brand ad doesn't. It needs a clear call to action, a way to give and some reassurance about who you're giving to. Fundraisers have used the long format for years on the logic that a fuller argument gets a bigger response, the same way a long letter can outperform a short one in the post.

I'm a film maker, not a fundraising media buyer, so I won't pretend to know any charity's response data. What I can tell you is what I see on the creative side: the ask is rarely tacked on at the end. The best appeal films build towards it, so the last 15 seconds feel like the natural next step rather than a sales pitch bolted on. If you strip one out of a 90 second film and cut to 30, the ask survives but the reason to say yes doesn't.

Brand-led charity ads work differently. A charity might run a 60 second film to build awareness and goodwill with no donation line at all, which has more in common with a product campaign. Both exist, and part of the confusion about "charity adverts" is that people lump the two together.

How is airtime sold, and does length change the maths?

TV airtime is sold on a cost per thousand basis, depending on who's watching, and a longer ad takes up more of the break. Thinkbox publishes conversion tables showing, for example, that 100 thirty-second spots equal 50 sixty-second ones in airtime. So a 90 second ad takes three times the airtime of a 30 second one for the same number of showings.

That's why length isn't something a charity gets for nothing. Every extra second is paid for out of money that could have gone to the cause, and trustees know it. So when a charity chooses to run long, it's usually because it's tested the longer version and found it works harder per pound, or because it's decided a short version would leave out something it can't do without.

If you want the full picture on spend, the cost post covers what airtime and production run to in the UK.

What does a long charity ad do that a short one can't?

Thinkbox's own guidance says longer ads have benefits over shorter ones and can act as memory anchors, meaning the fuller film helps people remember the shorter versions that follow it. That's a general finding about television, not a charity-specific one, but it matches what I'd expect: a viewer who's seen the full story once only needs a few seconds of it later to bring the feeling back.

In practice a lot of charities do exactly that. One long film carries the story. Shorter cuts, 30 seconds, 15 seconds, vertical edits for the phone, then do the reminding. It's the same shoot, cut several ways, which is how we'd plan any brand film. I've gone through that approach in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

Nobody's ever said "I wish that charity ad had been shorter" while reaching for their wallet. They say it while reaching for the remote.

When is a long charity advert a mistake?

When the length isn't earned. I've watched plenty of films, charity and commercial, that run long because nobody was brave enough to cut. Here's what that looks like:

  • The same point is made three times. Once with a statistic, once with a person, once with a voiceover. Pick the person.
  • The first 10 seconds are a logo and a mission statement. On TV, and especially on social, you've lost people by then.
  • Too many voices. Four people each get 20 seconds and nobody gets enough time to become real.
  • The ask is buried. If someone watches to the end and still isn't sure what to do, the length was wasted.

The test I'd use is simple. Take any 10 second chunk out of the middle. If the film still works, it didn't need to be there. If you can feel the hole, it was doing its job.

Does the same logic apply to online films?

Not in the same way. A TV ad is shown to people who didn't ask for it, in a break, alongside other ads. An online film is usually watched by someone who chose to, on a website, an email link or a social feed, and what holds them is different. We cover the length question for online fundraising film in its own post, and the general version in how long a brand film should be.

The short version is that attention online is earned per second. A three minute film on a donation page can work well because the viewer is already interested. The same film as a cold social ad usually needs a much shorter cut. That's why I'd always plan a long film, a mid-length one and a vertical edit together at the start, rather than hoping one file will do every job.

What can a smaller charity take from this?

You don't need a national TV budget to learn from how the big charities build their films. A few things carry over to any size of organisation.

Decide the one job first

Is the film there to raise money now, to build awareness, or to thank and reassure existing supporters? Each one wants a different length. A film trying to do all three is how you end up with four minutes of vague.

Build toward the ask

If there's a donation call at the end, the film should be heading there from the first scene. Work backwards from the ask and work out what the viewer needs to feel and know right before it.

Plan the cuts at the start

Shoot once, edit several lengths. It's much cheaper than commissioning a second film later, and it means your supporters see a consistent story wherever they meet you. Our Ohme Christmas raffle work is a campaign rather than a charity film, but it's built the same way, with one idea cut to suit the places it ran.

Let one real person carry it

A single person who's lived the thing, speaking plainly, will hold attention longer than any narrator. How to do that with care is covered in brand films for charities: dignity, consent and budget.

If you want the wider picture of how these pieces fit together, the complete guide to charity and fundraising films pulls it into one place.

So should your charity make a long advert?

Only if the story needs the time. If you can tell it in 30 seconds without losing the reason to care, do that. If you can't, don't squash it, because a rushed emotional film feels manipulative. And if you're not buying TV at all, which is true of most small charities, the question is really about the film on your website and in your supporters' feeds, where length is a different calculation altogether.

The useful habit is to say out loud, before anything is written, what the viewer should feel at the halfway point and what they should do at the end. If you can't, the film will wander, and wandering is what makes a film long in the bad way. If you're working out what length your story deserves and what it would take to make, get in touch and tell us about it. We'll say plainly whether a film is the right spend for you.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Are charity adverts longer than normal adverts?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Thinkbox says roughly half of UK TV ads are 30 seconds, and charity appeals more often run to 60 or 90 seconds, or two minutes. The reason is the job: a charity has to explain an unfamiliar cause, make the viewer care and ask for action, and that rarely fits into half a minute.

faqs.q: Why do charity adverts show upsetting scenes?
faqs.a: Because a feeling is what moves most people to act, and a statistic alone rarely does it. Good practice has shifted towards showing people with dignity and agency rather than pity, and towards consent that is checked repeatedly. If you're planning one, read the guidance on putting people first before you write a script.

faqs.q: Does a longer charity advert raise more money?
faqs.a: Not automatically. A longer film gives more room for the story and the ask, but it also costs more airtime and loses viewers if it drags. Charities that run long ads usually do so after testing, so look at your own results rather than copying someone else's length.

faqs.q: How long should a charity video be online?
faqs.a: It depends on where it sits. On a donation page or website, two to three minutes can work because the viewer is already interested. As a social ad to people who don't know you, much shorter cuts do better. Plan a long film and several short edits from the same shoot.

items.title: How much do charity TV adverts cost in the UK?
items.excerpt: A charity TV advert has three costs: making the film, Clearcast approval and airtime. Here's what each involves and where a smaller charity's budget should go.
items.coverAlt: A three person crew setting up a camera, boom and light in a plain community centre hall
items.body:
A charity TV advert has three separate costs: making the film, getting it cleared by Clearcast, and buying the airtime. Making it ranges from a few thousand pounds to six figures. Clearance is usually paid for by the broadcasters. Airtime is the big variable, and in 2025 hundreds of advertisers spent under £50,000 on TV in total.

This post breaks those three costs apart so you can see where a budget actually goes, and what a charity of modest size can realistically do. It sits alongside why charity adverts are so long, which is the creative side, and how charities advertise, which covers the channels beyond TV. I'm a film maker, so I can speak with authority on the first cost and I'll be straight about where I'm relying on published figures for the rest.

What are the main costs of a charity TV advert?

People tend to quote one number for "a TV advert" when there are really three, and mixing them up is how budgets go wrong.

  • Production. Writing, filming, editing, sound, music and any contributors' time. This is the part I work on.
  • Clearance. Every UK TV ad has to be approved by Clearcast against the advertising codes before it can run.
  • Airtime. The cost of placing the ad in front of an audience, which can dwarf the other two.

A fourth item sits quietly behind them: the cuts. A 60 second master plus a 30, a 15 and some vertical edits for social is more editing time, though it's a small cost beside the original shoot. If you're after that detail, it's a separate conversation, and turning one film into a year of content goes through it.

How much does it cost to make a charity TV advert?

The honest range is wide. A simple, well made ad built around one real person and a single location can be done for a modest sum. An ad with a big crew, a studio set, actors, a composed score and a lot of post production can run well into six figures. The difference is mostly crew size, days, locations and how much is built rather than found.

Our documentary style films start at £15,000 + VAT, and most land between £15,000 and £25,000, depending on the research, the number of shoot days and the size of the crew. That's the film itself, and it's built to be used across a website, social, events and funding pitches, not just on TV. I've set out where that money goes in how much a brand film costs in the UK.

A few things push production cost up that charities don't always expect:

  • Contributor care. Time spent on consent, preparation and review with people you support is slower than filming staff, and it should be.
  • Music. A track licensed for broadcast costs more than one licensed for the web. Check the terms before you fall in love with a song. I've covered the basics in music licensing for brand videos.
  • Multiple lengths. TV airtime is sold in tens of seconds, so you'll likely need more than one cut.
  • Broadcast delivery. The technical specification for TV is stricter than for a website, so the sound and picture mastering take more care.
The cheapest TV advert is the one you've decided the purpose of before anyone picks up a camera.

Who pays for Clearcast approval?

For most advertisers, the broadcasters do. Clearcast's own guidance says clearance is paid for by its stakeholders if the ad is transmitted on a channel it clears for. So for a standard submission you're not usually handed a bill by Clearcast, although you should plan for time: a script generally takes at least two weeks to clear, and the finished ad two to three working days if it matches the approved script.

If you're in a hurry, Clearcast offers a Fast Track service, which at the time of writing is £660 + VAT per submission with feedback within one working day. Check the current fee on their site before you rely on it. The practical lesson is to send the script early. A late script squeezes a schedule more than almost anything on set.

How much does it cost to put a charity advert on TV?

This is the number everybody wants, and the honest answer is that you decide it. TV airtime is sold on a cost per thousand basis, so you pay for the audience you reach, and what you pay depends on the programme, the time of day, the time of year and the audience you're targeting. Viewing is measured by Barb. You can buy through a media agency, directly from broadcasters, or through the Universal Ads self-serve platform that Thinkbox says lets smaller businesses buy and measure campaigns across the three major broadcasters from a single interface.

The common belief is that you need a fortune. Thinkbox, the industry's marketing body, argues that perception is wrong, and the numbers it publishes back up the point that spend ranges widely. They're from a body with an interest in selling TV, so read them as a ceiling on how little it can cost, not a promise.

Most of the "TV is too expensive" talk comes from people who've never priced it, and most of the "TV is easy" talk from people selling it.

Is TV the right place for a small charity's money?

Sometimes, but not usually first. TV gives broad reach, and a big appeal like a seasonal campaign can use it well. But a small charity has other places to spend a first £20,000 that a film can work in for years: a flagship film on the website and in funding bids, cut-downs for social, material for events and for trustees. A film that does four jobs is worth more than one that does one.

My rule of thumb is that TV makes sense when three things are true. You already have a story that works elsewhere. You have a clear, measurable action you want people to take. And you can afford the airtime to run long enough for it to matter, because a campaign that flashes up for a week and disappears has mostly paid for a very expensive reminder.

Before you commit, it's worth looking at how else charities get in front of people. How to promote a fundraising campaign covers the wider mix, and the social media version covers the cheapest end of it.

What hidden costs catch charities out?

In my experience the surprises are rarely in the headline numbers. They tend to be:

Airtime booked before the film is ready

Late edits or a rejected script mean you either pay for dead airtime or scramble. Book against a delivered, cleared film wherever you can.

Rights that expire

Music, stock footage and contributor releases can be limited by time or territory. If you want to reuse the film in a second appeal, check what you've actually licensed. Who owns copyright in commissioned video is worth a read before you sign anything.

No money for the follow-up

If the ad works, you need people to answer calls, emails and web enquiries, and a way to thank the new supporters. Budget for the system behind the ad as well as the ad.

Measuring nothing

Set up how you'll tell whether it worked before it airs: a dedicated web page, a unique phone number or a tracked code. Otherwise you'll have spent the money and learned nothing.

What does a realistic budget look like for a mid-sized charity?

I can't give you a universal figure, because it depends on the appeal, but I can show you how I'd think about it. Start from the total you can commit and split it into three buckets before you talk to anyone: the film, the clearance and delivery, and the airtime. Then add a small fourth bucket for measurement and follow-up.

The mistake I see most is spending nearly everything on the film and leaving a token amount for airtime, or the reverse. A beautiful film that runs for a week has barely been seen. A heavily bought campaign built on a weak film wastes the airtime. Neither is a good use of supporters' money, and trustees will rightly ask about it.

A sensible sequence is to make the film first, test it where it's cheap to learn, and only then decide how much airtime to buy. If it moves people on your website and in a small paid social test, that's real evidence. If it doesn't, you've found out for the price of a social budget rather than a TV one.

What should you tell a production company to get an accurate quote?

The more you share up front, the less padding goes into the price. When someone asks me for a quote, these are the things that change the number most:

  • Your ceiling. Give a range and a hard stop. It lets us scope the film to the money instead of guessing.
  • Where it will run. TV, web, events and social all need different deliverables and different licences.
  • How many people are in it. Every contributor adds preparation, filming and review time.
  • How many cuts you need. A 60, a 30, a 15 and a set of vertical edits is a different job from a single film.
  • Your deadline. A fixed broadcast date, or a campaign tied to a season, takes away flexibility and can add cost.

It also helps to say what's already in place. If you have a script cleared, a campaign page ready or a media agency booked, we can fit around it. If none of that exists yet, a good production company will tell you what to sort out first, and sometimes that advice is worth more than the quote.

How can a charity make an advert for less?

Plan hard, shoot fewer things and use what you've already got. One strong contributor, one or two locations, real light and a short, honest script beat a complicated shoot every time. Build the cuts into the first brief. Ask funders whether communications costs can sit inside a project grant, and tell the production company your number early so they can scope to it.

Our work with char.gy on their B Corp film is a good example of the principle in another sector: one interview-led film cut eleven ways, which is why it kept earning its keep after launch. If you're trying to work out what a film like that could do for your charity, the complete guide to charity and fundraising films is the best map.

If you want a straight view on whether TV makes sense for your appeal, or whether the money would work harder somewhere else, tell us about it. If a film isn't the right spend, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a small charity afford a TV advert?
faqs.a: It can be possible, but TV is rarely the first place to spend. Thinkbox reports that 598 advertisers spent under £50,000 on TV in 2025, and a self-serve option exists for smaller businesses. The film itself is a separate cost, so many small charities get more from a film that works across web, social and events.

faqs.q: Do charities get cheaper airtime on UK TV?
faqs.a: I can't point you to a standard charity discount, so don't build a budget on one. It's worth asking the broadcasters or a media agency whether any reduced-rate or donated airtime exists for your cause and timing, and getting anything offered confirmed in writing before you commission the film.

faqs.q: How long does Clearcast approval take?
faqs.a: Clearcast says a script usually takes at least two weeks, and longer if it needs a lot of supporting evidence. A finished ad that matches the approved script is usually cleared in two to three working days. A Fast Track option exists for a fee, but sending the script early is cheaper.

faqs.q: What is cheaper than TV for a charity film?
faqs.a: Putting the film on your website, in emails, at events, in funding bids and on social channels costs far less than buying airtime, and the same film can do all of those jobs. Paid social lets you start with a small budget and test. TV is best treated as a later step once you know the film works.

stat.takeaway: TV airtime isn't only for national brands. Hundreds of advertisers started small, though the film still has to be paid for on top.

items.title: How to run a successful fundraising campaign: a planning guide
items.excerpt: A successful fundraising campaign starts with one goal, one audience and one story. Here's how to plan it, where a film fits and how to tell if it worked.
items.coverAlt: Villagers walking towards fundraising stalls and a painted target board on a village green at golden hour
items.body:
A successful fundraising campaign starts with one clear goal, one audience and one story, and works backwards from a fixed end date. Set a target that's tied to what the money does, plan who you'll ask and when, tell the story through a real person, and decide in advance how you'll measure it. Most campaigns that struggle skipped one of those four.

This post is the planning side: how to build a campaign that has a decent chance of working, with the film's role in it. It doesn't cover getting the word out, which is in how to promote a fundraising campaign, or the social side, which is in promoting one on social media. I'm a documentary film maker rather than a professional fundraiser, so I'll stick to what I've seen from the creative side and to published sources for the rest.

Why do so many fundraising campaigns fall short?

Mostly because they start with the tactics. Someone decides to do a video, a Facebook push and an email, and only then asks what the campaign is for. By then the money and time have been committed, and the goal turns out to be vague: "raise as much as we can".

The wider backdrop isn't easy either. The Charities Aid Foundation's UK Giving Report 2026 found that one in five people say they can't afford to give to charity, and that the sector has lost almost six million donors over a decade. That doesn't mean campaigns can't work. It means supporters have to be given a clear and believable reason, and a campaign that asks for "support" without saying what it's for gives them none.

So the first job isn't creative at all. It's deciding what you're trying to change, by how much and by when.

There's also a crowded field. At the end of June 2026 the Charity Commission counted 171,539 charities on the register in England and Wales, so any supporter's attention is being asked for many times over. A campaign that sounds like everyone else's disappears. One that is specific about a place, a person and a result stands out.

How do you set a goal that people will back?

Make it specific enough to picture. "Raise £30,000" is a number. "Raise £30,000 to keep the youth club open for another year" is a reason. The second is the one a donor can say yes to, and the one a trustee can check afterwards.

A few habits help:

  • Tie the target to a result. Work out what a gift of a given size does, then say so plainly. Only use figures you can stand behind.
  • Pick an end date. A deadline gives people a reason to act now. It should be real, such as a funding match, an event or the end of a season, rather than invented.
  • Set three numbers, not one. A target you'd be delighted with, one you need and one that means rethinking. It stops a decent result being treated as a failure.
  • Name who it's for. Existing donors, local businesses, a community, past service users. One main audience and perhaps one secondary.
A campaign with a vague goal gives supporters nothing to say yes to.

Who should you ask first?

The people who already know you. It's a far easier conversation to ask someone who has given before, volunteered or been helped than to win over a stranger. Most campaigns I've watched from the outside are won or lost in how well the charity looks after the warm audience before it goes anywhere near cold ones.

A sensible order is:

  1. Trustees, staff and close volunteers. If they aren't giving and talking about it, nobody else will.
  2. Regular supporters and past donors. A personal message beats a mass email.
  3. Partners, local businesses and funders. A lead gift or a match gives everyone else a reason to move.
  4. The wider public. Only when the first three are underway, so there's momentum and proof to show.

That last step is where promotion comes in, and I'd rather you read that as its own planning job. It's in the promotion post.

What story should the campaign tell?

One story, told by one person who has lived it, will do more than a list of statistics. Facts tell people the problem exists; a person makes them care. This is the part of the work I do know well, because it's the whole of documentary storytelling.

The best campaign stories share a few things. There's a real individual, not a composite. There's a before and an after, or a before and a "what happens if nothing changes". There's a moment of choice that the donor can imagine themselves being part of. And the ask follows from the story, rather than sitting beside it.

How you treat the person in it matters as much as what you show. I've written about consent, dignity and what to avoid in brand films for charities. Read that before you ask anyone to be in a campaign, because a rushed request to someone in a hard place damages them and the charity.

If your campaign story could belong to any charity in the country, it doesn't belong to yours yet.

Where does a film fit in a fundraising campaign?

A film is the piece that carries the story to everyone at once. It sits at the top of the campaign page, goes in the launch email, gets cut down for social and gets played at any event. Done well, it's the thing your supporters share when they want to explain why they gave.

What makes one work is covered in what makes a good fundraising video, and the practical steps are in how to make a fundraising video. For the campaign plan, the points that matter are these:

  • Film early. You need it ready before the launch, not during it. Allow time for contributor review.
  • Plan every cut at once. A main film, a short version and vertical edits all come from one shoot.
  • Keep the main film clean of dates. Put the deadline in the short cuts, so the main film can be reused.
  • Give it one place to send people. A single campaign page with the film, the story, the goal and one clear way to give.

We built a campaign this way with Ohme: one idea, one film, cut to suit the places it ran. It was a Christmas giveaway rather than a charity appeal, and you can see how it came together in the Ohme Christmas raffle case study. The mechanics of planning the cuts are the same.

What should the campaign timeline look like?

I'd split it into four stages, whatever the scale.

Before: build and test

Set the goal, agree the story, film, write the campaign page and line up the first gifts. This is the longest stage and the one most often rushed. If you only have two weeks, you'll spend them here and shorten the public part.

Launch: warm audience first

Go to the people closest to you before anyone else, so the campaign page already shows momentum when strangers arrive. Early progress is persuasive in a way a blank counter isn't.

Middle: keep it moving

Campaigns sag in the middle. Plan updates, new angles and thank-yous for the days you know will be quiet. A new short cut, a message from a supporter or a milestone gives you something true to say.

Close: the last push and the thanks

The final days are often the strongest, because the deadline is real. Afterwards, thank people properly and say what the money did. That follow-up is what turns a one-off giver into a regular supporter, and it's the part campaigns most often forget.

How do you tell whether it worked?

Decide what you'll measure before launch. Total raised is the obvious one, but it doesn't tell you much by itself. I'd also want to know how many people gave, how many were new, what the average gift was, where visitors came from and how many watched the film and then gave.

Use a campaign page that you can track, and a way to tell the sources apart, even if it's only a different link in each email. Afterwards, write down what you'd change. A campaign that raises less than hoped but teaches you which audience responds is worth more than a lucky one nobody can explain.

Who should be on the campaign team?

Fewer people than you think, with clear roles. Someone owns the goal and the budget. Someone owns the story and the contributors, which is usually the person closest to the service. Someone owns the supporter list and the emails. Someone owns the campaign page and the numbers. In a small charity that might be two people wearing four hats, and that's fine as long as everyone knows which hat they're in.

Add a trustee or senior sponsor who will make the early personal asks, and agree one person who can sign off the film and the copy quickly. The campaigns that stall are usually the ones where every change goes round six people. If you work with an outside film maker, give them one point of contact and agree the review rounds up front, so the edit doesn't drift past your launch date.

It's also worth writing a short one page plan that all of them can see: the goal, the audience, the key dates, who's doing what and how you'll measure it. Nobody enjoys writing it, and everybody uses it when the middle of the campaign gets noisy.

What are the most common mistakes?

  • No single audience. Trying to speak to everyone, and reaching no one.
  • The ask comes too late or too often. Both feel wrong. Build towards it, then make it clearly and more than once.
  • Leaving the film until the end. It then becomes a rush job, and the contributors get the least care.
  • Forgetting the thank-you. The campaign isn't over when the counter stops.
  • Copying someone else's campaign. What worked for a national charity won't map onto a local one. Use the structure, not the story.

If you want the wider picture, the complete guide to charity and fundraising films ties the campaign, the film and the channels together, and what charity marketing is explains where campaigns sit in the bigger plan.

Do you need a film for your campaign?

Not always. A small community appeal can work with good photographs and a clear page. But if your story is about people and change, a film is the most direct way to put a real voice in front of a supporter, and it keeps working after the campaign closes. If you're thinking about one, tell us about the campaign and we'll say honestly whether a film is the right use of the money.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What makes a fundraising campaign successful?
faqs.a: A specific goal tied to a result, one main audience, one real story and a fixed end date. Successful campaigns also ask warm supporters first, so there's momentum before the public sees it, and they plan measurement and thank-yous in advance. Vague goals and last-minute planning cause most failures.

faqs.q: How long should a fundraising campaign run?
faqs.a: It depends on the goal, but a clear deadline matters more than a long window. Many campaigns work best over a few weeks, with more time spent preparing than running. A real deadline, such as an event or a match funding date, gives people a reason to give now.

faqs.q: How do you plan a fundraising campaign step by step?
faqs.a: Set the goal and deadline, choose one audience, agree the story and make the film or content, then build a single campaign page. Ask close supporters first, then widen out. Plan updates for the quiet middle, then finish with a thank-you and a report on what the money did.

faqs.q: Do you need a video for a fundraising campaign?
faqs.a: No, but it helps when your story is about people. A film carries a real voice to everyone at once and can be cut for web, email, social and events. If the budget is tight, start with strong photographs and a clear page, and add a film once you know what resonates.

stat.takeaway: Your campaign is competing for attention with a very large field, so a specific goal and a story only you can tell matter more than a bigger budget.

items.title: How to promote a fundraising campaign: channels and timing
items.excerpt: Promote a fundraising campaign by reaching close supporters first, then partners, local press and paid channels. Here's the order, the timeline and the film's role.
items.coverAlt: A parade of musicians and vintage vehicles moves along a village road past thatched cottages
items.body:
To promote a fundraising campaign, start with the people who already know you, then widen out in stages: your supporter email list, your own website, trustees and volunteers, partners and local businesses, local press and radio, events, and only then paid advertising. Use one film and one campaign page to tie them together, and put dates on every step.

This post is about the whole mix of channels and the order to use them in. Social media gets its own post, how to promote a fundraising campaign on social media, and the planning that comes before any promotion is in how to run a successful fundraising campaign. I'm a documentary film maker, so I'll be clear about what I know first hand, which is how a film gets used across these channels, and lean on published sources for the rest.

What should you promote first?

A single page and a single film. Before you tell anybody anything, there needs to be one place to send them. It should open with the story, show the goal and the progress, and make giving a one step action. Everything else points there.

The reason is simple. If your emails, posts, posters and talks each send people somewhere different, you can't see what worked, and supporters get a muddled message. One address, one story, one goal. If you've got a film, it sits at the top of that page and everything else is a way of getting people to watch it.

It also helps to write the campaign down in a sentence you can say out loud. "We're raising £25,000 by 30 November to keep the winter food club open, and Maria will tell you why it matters." If a volunteer can say that at a bus stop, the promotion is half done.

How do you promote to people who already support you?

This is the audience that gives most reliably, and the one most campaigns underuse. Your own email list, your regular donors, your volunteers and the people you've helped are all more likely to respond than anyone you reach through advertising.

Some practical points:

  • Send a personal message before the public launch. Tell your closest supporters first and ask for their help, not just their money. Early gifts make the page look alive when strangers arrive.
  • Use more than one email. A launch, a mid-campaign update, a final reminder and a thank-you is the minimum. People miss emails, and most gifts come in response to the reminder.
  • Put the film in the email as an image that links to the page. A still frame with a play button usually does the job, and it avoids the problems of embedding video in an inbox.
  • Ask supporters to share, specifically. "Forward this to one person who'd care" works better than "please share".
The people who already know you are the campaign. Everyone else is the bonus.

How do you get your own website working for the campaign?

Your site is the one channel you fully control, and it usually carries more of the burden than the charity expects. Put the campaign on the homepage, not three clicks down. Show the film at the top. Show the goal, the amount raised and the days left. Keep the donation step short.

The film earns its keep here. A visitor who's never heard of you has about a minute to decide if you're real and if they care, and a short film does that faster than a page of text. We've covered the placement in more depth in where to use your brand film, and the principles are the same for a campaign film.

Don't forget the small things people look for to trust a charity: your registered charity number, a named contact and a clear line on how the money is used. They're easy to skip and costly to lose. This is also the moment to check your campaign page loads quickly on a phone, because that's where a lot of your visitors will arrive.

Who else can promote it for you?

More people than you'd think, if you ask them properly. Trustees, staff and volunteers each have networks you don't. Local businesses might sponsor, match donations or host a collection. Schools, clubs and faith groups often like a local cause with a clear goal. Partner charities can share without competing, as long as the audiences differ.

The trick is making it easy to say yes. Give each partner a short brief with the one-sentence campaign, the link, the film, a few images and the dates. Ask for one specific thing, such as a newsletter mention or a post, instead of a vague "help us spread the word".

For a business, a clear benefit helps: a mention, a thank-you on the campaign page or a short film moment that credits them. Be careful to keep those mentions accurate, and never imply they're backing more than they've agreed to.

Can local press and radio help?

Often, yes, particularly for a local or community cause. Local papers and radio stations look for a real person, a clear reason now and a good picture or clip. A campaign with a deadline and a human story fits that better than a general appeal.

Offer them something they can use. A short, well shot film clip, a couple of strong photographs and a spokesperson who's relaxed on camera make a journalist's job easier. If you're sending video to a newsroom, keep it short and accurate, and be ready for the answer to be no. You'll get more from a handful of personal, well timed pitches than from a mass release.

The same material helps at events. A film playing on a laptop at a community day or a talk makes a stranger stop in a way a leaflet doesn't. We did this on Fully Charged Live, where content from one show was used to sell the next, and the principle carries over to a fundraising event.

Nobody ever shared a press release because it moved them. They shared the film of the woman who explained it.

Is paid promotion worth it?

It can be, once the campaign page converts and you've tested the message. Paid social is the cheapest place to start, and it's covered in the social media post. Search advertising can work too, and eligible charities may qualify for free advertising credit through Google's grants programme, so check whether yours does.

TV is a different scale of decision. Ofcom's Media Nations report shows that broadcast TV still reaches around three quarters of people in a typical week, but very unevenly: 94% of people aged 65 and over, and 45% of 16 to 24 year olds. If your supporters are older, it's worth a look. If they're younger, the money will usually go further elsewhere. I've broken down what it costs in how much charity TV adverts cost.

Whatever you pay for, set a small test first, measure the cost of each gift and only then put more behind what works. A film cut into several versions lets you test different openings cheaply.

What should be in a promotion kit?

A small bundle of ready-made material saves everyone time and keeps the message consistent. It's worth building before launch, because once the campaign is live nobody has time to hunt for a photo.

  • The one-sentence campaign and a slightly longer version of 50 words for newsletters.
  • The film in a long version and a short one, plus a still frame for emails.
  • Six to ten photographs with captions and clear permission to use them.
  • The campaign link and a short, readable web address that fits on a poster.
  • A draft email, post and press note that partners can adapt rather than start from nothing.
  • A thank-you line for anyone who shares, so they feel noticed.

Shooting stills and film on the same day is cheaper than commissioning them separately, and it means everything looks like it came from the same place. If you're planning a shoot, mention the kit at the start, so the photographs and cuts are planned in rather than begged for later.

Does timing in the year matter?

It does, though not in a way that guarantees anything. Many charities concentrate appeals around Christmas, so inboxes and feeds are busy and your message has more to compete with. A quieter moment can work in your favour if your cause has its own natural date, such as an anniversary, a season or a local event. Pick the time that fits your story, then give it enough run-up.

Whatever you choose, avoid launching on top of a big event your supporters care about, and check your own calendar for staff holidays and school breaks. A campaign that goes quiet because the person running it is away is a very ordinary way to lose momentum.

What does a promotion timeline look like?

Two weeks before

Finish the film and page. Brief trustees, staff and partners. Ask a handful of close supporters for the first gifts or a match, so the page isn't empty on day one.

Launch week

Email your list, post on your channels, send the press pitches and ask partners to share. Put your best effort into the first 48 hours, because that's when the audience closest to you is paying most attention.

The middle

Plan updates before you need them. A short cut with a new voice, a milestone, a thank-you to a business or a behind-the-scenes photo each gives people a reason to look again. Resist repeating the launch message.

The final days

This is when the deadline does the work. Send the last reminders, tell the story of how close you are and thank everyone publicly. Then close properly, with a message to everyone who gave about what the money will do.

How do you know which channels are working?

Track them separately. Use a different link for each email, each partner and each ad, or at least for each main channel, so your giving platform or analytics can show where gifts came from. Look at the number of gifts and the average gift, not only visits. Note which version of the film or which opening line brought people in.

Then use it. If email brought most of the gifts, spend more time on your list next time. If a local radio slot brought a spike, build the relationship. The point of tracking is the next campaign, not a tidy report. How charities advertise goes deeper into the paid side of the picture, and the complete guide to charity and fundraising films pulls the whole set of posts together.

What's the most common promotion mistake?

Treating promotion as a single announcement. A campaign is a conversation over weeks. The ones that struggle say the same thing once, on one channel, and wait. The ones that work say it in different ways, to different people, at different moments, and keep thanking the people who've already helped.

If you want a film that's built to be used across all of these channels from one shoot, tell us about the campaign. We'll say plainly whether it needs a film, and what the right size of one would be.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How do you promote a fundraising campaign with no budget?
faqs.a: Start with people who already know you. Email your supporters, ask trustees, staff and volunteers to share, brief local businesses and community groups, and pitch local press and radio. A single clear page with a short film does most of the work. Organic promotion costs time rather than money, so plan it in advance.

faqs.q: What is the best way to promote a charity campaign?
faqs.a: There isn't one best channel. The strongest approach is to reach your warm audience first by email and in person, then widen out through partners, local media and events, and use paid promotion once the page converts. Send everyone to one campaign page so you can see what's working.

faqs.q: How early should you start promoting a fundraising campaign?
faqs.a: Prepare at least two weeks before launch, ideally longer. Use that time to finish the page and film, line up first gifts or a match and brief partners. Promote publicly only when the page already shows some momentum, because an empty progress bar puts people off.

faqs.q: Should a charity use video to promote a fundraising campaign?
faqs.a: Yes, where the story is about people. A short film on the campaign page, in emails and at events carries a real voice faster than text. Keep a long version for the page and shorter cuts for sharing, and make sure every contributor has agreed to how and where it will be used.

stat.takeaway: Where you promote depends on who you need to reach, because the same channel works very differently for different supporters.
