items.title: How to promote a fundraising campaign on social media
items.excerpt: Promote a fundraising campaign on social media with short vertical video of a real person, one campaign link and a steady rhythm of story, proof and thanks.
items.coverAlt: Two people play table tennis on a blue table in a leafy yard at a summer party
items.body:
To promote a fundraising campaign on social media, post the story through a real person in short vertical video, ask people to share rather than just give, and keep every post pointing to one campaign page. Start with the supporters who already follow you, vary the format across the weeks, report progress honestly and thank people in public.

This post is only about social. The wider mix of email, press, partners and events is in how to promote a fundraising campaign, and the day-to-day running of a charity's accounts is in how charities use social media. If you're after the longer-term job of building an audience, how to promote a charity on social media is the better fit. Here I'm focused on a time-limited campaign with a goal and a date, and on the video that carries it.

What makes social media different for a fundraising campaign?

It's fast and it's crowded. People scroll past dozens of posts a minute, so a campaign post has a second or two to earn attention and a few more to earn a reaction. That changes how you tell the story. The long, careful build that works on a donation page needs a sharp front door on social.

It's also public, which helps. When someone shares your post or comments that they've given, others see it. Social proof does a lot of the persuading, so a campaign that makes sharing easy and visible tends to travel further than one that only asks for money.

The trade-off is that social rewards people, not organisations. A post with a face and a voice usually gets a better response than a branded graphic with a donation link. That's good news for a charity, because you have plenty of real people to point a camera at, as long as they want to be filmed and have agreed to how it's used.

Is everyone on social media now?

Nearly. Ofcom's Online Nation 2025 report found that 93% of UK online adults used Facebook or Messenger in a typical month, 78% used Instagram and 56% used TikTok. So the audience is there, and so is every other charity asking for the same attention. WhatsApp reached 90%, which matters because supporters often pass on an appeal in private messages, where you can't see it happening.

The practical point is that "we posted it on Facebook" no longer sets you apart. What does is a clear idea of who you're talking to, a story that's honestly told and a consistent rhythm across the weeks of the campaign.

Which platforms should you use?

Go where your supporters already are, not where you think you should be. A local charity whose donors are mostly older may get more from Facebook and email than from a platform its volunteers use. A youth charity might lean on short video platforms. A professional cause may do better on LinkedIn.

A sensible approach is to pick one main platform and one support platform, not five. Doing two well beats doing five badly, and you can only look after so many comment threads during a campaign. If you don't know where your supporters are, ask them. A simple question in your next email or at your next event is worth more than a guess.

Use the platform's own giving tools where your charity qualifies and where they fit your set-up, since they remove steps between interest and gift. Check the current rules and fees on each platform, because they change, and make sure any donation route is clearly your charity's and clearly explained.

What should you post during the campaign?

Variety, built around one core story. If every post is "please donate", people stop seeing them. A better mix over a few weeks might be:

  • The story. One person, in their own words, in a short vertical video. This is the heart of it.
  • The reason. What a gift does, shown through one specific example rather than a list of figures.
  • The proof. Progress to the goal, gifts coming in, a milestone reached or a donor match being reached.
  • The people. A volunteer, a member of staff, a local business that's helping. Short, unpolished and real works well.
  • The thank-you. Public and specific. It rewards the people who've given and shows others what joining in looks like.
  • The ask. Clear and direct, repeated, and not buried in a long caption.
On social, a face and a voice beat a logo and a link almost every time.

How do you make video for a social fundraising campaign?

Short, vertical and built for sound off as well as on. Open on a person or a moment, not a logo. Put captions on everything, because many people will watch without sound. Keep the first line of the story in the first three seconds, then earn the rest.

You don't need a big shoot to do it. Some of the best campaign video is a supporter or beneficiary telling their story to a phone, with good light and clear audio. If you're recording yourselves, phone video for business content covers the basics, and sound matters more than the picture. Anyone on camera should have agreed to it and be shown the result before it goes live, which I go through in brand films for charities.

If you do commission a film, plan the social cuts at the start. One day of shooting can produce a main film, a handful of vertical shorts and some stills, and that's far cheaper than adding them later. We did exactly this with Super Efficient Drainage, where one day on a job became a longform film, a run of vertical shorts and carousels. The principle is the same for a campaign. For the wider approach, see social media videos for business and what makes a good fundraising video.

If the first three seconds are your logo spinning in, the campaign is already over.

How often should you post?

Enough to be seen and not so much that people mute you. For a campaign of a few weeks, a regular rhythm works better than bursts: perhaps a few posts a week, with more in the launch days and the final days, when attention peaks. Quality matters more than volume. A thin schedule you can keep up is better than an ambitious one that collapses in week two.

Plan it on a simple calendar before you start. Mark the launch, the milestones, the thank-yous and the final push, then fill the gaps with the story and people posts. Prepare most of the content in advance so you can respond to the day's events without scrambling.

How do you get supporters to share it?

Ask them, specifically, and make it effortless. Give them the link, a short line to copy, an image or clip and a reason. "Share this with one friend who'd care" lands better than "please spread the word".

Make the first supporters visible

Thank early givers by name, with permission, so others see it's normal. Quote a supporter's reason for giving. Real voices persuade better than yours.

Let people fundraise with you

Some supporters would happily set up their own page or challenge for your cause. Give them a simple way to do it, a welcome message and some content to use. A friend's request is often more persuasive than any charity post.

Get partners posting

Trustees, staff, volunteers and local businesses should each post once or twice in the first week, with the tags and link ready. Where it's appropriate, tag partners and organisations involved so they can see it and share it, and don't tag anyone who hasn't agreed to take part.

How do you report progress without nagging?

Give people news, not pressure. A progress bar and a number are fine, but they work better with a small human detail: who gave the gift that took you past halfway, what a particular milestone makes possible, or a message from someone the money will help. Each update should tell followers something they didn't know yesterday.

Be honest when it's slow. "We're at 40% with ten days to go, and here's what that means" is more persuasive than silence or false cheer. Supporters tend to rally round a campaign that's straight with them, and they remember the ones that weren't.

How do you handle comments and questions?

Assign one person to watch the campaign posts every day and reply quickly and warmly. Thank people who comment. Answer questions about where the money goes with specifics, and link to the page that explains it. If someone is critical, reply politely and factually once, and take longer conversations offline.

Treat anyone who appears in your content with care in the comments too. A contributor who has shared a hard story shouldn't be left to face unkind replies alone, so agree in advance who will moderate and what happens if something is posted that crosses a line. It's part of the consent you owe them, and I'd put it in the briefing before the film is ever shared.

What about paid social?

It can work, in small, tested steps. Run a small budget against two or three versions of the film opening, to an audience made up of people who already know you or look like them. See what each gift costs, then put more behind the best. Don't spend big on a version you haven't tested.

Be careful with targeting. Charities have responsibilities under data protection rules about how supporter information is used, so keep your audience building within the platform's tools and your own privacy policy, and check with whoever looks after data in your organisation. Think about the people you're showing too: an ad that appears next to someone's own difficult moment can feel unkind.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Only posting the ask. Mix in story, proof and thanks.
  • Landscape video built for a website. Re-cut for the platform.
  • No single link. Send everyone to one campaign page.
  • Ignoring comments. Reply, thank and answer. It's part of the campaign.
  • Quiet after the goal. Report back on what the money did, otherwise people won't give again.

The complete guide to charity and fundraising films ties these posts together, and the planning behind the campaign is in how to run a successful fundraising campaign.

Do you need a film to do this well?

You can start without one. A good phone video of a real person, shot with care and consent, is often enough to launch. But if your story deserves more, a short documentary film shot once and cut into a main piece, vertical shorts and stills gives you months of social content from a single day. If you'd like to talk about that, tell us about your campaign and we'll say plainly whether a film is the right spend.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the best social media platform for fundraising?
faqs.a: The one your supporters already use. Older audiences often respond well on Facebook and email, younger ones on short video platforms, professional causes on LinkedIn. Pick one main platform and one support platform and do them well, rather than posting thinly on five.

faqs.q: What should a charity post to promote a fundraising campaign?
faqs.a: A mix built around one story: a real person in short vertical video, what a gift does, progress to the goal, volunteers and partners, public thank-yous and a clear ask. If every post is a donation request, people stop noticing. Vary the format, repeat the link and report honestly on progress.

faqs.q: How long should a fundraising video be on social media?
faqs.a: Short, usually under a minute for a cold audience, with the main point in the first few seconds. Captions matter because many people watch without sound. Keep a longer version for your campaign page, where viewers have already chosen to watch, and cut shorter edits for each platform.

faqs.q: Can you run paid ads for a charity fundraising campaign?
faqs.a: Yes, but test small first. Try a few versions of the film opening on a modest budget, see what each gift costs and only then increase spend. Be careful with data protection and with where your ads appear, and check platform rules for charity and fundraising advertising before you start.

stat.takeaway: Facebook and Instagram still reach most of your supporters, and TikTok is now past half of online adults, so pick your platform by who you're asking.

items.title: What is a capital fundraising campaign? A UK guide
items.excerpt: A capital fundraising campaign raises a large sum for a building, equipment or endowment. Here's what it is, how it differs from annual fundraising and who's involved.
items.coverAlt: A lone figure outside a boarded up brick community building at sunset
items.body:
A capital fundraising campaign is a time-limited, goal-driven effort to raise a large sum for something lasting, usually a building, a refurbishment, major equipment or an endowment, rather than for day-to-day running costs. It's planned in phases, led by a small group of major donors first, and then opened up to the wider public.

This post covers what a capital campaign is, how it differs from the fundraising a charity does every year, what it typically pays for, and who's involved. How the phases run in practice is in how a capital campaign works, and the public-facing side is in what capital appeals are. It's all part of our guide to charity and fundraising films.

What does "capital" actually mean in fundraising?

It means money for things that last. A hospice that needs a new inpatient wing, a village hall whose roof has finally given up, a school that wants a sports hall, a theatre that has to be made accessible, a museum building a new gallery. The common thread is that the thing being paid for will still be there in thirty years, and that the cost is far larger than anything the organisation could raise in an ordinary year.

That's the key contrast with revenue fundraising. Revenue money pays for the work itself: staff, rent, energy bills, materials, the nurse on shift. Capital money pays for the asset the work happens in or with. Most donors find it easier to picture a new building than a year of electricity bills, which is partly why capital campaigns can raise sums that surprise the people running them.

I should be straight about what I do here. I'm a film maker, not a fundraising consultant, and I've never run a capital campaign. What I know comes from filming for organisations and watching where a film helped and where it didn't. For the technical side of campaign planning, talk to the people who do it for a living, such as a fundraising consultant or the Chartered Institute of Fundraising.

How is a capital campaign different from the fundraising a charity does every year?

Four things change.

  • It has a target and an end date. A regular fundraising programme just keeps going. A capital campaign says "we need £4.2 million by the autumn after next", and everyone can see how far along it is.
  • The money comes from fewer people. In a typical capital campaign a small number of large gifts make up most of the total. Fundraisers often say the top handful of donors give the bulk of it, though the exact split varies a lot between campaigns, so treat any neat ratio you read online with caution.
  • Gifts are often pledged over several years. A donor might commit to £50,000 paid over three years. That helps the donor and the project, because the pledge schedule can be matched to the builder's payments.
  • It needs a reason to give now. Ongoing fundraising can be steady and quiet. A capital campaign needs a clear case for why this project matters and why the moment is now, because a lease, a planning decision or a building's condition has set the clock.

None of this means the charity stops its normal fundraising. Trustees often worry that the capital campaign will drain the regular donors, and a good plan protects against that by keeping the two streams visible and separate.

What do capital campaigns usually pay for?

In the UK, the examples I see most often are these:

  • Buildings and refurbishment. New premises, extensions, accessibility works, a roof, a heating system.
  • Equipment. A scanner, a minibus, a recording studio, a commercial kitchen.
  • Land and community assets. A community buy-out of a pub, a shop or a playing field.
  • Endowments. A lump sum invested so the income supports the work for good. Universities and schools do this a lot.

The scale ranges enormously. A parish church tower might need £120,000. Great Ormond Street Hospital's charity launched what Civil Society reported as a £300 million appeal to fund a new cancer centre. The sums are miles apart, yet the shape is the same: a clear thing to build, a number, and a deadline.

Who's involved in a capital campaign?

More people than most trustees expect, and the mix matters.

Trustees and the chief executive own the decision and usually give first themselves. A campaign that asks the public to give while the board hasn't is a hard sell, and potential major donors will ask the question early.

A campaign lead or chair is often a well-connected volunteer, someone who can pick up the phone to people the charity doesn't know. This role is easy to underrate. Warm introductions raise more than cold letters.

Fundraising staff or consultants run the plan: the feasibility work, the list of prospects, the gift tables, the asks and the thank-yous.

Grant-makers and trusts often provide a big share. Many have their own rules on how much of a project they'll fund. The National Lottery Heritage Fund, for example, expects applicants to find part of the cost themselves, which I've covered in how a capital campaign works.

The public, local businesses and supporters arrive later, once the project has momentum and a visible total.

How much of the money comes from ordinary supporters?

Less than the public-facing side of the campaign makes it look, and more than a cynic would assume. The big gifts open the campaign and make the target believable. The wider public then closes the gap, and, just as importantly, tells everyone else the project is real.

It also helps to remember who's giving. The government's Community Life Survey found that 67% of adults had given money to charity in the previous four weeks in 2024/25, down from 82% in 2013/14. The most common ways were charity shops (28%), direct debits and standing orders (23%) and raffle tickets (20%). A capital campaign asks a smaller, more stretched giving public for something bigger and rarer than a raffle ticket, so the case has to be clear enough to justify it.

One practical point on tax: if the donor is a UK taxpayer and signs a Gift Aid declaration, the charity can claim 25p for every £1 given. On a pledge paid over three years from a single supporter, that adds up, and it's worth the charity checking each pledge is set up to claim it.

Why does a capital campaign need a story?

Because a building doesn't have a feeling, and the people funding it need one. A drawing of an extension and a cost schedule tell a donor what they're paying for. They don't tell them why it matters, or what will happen on a Tuesday afternoon in that room once it exists.

Nobody gives to a floor plan. They give to the person who'll finally be able to use the room.

That's the work a film does. It puts the future user of the building, or the person who struggles without it, in front of a donor in their own words. The best capital campaign films I've seen aren't about the building at all. They're about what the current space makes impossible. A hospice family room that's too small for a family. A rehearsal studio where the roof leaks over the drum kit. Show the problem honestly, and the solution explains itself.

Every capital campaign film has a shot of someone in a hard hat holding a plan. Please, someone, just once, film the plan being useful.

Our Southwick D-Day 80 work is an event rather than a campaign, but it shows how much a place and the people in it can say when they're given room. For the ethics of filming the people a charity supports, start with our piece on brand films for charities.

What does a capital campaign need before it starts?

Before any public launch, I'd expect to see these in place:

  1. A clear, costed project. A number the board trusts, with a contingency, not a hopeful guess.
  2. A case for support. A short document that explains the need, the plan, the cost and the impact. Everything else, including any film, is drawn from this.
  3. A feasibility check. Many organisations test the idea quietly with likely major donors first, to find out whether the target is realistic.
  4. Leadership gifts. The board and closest supporters commit before anyone is asked publicly.
  5. A plan for thanking people. Naming opportunities, plaques, updates and openings. Donors who are looked after give again.

Only then do you plan the public side, the communications and the content. Films made too early tend to show a project that hasn't quite decided what it is, and films made too late miss the moment when supporters were paying attention.

What tends to go wrong with capital campaigns?

Four things come up again and again when I talk to people who've been through one.

The target is set before anyone has tested it. A number chosen because it matches the builder's quote, not because any donor has said they'd give, is a risk that only shows itself six months in. The second is a public launch with nothing already in the bank. Supporters follow momentum, and an empty thermometer on launch day says the project is a long shot.

The third is a vague case. "Help us build a brighter future" could be on any appeal in the country. The campaigns that raise money say what the room is, who uses it and what they can't do now. The last is thanking badly. A donor who gave £10,000 and heard nothing until the next ask won't be there for the next project, and capital donors are often the people you'll want again.

None of those is about film, but a film made on top of any of them inherits the problem. If the story isn't clear on paper, a camera won't fix it.

Where does film fit in a capital campaign?

At three points, and they need different films.

The private film. A short piece, perhaps three or four minutes, shown to major donors and grant-makers in meetings. It's honest, it doesn't oversell, and it's built around one or two real voices. It sits next to the case for support rather than replacing it.

The public launch film. This is the one that goes on the website, social and at events. It has to work with the sound off in a feed and with sound on at a launch evening, so we plan the cuts together on the day. Whether the charity is a national name or a village hall committee, the principle is the same: someone speaks about why the space matters to them.

The progress films. The ones people forget. A short update at the halfway point, a film from the building site, an opening day. Supporters want to see the thing they paid for coming to life, and these are also the cheapest to make if the main film was planned well.

If your question is how this fits with a budget, our guide on how to set a video budget is a good next read, and there's more on how we work on the films page.

If you're at the stage of working out how to tell the story of a capital project, get in touch and we'll talk it through.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a capital campaign and a capital appeal?
faqs.a: In practice the two terms overlap, and many UK charities use them interchangeably. A capital campaign usually describes the whole planned effort, including the quiet phase with major donors. A capital appeal tends to describe the public-facing ask. I've written more on this in our post about what capital appeals are, so check that for the public side.

faqs.q: How long does a capital fundraising campaign take?
faqs.a: It varies with the size of the target and the strength of the organisation's donor base. A modest community project might take twelve to eighteen months, while a major building project can run for several years from first feasibility work to the opening. Allow for a quiet planning phase before any public launch, and for pledges that are paid over a number of years.

faqs.q: Can a small charity run a capital campaign?
faqs.a: Yes, and many do, especially for a village hall, a community building or a piece of equipment. The principles are the same, only scaled down: a clear costed project, a short case for support, trustees giving first, and a realistic mix of grants and local donors. A small charity might use one volunteer chair and a part-time fundraiser rather than a consultant.

faqs.q: Do we need a film for a capital campaign?
faqs.a: You don't need one, but it helps. A short film lets major donors and grant-makers hear the need from the people who feel it, and it gives the public launch something to share. It works best when it's planned with the case for support, made once, and cut into several versions for different audiences and platforms.

stat.takeaway: A capital campaign asks a smaller share of the public than a decade ago to give something bigger, so the case has to be clear and personal.

items.title: How does a capital campaign work? Phases, gifts and timing
items.excerpt: How a UK capital campaign works, from the feasibility check and the quiet phase to the public launch, grants and pledges, and where film helps at each stage.
items.coverAlt: A man in a cream jacket speaks to a seated audience beside a panel table in a map room
items.body:
A capital campaign works in phases. A charity tests the idea and sets a target, secures the biggest gifts privately from trustees and major donors, then launches publicly with a visible head start, and finally closes the gap with grants, community giving and events. Gifts are usually pledged over several years and tracked against the build programme.

This post walks through those phases in the order they happen, with the timings, the gift pyramid, how grants fit in and where a film earns its place at each stage. If you want the definition first, read what a capital fundraising campaign is. The public side of the ask is in what capital appeals are, and the whole subject sits inside our guide to charity and fundraising films.

As ever, I'm a film maker describing the fundraising I've seen from the camera side. Your own fundraisers or a consultant should own the plan.

What happens first in a capital campaign?

The unglamorous bit: working out whether the project is possible. Most campaigns start with a feasibility phase, which can take a few months. The organisation settles the scope and cost, writes a first version of the case for support, and quietly talks to a short list of people who might give or who know people who might. The question underneath is "if we asked for this much, would we get it?"

Done properly, this phase can change the project. A charity that wants £6 million for a new building finds that its likely donors would back £3.5 million, and the plan is rephased or phased down before a penny is spent on a launch. It's cheaper to learn that in a quiet room than in public.

By the end you want four things: a costed project, a draft case for support, a target the board believes in, and a first list of prospects.

What is the quiet phase, and why does it come before the launch?

This is the part the public never sees, and it's where most of the money is won. In the quiet (sometimes called leadership or nucleus) phase, the charity asks for the biggest gifts first, in private, before telling anyone else the campaign exists.

It starts at home. Trustees, the chief executive and the closest supporters give or pledge before anyone outside is asked. Then come the major donors, trusts and companies, approached one at a time by people who already know them. These are conversations, not mailings. A major donor will want to meet someone, see the site, ask hard questions and hear from someone who'll benefit.

The aim is to reach a meaningful share of the target before launching. Fundraisers use different figures for this, and I'd rather not give you a number I can't back up, so ask your own adviser what's realistic for a project your size. The principle is simple and widely held: launch from strength. A campaign that opens already part-way up the thermometer makes everyone else more confident to join.

A donor wants to back a project that's going to happen. The quiet phase is how you prove it.

How does the gift pyramid work?

It's the shape of the target. Fundraisers build a gift table that shows how many gifts of what size are needed to reach the total. A common pattern has one or two very large gifts at the top, a handful of large ones beneath, a bigger group of mid-sized gifts, and then a wide base of smaller donations from the community.

Say the target is £1 million. A simple table might look like this:

  • One lead gift of £200,000
  • Three gifts of £75,000 (£225,000)
  • Ten gifts of £20,000 (£200,000)
  • Thirty gifts of £5,000 (£150,000)
  • A broad base making up the remaining £225,000 in smaller gifts, grants and events

That's an illustration of the shape, not a rule. The use of the table is that it shows, early, how many conversations have to happen. If you need ten gifts of £20,000 and you can only think of four people who might give that much, you've found the problem in month one rather than month fourteen.

How do grants and match funding fit in?

Grant-makers can supply a big share, but nearly all of them want to see that the organisation is putting in its own effort. The National Lottery Heritage Fund is a good UK example. For grants of £250,000 to £10 million it asks applicants to provide at least 5% of the project costs as partnership funding for grants up to £1 million, and at least 10% for grants of £1 million to £10 million. That can be cash, non-cash contributions or volunteer time.

The wider lesson is that grants and donations support each other. A grant-maker wants to see local money behind the project, and local donors feel safer when a respected funder is behind it too. Many campaigns therefore time the asks so that one announcement helps the next.

Always read the funder's own current guidance, since percentages, caps and what counts as match funding change from one programme and one year to the next.

What does the public phase look like?

This is the launch the community sees: the website, the social posts, a launch event, the press story, the thermometer on the noticeboard. By now the campaign has a head start, so the public ask can be framed as "help us finish what we've started" and not "help us start".

It tends to mix a few things:

  • Community giving. Online donations, collection tins, sponsored events, local business support, school involvement.
  • Named opportunities. A brick, a seat, a room or a tree that a supporter or their family can put their name to.
  • Regular updates. People who've given want to know what happened with the money, which is why a campaign needs more than one burst of content.
  • Tax-efficient giving. The charity should make sure it claims Gift Aid where donors are eligible, at 25p for every £1 given by a UK taxpayer.

Our post on how to write a fundraising appeal goes into the words side of this phase, and why donors give explains what actually moves people to pay.

How are pledges and the build programme managed?

Capital gifts often arrive as pledges paid over two to five years, so someone has to track what's been promised, what's been received and what's coming. A pledge isn't cash. The finance lead and the project manager need to look at both numbers together, because a contractor wants paying when the work is done and not when a donor's third instalment lands.

Good campaigns agree a cash-flow plan before a spade goes in the ground. They also keep a contingency in the target, since building costs have a habit of moving. It's much better to say in the case for support that the target includes a margin than to go back to major donors later with a bigger number.

What do major donors ask before they commit?

Having sat in the room while a few of these conversations went on, I can tell you the questions are remarkably consistent, and a good case for support answers them before they're asked.

  • Is the project really going to happen? They want evidence: planning permission, a costed scheme, a board that's given, a timetable.
  • Who else is giving? Nobody wants to be first, and few want to be alone. This is why leadership gifts come first and why a campaign can quote what's already pledged.
  • What happens if you don't reach the target? A sensible answer is a plan B, such as phasing the build or refunding restricted gifts according to what was promised.
  • Can the charity run it afterwards? A new building adds running costs. Donors who understand charities will ask who pays for the heating once the ribbon is cut.
  • What will I see for it? Updates, a visit, a naming opportunity if they want one, and honest reporting.

The last question is the one most campaigns underinvest in. Capital donors who get regular, honest updates are the ones who come back for the next project or tell a friend. A short film from the site every few months costs far less than recruiting a new major donor, and it shows the work is real.

How long does a capital campaign take?

It depends on size and starting point, and I'd distrust anyone who gives you a single number. As a rough pattern, expect feasibility and planning to take months, the quiet phase to take the better part of a year or more for a large project, the public phase to run for several months, and pledge collection and the build to go on well beyond that. A smaller community project can move faster.

The thermometer is the only graphic in fundraising that's allowed to be hand painted and still look serious.

What matters for planning is that the campaign is a run of stages, and each has a different audience and a different bit of content. Which brings us to film.

Where does film fit in each phase?

Each phase needs something different, and it's a mistake to make one film and expect it to do everything.

Feasibility and quiet phase. A short, honest film for use in meetings. Two or three voices, the problem shown plainly, no soundtrack doing the emotional work for you. This is the one that sits alongside the case for support. It helps if the people in it are the ones who'll actually use the building, since major donors are good at spotting a staged moment.

Public launch. A film for the website, social and the launch event, with shorter cuts for feeds. This is where I'd plan the shoot so that one day produces every version, a point I make in brand films for charities too. Adding cuts later always costs more than planning them at the start.

Mid-campaign progress. Short updates showing the total moving, the site coming to life and people's thanks. These keep supporters engaged and give people a reason to share again.

The opening. A film that closes the story. It's what donors want most, and it's also the one that gets forgotten because everyone is exhausted. Plan it from the start.

For a sense of how we work with real people on camera, see our Nimrod Road film, a house renovation told by the couple who lived through it. It isn't a charity piece, but the approach, letting the people closest to the project explain it, is the one I'd use. Consent matters more than usual when the people on camera are beneficiaries, so read our interview guidance too.

Planning the film side of a campaign? Tell us the project and the timeline and we'll say what we'd make and when. You can also see how our films work.

faqs.q: What is the quiet phase of a capital campaign?
faqs.a: It's the private stage before the public launch, when the charity secures its largest gifts and pledges from trustees, major donors, trusts and companies. Because the campaign hasn't been announced, the asks are made face to face by people who know the prospect. The goal is to launch with a meaningful head start, which makes the public more confident to give.

faqs.q: Do capital campaign donors have to pay everything at once?
faqs.a: No. Capital gifts are often pledged and paid over two to five years, and that suits many donors who can give more by spreading it out. The charity needs a cash-flow plan that matches pledges to the building payments, and should be clear in its records between money pledged and money received.

faqs.q: How much do grant-makers expect a charity to raise itself?
faqs.a: It depends on the funder and the programme. The National Lottery Heritage Fund, for example, asks for at least 5% partnership funding on grants from £250,000 to £1 million and at least 10% on grants from £1 million to £10 million, and that can include non-cash contributions and volunteer time. Always check the funder's current guidance before you plan around it.

faqs.q: When should a charity make its campaign film?
faqs.a: Plan it alongside the case for support, before the public launch, and shoot once for several cuts. A short private version helps in major donor meetings, and a launch film with shorter social edits serves the public phase. Leave budget and time for progress updates and an opening film, because supporters want to see what their money did.

stat.takeaway: Big funders expect the organisation to put its own effort in, so the grant and the campaign have to be planned together.

items.title: What are capital appeals? A plain guide for UK charities
items.excerpt: What capital appeals are, how they differ from regular and emergency appeals, the main types in the UK and what makes the public believe in one.
items.coverAlt: Volunteers and builders repairing a scaffolded village church roof under an overcast sky
items.body:
A capital appeal is the public request for money to pay for a specific, lasting project: a new building, a restoration, a piece of equipment or a purchase of land. It has a named goal, a target figure and usually a deadline, and it asks ordinary supporters, businesses and funders to help close the gap.

This post looks at capital appeals from the public's side of the fence: what you'll see, the types of appeal, how the language works and what makes one believable. The planning behind the scenes is in what a capital fundraising campaign is and how a capital campaign works. It also belongs to our guide to charity and fundraising films.

What is the difference between a capital appeal and a capital campaign?

Not much, in everyday UK use, and people swap the words freely. If you want a tidy split, a campaign is the whole planned effort, including the private fundraising among major donors, and an appeal is the visible part: the ask that reaches the public through the website, a letter, a poster, a film or a collection bucket at the door.

You'll also see "building appeal", "restoration appeal" and "roof appeal". They're all capital appeals with a description of the project in front. The ones with the clearest name tend to do best, since a donor can say in one sentence what they gave to. "The Roof Appeal" is a better name than "Securing Our Future".

What kinds of capital appeal are there in the UK?

They fall into a handful of types, and each one asks the public something slightly different.

  • Building and restoration appeals. A church tower, a village hall roof, a theatre, a lido. The thing is visible, local and often loved. These often rely on the community's emotional attachment to a place.
  • New-build and expansion appeals. A hospice wing, a school hall, a children's ward. The pitch is about people who'll be helped, rather than a place being saved.
  • Equipment appeals. A scanner, a community minibus, an air ambulance helicopter. The gift buys one specific, countable thing.
  • Community purchase appeals. Local people raising money to buy the pub, the shop or the green. Giving is usually tied to a share in the outcome or a pledge of local ownership.
  • Major national appeals. At the top end are projects such as the £300 million appeal that Great Ormond Street Hospital's charity launched, as Civil Society reported, for a new cancer centre. Those have corporate partners, major donors and mass-market giving all running at once.

What links them is a single outcome that can be seen when it's finished. That's a strength, because supporters can come to the opening and see what their money did.

How is a capital appeal different from an emergency or regular appeal?

An emergency appeal is urgent and reactive: a flood, a famine, an earthquake. The charity can't plan the timing and the message is "act now". A regular or revenue appeal funds the work itself, such as a Christmas appeal for a homelessness charity, and it comes round every year.

A capital appeal sits between the two. It's planned, so the charity chooses the moment. It's finite, so there's an end point. And it tells the donor something they rarely hear in fundraising: a clear picture of where the money is going and what will exist as a result. That clarity is the strength of a capital appeal, and the temptation is to lose it under vague phrases like "a better future for our community".

Why are capital appeals harder in some years than others?

Because they compete with everything else people are giving to, and the total available isn't fixed. The Charities Aid Foundation's UK Giving Report estimated that the public donated about £14 billion in 2025, compared with £15.4 billion in 2024, and that the share of people giving had fallen from 69% in 2016 to 55%.

A fall like that doesn't make capital appeals impossible, but it does mean the case has to work harder. A supporter deciding between the roof appeal and the food bank has to understand why this matters, to them, now. You can see this in the way successful appeals are written: they're local, specific and honest about the cost. For the words themselves, our guide on how to write a fundraising appeal goes line by line.

A capital appeal succeeds when a stranger can say, in one sentence, what the money will build and who it's for.

What makes a capital appeal believable?

Donors, particularly local ones, are quick to spot an appeal that isn't quite straight. These are the things I see in the ones that land:

  1. A real number and a real breakdown. "We need £480,000, and here's roughly where it goes." You don't need a ten-page budget, but people want to see it isn't a guess.
  2. Visible progress. The total so far, what's already pledged and the next milestone. A thermometer is old-fashioned and it still works.
  3. Named, reachable people. A chair of trustees, a manager or a volunteer who'll answer an email. Faceless appeals feel like they could be anywhere.
  4. An honest "what if we fall short?" Even one sentence helps: what happens to the money if the target isn't met.
  5. A registered, regulated organisation. Fundraising in the UK is covered by a self-regulatory code, and the Fundraising Regulator publishes it. In its May 2026 research, 45% of people said seeing the Fundraising Badge would make them more likely to donate. Showing your registered charity number and, where you're entitled to, the badge answers the "is this genuine?" question.

Every one of those is also something a film can support. People on camera giving real names and describing real problems is more convincing than a paragraph of copy on the same subject.

If your appeal film opens with a drone shot of the building at sunrise, assume your supporters have already seen it. They live there.

How do capital appeals use film?

Usually in three places: at the heart of the website, in the social posts, and in the room at the launch or an event. The film's job isn't to explain the building. It's to make a stranger care about the people who'll use it.

The strongest appeal films I know of share a pattern. They begin with the problem the way a user experiences it. A choir rehearsing in a damp church. A hospice team unable to find a quiet room to talk to a family. A sports club turning children away because there's one changing room. They give the person speaking time, and they don't rush to the ask. When the ask arrives, it's short, and it follows naturally from what the viewer has just seen.

Look at how this plays out in a place-based story, such as our Southwick D-Day 80 coverage. It's an event record rather than an appeal, but the lesson holds. People remember a place through the people in it, and a capital appeal film should work the same way.

A note on ethics: if the film features people the charity supports, especially children or vulnerable adults, the consent has to be real, not rushed. Our post on brand films for charities covers the detail on dignity and consent, and I'd read it before you plan a shoot.

How do people actually give to a capital appeal?

In more ways than the appeal usually offers. The government's Community Life Survey (2024/25) found the most common ways UK adults gave were buying from a charity shop (28%), direct debit or standing order (23%) and buying raffle tickets (20%). A capital appeal can learn from that: give people small, easy ways in, as well as the big ask.

  • One-off online gifts with Gift Aid, so that a UK taxpayer's £100 can become £125 for the charity.
  • Monthly gifts toward the appeal, which suits people who can't give a lump sum.
  • Events and community fundraising such as sponsored walks, quiz nights and school challenges.
  • Naming and dedication opportunities for those who want to mark someone's memory or a family's link to the place.
  • Gifts in wills, for appeals with a long horizon.

For those who give at the top end, the appeal needs a separate, personal route, as described in our post on how a capital campaign works. A public appeal and a quiet phase aren't alternatives. They're two halves of the same plan.

Who gives to a capital appeal, and who doesn't?

The people who give are rarely the ones a committee imagines. They aren't random passers-by. They're past users, families, neighbours, former pupils and patients, local businesses, and people who simply like the place or the cause. The Community Life Survey found that people aged 65 to 74 (80%) and 75 and over (81%) were the most likely to say they'd given in the last four weeks, and rural adults (73%) more than urban ones (65%). That's the typical audience for a village or town appeal, and it's why the printed letter, the noticeboard and the local paper still matter alongside social media.

Younger supporters tend to arrive through a specific person, an event or a film they've been sent. They need it to be easy to give on a phone, and they need to see why they'd be part of it. If your appeal only speaks to the people who already know the building, it'll raise what you'd have raised anyway.

When is the best time to launch an appeal?

There isn't a magic date, but there are sensible choices. Most people give more around Christmas, though that's also when every other charity is asking, so a building appeal can get lost. A launch tied to something real works better: the day the scaffolding goes up, the anniversary of the place opening, the start of a school year, or the moment a lead gift is announced. A reason to talk now beats a calendar slot.

Whatever the date, avoid launching with a film that isn't ready. We've seen appeals rush a poor edit out to hit a launch evening and then spend months apologising for it, when a week's delay would have made the whole thing land. Your supporters will forgive a later start far more easily than a rushed one.

What mistakes do capital appeals commonly make?

The first is launching before the case is clear. The second is spending the whole film budget on the building and none on the people. The third is going silent after the launch, so supporters never find out how it's going. And the fourth is treating the opening as the end, when it's the best moment to thank everyone and begin the next relationship.

If you're planning an appeal and want to talk through a film that does the job without sentimentality, drop us a line, and have a look at our films to see how we work.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What does capital appeal mean?
faqs.a: A capital appeal is a public fundraising request for a specific, lasting project such as a building, a restoration, new equipment or a land purchase. It has a clear target and usually a deadline. It differs from a regular appeal, which pays for day-to-day running costs, because the money turns into something that will still exist for years.

faqs.q: Are capital appeals the same as capital campaigns?
faqs.a: In everyday UK use, mostly yes. If you want a distinction, a capital campaign is the whole planned effort, including private conversations with major donors, while the capital appeal is the public-facing ask that supporters see through letters, the website, social media and events. Charities often use the two words interchangeably.

faqs.q: Can anyone launch a capital appeal?
faqs.a: Not quite. A charity, community group or committee can run one, but there are rules on how money is raised, held and spent. A registered charity has legal duties to its trustees and regulator, and fundraising in the UK is covered by the Code of Fundraising Practice. A group without charitable status should take advice before collecting money from the public.

faqs.q: How long does a capital appeal usually run?
faqs.a: It depends on the size of the project. A small community appeal might run for a year or so, while a major building appeal can take several years including the private planning before launch. The public phase is often months rather than years. A clear end date helps, because supporters like to know when the campaign will close.

items.title: How to write a fundraising appeal that gets read and funded
items.excerpt: How to write a fundraising appeal: the structure, the opening, a specific ask, the tone to use and avoid, how to test it, and how to turn it into a film.
items.coverAlt: A postwoman posting letters through a terraced house door on a misty London street in early morning
items.body:
To write a fundraising appeal, pick one person or one clear need, tell their story in plain words, say exactly what a gift will do, make a single specific ask, and give a reason to act now. Write it to one reader, keep it honest, and finish with a simple way to give and a genuine thank you.

This post is the practical version: the order I'd put things in, the words that work and the ones that don't, how to check it before it goes out, and how the same writing becomes the script for a film. If you're asking for money for a building, read what capital appeals are first. To understand the reader's side, why donors give is the companion piece, and the wider picture is in our guide to charity and fundraising films.

I'm a film maker, not a copywriter by trade, but I spend a lot of time turning a charity's written appeal into something people say out loud on camera, and that's taught me what survives being spoken and what doesn't.

What goes into a fundraising appeal?

The skeleton is the same whether it's a letter, an email, a web page or a film script. Six parts, in this order:

  1. A way in. A person, a moment or a problem, not an organisation. "Last winter, Margaret couldn't get up the stairs to her own bedroom" works. "We are a leading provider of support services" doesn't.
  2. The need, made specific. What's wrong, for whom, and why it can't wait.
  3. What you'll do about it. The plan in a sentence or two.
  4. What the gift does. Concrete, honest, and tied to an amount.
  5. The ask. One clear request, stated plainly.
  6. Why now, and how. A deadline or a reason, and the easiest possible way to give.

Most weak appeals fail at the first step. They open with the charity, its history or its mission, and the reader's attention has gone by paragraph two. Start where the reader can picture something.

Why does one person's story raise more than statistics?

There's research on this, and it's worth knowing because it should change how you write. In a well-known set of experiments, Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic gave people a Save the Children style request in different forms. In one study, people who read about a single named child gave an average of $2.38, against $1.14 for those who read statistics about the wider problem. Adding the statistics to the child's story pulled the average down to $1.43.

It's a small American study with university participants, so I wouldn't treat the exact figures as a UK rule. The pattern is what's useful: people respond to a person, and cold numbers can weigh down a warm story. Use the number once, as support, and let the person carry the appeal.

Lead with the person. Use the number to back them up, not to introduce them.

One caution. An identifiable story isn't permission to exploit someone. The person has to agree to it, understand where it will appear, and be shown in a way that respects them. I've written about consent and dignity in brand films for charities, and the same rules apply to a letter. If the story is composite or anonymised, say so.

How should you open the appeal?

With a sentence that could only belong to this charity. Test it by swapping in another organisation's name. If the sentence still works, it's too generic.

Good openings tend to be one of these:

  • A moment: "At 6.40 on a Tuesday morning, the minibus still hadn't started."
  • A quote: a service user's own words, with their agreement.
  • A plain statement of the problem: "Our roof has 14 weeks of life left."
  • A direct question that the reader can answer from their own life, used sparingly.

Avoid the dramatic stat, the thundering "Imagine a world where", and anything that sounds like a mission statement. Short sentences help. So does a real place, a real month and a real name, within what the person's consent allows.

How do you make the ask?

Specifically. "Please give what you can" does less than "£25 pays for one afternoon session for six people". An amount tied to an outcome helps the reader see what they're doing, and it sets a sensible anchor.

Be careful with the arithmetic. Don't claim that £25 does something unless the charity has worked out that it does. If a figure is an average or a contribution towards a cost, say so. An honest "£25 helps cover the cost of..." beats a falsely precise one, and the UK's Fundraising Regulator expects fundraising material to be honest and not misleading.

A few habits that help:

  • Offer three amounts, not ten. One sits in the middle with an outcome attached.
  • Ask once, clearly, early and again at the end. Don't hide the ask in paragraph eight.
  • Mention Gift Aid where it applies. A UK taxpayer's gift can be topped up by 25p for every £1, and it helps to say so plainly.
  • Make the next step small. One link, one button, one return envelope.

If your appeal needs a glossary, the reader has already left. Write it so your nan could read it aloud in the pub.

What tone works, and what should you avoid?

Warm, direct and specific. Write to one person, using "you", and read it aloud as you go. If a sentence sounds odd in your mouth, it'll sound odd in their head. You aren't writing to "supporters" or "the community". You're writing to a person at their kitchen table.

The things I'd cut every time:

  • Jargon from inside the sector, such as "beneficiaries", "stakeholders" or "interventions".
  • Guilt. Telling people they should feel bad, or implying that they're letting someone down, tends to make them close the page.
  • Pity language that reduces the person to their worst day. People want to help someone, not look at them.
  • Fake urgency. If the deadline is real, give it. If it isn't, don't invent one.
  • Long openings about the organisation. The reader will get to you later.

The sector has moved a long way on this, and so has the public. Showing someone with agency, skills and a future is both kinder and more persuasive.

How do you write a capital appeal differently?

A capital appeal has an extra job. The reader has to picture something that doesn't exist yet. So the best ones do two things: they describe the problem with today's space clearly enough that it hurts a little, and they describe the future in terms of what people will do there, not what the building looks like.

"A new activity room with a kitchen where six members at a time can learn to cook for themselves" gives the reader more than "a state-of-the-art multi-purpose facility". Give a figure for the target, say how much is already pledged, and name the things a gift would pay for. If you can link a gift to a visible part of the building, such as a room, a window or a bench, do. If you want the full picture of the planning behind it, see how a capital campaign works.

How do you test an appeal before sending it?

Four quick checks, none of which need software.

  1. The stranger test. Give it to someone who doesn't know the charity. Ask them, after 30 seconds, what the charity does, who it helps and what you want them to do.
  2. The read-aloud test. Anything you trip over, rewrite.
  3. The fact test. Every number, name and claim checked against a source. Get the person in the story to read their part.
  4. The skim test. Can the reader get the point from the first line, the subheadings and the final ask alone?

If you send the appeal to a list, split it into two versions occasionally and see which does better. Small samples can mislead, so use the results as a nudge, not gospel. For campaigns beyond a single appeal, our sibling piece on running a successful fundraising campaign picks up from here.

What happens after someone gives?

The appeal isn't finished when the gift lands. The thank-you is part of the writing, and it's the part most charities rush. A prompt, personal, specific thank-you tells a donor their money arrived and mattered, and it makes the next ask feel like a conversation instead of a demand.

Good thank-yous do three things. They arrive quickly. They say what the gift will do, using the same specifics as the appeal, and not a generic "your generosity makes a difference". And they come from a real person, with a name, who works there. Later, a short update on what happened tells the donor the story didn't stop at the ask.

This is also where film earns its keep for charities with small teams. A 60-second thank-you from the person you helped, or from the volunteer who was there, is easy to share and easy to drop into every thank-you email. We plan these into a shoot from the start so they're not an afterthought.

What should the subject line and first screen say?

For an email or web appeal, the subject line and the first screen do the work of the envelope. Keep the subject honest and specific. "Margaret's stairlift" tells the reader more than "Urgent appeal". Avoid shouting, avoid false deadlines and avoid pretending to be a personal email when it isn't.

On the page itself, the first screen should carry the person, the need and the way to give. Many readers on a phone won't scroll. If the donation button is two screens down, you've asked them to do extra work for the privilege of helping you. Place it early and repeat it at the end.

How does a written appeal become a film?

The best film scripts I've worked from started as good appeals. The structure is the same: a person, a need, a plan, an ask. The difference is that on camera, you don't write the person's words. You ask them questions and let them answer.

What we take from the written appeal is the order. We make sure the film opens on the person and the problem, gets to the plan quickly, and ends with the ask said in one plain sentence and shown on screen. We then cut shorter versions for social, where the first few seconds do the work of your first line. To see the approach in action with real people and their own words, see how we did it on La Fromagerie. It's a founder story rather than an appeal, but the discipline of letting the person tell it is the same. You can also look through our films.

One tip: record the person telling the story before you finalise the written appeal. Their phrasing is nearly always better than yours, and you can lift a line straight into the letter.

If you'd like help turning an appeal into a film that sounds like your charity, send us a message and we'll talk about it.

faqs.q: How long should a fundraising appeal be?
faqs.a: As long as it needs to be to make the case, and no longer. Direct mail letters often run to two pages because the reader has time with them, while an email or social post needs to make the point in a few lines and link to more. Whatever the format, put the person and the ask early, so a skimming reader still gets the point.

faqs.q: Should a fundraising appeal use statistics?
faqs.a: Sparingly. Research by Small, Loewenstein and Slovic found that people gave more to a single named child than to statistics about the wider problem, and that adding the statistics reduced giving. One well-chosen, verified figure can support a story, but the person should lead. Make sure every number can be traced to a reliable source.

faqs.q: What should you never say in a fundraising appeal?
faqs.a: Anything misleading, such as an exaggerated claim about what a gift achieves, an invented deadline or a story that's been altered without saying so. Avoid guilt, pity language and sector jargon. UK fundraising is covered by the Code of Fundraising Practice, so check the rules on honesty, consent and how you describe your beneficiaries before it goes out.

faqs.q: Can a fundraising appeal be turned into a video?
faqs.a: Yes, and it often works well. The structure carries over: a person, a need, a plan and a clear ask. The difference is that on camera the person tells their story in their own words, so you interview rather than script. Record that conversation early, since their phrasing can improve the written appeal too.

stat.title: Average donation by how the request was framed, in one US experiment

bars.label: One named child, plus the statistics

stat.takeaway: People gave most when the appeal was about one person, so lead with them and keep the numbers in support.

items.title: Why do donors give? What UK research says
items.excerpt: Why donors give in the UK: belief in the cause, visible impact, personal connection and trust, with Charity Commission data and what it means for charity storytelling.
items.coverAlt: Sausages and halloumi grill on a barbecue in a cloud of smoke, a gloved hand turning them
items.body:
Most donors give because they believe in the cause and trust that the charity makes a real difference. The Charity Commission's 2026 research found that 54% of donors gave because they believe in the cause and 45% because the charity makes a positive difference. Personal connection, and being asked by someone they know, matter too.

This post looks at what the evidence says about why people give, what that means for the way a charity tells its story, and where a film helps. The flip side, why people stop, is in why donors stop giving, and finding new ones is covered in how to find donors. It's part of our guide to charity and fundraising films.

What do donors say is their reason for giving?

The best evidence I know of for England and Wales is the Charity Commission's annual public trust research, run by BMG Research. In 2026 it asked people who had donated money to charity why they did. These are the answers, with the share who gave each reason:

  • I believe in the cause that this charity supports: 54%
  • The charity makes a positive difference: 45%
  • The charity does important work in the UK: 37%
  • I knew it was a registered charity: 27%
  • The charity tackles an issue that directly affects me or people close to me: 25%
  • The charity does important work in the area where I live: 21%
  • A friend or family member asked me to: 13%
  • I saw or heard an effective advert or appeal: 11%
  • The fundraiser was persuasive or admirable: 9%

People could pick more than one, so the figures don't add up to 100. The list is worth sitting with. The top two reasons are about belief and impact. Nowhere near the top are the things charities spend the most time agonising over: the slickness of the advert, the cleverness of the ask, the persuasiveness of the person holding the clipboard.

The Charities Aid Foundation's UK Giving Report points the same way. Among people who donate, 78% were motivated by an emotional reason, such as caring about the cause, and 53% by wanting to be part of something bigger.

Is giving emotional or rational?

Both, and in a particular order. The emotional bit gets someone to care. The rational bit lets them feel okay about acting on it. A person sees something that moves them, and then asks quietly: is this real, is it a proper charity, will the money go where they say?

That's why a film that is all feeling and no evidence can fall short, and why a report that is all evidence and no feeling doesn't get read. Donors want the heart first, and then proof to back up the instinct. I try to build both into a shoot: the person speaking from the heart, and a clear, plain moment about what the work actually does.

People give with their hearts and check with their heads. A good appeal does the first and makes the second easy.

Why does a single person's story move people more than facts?

Because we respond to people more than numbers. In experiments by Small, Loewenstein and Slovic, people gave more to a single named child than to statistics about the wider problem, a result I set out in more detail in how to write a fundraising appeal. It's one study from the US, and not a law, but it fits what I see on shoots. Someone talking calmly about the day things changed does more than any graph.

The lesson isn't to use sad stories. It's to be specific. A real person, a real detail and a real change. Dignity matters here, and I'd point you to our piece on brand films for charities for how to get consent right.

Does personal connection matter?

A lot. A quarter of donors in the Charity Commission's research said they gave because the charity tackles an issue that directly affects them or people close to them, and 21% because it does important work in their area. Another 13% gave because a friend or family member asked.

That's a big clue for how a charity should plan. People give to causes they have a reason to care about, and they give to people they know. That's why community fundraising, sponsorship asks and peer-to-peer giving can outperform a cold advert. It also explains why a local, personal film of a real person from the community can travel further than a polished national piece.

The most persuasive channel on the Charity Commission's list is a friend saying 'go on then'. Nobody has made a brand film about that.

How much does trust matter?

More than most charities admit. 27% of donors said they gave partly because they knew it was a registered charity. The same research found that overall trust in charities sits at a mean of 6.5 out of 10, and that people's biggest trust drivers are knowing most of the money goes to the cause and seeing that the charity makes a real difference.

Giving is also an act of faith. The donor can't check the work themselves, so they look for signals: a registered number, named people, honest figures, a clear account of what happened with the last gift. Film can supply some of those signals. A trustee on camera, a frontline worker describing the week, or a short film from a project a year on, all say "this is real".

What stops people giving?

Money is the main reason. The Charity Commission found that 40% of non-donors said they couldn't afford to donate. That's an honest fact of the times, not an objection to be argued with. A charity can't tell someone with no spare cash that giving is cheap. What it can do is make the ask proportionate, offer small amounts and recognise other ways to help, such as volunteering, sharing or fundraising.

The second set of reasons is about trust: doubts that donations are used properly, or that a charity is genuine. These are answerable, with transparency. The third is simply never being asked well, or being asked too often. For what happens to people once they've given, see why donors stop giving.

Do major donors give for different reasons?

Often the same ones, with a few additions. I'm describing what I've seen rather than publishing research, so take it as experience and not data. Major donors tend to care about outcomes, want to know the organisation is run well, and like to feel they're part of a project they can see. Many want a relationship with the people doing the work, not just a receipt. Some want recognition, some want anonymity, and a good fundraiser asks instead of guessing.

That's why the private film for a major donor is different from the public one. It's shorter, quieter and built around the hard facts and the people. It's also why, in a capital campaign, you show donors the real need. More on that in how a capital campaign works.

Who gives, and how much do they give?

It helps to know the shape of the giving public before you write for them. The government's Community Life Survey for 2024/25 found that 67% of adults had given money to charity in the previous four weeks. Among those who had, the median amount was £20, and the average was £32 (excluding donations of £300 or more). Nearly a quarter (23%) gave over £50 in the period, and 11% gave up to £4.

Age and place make a difference too. Adults aged 65 to 74 (80%) and 75 and over (81%) were the most likely to have given, and so were people in rural areas (73%, against 65% in urban ones). If your film is aimed at the people most likely to give, it's worth thinking about where they'll see it. Many of them aren't on the platforms that marketing teams default to. The same film can go to a local newsletter, a screening at a community event, a charity's own website and a Facebook page, as well as the feeds younger supporters use.

The amounts matter for your ask. If the typical gift is £20, an appeal film that only talks about thousands of pounds will feel like it's for someone else. A good one makes room for the person who can give £10 a month and for the person who can give £10,000.

None of this is a reason to fixate on the average donor. Most charities have a handful of very different supporters: the regular monthly giver, the person who gave once at an event, the local business, the trust officer and the person who left a gift in their will. They give for overlapping reasons, but they each need to hear something slightly different. One good shoot, planned with those audiences in mind, can supply all of it.

What do small charities get wrong about donor motivation?

They tend to assume that people give because of the charity. Mostly, they give because of the cause and the difference. A small charity doesn't need to look like a big one. It needs to be clear about who it helps, how, and what changed this year.

The other mistake is to assume that donors know what the charity does. They don't, even the ones who gave last year. A film shouldn't assume knowledge. It should let a new viewer understand, in the first thirty seconds, who the people are and why it matters, and let an existing supporter feel proud to share it.

What does this mean for a charity's films and content?

If the research is right, a charity film should do five things, roughly in this order.

  1. Make the cause clear and personal. Who is helped, with what, and why it matters. The top reason people give is belief in the cause, so give them something to believe in.
  2. Show the difference. Impact is the second reason. Specific, observable change beats a claim about transformation.
  3. Show the work close up. People give to charities that do important work. Let them see what a day looks like.
  4. Signal trust. Name the charity, show the people, and be straightforward about how the money is used.
  5. Make the ask small and obvious. One action, one link, a clear next step.

Notice what isn't on that list: spectacle. In my experience filming real people at work, honest and specific beats big and slick. Take our Signwriting Jack film, which follows a craftsman at his work. It isn't a charity piece, but it holds attention on the strength of a person doing something he cares about. The same applies to a hospice nurse or a youth worker. See more in our films.

If you're working out how to tell your charity's story so people understand why to give, get in touch. We'll tell you honestly whether a film is the right next step.

faqs.q: What is the main reason people donate to charity?
faqs.a: Belief in the cause. In the Charity Commission's 2026 research, 54% of people who donated said they gave because they believe in the cause the charity supports, and 45% said it was because the charity makes a positive difference. The Charities Aid Foundation found a similar pattern, with 78% of donors citing an emotional reason such as caring about the cause.

faqs.q: Do people give because of adverts?
faqs.a: Sometimes, though not as often as charities hope. In the Charity Commission research, 11% of donors said they gave because they saw or heard an effective advert or appeal, and 9% because the fundraiser was persuasive. Belief in the cause and trust in the charity's impact came far higher. Adverts matter most when they build on a cause people already care about.

faqs.q: Why do people give to charity in the UK?
faqs.a: They give because they care about the cause, believe the charity makes a difference, have a personal connection to the issue or were asked by someone they know. Trust matters too, as 27% said they gave partly because they knew it was a registered charity. Money is the main barrier, with 40% of non-donors saying they couldn't afford to give.

faqs.q: How can a charity film encourage donations?
faqs.a: By making the cause clear and personal, showing the difference the charity makes through real people and specifics, and signalling trust with honest detail about how money is used. A short film should end with one simple ask. Treat the people in it with dignity, get proper consent and avoid pity or spectacle, since the research suggests belief and impact motivate people most.
