items.title: Why do donors stop giving? The reasons and what to do
items.excerpt: Why donors stop giving to charity, what the latest UK figures show, and what to do about lapses, failed payments and win-back, with a film where it helps.
items.coverAlt: A person walking away down an empty community centre corridor past a noticeboard and coat hooks
items.body:
Donors stop giving for ordinary reasons. Money gets tight, nobody tells them what their gift did, the asks arrive too often or feel generic, or a regular payment fails quietly because a card expired. Very few leave in anger. Most just drift, and the charity never sees the moment it happened.

This post goes through the reasons in the order they tend to happen, what the latest UK figures say, and what a charity can do about each one. I'm a film maker rather than a fundraiser, so I'll also be straight about where a film helps with keeping donors and where it doesn't. Why people start giving is covered separately in why do donors give, and the wider picture sits in our guide to charity and fundraising films.

Why do people stop giving to charity?

Usually it isn't one decision. A donor gives once, maybe after a TV appeal or a friend's sponsored run, and then nothing much happens. They get a receipt, perhaps a generic newsletter, perhaps an immediate second ask. Six months later they don't remember what the charity does, so when money is short that gift is the easiest thing to cut.

The reasons that come up again and again are these:

  • Money. The household budget changed and giving went first.
  • No connection. The donor never felt part of anything, so there was nothing to stay for.
  • No sense of what happened. They gave and never heard what it did.
  • Too many asks, or the wrong ones. Every message was a request, and none of them sounded like it was meant for them.
  • A bad moment. A clumsy phone call, a mistake with their details, a message after they'd asked to be left alone.
  • Life. They moved, retired, had a baby, lost a job, or died.
  • Admin. A regular gift failed and nobody followed it up.

Only some of those are things a charity can fix, but more of them than you'd think.

Is it all down to the cost of living?

Money is a real part of it, though not the biggest part of the story. The Charities Aid Foundation's UK Giving Report, published in March 2026, found that 55% of people gave to charity in the previous year, down from 69% in 2016. Total giving fell to £14bn, nearly 10% down in a year. Of everyone surveyed, 22% said they don't donate because they can't afford it.

The figure that interests me more is the other one. Among people who didn't donate, 28% said they just weren't interested in charities, rising to 49% of higher and additional rate taxpayers. Affordability can't explain that. It looks like a lot of people who could give have simply never been given a reason that landed.

What do the latest UK figures say?

I've put the headline numbers in the chart, because the scale of the drop is easy to miss in a paragraph. Take the 14 percentage point fall and apply it to a donor base of thousands and you can see why retention has become the thing finance directors worry about.

The same CAF report found that among people who do give, 78% are motivated by an emotional reason such as caring about the cause, and 53% want to be part of something bigger. Read that the other way round and you get a decent list of why people leave: they stop feeling the cause, and they stop feeling part of anything.

People rarely stop caring about the cause. They stop being reminded why they cared.

What goes wrong in the first year?

The first twelve months decide most of it. A new donor is at their warmest the day they give, and what the charity does in the next few weeks sets the tone.

The common failures are dull ones. The thank you arrives late or reads like a template. The second message is another ask. Nothing arrives that shows what the first gift did. By the time the charity does tell a story, the donor has forgotten who it is.

A better first year is simple to describe. Say thank you quickly and mean it, ideally in a human voice rather than a letterhead. Say what happens next. Then, within a few weeks, send one thing that makes the cause real: a short story from the work, a photo with a name and a place, or a short film. Only after that do you ask for anything else.

That order matters more than any single piece of copy. Nobody leaves a charity because they were thanked too warmly or too quickly.

Do too many asks drive donors away?

Too many of the wrong ones do. A donor who gets a monthly newsletter that is also a monthly appeal learns to read it as a bill. A donor who gave to a specific appeal, such as an animal rescue after a flood, and then gets something unrelated about a different campaign, starts to wonder whether the charity has any idea who they are.

Frequency complaints are real, and the UK has a framework for them. The Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice sets the standard charities are held to, and the Fundraising Preference Service lets people stop contact from the charities they choose. A donor who has to use that service has already left emotionally. The better fix is earlier: let people choose how often and about what, and then do what they chose.

Tone is the other half. Pressure and guilt work in the short term and cost you the relationship. The Charity Commission's 2026 trust research found that 57% of the public have high trust in charities, and 11% have low trust, up from 9% in 2024. That's a small shift, but the people at the low end tend to be the ones who've had a pushy experience.

Why do regular givers lapse without ever deciding to?

This is the most fixable cause and the one that gets least attention. A direct debit fails. A card expires. A donor changes bank. The payment bounces, the charity's system sends one automated message, and the donor never sees it. The gift is gone, and no human ever decided anything.

If you have regular givers, treat failed payments as a service issue and look at them every week. A short, friendly note that says "your payment didn't go through, here's how to fix it, and thank you for everything so far" will recover a good number of them. Do it once or twice, then stop. Chasing someone five times turns an admin problem into an irritation.

Life events are the other quiet cause. People move house and the letters go to an old address. People die, and a thoughtful charity notices and responds with care rather than another appeal. Some of those supporters might have left a gift in their will if anyone had talked to them about it earlier, which is a topic we cover in how to talk about legacy giving.

How do you win lapsed donors back?

Start by splitting them. A donor who stopped after four years is a very different person from one who gave once and vanished. The long-standing supporter deserves a personal message, ideally from someone who knows the work, that says what's changed and what their past gifts helped build. The one-time donor probably needs reminding who you are before anything else.

Ask them why. A short, honest question, sent by email or a quick phone call if you have consent, will tell you more than another year of guessing. You'll hear "I couldn't afford it", and you'll also hear "I never heard what happened". Both are useful. One tells you to leave the door open, and the other tells you what to fix.

Then give them something that isn't an ask. A story that shows what happened since they left, with a face and a result. This is where a film earns its place. Someone who has drifted away from a charity will watch two minutes of a real person talking about the work much more readily than they'll read a four-page update.

If your win-back email opens with "We miss you", the donor is already composing the unsubscribe.

Where can a film help keep donors?

A film can't fix a failed direct debit or a rude phone call. What it can do is give a donor the thing most of them say they're missing, which is a sense of what happened. On shoots, the thing people want to see is the work itself, in the words of the people doing it, and that's rarely a pie chart.

The films that retain donors are usually modest. A programme lead talking for a minute about a normal week. A volunteer explaining why they turned up. Someone the charity supports, with their consent and on their terms, describing what changed. A short documentary-style piece like that can go in a thank you email, a welcome series, an update to regular givers, or the first message to a lapsed supporter. I wrote about doing this with proper consent and dignity in brand films for charities, and it's worth reading before anyone is asked to appear.

The same material feeds your impact reporting, which is where donors, trustees and funders look when they want proof. If you're building that, what is an impact report is the place to start. For an idea of how we work with real people on location, see the Southwick D-Day 80 film or browse our films.

What should you do this month?

You don't need a new strategy. You need to look at what's happening to the donors you already have, and measure it the same way every quarter so you can see whether anything you change is working. The numbers worth tracking are few: how many first-time donors give a second time, how many regular givers are still paying after twelve months, how many payments fail and get recovered, and how many lapsed donors come back after you contact them. Compare each new group of donors with the last one, rather than only looking at the total, because a healthy total can hide a leaky first year.

  • Pull the lapse data. How many first-time donors gave a second gift? How many regular givers stopped, and how many of those were failed payments?
  • Read your own welcome journey. Sign up as a donor and see what arrives, and when. Most charities are surprised.
  • Fix the thank you. Quick, personal, specific. Nothing else in the first week.
  • Send one piece of proof. A story or short film that shows what the money did, before the next ask.
  • Ring ten lapsed donors. Ask them what happened. Listen more than you talk.

If you're thinking about how film could sit inside that, and you'd like a straight view on whether it's worth it for your charity, tell us what you're working on.

faqs.q: Why do donors stop giving after one gift?
faqs.a: Mostly because nothing happens after the gift that makes them feel part of the work. A late or generic thank you, an immediate second ask and no sign of what the money did all push a first-time donor to drift. A quick personal thank you, followed by one clear story about the impact, does more for a second gift than another appeal.

faqs.q: What percentage of UK people give to charity?
faqs.a: The Charities Aid Foundation's UK Giving Report, published in March 2026, found that 55% of people gave to charity in the previous year, down from 69% in 2016. Total giving was £14bn, nearly 10% lower than the year before. The Community Life Survey measures a different period, the last four weeks, so the two numbers can't be compared directly.

faqs.q: How do you re-engage lapsed donors?
faqs.a: Split them by history first. Long-standing supporters deserve a personal message that says what their past gifts helped achieve. One-time donors need reminding who you are. Ask why they stopped, offer something that isn't a request, such as a short film or story, and only then invite them back. Always respect any contact preferences they've set.

faqs.q: How many asks are too many?
faqs.a: There's no fixed number, and it depends on the donor and the cause. A useful rule is to keep a clear ratio of updates to requests, let people choose how often they hear from you, and make sure what you send relates to what they gave to. Check the Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice for the standards you're held to.

items.title: How to find donors for a nonprofit: a UK guide
items.excerpt: How to find donors for a UK charity: where they come from, who to ask first, how to research trusts and companies, the rules to follow, and where film helps.
items.coverAlt: A barista in a bun serves an older customer in a flat cap at the counter of a deli, with fruit and a coffee grinder beside
items.body:
You find donors by starting with the people already closest to your cause: past supporters, volunteers, service users' families and local businesses. Then you widen out to trusts and foundations, companies, community groups and wealthier individuals, using public data to find the right ones and a clear story to make them care. Most skip the first step.

This post is a practical map of where UK donors actually come from, how to research them, how to ask without burning the relationship, and where film earns its keep. It doesn't cover the psychology of giving, which is in why do donors give, or how to keep them once they've started, which is in why do donors stop giving. The wider picture is in our charity and fundraising films guide.

Where do charity donors come from?

In the UK they come from six places, and a small charity usually only needs two or three of them to work well.

  • Individuals. Members of the public who give once, give regularly, sponsor someone or give in memory of a person.
  • Trusts and foundations. Grant makers with a stated purpose and an application process.
  • Companies. Sponsorship, staff fundraising, matched giving, in-kind support and community pots.
  • Major donors. Individuals able and willing to give at a much higher level, usually after a relationship has built up.
  • Community and events. Fun runs, quizzes, schools, faith groups, clubs, local shops.
  • Legacies. Gifts in wills, which take a long time to arrive and depend entirely on trust built earlier. There's more in how to promote legacy giving.

The scale of the first group is easy to underestimate. NCVO's Civil Society Almanac found that the public supplied 48% of the voluntary sector's income in 2021/22, well ahead of government at 26%. That figure includes shop sales and memberships as well as donations and legacies.

Which mix suits you depends on size and cause. A hospice leans on community and legacies. A new youth project with no track record may do better with two or three trusts and a handful of local businesses before it tries to build a public audience.

Who is most likely to give, and does age matter?

Age matters a lot, and it surprises people. The government's Community Life Survey asks adults whether they've given to charity in the last four weeks. The overall figure for 2024 to 2025 was 67%, but it climbs steeply with age, from 48% of 16 to 24 year olds to 81% of people aged 75 and over.

It doesn't mean you should only chase older givers. It means the audience you pick decides what you say and where you say it. Older supporters are more likely to give through direct debit, shops and raffles. Younger people are less likely to have given recently, and they're more likely to be reached through someone they know or a cause that feels like theirs.

The same survey found that the most common ways of giving were buying from a charity shop or catalogue (28%), direct debit or standing order (23%), buying raffle tickets (20%), collection tins (17%) and online donations (17%). The median gift was £20. If your plan assumes everyone will click a Donate button, that's worth a second look.

Who should you ask first?

The people nearest to you, because they're the easiest to find and the most likely to say yes. Go through this list before you spend a penny on advertising:

  • Past donors. Including the ones who stopped. A thank you and a short update is a better start than a cold appeal.
  • Volunteers and their families. They already give time and they know the work.
  • Trustees, staff and their networks. A trustee's introduction to a local firm is often worth more than a campaign.
  • People you've helped, and their families. Some will want to give back, but never make it feel expected.
  • Local businesses and employers. Particularly ones with a link to your cause or your area.

Rank them by how warm they are and work down. Each group tells you something about who else to approach, because people give to causes their friends and colleagues care about.

How do you research potential donors?

Without paying for anything, you can learn a lot. For trusts and foundations, the funders' own websites list what they fund, how much, and what they won't touch. Their annual accounts are public on the Charity Commission register and list recent grants, which tells you which causes and sizes they actually support rather than what they say they support. There are also free open data sources on UK grants which let you search past awards.

For companies, look at who's local, who has a staff volunteering or charity-of-the-year programme, and who's already in your sector. For individuals, public information is limited and the rules matter, which I'll come to in a moment. Any research should help you decide who to talk to and what to say. Collecting names for the sake of it doesn't.

The best prospect lists I've seen were short. Thirty well-matched trusts and companies, with a note on what each cares about and who to approach, will do more than a spreadsheet of three thousand.

What does a good first approach look like?

Short, specific and about them. Say who you are in a sentence, what changed because of your work in another, and why you're writing to this particular person or funder. Ask for something small and clear: a conversation, a visit, a look at a proposal. Don't open with an amount.

For a grant application, follow the guidelines to the letter and read the last funded projects. If the funder says it prioritises under-served communities and your work doesn't, say so in the first call rather than bending your application out of shape. Funders can smell that quickly.

For individuals, the first ask should match the relationship. A new contact is invited to see the work before they're asked for money. An existing supporter might be asked to become a regular giver. A very small number might be ready for a conversation about a larger gift, but that happens after months of attention, not on a first meeting.

A prospect list with 3,000 names isn't research, it's a mailing list with ambitions.

What do the UK rules say about contacting people?

A lot of fundraising advice from the US doesn't fit here, so it's worth getting this right. In the UK, charities are held to the Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice, and data protection law and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) apply to how you use people's details. In practical terms, you need a lawful basis to use someone's data, you need to be careful with consent for emails, texts and calls, and you have to honour requests to stop contact.

I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice. Your charity's data protection lead, the Information Commissioner's Office guidance for charities and the Fundraising Regulator are the places to check before you buy a list or start a campaign. Gift Aid is the other UK-specific piece: if a UK taxpayer gives and signs a declaration, the charity can claim an extra 25p for every £1, so collect that information properly from day one.

How can a film help you find donors?

A film doesn't find donors by itself. It does three jobs that make everything else work better.

First, it makes the first conversation easier. When a trustee emails a local company director, a link to a two minute film about the work is far more persuasive than a PDF. Second, it helps funders check you out. Almost every funder will visit your website before they reply, and a real person describing what the charity does tells them more in two minutes than a paragraph of mission statement. Third, it gives supporters something to share, which is how a warm contact turns into a warmer one.

The films that do this are usually documentary in style: real people, real places and an honest account of what happens. I've written about the consent and dignity side in brand films for charities, and the practical side of making one in how to make a fundraising video. A film can also be cut shorter for social posts and for supporters to share, and you can find out how to promote it in how to promote a fundraising campaign.

A good film doesn't replace the conversation. It gets you invited into one.

If you'd like to see how we film real communities rather than staged ones, the Southwick D-Day 80 project is a good example, and the rest of our work is on the films page.

Is it worth paying for ads or social media to find donors?

Sometimes, but not first. Paid social can reach people who've never heard of you, and it works best when you send them somewhere that already makes sense: a clear page, one story and one action. Sending cold traffic to a general homepage with six different asks wastes the money. Test with a small budget, measure what each new supporter costs, and compare it with what a supporter is worth over a couple of years. Many small charities find that a modest budget behind a strong local story brings in more than a broad national campaign.

Organic social is cheaper and slower. People discover a charity because someone they know shared it. That's why a film or story that supporters are happy to pass on matters. Our post on how to promote a charity on social media goes into the detail.

What mistakes do charities make when looking for donors?

  • Starting with strangers. The cheapest supporters are already in your orbit.
  • Asking before explaining. Nobody gives to an organisation they can't describe.
  • Applying to everyone. Funders notice a mismatch immediately, and chasing grants that don't fit takes weeks of staff time.
  • Forgetting to say thank you. New donors are the best prospects for a second gift, and they drift if nobody speaks to them.
  • Having no record of where people came from. If you can't say which source works, you can't do more of it.

What should a small charity do first?

Pick one audience, one message and one thing to ask for. Then run it for a few months before deciding whether it works.

  1. List your warmest 50 people and write to each one properly.
  2. Choose five trusts or companies that clearly fit, and learn what they funded last year.
  3. Get the Gift Aid and consent basics right before any campaign.
  4. Make one honest piece of content, a short film or a story with photos, that shows the work.
  5. Track where every new supporter came from, so you know what to do more of.

Fundraising appeals themselves are covered in how to write a fundraising appeal, and the marketing side in what is charity marketing. If you want to talk through whether a film would help your fundraising, get in touch and we'll give you a straight view.

faqs.q: Where do most UK charities find their donors?
faqs.a: Most start with people already close to them: past donors, volunteers, trustees' networks and local businesses. After that come trusts and foundations, companies and community fundraising. Cold advertising to strangers usually costs the most for the least return, so it tends to come later. Track where each new supporter came from so you know which source to build on.

faqs.q: How do you find donors for a new charity with no track record?
faqs.a: Begin with your own network and two or three funders who back early-stage projects, then show real activity. Funders and local businesses want evidence that you do what you say, so start small, record the results and tell the story honestly. A short film or a clear case study of your first project gives you something solid to show people.

faqs.q: Can you buy a list of donors?
faqs.a: Be very careful. Under UK data protection law and PECR, you need a lawful basis to use someone's details and valid consent for much electronic marketing. Bought lists often fail that test and damage trust. Speak to your data protection lead and check Information Commissioner's Office and Fundraising Regulator guidance before you consider it.

faqs.q: How long does it take to find and win a major donor?
faqs.a: Usually months, and often years. Major gifts come out of a relationship: the person sees the work, meets the people involved, and gets to know the charity before anyone discusses an amount. Rushing it tends to end the conversation. Keep notes on every interaction and let the supporter set the pace.

items.title: What is an impact report? A plain guide for UK charities
items.excerpt: What an impact report is, how it differs from a trustees' annual report, who reads it and the forms it can take, including a short film, for UK charities.
items.coverAlt: Families mingling in a bright community hall with children's paintings strung across the room
items.body:
An impact report is a document or film that shows what a charity achieved with its money and time, and who benefited. It goes beyond listing activities. It sets out the change that happened, with evidence, so donors, funders and trustees can see the difference their support made. It's usually separate from the legally required trustees' annual report.

This post explains what an impact report is, how it differs from the other reports a charity produces, who reads it, and the different forms it can take, including a short film. What to put in one is covered in what should an impact report include, and the process of producing one is in how to write an impact report. The wider context is in our charity and fundraising films guide.

What is an impact report in plain terms?

It's the answer to "so what happened?" A charity says it supports people into work, cleans up a river or runs a youth club. An impact report shows how many people, what changed for them, how you know, and what it cost. It looks back over a period, usually a year, and it's written for people who gave something and want to see what came of it.

Three things set it apart from a brochure. It has evidence, in the form of numbers, outcomes and the words of the people involved. It's honest about what didn't go to plan. And it connects the money to the result, so a supporter can see where their gift sits in the story.

What's the difference between outputs, outcomes and impact?

This is where most impact reports go wrong, so it's worth being clear. Outputs are what you did: 120 workshops, 800 meals served, 15 volunteers trained. Outcomes are what changed for people as a result: more confidence, a job, a warmer home. Impact is the wider, longer-term difference, and it's the hardest to prove because other things also affect people's lives.

A good report moves through all three without confusing them. Outputs show the scale of the work, outcomes show it mattered, and impact shows what it adds up to. Most charities have plenty of output figures sitting in a spreadsheet. The honest work is finding some outcome evidence, even if it's imperfect: a before-and-after survey, a follow-up call six months later, or a set of quotes gathered with consent. You can say where the evidence is thin. Funders respect a charity that knows the limits of its own data far more than one that claims to have changed the world.

What does an impact report sound like in practice?

Here are three made-up lines to show the difference in tone. They're illustrations, not real results.

  • Activity: "This year we ran 60 sessions for young people."
  • Outcome: "Of the 48 young people who attended regularly, 35 told us they felt more confident speaking in a group."
  • Learning: "Attendance dropped in the winter term when sessions moved to evenings, so next year we're moving them back."

The second line tells a donor something happened. The third tells a funder you pay attention. Neither needs fancy design. They need honest data and the nerve to include the awkward bit.

How is it different from an annual report?

Every registered charity in England and Wales has to produce a trustees' annual report. It's a legal document, with required content on the charity's purposes, activities, finances and public benefit, and charities above a certain income send theirs to the Charity Commission. Its audience is the regulator, auditors and anyone who wants to check the charity's governance.

An impact report is voluntary, and written for people. It borrows from the annual report but it's shorter, more visual and focused on results. Some charities fold the two together into one document, and plenty keep them apart: the annual report for the formal record and the impact report for donors and funders.

Size matters here. NCVO's Almanac counts about 166,000 voluntary organisations in the UK, and 80% of them are micro or small, with an income under £100,000. Between them they hold just 3% of the sector's income, while the 4% with more than £1m hold 84%. Most charities, in other words, have no communications team and a legal annual report that tells the reader what they did, not what changed. The chart above shows the split. An impact report doesn't have to be a big document to fix that, and a short, honest one is a realistic aim for a small charity.

Why does trust come into it?

Because people judge a charity by what it can show them. In the Charity Commission's 2026 public trust research, the money reaching the cause came first when people were asked what makes them trust a charity, but making a real difference and being able to see how money is raised and spent both ranked high.

That second group is an impact report's territory. It's the document that lets someone check, rather than take your word for it.

What else is it called?

The name varies, which causes confusion when you're searching or briefing someone. You'll see "impact report", "social impact report", "outcomes report", "annual review" and "social value report". They overlap, and a few have specific meanings. An annual review is usually a lighter, designed version of the year's highlights. A social value report is more common with organisations that deliver public contracts and have to evidence the wider benefit of their work.

It's also different from a case for support, which looks forward and asks for money to do something next. An impact report looks back and shows what the last lot of money did. The two work together: a strong impact report is the best evidence you can put inside a case for support, and our post on how to write a fundraising appeal shows where that evidence goes.

Whatever you call yours, make the title say what it is. "Our year in numbers and stories" tells a reader more than "Annual Review 2026" ever will.

Who reads an impact report?

Different people open it for different reasons, and it helps to know who you're writing for before you start.

  • Individual donors want to know their gift mattered, in terms they can picture.
  • Trusts and foundations want evidence against the outcomes they funded, and a sense that you learn from what didn't work.
  • Corporate partners want something they can share with staff and customers.
  • Trustees want a view of whether the charity is achieving its purpose.
  • Potential supporters read it to decide whether to get involved.
  • Staff and volunteers often read it most closely of all, and it affects how they feel about the work.

One document can serve several of these, but not all of them at the same depth. Many charities produce a full report for funders and a shorter, more visual version for the public.

An impact report with no numbers and eleven photos of people holding a giant cheque is a scrapbook.

What forms can an impact report take?

There's no required format, and the best ones match the audience.

The full written report

Ten to thirty pages, with data, case studies, finances and learning. This is the version funders tend to expect and keep on file. It needs to be skimmable, with the headline results up front.

The one-page summary

A single sheet or short PDF with the key figures, one story and a clear thank you. It's what most donors will actually read.

The web page or microsite

A page that updates through the year. It suits charities with regular, measurable work, and it can link to the detail for the people who want it.

The film

A two to five minute film, with the people involved speaking for themselves, covering the same ground in a way people will watch to the end. Done with consent and care, it is often what a supporter remembers. It doesn't replace the numbers, it carries them. A film sits well alongside a written report, and the same shoot can produce a main film, a short cut for social and a set of clips for a donor update. I go through the consent side in brand films for charities, and there's a practical guide to film length in how long should a fundraising video be.

The best arrangement is usually a combination: a written report for the record, a one-page summary for the casual reader and a short film for people who'd rather watch than read.

What makes an impact report good?

From the shoots I've been on, the clearest ones share a handful of qualities.

  • It starts with the result. The headline is what changed, not what the charity did.
  • It's specific. "Forty-two people into work, thirty-one still in work six months later" says more than "transformed lives".
  • It uses real voices. Quotes from the people involved, in their own words, with their agreement.
  • It's honest. A report that includes what you learned and what you'll change reads as more believable than one that has only good news.
  • It's short enough to finish. Fewer, stronger pages beat a long list of everything.

Do small charities need one?

They don't need a glossy one, but they do need to be able to answer the question. A small charity with a four page document, a handful of figures and two quotes is giving funders what they want. The cost isn't the point. Knowing what you set out to change, and checking whether it happened, is.

It also helps with fundraising. A supporter who has seen your impact report is more likely to give again, and a funder who's seen one is more likely to treat your next application seriously. The report becomes part of how you find donors and part of how you hold on to them, which is the subject of why donors stop giving.

The point of an impact report is to let people check you, not to ask them to take your word for it.

Where does film fit?

A film is one way to tell the impact story, and it's most useful when the change is hard to capture in a table: confidence, belonging, a family back in a home, a young person on a team. If you can see it and hear it, put it in a film. If it's a number, put it in a chart.

We make documentary-style films for organisations, and charities are one of the places that work best when the people are comfortable and the story is theirs. You can see how we film real communities in the Southwick D-Day 80 project, and the rest of our work is on the films page. If you're considering a film as part of an impact report, get in touch and we'll tell you honestly whether it's worth it for you.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an impact report and an annual report?
faqs.a: An annual report is a legal document that registered charities must produce, covering purposes, activities, finances and governance, mainly for the regulator and the public record. An impact report is voluntary and written for donors, funders and supporters. It focuses on the change the charity achieved, backed by evidence, rather than a record of what it did.

faqs.q: How long should an impact report be?
faqs.a: As short as it can be while still showing evidence. A full report for funders might run to ten or twenty pages, with a one-page summary for donors and a short film for people who prefer to watch. A small charity can do a good job in four pages. Length isn't what makes a report credible, specifics are.

faqs.q: Do charities have to publish an impact report?
faqs.a: No. In England and Wales, registered charities must produce a trustees' annual report, and many must also file accounts, but an impact report isn't a legal requirement. Many funders ask for evidence of outcomes, though, and donors respond well to it, so most charities that can produce one find it worth the effort.

faqs.q: How often should a charity publish an impact report?
faqs.a: Most do it once a year, to match the financial year, with shorter updates through the year for regular supporters. Some publish after each project or campaign. Pick a rhythm you can keep up. A modest, honest report every year does more for trust than an ambitious one that appears once and never again.

items.title: What should an impact report include? A UK charity checklist
items.excerpt: What an impact report should include: ten sections from the headline result to the thank you, how long each should be, and what to leave out, for UK charities.
items.coverAlt: Charity trustees walking across a frosty community allotment past a polytunnel
items.body:
A good impact report includes a headline result, who you help and why, what you did, what changed as a result, real voices and stories, a clear account of the money, what you learned, and what happens next. Add a short note on how you gathered your evidence and a genuine thank you. Leave out the rest.

This post is the checklist: each section, what goes in it, how long it should be and the mistakes that make readers stop. What an impact report is lives in what is an impact report, and the step-by-step process of producing one is in how to write an impact report. Our charity and fundraising films guide covers the film side.

What are the essential sections of an impact report?

There's no legal template for an impact report, so this is a structure that works for UK charities of most sizes. Ten sections sounds like a lot, but several are a paragraph each.

  1. The headline result
  2. Who you help and why it matters
  3. What you did
  4. What changed
  5. Voices and stories
  6. The money
  7. What you learned
  8. What's next
  9. How you know
  10. Thank you and how to get involved

Take them in turn.

What goes at the top?

The headline result: the one or two figures that best sum up the year, in plain language, with a sentence of context. "Over the year, 214 people found work through our programme, and 160 were still in work six months later." A reader who stops after the first page should still know what you achieved.

Leave out the long welcome from the chair. If it needs to be there, keep it to three sentences and put it after the headline. The people who opened your report want the result before the greeting.

Who you help and why it matters

A short description of the need you exist to meet, with one credible statistic about the problem and the area or group you serve. Keep it local and concrete. If you're a food bank in a London borough, the useful fact is about that borough, not the national picture.

This section reminds the reader what is at stake and stops the report reading like a list of activities with no purpose. One page is plenty, half a page is better.

What you did

Your outputs: sessions run, people reached, meals served, hours given by volunteers, sites visited. Present them as a simple list or a row of figures, and compare with the previous year if the trend is useful. Volunteers' hours deserve a mention, because they show scale and they're a way of thanking people.

This is the part most charities already have. It's necessary but it isn't the point of the report, so keep it brief.

What changed

This is the section that makes it an impact report. Outcomes are what is different for the people you work with because of what you did, and ideally you have some evidence: survey results, follow-up data, staff assessments or distance travelled. Three or four outcomes, each with a figure and a sentence saying how you know, will do more than ten vague ones.

Charities that do report impact tend to agree on the test. In a survey for ICAS of UK charities, 87% said the importance of the information to its users guided how they report impact in their annual report, 77% said being measurable and 67% said being verifiable. The chart above shows it. It's a handy filter for this section: would a reader care, can you count it, and can you show how you know?

Voices and stories

Quotes and case studies that show the numbers in human terms. One or two in depth, plus short quotes scattered through, is plenty. Use people's own words, get written consent, and decide together how they're described and whether they're named. I covered the consent side in brand films for charities, and the same principles apply on the page.

A case study should start with the person rather than the programme, show a before and after in their words, and be specific. "Sam" with no detail doesn't persuade anyone. It also shouldn't be the sad-face version. People trust a story more when it shows someone with agency than when it shows someone being rescued.

If every quote in your report is a five-star review, the reader assumes you wrote them yourself.

How do you show the money?

Simply. Where the income came from and where it went, in a chart or a short table, with a sentence a donor can understand. If you can, give a unit cost that connects spending to results, for example roughly what it costs to support one person through the programme. Don't hide behind percentages that look good but say nothing.

The detailed numbers are in your statutory accounts, so point to them rather than copying them. The Charity Commission's 2026 trust research found that only 40% of people said it's easy to see how much a charity has raised and how it's been spent, so clear presentation here earns more goodwill than you might expect.

What did you learn?

One short section on what didn't work and what you'll change. It's the part most charities are nervous about, and the part funders say they like most. A report with only good news raises suspicion. One that says "we reached fewer people than planned because of X, and we've changed Y" sounds like a charity that pays attention.

What's next, and how do people help?

A paragraph on your plans for the coming year, a clear single call to action, and a thank you that names the people who made it possible. Funders, volunteers, partners, supporters. Be specific, because "thank you to everyone who supported us" is the sort of line no one remembers.

If the next step is a gift, a volunteer sign-up or a conversation, give them one clear link. The report is where a warm supporter is most ready to act, so don't waste it.

How do you explain where the evidence came from?

A short method note, usually a box near the end: how many people you surveyed, over what period, how you collected the stories, and anything you couldn't measure. It takes a few lines and does a lot for credibility. It also protects you, because it tells readers which claims are strong and which are indicative.

How do you choose which numbers to include?

Pick the ones that answer a reader's question: how many, how much did it change, and what did it cost. Three to five headline figures are plenty. Each should have a comparison, either against last year, against a target or against a baseline, because a number on its own doesn't tell anyone whether it's good.

Check each figure before it goes in. Know where it came from, what period it covers, and who counted it. If two figures can't both be right, find out which one is. A single wrong number in an impact report does more damage than a dozen missing ones, because funders read these carefully and remember the mistake.

Round sensibly. "Nearly 1,200 people" is easier to read than "1,187", and you can keep the exact figure in the method note. And be careful with percentages from very small groups: "50% improved" means something very different if you worked with six people than if you worked with six hundred. Say the number of people alongside the percentage.

How do you make it easy to read?

Design matters, but plain clarity matters more. A few habits help.

  • One idea per page. Headline figure large, a sentence or two beneath, one picture.
  • Real photographs. Pictures of the work, with captions that say who and where.
  • Readable type and contrast. Many of your supporters are older, and accessible design is just good design. Provide a text version for screen readers.
  • Descriptive headings. "214 people found work" beats "Our impact".
  • Consistent comparisons. Use the same layout for each outcome so people can scan.

If you're publishing online, put the headline results in the page itself rather than only in a PDF, so search engines and people on phones can find and read them.

How do you adapt it for different readers?

The same material can be cut three ways. For funders, keep the evidence and method prominent and tie your outcomes to what they funded. For individual donors, lead with stories and a simple statement of what their money did. For corporate partners, include the figures they can share, and a short passage on what their support made possible.

You don't need to write three reports. Build a full version once, with the structure above, then pull out the pieces each audience wants. That also makes a natural plan for a film and its cuts: the long version for the website, a short one for a funder meeting and a thirty second clip for the donor email.

What should you leave out?

  • Jargon. "Stakeholder engagement outcomes" means nothing to a donor.
  • Every single activity. If it doesn't support the story, it can go in an appendix.
  • Stock photos. Real people and real places are worth far more than a generic image of hands.
  • Claims you can't back. If you can't evidence it, say it's what you hope for or leave it out.
  • Internal structure. Readers don't care how your teams are organised.
  • Overpromising. No report should promise results to come.

How long should each section be?

As a guide for a 10 to 12 page report: headline half a page, the need half a page, activities one page, outcomes two pages, stories two pages, money one page, learning half a page, what's next half a page, method a few lines and thanks a short paragraph. A one-page version takes the headline, three outcomes, one quote, a simple finance chart and the thank you.

Should a film be part of the report?

It can be, and it often should be. A short film of two to four minutes works best as the human centre: a few people describing what changed, with the key figures on screen. It sits alongside the written report. The full report links to it, and the film points back to the report for the numbers. The same shoot can produce a longer version for the website and shorter cuts for social, which keeps the cost per use down. There's more on length in how long should a fundraising video be and on what makes one work in what makes a good fundraising video.

If you'd like to see how we film real people and places, there's the Southwick D-Day 80 project and the films page. And if you'd like to talk about a film for your own report, get in touch.

The best impact reports are the ones where you can find the result in ten seconds and the proof in a minute.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What are the main sections of an impact report?
faqs.a: A headline result, who you help and why, what you did, what changed, real voices and stories, the money, what you learned, what's next, a short note on how you gathered your evidence, and a thank you. Not every report needs every section at length. A small charity can cover all of them in four pages, as long as the outcomes and the evidence are clear.

faqs.q: Should an impact report include financial information?
faqs.a: Yes, in a simple form. Show where the money came from and where it went in a short chart or table, and link to your full accounts for the detail. If you can give a unit cost, such as what it costs to support one person, it helps donors see what their gift does. Avoid burying people in tables.

faqs.q: Do you have to include negative results in an impact report?
faqs.a: You don't have to list every setback, but an honest 'what we learned' section is one of the most trusted parts of a report. Saying what didn't go to plan and what you changed shows funders you pay attention. A report that contains only good news tends to look like marketing, which weakens the good news that's true.

faqs.q: Can an impact report be a video instead of a document?
faqs.a: It can be, though most charities do best with both. A short film is good for the human side and for people who won't read a PDF, while a written report holds the detailed evidence funders expect. Link them together, and cut the film into shorter clips for social media and donor emails.

bars.label: Matters to the people who use the report

stat.takeaway: Charities that report impact say the test is relevance, measurability and proof, so every section you include should pass all three.

items.title: How to write an impact report: a step-by-step UK guide
items.excerpt: How to write an impact report in about eight weeks: gather evidence, collect stories with consent, draft the headline first, check every figure and reuse it.
items.coverAlt: Two people mid interview on a sofa in silhouette against a big window, with a camera on a tripod
items.body:
To write an impact report, decide who it's for, gather the data and stories you already hold, work out the three or four changes you can evidence, draft the headline result first, then build the rest around it. Write plainly, check every figure, get consent for every story, and give yourself about two months. Most of the work is gathering.

This post is the process, in the order I'd do it. What a report is lives in what is an impact report, and the section-by-section checklist is in what should an impact report include. The wider picture for charities using film is in our complete guide.

Where do you start?

With the reader, not the page. Write down who the report is mainly for and what you want them to do afterwards. A funder deciding on renewal needs different things from a donor deciding whether to give again. If you try to write for everyone you'll end up with a document that satisfies nobody, so choose a main reader and let the others get a shorter version later.

Then write two sentences: what you set out to change this year, and what happened. If you can't write those yet, that's useful to know early. It means the first job is finding the evidence, not drafting.

How do you gather the evidence?

Start with what you already hold. Most charities have more than they realise: attendance sheets, referral records, case notes, feedback forms, surveys, emails from grateful families, volunteer logs, finance reports and the monitoring returns you've already sent to funders. Put them all in one place and list what each tells you.

Then look for gaps. Typically you'll have plenty on activity and little on outcomes. Fill what you can cheaply:

  • A short follow-up survey of the people you've supported, three to five questions, with a way to answer by phone or in person for people who won't use a form.
  • A before and after measure, if you did one, such as a confidence scale at the start and end.
  • A few structured conversations with staff and volunteers about what they saw change.
  • Partner feedback from schools, GPs or other agencies who refer to you.

Mind the data protection side. Only use personal information in ways people understood when they gave it, report in aggregate where you can, and ask your data protection lead if you're unsure.

How do you collect stories properly?

Choose people who are happy to talk, and who show something typical, not only the best outcome you ever had. Explain what the story will be used for and where it will appear. Offer them the chance to read it, change it or say no, and get that agreement in writing. If you're working with children or vulnerable adults, your safeguarding policy leads.

When you interview, ask open questions and then leave the silence. "What was life like before?" "What changed?" "What would you say to someone in the same position?" The best quotes come from the second or third question, once the person has relaxed. It's the same method we use on film shoots, and I explain more about how to make people comfortable in brand films for charities.

The best quote in the whole report is usually the one somebody says after the recorder's been switched off.

What does the plan look like?

Once you have the evidence, pick three or four outcomes you can back up and build the report around them. Cut anything that doesn't support them. Then outline, using the structure in the checklist post: headline result, need, activity, outcomes, stories, money, learning, next steps, method, thanks.

A rough timeline for a full report, working back from the date you want to publish:

  1. Weeks 1 to 2: agree audience and purpose, list sources, start any follow-up surveys.
  2. Weeks 3 to 4: gather data, interview people, get consents.
  3. Weeks 5 to 6: analyse, outline and write the first draft.
  4. Week 7: check figures, get sign-off from trustees, staff and the people quoted.
  5. Week 8: design, proof and publish.

A short report can be done in half that time. A film adds some weeks, and it's best to plan it from the start so the interviews serve both.

Who should write it?

One person should hold the pen, usually whoever owns communications or fundraising, with a named owner for the data and another for the stories. Programme staff know what happened, so they should supply facts and read the draft, but they shouldn't write it from scratch while delivering the work. A trustee or an outside reader gives the final sense check.

If you hire a writer or a production company, brief them with the evidence you already have and the audience you're aiming at. We do the same with film: the more a client can tell us at the start about who they want to reach and what changed, the less time gets spent guessing. Our guide to writing a video brief works just as well for a written report.

What does a first draft of the headline look like?

Here's an illustration, with made-up figures, of the move from activity to outcome. A first attempt reads: "This year our team delivered 90 workshops and supported 300 people." It's accurate and flat. After asking "so what changed?" it becomes: "This year 300 people came to our workshops, and 212 of them told us three months later that they'd started a course, found a job or got a benefit decision sorted." The second version has a clear result, a time frame and a sense of how you know.

If you have to hedge, hedge in the open: "212 of the 240 people we followed up with." The honest denominator makes the claim stronger, not weaker.

How do you write it so people read it?

Write the headline first, then everything else around it. Keep sentences short and say who did what. Prefer "we helped 214 people find work" over "214 positive employment outcomes were facilitated". Use the words your supporters use, and explain any term you can't avoid.

Some habits make a real difference:

  • Lead each section with the finding, then the explanation.
  • Put numbers in context: compared with what, out of how many?
  • Use people's own words for the feelings. Use yours for the facts.
  • Cut adjectives. "Life-changing" is for the reader to decide.
  • Read it aloud. Anything you stumble over, rewrite.
If a sentence could appear in any charity's report, it doesn't belong in yours.

Should you use AI to help write it?

Many charities already do. The Charity Digital Skills Report 2026 found that 79% of charities are now using AI, though 56% say a lack of skills is their biggest barrier and 35% don't trust AI tools. Funders are watching too: 58% say AI is changing the bids they receive.

Used carefully, it can help with the dull parts: tidying a rough draft, summarising survey comments, suggesting headings, checking tone. It shouldn't write your outcomes. A tool doesn't know what happened in your project, and an invented statistic in an impact report is a serious problem. Never paste in personal information about the people you support, keep a human responsible for every fact, and be open about it if a funder asks. The stories especially need to sound like your charity's real voices, because that's what readers trust.

How do you check it before it goes out?

Check in three passes. First, every number against its source, with a named person responsible. Second, every quote and story against the consent you hold, and show the people involved their part. Third, a fresh reader: someone who doesn't work for you reads it and tells you what they think you achieved. If their answer isn't your headline, the report needs another pass.

Then ask trustees to approve it, because the report speaks for the charity. Where your report touches regulated areas such as fundraising claims, make sure your wording meets the Fundraising Regulator's Code of Fundraising Practice.

What mistakes are most common?

  • Leaving it to the end. Collecting evidence after the year closes is far harder than building it in as you go.
  • Writing for the trustees. The people who need convincing are outside the building.
  • Hiding the bad bit. Funders have seen every kind of report. Anything you leave out, they'll wonder about.
  • Asking for consent late. Getting agreement the week before printing puts pressure on the person and risks losing the story.
  • Treating it as a one-off. The charities that do this well use the same questions every year, so the figures can be compared.

How do you handle numbers that look disappointing?

Put them in with context. If you reached fewer people than planned, say what the plan was, what got in the way and what you did about it. A shortfall caused by a funding gap, a venue closing or a referral route drying up is a perfectly respectable thing to report. Trustees and funders deal with it all the time. What they can't forgive is finding out later that a figure was quietly dropped.

Sometimes the number is small because the work is intensive. Ten people supported through a hard year can be a bigger result than a thousand leaflets handed out, and the report is the place to explain that. Give the cost, the depth of the support and the change you saw, and let the reader judge.

How do you get more out of it once it's done?

A report that sits in a PDF folder has done a tenth of its job. Send the short version to every donor with a personal thank you, thank the people who appear in it, put the headline results on your website, and share them with funders and partners. Cut the best stories into social posts and email updates, which also helps with keeping donors giving.

This is where film pays back. One shoot for the report can give you a main film, a shorter cut for the funder meeting and clips for social. The time you've spent gathering stories is the same time that makes a film possible. For length and format, see how long should a fundraising video be and how to make a fundraising video. The wider question of finding supporters to share it with is in how to find donors.

What if you're a small charity with no time?

Do less, but do it honestly. Pick one outcome. Collect one good case study with consent. Write four pages: headline result, what you did, what changed with two quotes, the money in a simple chart, what you learned and a thank you. That's more useful to a funder than an unpolished forty page report, and you can build on it every year.

If a film would help, we make documentary-style ones for organisations, filmed with the people in them on their terms. See the Southwick D-Day 80 project or browse the films page, and get in touch if you'd like to talk it through.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long does it take to write an impact report?
faqs.a: A full report usually takes about eight weeks from planning to publication, most of it spent gathering data, collecting stories and getting sign-off rather than writing. A short four page version can be done in three or four weeks. If you add a film, plan it from the start so the same interviews serve both.

faqs.q: What is the first step in writing an impact report?
faqs.a: Decide who it's for and what you want them to do afterwards, then write two sentences: what you set out to change and what happened. If you can't write those yet, your first job is finding evidence, not drafting. Pick one main reader and make shorter versions for the others later.

faqs.q: How do you measure impact if you don't have much data?
faqs.a: Use what you already hold, then add cheap evidence: a short follow-up survey, a simple before and after question, structured conversations with staff and volunteers, and feedback from referral partners. Be open about the limits of the evidence in a method note. Funders respect honest, modest evidence more than confident claims that don't stand up.

faqs.q: Can I use AI to write my impact report?
faqs.a: You can use it for tidying drafts, summarising survey comments and suggesting structure, but not for facts. It doesn't know what happened in your project, and an invented figure would damage trust. Don't paste in personal data about the people you support, check every number yourself, and be ready to say how you used it if a funder asks.

items.title: How to promote legacy giving: a practical plan for charities
items.excerpt: A practical plan for promoting gifts in wills: who to reach, where to do it, what to say, the rules to follow and how a short film can help without being pushy.
items.coverAlt: A woman sits reading a paper in a white armchair in a bay window with plantation shutters and a monstera plant
items.body:
You promote legacy giving by making a gift in a will feel like a normal, easy thing your supporters can do, then reminding them it exists at the moments they're already thinking about their wishes. That means a clear page on your website, a steady drip of real stories, a named person who can answer questions, and proper thanks for anyone who tells you they've left a gift.

I'm a film maker, not a legacy fundraiser, so this post stays on the promotion side: who to reach, where to reach them, what to say, how to avoid being pushy and how to tell whether any of it is working. Where it helps, I'll say what a film can and can't do. The wording of the conversation itself gets its own post in how to talk about legacy giving, and the case for doing it at all is in why legacy giving is important.

Who are you actually promoting legacy giving to?

Start with people who already know you. The people most likely to leave a gift in a will are the ones who've given before, volunteered, used your service or watched someone they love use it. A cold audience on social media is the hardest place to begin, and the most expensive.

It helps to split your own list into three rough groups:

  • Long-standing supporters. Regular givers, past fundraisers, volunteers and members. They already trust you, so they're the natural first audience.
  • People with a personal story. Families who've been helped, bereaved relatives, former service users. They often have the strongest reason to give and the clearest story to tell.
  • Everyone else who's warm. Event attendees, newsletter readers, people who've signed a petition or bought from your shop.

Age matters less than people assume. The Remember A Charity tracking study found that supporters in their 40s and 50s who had a will were the most likely to have included a charity (37%), ahead of those over 60 (27%). If your legacy messaging only ever shows people in their eighties, you're ignoring the group most ready to act.

It also pays to think about the people around your supporters. Solicitors, financial advisers and will writers sit in the room when the decision actually gets made. Remember A Charity has published work on the role of wealth advisers in growing legacies, and a short, clear explainer you can hand to a professional is worth more than another poster.

Why don't more people leave a gift in their will?

Mostly because nobody has asked, and because the practical steps feel like a hassle they'll get to later. Many people have simply never considered it. That's good news, because a barrier of "I hadn't thought of it" is one you can do something about.

Remember A Charity surveyed 500 people in the UK with over £1 million in investable assets in 2025 (the research was done by Savanta). Half of them had already included a charity in their will. Of those who hadn't, 58% said they were open to doing it. That's a group with plenty of goodwill and a gap where a prompt should be. More than a third of those aged 55 to 65 had no will at all, which tells you the first job for many people is getting a will written, before anything can be said about charity.

The other brake is family. In the 2024 tracking study, 63% of supporters said the reason they hadn't left a gift was that they wanted to leave everything to family or friends. Good promotion respects that. It doesn't ask people to choose between you and their children. It asks if they'd consider a small share once their family is looked after.

Nobody has ever left a gift in their will because of a stock photo of a sunset.

Where should you promote legacy giving?

In the places your supporters already pay attention, and in more than one of them. A single leaflet in a thank-you pack won't build much. Over a year, a handful of modest, consistent touches will.

On your own website

Give legacy giving a page of its own, linked from your main navigation and your donate page. Cover the basics in a few short paragraphs: what a gift in a will is, the different types, that you don't need to be wealthy, how to tell your solicitor, and who to contact. Include your charity name and registered number, because a legacy donor wants to be sure their solicitor has the right details.

In your existing communications

Newsletters, annual reviews, supporter magazines and thank-you letters are already read by the right people. A short, warm paragraph about legacy gifts, with a real person's story now and then, does more than a sudden campaign. Keep the tone the same as the rest of your writing. A sudden switch to formal, solemn language tells readers something big is being asked of them.

Through partners and professionals

Will-writing campaigns give people a reason to act at a set time. Will Aid runs every November, when participating solicitors waive their fee for a basic will in return for a suggested donation to its partner charities (currently £120 for a single will and £200 for mirror wills). Free Wills Month runs in March and October, according to Macmillan's explanation of it. If you're a partner, those dates are natural peaks. If you're not, they're still a good prompt for your own messaging.

At events and in person

Talks, open days, anniversaries and memorial services are where people feel closest to a cause. A quiet conversation with a trained team member, no pressure and no hard sell, can start things in a way a mailing can't. Train whoever's there to listen first.

What should your promotion say?

It should say what a gift does, in the voice of someone who's seen it. Statistics are fine in the background, but people leave gifts because of a person, a place or a moment they care about.

A few things that tend to hold up:

  • Use the supporter's own words. A volunteer explaining why they've left a gift will land better than a paragraph in your voice about "your lasting legacy".
  • Be specific about what a gift makes possible. "A gift of any size keeps the minibus running" beats "make a difference for generations".
  • Say that family comes first. It's what most people feel anyway, and saying it out loud takes the pressure off.
  • Make the next step tiny. A phone number, an email address and a one-page guide. Not a form with twelve fields.
People don't leave a gift to a mission statement. They leave it to a place, a person, a Tuesday afternoon they remember.

Watch out for euphemism overload. Phrases like "passing on your values" can end up obscure. "A gift in your will" is plain, and it's what people search for. If you're wondering how to word that conversation with someone face to face or on camera, the next post in this series is the one to read.

Can a film help promote legacy giving?

Yes, and it's one of the better uses of a charity film, because the thing you're asking for is trust and the person asking is invisible. A film puts a face and a voice on it. A supporter who watches someone talk about why they left a gift sees the decision as ordinary, which is half the battle.

What works is short and human. One person, filmed where they feel at home, talking about why they gave and why they decided to put it in writing. No music swelling, no slow-motion hands on a tombstone. If you've seen how we approach charity films with dignity and consent, the same rules apply here, with an extra layer of care, because a legacy story often involves someone who has died and a family who'll watch it.

Some practical points from filming real people on real shoots:

  • Film living supporters who've pledged. They can speak freely, approve the cut and change their minds.
  • Get consent that covers reuse. A film may run for years, so agree how long, where and how someone can ask for it to come down. There's more on the ownership side in who owns the copyright in commissioned video.
  • Shoot more than one length. A full story for the legacy page, a short cut for email and a vertical clip for social all come from the same day. Turning one film into a year of content covers how.
  • Put the contact line on screen. A film that moves someone and then gives them nowhere to go has wasted the moment.

A film about a place with deep roots can carry legacy themes without saying the word. When we filmed the D-Day 80 commemoration at Southwick, it was a reminder of how strongly people feel about a place and a history they want to see continue. That feeling is what legacy giving rests on.

How do you promote legacy giving without being pushy?

By following the rules, which are more detailed than most people expect, and by treating the person as a person. The Fundraising Regulator's page on legacy fundraising says fundraisers need to make sure they haven't put any undue pressure on potential donors, that they shouldn't give legal advice (they should point people to independent advice instead), and that legacies "can be a sensitive issue for individuals and their families". The Code of Fundraising Practice goes further on visits and on vulnerable people, so read the current version before you plan anything face to face.

In practice that means:

  • Never rush anyone, and make it easy to say no.
  • Send people to a solicitor for the legal side.
  • Take extra care with people who may be vulnerable, bereaved or unwell.
  • Keep records of who you've spoken to and what they said they wanted.

Trust matters throughout. The Charity Commission's 2026 research found that the top reason people trust charities is that most of the money raised goes directly on the cause (55%), followed by the charity making a real difference (51%). A legacy page that's honest about both will sit comfortably with that.

How do you look after people who tell you they've left a gift?

Thank them properly, quickly and personally. This is the part many charities skip, and it costs them. The same tracking study found 64% of people who had pledged a gift hadn't told the charity, and nearly half (47%) said it had never occurred to them to tell you. Every one of those is a supporter you can't thank, can't keep in touch with and may not know about until it's too late to hear their story.

Make telling you easy. Add a line to your legacy page and your thank-you pack: "If you've left us a gift, we'd love to say thank you." Then do it, with a handwritten note or a call from someone senior. Offer people the chance to join a recognition group if you have one, and let them choose how public to be. Some will be happy to feature in your communications. Plenty won't, and that's fine.

How do you tell whether your promotion is working?

Legacy income lags by years, so don't judge a campaign by this quarter's cheques. Track the things you can see sooner:

  • Visits to your legacy page, and how many people download the guide or get in touch.
  • Enquiries and conversations started, and where they came from.
  • The number of people who tell you they've left a gift, over time.
  • Responses to individual stories, whether by film, email or letter.

Be patient and consistent. A charity that mentions legacy giving gently and often over five years will usually do better than one that runs a loud campaign for six weeks and goes quiet.

If you're thinking about a film as part of this, start with the people rather than the format. Read how to make a charity video and what makes a good fundraising video, and come back to the hub guide to charity and fundraising films for the full picture. When you're ready to talk about a film for your own supporters, you can get in touch, and if a film isn't the right next step we'll tell you.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: What is the best way to promote legacy giving?
faqs.a: Make it easy and keep it consistent. A clear page on your website, regular real stories from supporters, a named contact who can answer questions and a good thank-you process do more than any single campaign. Start with people who already know and trust you, since they're the most likely to leave a gift. Promote gently and often over several years rather than loudly for a few weeks.

faqs.q: Who is most likely to leave a gift in their will?
faqs.a: People who already have a relationship with your charity, such as regular donors, volunteers, members and families you've supported. Remember A Charity's 2024 tracking study found supporters in their 40s and 50s with a will were the most likely to have included a charity (37%), ahead of those over 60 (27%). Having a will in the first place is the biggest step.

faqs.q: Can you promote legacy giving on social media?
faqs.a: Yes, but treat it as a slow, supportive channel. Short stories from supporters, a reminder around Will Aid in November or Free Wills Month, and a link to your legacy page work better than direct asks. Keep it respectful, avoid pressure and never give legal advice. Real people talking about why they've left a gift will always do better than stock images or slogans.

faqs.q: How long does it take for legacy promotion to bring in income?
faqs.a: A long time, which is why patience matters. A gift only arrives after someone has died, the estate has been settled and probate has been granted, which can be years or decades after they decided. Judge your promotion by earlier signs: visits to your legacy page, enquiries, and the number of people telling you they've pledged a gift.
