items.title: How to talk about legacy giving, in plain and kind words
items.excerpt: How to talk about gifts in wills with supporters: the plain words to use, a simple script, how to answer common reactions and how to handle it on camera.
items.coverAlt: Two people sharing tea at a table in a community hall cafe, seen from behind
items.body:
Talk about legacy giving the way you'd talk about anything else that matters to someone: plainly, warmly and with no hurry. Say "a gift in your will" rather than "bequest" or "legacy", make clear that family comes first, mention that any size of gift helps, and let the person take their time. Ask what matters to them before you say a word about what you need.

This post is about the conversation itself: the words, who should start it, how to answer the usual reactions and how to handle it on camera. If you're after the wider plan for reaching people, that sits in how to promote legacy giving, and the reasons it matters are in why legacy giving is important. I'm a film maker, so I come at this as someone who has spent a lot of time asking people to talk about things that are personal. The same instincts apply.

What words should you use when you talk about legacy giving?

Plain ones. "Legacy" is a sector word. To most people it suggests a grand inheritance or something to do with their reputation. "Bequest" sounds like a solicitor's letter. "A gift in your will" is what people understand, and it's the phrase they'd type into Google.

A few swaps that tend to help:

  • "A gift in your will" instead of "legacy" or "bequest".
  • "After you've looked after your family" instead of "when you die". It's kinder and it's honest about priorities.
  • "A share of your estate" or "a small percentage" instead of "a large donation". Most gifts are modest.
  • "Remembering us" only if the person already uses that language. Otherwise it can come across as vague or sentimental.

Avoid jargon like "pecuniary", "residuary" and "testator" in anything a supporter sees. Those terms matter to the solicitor writing the will, and they're a good reason to point people to one. They don't belong in a first conversation.

Tone matters as much as vocabulary. Earnest or solemn language tells people something heavy is coming. Most of us would rather talk about this the way we'd talk about a favourite place or a person who changed our lives, with a bit of warmth and sometimes a laugh. Humour has a place here, if it's the person's own.

Who should start the conversation?

Someone the supporter already trusts, and ideally someone who isn't asking for money. A volunteer co-ordinator, a long-standing member of staff, a trustee, or another supporter who's left a gift will usually be better received than a fundraiser they've never met.

Peer stories are strong for this reason. Hearing a fellow supporter explain why they decided to put a charity in their will can make the idea feel ordinary, and that's often all it takes. A short written story or a filmed one can do that at scale. I'll come back to that near the end.

When a member of staff does start it, they should have been trained in how to listen, how to stop, and what the rules are. The Fundraising Regulator is clear that fundraisers need to ensure they haven't exerted any undue pressure on potential donors, and that a fundraiser shouldn't give legal advice but should recommend independent advice if asked. The same guidance says responsible fundraisers will give people time and space to consider a request if they ask for it.

It also helps to talk about it inside your own organisation before you talk about it outside. Trustees, staff and volunteers will be asked questions by supporters, often when no fundraiser is in the room. If they know the plain wording, know where the information guide is and know who to pass a question to, the conversation stays warm instead of awkward. A ten minute session at a team meeting does more than a long policy document nobody reads.

What do you actually say?

Start by listening. Ask what brought them to your charity, what they remember most, what they'd like to see continue. A person who's talking about why they care is already halfway to the answer, and you'll hear what to mention.

When it feels right, you can say something like this:

Lots of people who care about our work like to remember us in their will, once their family are looked after. Even a small share can make a real difference. Would you like me to send some information, with no obligation?

It's short, it puts family first, it says a small gift is welcome and it makes the next step light. That's about all the pitch you need. Everything else is answering questions.

Some things I'd keep in the mix:

  • Be honest about what the gift does. Naming the real service it supports, with a real figure if you have one, is more persuasive than "help us plan for the future", as long as it's true.
  • Say you'd be happy with a no. It sounds odd, and it works. People relax when they know they won't be chased.
  • Mention the practical route. A solicitor can add a gift to an existing will, so nobody has to start again.
  • Offer a short guide. One page, short sentences, with a phone number and a name.

After the conversation, follow up once, lightly. A short note saying it was good to talk, with the guide and one name to contact, is plenty. If the person wants to take it further they will, and if they don't, you've left a good impression. Nobody has ever been put off by being thanked for their time.

The Remember A Charity tracking study from 2024 gives a feel for why this approach fits. Among the supporters surveyed, 77% said they'd be willing to leave a small percentage of their estate to charity, and 13% would consider 10% or more. The main reason people hadn't left a gift was that they wanted everything to go to family or friends (63%). So a conversation that respects family first and asks for a modest share is aimed at the right place.

If your opening line sounds like it came from a funeral director's brochure, start again.

How do you answer the things people say?

Most reactions fall into a handful of types. None of them need a clever comeback, just a calm, honest reply.

"I haven't got a will"

That's useful to know, and it's common. The tracking study found almost two thirds of supporters had written a will, which leaves plenty who hadn't. Don't push the charity angle yet. Say that having a will is worth doing whatever happens, and point them to a solicitor or a scheme such as Will Aid in November, where participating solicitors waive their fee for a basic will in return for a suggested donation.

"I want to leave everything to my family"

Respect it. Say that's what most people feel, and that some people simply choose to include a small share once their family are looked after. Leave it there. If it isn't for them, it isn't for them.

"I haven't got much to give"

Gifts of all sizes count. Say so, and mean it. A person on a modest income may be the one who cares most.

"I don't like thinking about it"

Nor does anyone. Say you understand, and that there's no rush. You might offer to send something they can read in their own time, or to leave it for another conversation.

"Let me think about it"

That's a good answer. Say thank you, leave them your contact details and don't chase. If they come back, it's because they want to.

How should supporters talk to their own families about it?

Because the person who wants to leave a gift usually needs help with the next conversation too. Surprises at the reading of a will cause hurt, and sometimes disputes. If you're supporting someone who's decided to leave a gift, suggest that they:

  • Tell the people closest to them what they've decided, and why, while they're around to explain it.
  • Talk to a solicitor, who can word the gift properly and make sure it stands up.
  • Tell the charity, if they feel comfortable, so you can thank them and keep in touch. According to the same study, 64% of people who had pledged a gift hadn't told the charity, and 47% said it had never occurred to them.

It's not for the charity to tell anyone what their will should say. That's the solicitor's job, and the Fundraising Regulator is clear that fundraisers shouldn't give legal advice. What you can do is make the family conversation feel normal, perhaps with a story from someone who's already had it.

How do you talk about legacy giving on camera?

With the same care, plus a few things that only matter once a camera's running. I've interviewed enough people about personal subjects to know that how you ask decides almost everything.

  • Ask open questions. "What made you decide?" and "What was the conversation with your family like?" will get you more than "Why did you leave a gift?"
  • Don't script it. A rehearsed line about "leaving a lasting legacy" sounds exactly like that. Let the person find their own words, and be ready to wait through a pause.
  • Agree what's off limits first. Money amounts, family disagreements and anything about health are usually best left out unless the person raises them.
  • Show them the cut. Someone talking about their will deserves to see how it's been edited before it goes anywhere. If you're nervous about being filmed yourself, here's how to prepare.
  • End on the human bit. The place, the person or the memory that made them give, then a plain line saying how to find out more.

The aim is for a viewer to think, "That could be me." A film that does that quietly will do more for a legacy programme than one that tries to make anyone feel guilty. The thinking behind it is the same as in nonprofit storytelling: a real person, a real reason and no pressure. Our La Fromagerie documentary is a good illustration of how much a single person speaking honestly about what they've built, thirty-three years in, can carry.

What should you never say?

A short list, and worth sticking up where your team can see it:

  • Anything that suggests the person ought to leave you a gift, or that they'd be letting you down if they didn't.
  • Legal or tax advice. Tell people that a solicitor can explain how it works. If you want to mention the tax side, you can say that the estate can pay Inheritance Tax at a reduced rate of 36% on some assets if 10% or more of the net value is left to charity, and leave the detail to the professionals.
  • Comments about someone's age, health or family.
  • Any suggestion that the offer is running out or that they need to decide today.
  • Promises you can't keep about exactly how a gift will be used. A solicitor and your finance team can tell you what's possible.

If a conversation goes quiet, let it. If someone becomes upset, stop, be kind and follow up another day if they'd like you to.

For the wider picture on charity storytelling and films, there's a full guide in charity and fundraising films, and a closer look at the supporters side in why donors give. If you'd like to talk through a film in which your own supporters speak about why they give, get in touch.

faqs.q: What should you say when asking someone to leave a gift in their will?
faqs.a: Keep it short and kind. Something like: lots of people who care about our work remember us in their will once their family are looked after, and even a small share can make a real difference. Then offer some information and say there's no obligation. Listen first, never pressure anyone, and send them to a solicitor for the legal side.

faqs.q: Why is legacy giving a difficult subject to talk about?
faqs.a: It involves death, family and money, three things many people avoid. The Fundraising Regulator describes legacies as a sensitive issue for individuals and families. The way through is a calm tone, plain words such as a gift in your will, and making it clear that family comes first and that there's no hurry. People soften quickly when they feel heard.

faqs.q: Should you say legacy or gift in your will?
faqs.a: A gift in your will is clearer for most supporters. Legacy and bequest are sector words that can sound grand, formal or unclear. Use the plain phrase on your website, in letters and in conversation, and keep technical terms for solicitors. It's also the wording people are most likely to search for, which helps them find your page.

faqs.q: Can a charity give advice about writing a will?
faqs.a: No. A fundraiser shouldn't give legal advice, and should recommend independent advice if asked. What you can do is explain that people can add a gift to an existing will with a solicitor, point them to schemes such as Will Aid or Free Wills Month, and provide a plain information guide. The solicitor handles wording, tax and legal checks.

items.title: Why is legacy giving important? The case for gifts in wills
items.excerpt: Why legacy giving matters: the £4.4bn it raises, why charities rely on it, what it means to the person leaving a gift, the risks and the role of real stories.
items.coverAlt: A hospice garden bench with a brass plaque in late afternoon light, with a gardener behind
items.body:
Legacy giving is important because it funds a huge share of UK charity work, and it lets ordinary people give far more than they could from their monthly budget. Gifts in wills raised over £4.4 billion in 2025, and for the biggest legacy charities they bring in around 30% of fundraised income. For many causes, it's the difference between planning ahead and hoping.

This post makes the case: what the money is, why charities lean on it, what it means for the person giving, and where the risks are. It doesn't cover how to run a campaign, which is in how to promote legacy giving, or how to word the ask, which is in how to talk about legacy giving. I make films for a living, so I've also added a section on why the stories people tell about their reasons matter more than any statistic.

How much money does legacy giving raise in the UK?

A lot. Remember A Charity's 2026 update reports that legacy income raised over £4.4 billion for charities in 2025, with a record 17.4% of estates at probate now including a charitable gift. There were almost 44,000 charitable estates, the second highest level on record, and an estimated 104,000 charitable bequests.

The size of gifts is worth noticing. The average comes to around £44,000 overall. A percentage or residual gift (a share of what's left after other gifts and costs) averages £98,000, while a fixed lump sum gift averages £6,100. Most of the money, in other words, comes from people leaving a share rather than a set amount.

The forecast is for growth. The same report expects legacy income to reach £5 billion by 2029 and £10 billion by 2046. Forecasts are forecasts, and they depend on how many people write wills, how property values move and how many estates charities are named in. But the direction of travel is clear enough that most large charities have a team built around it.

More people are also naming charities. Earlier tracking research from the same organisation found that 21% of supporters said they'd included a charitable gift in a will, up from one in seven (14%) in 2010. That's a slow, steady cultural shift, and it's the kind of thing that's easy to miss when you only look at annual income.

Why do charities depend on legacy income?

Because it's large, and because it reaches work that ordinary giving struggles to fund. For the top 1,000 legacy charities, gifts in wills drive about 30% of their fundraised income. That's nearly a third of the money they raise from the public, from one source.

It tends to pay for things that take time. A hospice building programme, a research project that runs for a decade, a rescue service that needs boats replaced, a youth project that wants a stable team. Monthly donations and event fundraising are brilliant at keeping the lights on and responding to what's happening now. A large gift left in a will can fund the longer game.

It also tends to come from people who care deeply. Someone who decides to put a charity in their will has usually been connected to it for years, as a supporter, volunteer or family member of someone it helped. That connection is useful to a charity in its own right, quite apart from the money. These are people who understand why the work exists.

Over four billion pounds a year, and the main marketing tool is still a leaflet in a drawer.

Why does it matter to the person leaving the gift?

It lets them give in a way they otherwise couldn't, and it gives them a say in what their life's work goes toward. Plenty of people can't afford a big donation while they're alive because they're paying a mortgage, supporting children or saving for care. A gift in a will costs them nothing in their lifetime. They stay in control of their money until they no longer need it.

It's also a way to say something about what mattered. Most of us don't get many chances to do that. A line in a will can honour a person, a place, a cause or an experience. People I've interviewed on shoots often describe a charity that looked after someone they loved, and the way they talk about it is wholly different from the way anyone talks about a standing order. It's personal in a way that's hard to match.

There's a tax side too, and it's worth knowing about without leaning on it. Gifts to UK charities in a will are normally exempt from Inheritance Tax, and under the government's rules the estate can pay Inheritance Tax at a reduced rate of 36% on some assets if you leave 10% or more of the net value to charity. That can make a gift cost the family less than people expect. It's a reason for a conversation with a solicitor, not a reason for a charity to promise anything.

Does it matter for smaller charities too?

Yes, and often more than people realise. The headline numbers are dominated by big names, but the average gifts above show that a single residual gift can be worth tens of thousands of pounds. For a local charity with a budget of a few hundred thousand, one gift like that can fund a post or a new project.

The catch is that smaller charities usually have fewer resources to ask. They may not have a legacy team, a dedicated page or any written guidance. The good news is that the basics are cheap: a clear web page, a short guide, a named contact and a habit of mentioning it in newsletters. Smaller charities can also be more personal, which suits this kind of giving. A supporter who knows the chief executive by name may find the conversation easier than they would with a national body.

For a small charity the real obstacle is often confidence. People worry about seeming greedy or morbid. They needn't. If your supporters value what you do, they'll often be glad to be told that this is an option, as long as it's offered gently.

What are the risks of relying on legacy income?

It's unpredictable, and it's late. A gift in a will arrives after a death, after probate, sometimes years after the person made their decision. You can't plan to the penny, you can't bring a gift forward and you can't easily influence a particular year. Income can also swing: a single very large gift can distort one year's figures, and a slow year can follow.

That means a few sensible habits:

  • Don't spend what you haven't got. Budget on a cautious average over several years, not on the best year you've had.
  • Keep other income going. Regular giving, grants and events pay for the things legacy income can't.
  • Be wary of dependence. If a large share of income comes from gifts in wills, a bad run can hit hard.
  • Invest in the long term. Because the pipeline takes years to fill, charities that start late are always behind.

There's also the question of how you ask. Legacy fundraising has rules because it deals with people at sensitive moments. The Fundraising Regulator's guidance on legacy fundraising says fundraisers must avoid undue pressure and shouldn't give legal advice. A charity that gets this wrong can lose more than a gift: it can lose trust.

What does it mean for the people a charity helps?

It means stability, which is something people who use charity services rarely get from the rest of their lives. A drop-in centre that knows it can keep its doors open for another five years can plan, hire and make promises. A research team that has secured a long-term funding source can take on questions that don't have quick answers. The people on the receiving end seldom see the line in a will that made it possible, but they feel the difference in whether the service is still there.

It also changes what a charity can be brave about. Income that arrives without an appeal attached lets an organisation try things, test a new service or respond to a need before a funder has been found.

Will legacy giving keep growing?

Probably, though nobody can promise it. The numbers point up, with legacy income forecast to reach £5 billion by 2029 and £10 billion by 2046. The things that move it are likely to include how many people write a will, how much wealth passes between generations and how many of them name a charity.

A few things could slow it. Fewer people having wills, more estates being spent on care, or a squeeze on property values would all matter. What the sector can influence is the part that depends on conversation: how many people hear about it, how comfortable they feel and how well charities thank those who do it. That's why the quality of the communication matters so much, and why it's worth putting effort into it before the next peak rather than after.

Why do the stories behind legacy gifts matter?

Because the numbers explain why it matters to a charity, and the stories explain why it matters to a supporter. Nobody decides to leave a gift because they've read that sector income is forecast to hit £5 billion. They decide because of what happened to someone they love or what they saw with their own eyes.

The statistic gets a trustee's attention. The story gets a supporter's signature.

This is where film can help. A short, honest piece with a real supporter explaining why they decided to leave a gift can do something a leaflet can't. It shows the decision as something ordinary and personal. It also lets a charity say thank you in public, if the supporter's happy for that. The same instincts apply as for any charity film made with dignity and consent: real people, their words, their approval of the cut.

It also connects to the rest of your story. Supporters who give in a will are usually the ones who've seen what you do most clearly, so the strongest legacy content is often the same material you use to show impact. A good impact report and a film that shows the work in action both feed the decision. And the reasons people give in the first place, which we cover in why donors give, are the same ones that move them to leave a gift later.

Our own documentary work, such as the film we made for La Fromagerie, is built on the same idea: someone with a long history explaining in their own words why it matters. If a charity wants a film of that kind, for legacy giving or for the wider cause, get in touch. The full set of guides on this subject is in the charity and fundraising films hub.

What's the simplest way to summarise why it matters?

It funds the long game, it gives supporters a way to give more than they could in life, and it only grows when people feel able to talk about it. Charities that treat it as a relationship built over years, with real thanks and real stories, tend to do best. Charities that avoid the subject out of awkwardness leave it to chance.

faqs.q: Why is legacy giving important to charities?
faqs.a: It funds long-term work that regular donations struggle to cover. According to Remember A Charity, legacy income raised over £4.4 billion in 2025, and gifts in wills drive about 30% of fundraised income for the top 1,000 legacy charities. For many causes it pays for buildings, research and services that take years to plan, so it shapes what a charity can promise.

faqs.q: How much of charity income comes from legacies?
faqs.a: For the largest legacy charities, around 30% of fundraised income comes from gifts in wills. Across the whole UK, legacy income was over £4.4 billion in 2025. The share varies a great deal between charities: some rely on legacies for most of what they raise from the public, while many smaller ones receive very little and could grow it.

faqs.q: Is leaving money to charity in a will tax efficient?
faqs.a: Gifts to UK charities in a will are normally exempt from Inheritance Tax, and if 10% or more of the net value of the estate goes to charity, the estate can pay Inheritance Tax at a reduced rate of 36% on some assets. The rules have detail, so anyone considering it should talk to a solicitor or financial adviser before deciding.

faqs.q: What is the downside of relying on legacy income?
faqs.a: It's unpredictable and slow. Gifts arrive after a death and after probate, so a charity can't forecast a single year accurately or speed things up. One very large gift can distort a year's figures. Sensible charities budget cautiously, keep other income streams going and start building their legacy work early, because the pipeline takes years to fill.

stat.takeaway: Legacy income is already one of the biggest sources of charity funding in the UK and is forecast to keep growing, which is why more charities are learning to talk about it well.

items.title: Is a charity a brand? What it is and why it matters
items.excerpt: Yes, a charity is a brand. Here's what a charity brand is made of, how it differs from a company's, why it matters as fewer people give, and how film shows it.
items.coverAlt: A volunteer hanging a coat in a charity shop window while shoppers queue in the rain
items.body:
Yes, a charity is a brand. A brand is the sum of what people think, feel and expect when they hear your name, and every charity has that whether it's designed it or not. The difference from a company is what the brand is for: it exists to earn trust, support and action for a cause rather than to sell something for profit.

Plenty of people in the sector wince at the word, because it sounds like logos and spending that donors didn't agree to. This post explains why it's still the right word, what a charity brand is actually made of, what makes it different from a commercial one, and how a film shows it. For the wider picture of how charities use communication to raise money, see what charity marketing is, and for the people who speak on a charity's behalf, what a charity brand ambassador is.

What does it mean to call a charity a brand?

It means people hold a picture of you in their heads, and that picture drives what they do. When someone sees a red nose, a paper poppy or a particular shade of green on a charity shop front, they know straight away what it stands for and whether they feel warmly about it. That's brand at work, and it was built over years.

A good example is the poppy. The Royal British Legion held its first Poppy Appeal in 1921, the year the Legion was formed, and the flower became shorthand for remembering the fallen. Comic Relief, set up in 1985, held its first Red Nose Day on BBC One in 1988, and the red nose gave a comedy night a symbol people could wear. Neither started with a branding agency presentation. They started with a clear purpose and a simple, repeatable sign of it.

So when people say "we're a charity, not a brand", they usually mean "we don't want to be slick". Fair enough. But the thing they're worried about, a slick surface with nothing underneath, is a bad brand rather than the absence of one. Every time a supporter hears from you, meets a volunteer or reads your annual report, they're deciding what you're like. That decision is your brand.

What is a charity brand made of?

More than a logo. A logo is the label on the tin. The brand is everything inside it, and most of that is behaviour. It helps to split it into five parts:

  • Purpose. What you exist to change, in a sentence a stranger could repeat.
  • Reputation. What people say about you when you're not in the room: supporters, beneficiaries, staff, funders, journalists.
  • Behaviour. How you treat people. How fast you answer an email, how a volunteer is thanked, what happens when something goes wrong.
  • Voice and look. The tone of your writing, the way you photograph and film people, your colours and typefaces.
  • Promise. What someone can expect if they back you, and how you show them the result.

The last two get the most design attention, but the first three carry the weight. A charity with a beautiful identity that answers donor complaints slowly has a weaker brand than one with a basic leaflet and a team that rings people back.

It's also why a charity brand can't be created by one department. The finance team, the fundraisers, the shop volunteers and the trustees all shape it. Whoever writes the thank-you letter is doing brand work, whether they know it or not.

Why does a charity brand matter?

Because giving is getting harder to win. The CAF UK Giving Report 2025, which covers 2024, found that the proportion of people donating to charity had fallen to 50% for the first time since the measure began. Including sponsorship, 55% of people gave in the last 12 months. London was the first region where fewer than half of people reported giving (49%, down from 64% in 2017), and only 36% of 16 to 24 year olds said they had donated or sponsored someone.

The same report estimates the public donated £15.4 billion in 2024, and that those who do give are giving more, with an average donation of £72. So the money's still there. It's concentrating in fewer hands, and those hands choose who to back based on who they recognise, trust and feel something about.

The Charity Commission's research points the same way. Its 2026 survey of 4,681 adults found that the things that matter most when deciding whether to trust a charity are that most of the money goes to the cause (55%), that it makes a real difference to the people it serves (51%) and that it's easy to see how much it raised and spent (40%). Every one of those is a brand promise that you either keep or you don't. You can read the full findings in the Commission's public trust in charities 2026 report.

If your brand guidelines are longer than your thank-you letter, something's gone wrong.

How is a charity brand different from a company brand?

In what it's asking for, who it's accountable to and what it can say. A company asks for a purchase. A charity asks for belief, time, money or a change in behaviour, with nothing physical in return. That makes trust the main currency, and trust is slower to earn and quicker to lose.

The differences that matter in practice:

  • Many audiences at once. Donors, volunteers, beneficiaries, funders, trustees, regulators and the press all look at the same brand. A company mostly has customers and staff.
  • Money is under a microscope. Any spending on communication can be questioned. Good brand work is easier to defend if it's tied to something specific, such as more regular givers or more people coming forward for help.
  • Beneficiaries have rights. You can't use the people you help as props. Their dignity and consent are part of the brand. We cover that in more detail in brand films for charities.
  • The rules are different. Registered charities in England and Wales must show their registered charity number on their official materials. Fundraising has its own code of practice. Check the current Charity Commission and Fundraising Regulator guidance for the detail.
  • The goal isn't growth for its own sake. A charity may want to shrink the problem until it doesn't need to exist.

None of that makes a charity less of a brand. It makes it a brand with more responsibilities.

Do charities need to think about branding?

They do, and the ones that treat it seriously tend to get further with less money. Awareness, familiarity and understanding are what turn a stranger into a supporter. The usual path runs from awareness to understanding, then support, then trust, and each step depends on the one before. A charity nobody has heard of has to start from zero every time it asks.

Smaller charities can do this on a tight budget. The important decisions are free: say clearly what you do, use the same words and tone everywhere, tell true stories about real people and keep your promises. A modest identity used consistently beats a smart one used differently by every volunteer.

Where a charity does spend, it should be able to say why. A film or a rebrand needs a purpose you can explain to a trustee: more regular givers, better volunteer recruitment, stronger funder relationships. If you can't name the job, wait.

How does a film show a charity's brand?

Better than almost any other format, because it shows behaviour, which is the biggest part of a brand. A logo says who you are. A film shows how you treat a person who walks through the door.

When we film for an organisation, I'm looking for the moments that show what it's like to deal with them: how the team talk to each other, what a normal afternoon looks like, what the people they help say in their own words. Those moments are the brand. They're what a viewer carries away. That's also the thinking behind our purpose-led film for char.gy and the wider idea of a brand documentary versus a corporate video.

A few things make a charity film strengthen the brand rather than dilute it:

  • Let real people speak. Staff, volunteers and the people you help, with their consent. Scripted lines about "our journey" make the brand sound generic.
  • Match the tone of the rest of your communication. A warm, funny charity shouldn't release a film that sounds like a documentary about a disaster.
  • Show change, not just need. The Commission's trust research puts "makes a real difference" near the top of what people look for.
  • Use it everywhere. A film should appear on your site, in funder pitches and in short cuts for social. Our guide to making a charity video covers planning that from the start.
A charity's brand is what a supporter would say about you to a friend, without the logo in front of them.

How can you check how your own charity's brand is doing?

You don't need a research budget to get a first read. A simple audit gives you more than most people expect:

  • Ask five supporters and five non-supporters to describe your charity in one sentence. Compare the answers with how you'd describe yourselves.
  • Walk through three touchpoints as a stranger: your website's front page, your donate page and your thank-you email. Do they sound like the same organisation?
  • Read your last ten pieces of communication in a row. Look for changes in tone, vocabulary and the way people are photographed or filmed.
  • Ask a volunteer or frontline member of staff what they tell people when they're asked what the charity does. That's the brand in daily use.

The gaps you find are the work. Sometimes it's as simple as agreeing a one-line description and using it everywhere. Sometimes it's a deeper conversation about what you stand for. Either way, it's cheaper and more useful than starting with a new logo.

What are the common mistakes with charity branding?

I see the same few again and again:

  • Treating it as a logo project. A new identity can't fix a service people have stopped trusting.
  • Copying commercial tricks. Slogans, stock photography and polished corporate language don't suit most causes.
  • Changing too often. Constant redesigns confuse supporters and cost money.
  • Letting each team do its own thing. Fundraising, services and campaigns end up sounding like three different charities.
  • Using beneficiaries as props. Short-term emotional pull costs long-term trust.
  • Forgetting the internal audience. If staff and volunteers don't understand the brand, nobody else will.

For how storytelling feeds a brand, there's a closer look in what nonprofit storytelling is, and the full set of guides is gathered in the charity and fundraising films hub. If you'd like to talk about a film that shows what your charity is actually like, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is a charity a brand or a business?
faqs.a: A charity is a brand, and it can also run like a business in how it manages money and people. It has a name, a reputation and a promise that supporters respond to, which is what makes it a brand. The difference from a company is that any surplus goes back into its cause, and it's accountable to trustees, regulators and the public.

faqs.q: Why do charities need branding?
faqs.a: Because supporters choose who to give to based on who they recognise and trust. CAF's UK Giving Report 2025 found that only half of people donated in 2024, so charities are competing for a smaller pool. A clear, consistent brand makes it easier for people to understand what you do, remember you and decide to back you.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a charity logo and a charity brand?
faqs.a: A logo is a visual mark that identifies you. The brand is the whole impression people have of your charity: your purpose, reputation, behaviour, tone of voice and promise. A good logo helps people recognise you, but if the service, communication or reputation falls short, no logo will repair it.

faqs.q: Can a charity spend money on branding?
faqs.a: Yes, if it can show the spend serves the cause. Trustees should be able to say what the work is meant to achieve, such as more regular donors or better volunteer recruitment, and how they'll judge it. Many branding improvements, like clearer language and consistent tone, cost very little. Larger projects, such as a film, are best tied to a specific goal.

stat.title: Share of UK adults who gave to charity in the last 12 months (2024)
stat.takeaway: Fewer people are giving, so a charity has to earn recognition and trust from a smaller pool, which is what a brand does.

source.name: Charities Aid Foundation, UK Giving Report 2025

items.title: What is a charity brand ambassador? Roles, types and rules
items.excerpt: What a charity brand ambassador is, the different types, how they differ from patrons and influencers, how to recruit them, the ASA rules and how film helps.
items.coverAlt: A smiling woman in a red scarf chats to two men at an exhibition, with soft green foreground
items.body:
A charity brand ambassador is a person who speaks up for a charity and its cause, usually without being on its payroll, and who gives it a human face, a voice and an audience. Ambassadors can be celebrities, but they're just as often people with lived experience, long-serving volunteers or local figures whom the community already trusts.

This post covers who ambassadors are, what they do, how they differ from patrons and influencers, how to recruit and look after them, and what the rules say. It leans on the point that a charity's reputation is carried by people, which ties into whether a charity is a brand and into nonprofit storytelling. I'm a film maker, so I'll also say how film can help an ambassador tell their story well.

What does a charity brand ambassador actually do?

They lend their credibility and their voice to the cause. In practice that covers a range of things, depending on the person and the charity:

  • Sharing the charity's work with their own audience, online or in person.
  • Appearing in campaigns, films, photographs and press stories.
  • Speaking at events, launches and fundraising dinners.
  • Opening doors to other people: funders, businesses, journalists and policy makers.
  • Taking part in challenges or appeals that give the charity something to talk about.
  • Telling their own story, when it's relevant, to help others understand what the cause means.

What they don't do is run the charity or make decisions for it. An ambassador speaks for the cause, while trustees and staff are responsible for governance and operations. Being clear about that line at the start avoids a lot of misunderstanding later.

The title doesn't have a legal definition. Different charities use it in different ways, and some use words like supporter, champion, advocate or patron to mean the same thing. What matters is that there's a written understanding of what the person's role is.

What types of charity ambassador are there?

Most fall into a few groups, and a charity often has more than one.

Celebrity and high-profile ambassadors

Well-known people from entertainment, sport, the arts or public life. UNICEF UK is a good illustration of how structured this can get. Its site describes UNICEF Goodwill Ambassadors, who support its work globally and are appointed by UNICEF headquarters in New York, UNICEF UK Ambassadors, who promote its work in the UK and have shown a commitment over a number of years, and High Profile Supporters, who back its work in the UK. It traces its celebrity support back to Danny Kaye in 1954. A tiered approach like that shows the value of committing for the long term.

Ambassadors with lived experience

People who've used the charity's services or who live with the issue it addresses. They're often the most compelling ambassadors, because they can speak from direct experience. The Charity Commission's 2026 research found that 27% of people said being a voice for the people or causes it supports was important in whether they trusted a charity. Lived-experience ambassadors can do that more convincingly than anyone. They also need more care and support, which I'll come to below.

Volunteer and supporter ambassadors

Long-term volunteers, fundraisers and donors who talk about the charity among friends, in their workplace or at community events. They're the quiet backbone of the whole thing, and they're often the ones who influence people the most.

Local and community ambassadors

For smaller charities, a local business owner, a councillor, a head teacher or a sports coach can do far more than a famous name would. People trust those they see in the high street.

Corporate ambassadors

Businesses and their staff who champion a charity partnership. That can bring funding, volunteers and reach, though it needs the same clear agreement and checks as any other tie-up.

Why do ambassadors matter to a charity's brand?

Because people trust people more than they trust organisations, and a recommendation from someone they know beats any advert. The Charity Commission's 2026 public trust research asked people who had had contact with a charity where they first heard of it. Friends and family came top at 35%, ahead of social media, TV, radio or newspaper adverts and the charity's own website (each 19%).

Your best ambassador is usually already in the building, wearing the hi-vis, making the tea.

That's a useful number for a small charity. Your most effective channel is likely to be the people who already talk about you. An ambassador is that effect with a bit of structure and support behind it.

The pool to draw from is big. The government's Community and Engagement Survey 2025/26, which had over 175,000 responses, found that 66% of people aged 16 and over in England had given money to charitable causes in the last four weeks. About 35% volunteered, formally or informally, at least once a month, and 18% did so formally. Not all of those people will want a title, but plenty will happily tell friends why they care, if you ask them and give them something to share.

A famous face on the poster gets a glance. A neighbour saying "I volunteer there" gets a phone call.

What's the difference between an ambassador, a patron and an influencer?

The lines blur, and each charity uses the words differently, but these are the usual distinctions:

  • Patron. Usually a senior or distinguished person who lends their name and standing to a charity, often for a long period and sometimes in a formal capacity. The role tends to be more ceremonial.
  • Ambassador. A more active role, with specific things the person agrees to do, such as attending events, appearing in campaigns or talking about the cause.
  • Trustee. A legal role. Trustees govern the charity and carry legal responsibility. An ambassador doesn't.
  • Influencer. Someone with a social media audience who may promote a cause, often as a one-off or a paid collaboration. A long-term ambassador can also be an influencer, but not every influencer is an ambassador.

The practical point is to agree on what the title means before you use it, and to put it in writing. "Ambassador" sounds grand, and it's easy for the person and the charity to have different ideas of what it involves.

How do you find and recruit a good ambassador?

Start with real connection, not reach. Someone with a personal reason to care will outlast someone who's simply available, and an audience of a million that doesn't care about your cause does little for you.

A sensible process looks like this:

  1. Work out what you need. A face for a campaign, a voice for lived experience, a door-opener to funders? Different needs mean different people.
  2. Look close to home first. Existing supporters, volunteers, beneficiaries and local figures are often the best candidates.
  3. Do your homework. Check their public history, past statements and affiliations. An ambassador's behaviour reflects on the charity, so look at it honestly before you announce anything.
  4. Have an honest conversation. Explain what you'd like, what you can offer in return (expenses, support, recognition) and what they can say no to.
  5. Agree it in writing. Roles, expectations, how long, how either side can step back, what they'll be asked to say and what they won't.

Take extra care with anyone who has lived experience of the issue. They're being asked to share something personal for the charity's benefit, so they need proper support, a clear say in how their story is used and the right to stop. The safeguarding and dignity principles in our post on brand films for charities apply here too.

What do the rules say about charity ambassadors and advertising?

If the relationship involves payment or control, the UK advertising rules are likely to apply. The Advertising Standards Authority says it uses two tests, which both have to be met: payment and editorial control. In its influencer marketing advice, it explains that payment covers gifts, discounts, event access and even charity donations, and that editorial control means any influence over what a post says, such as approval rights, scripts or required hashtags. If both apply, the post should be clearly labelled as an ad, and the ASA recommends "#ad" as the simplest way.

That doesn't mean every post from an unpaid volunteer is advertising. But if you're paying an influencer, giving someone perks or approving what they say, label it and check the current guidance from the ASA and the Committee of Advertising Practice. It's also sensible to check your own fundraising code and keep the Charity Commission's expectations about reputation and risk in mind.

On the practical side, agree up front who owns any content the ambassador creates, who can reuse it and for how long. The same principles that apply to any commissioned video are explained in who owns the copyright in commissioned video.

How can film help an ambassador tell their story?

Film shows who someone is in a way that a quote can't. A well-made short piece lets an ambassador speak in their own words, in a place they know, at their own pace. That's what makes people believe them.

A few lessons from sitting down with people in front of a camera:

  • Let them choose the setting. Their kitchen, the charity's drop-in or a place that matters to them. People are calmer on familiar ground.
  • Don't script it. Ask open questions and let them find the words. If they're nervous, here's how to prepare for being filmed and how to speak on camera are good places to send them.
  • Show them the cut. Nobody should see themselves for the first time on a charity's feed.
  • Give it several lives. A full story for the website, a short for email and vertical clips for social, all from the same shoot. If it helps, our post on how charities use social media shows where they go.

Our own film for Isaac Chamberlain and Boxraw, a professional boxer filmed training for a boxing brand, is a different sector but shows the same principle of letting an athlete's work speak for itself. A good ambassador film does the same for a cause. For the whole set of guides on this subject, see the charity and fundraising films hub, and if you want to discuss a film for your ambassadors, get in touch.

How do you look after ambassadors once they've signed up?

Treat them as partners. Give them a named contact, a short briefing pack and the facts they need to speak accurately. Tell them about results, so they can see what their effort did. Thank them in private and, if they're happy with it, in public.

Check in regularly, particularly with anyone whose personal story is being shared. Circumstances change, and what felt right a year ago may not now. Make it easy for them to step back without awkwardness. A good ambassador relationship should leave both sides with a better reputation, and a respectful exit is part of that.

Whatever's agreed, put it in writing and check the current ASA and CAP guidance.

faqs.a: Yes. Celebrities are the best known type, but volunteers, supporters, people with lived experience and local figures can all be ambassadors, and often are the most effective. What matters is a real connection to the cause and a clear agreement on the role. A charity should check a person's public record before announcing them.

faqs.a: A patron is usually a distinguished person who lends their name and standing to a charity, often in a more ceremonial role. An ambassador has a more active job, such as appearing in campaigns, speaking at events or sharing the cause with their audience. items.title: Employer brand and culture films: the complete guide
items.excerpt: A complete UK guide to employer branding and culture films: what it is, why it matters, how to build it, employee advocacy, and how to make a recruitment video.
items.coverAlt: A factory worker in gloves leans over a workbench fitting a metal part while a colleague watches
items.body:
Employer branding is the reputation your business has as a place to work, and the things you do to shape it. It's what a stranger would say if you asked them what it's like to work for you, whether you've told them or not. A film is one of the most honest ways to show it. The short version is in what employer branding is, and this guide covers the rest.

I make documentary brand films, and a fair number of them have been about people and places rather than products. That's given me a good view of what makes a workplace look real on camera and what makes it look staged. This guide walks through the subject in the order a UK HR lead, comms manager or founder usually needs it: what employer branding is, why it matters, what goes into it, who owns it, how your own people fit in, and how culture and recruitment films work in practice. Each section links to a deeper answer, so you can read it straight through or jump to the part you're stuck on.

What is employer branding, in plain words?

Start with the simplest version. Your employer brand is the picture people carry of you as an employer: what the work is like, how people are treated, whether it's a place they'd want to be. If you'd like it without the jargon, employer branding in simple words is the one to read first. Every business has one. Most just haven't looked at it.

The phrase gets used loosely, which is why people search for what employer branding means as well as what it is. In practice the meaning sits in two halves. One is the reputation that already exists, built from your reviews, your leavers, your managers and what staff say at the school gate. The other is the deliberate effort to make that reputation accurate and visible. You can't fully control the first. The second is the work.

Recruiters use the term a little differently. Employer branding in recruitment is about the moment a candidate meets you: the job advert, the careers page, the first call, the interview. And employer branding in talent acquisition is the wider, longer game of keeping a pool of people warm so that when a role opens, the right ones already know who you are. A candidate who's watched a film about your team before applying turns up better informed, and that saves everyone time.

Why does employer branding matter, and how does it affect hiring?

Because hiring is a two-way decision, and candidates now do their homework before they ever speak to you. Why employer branding is important comes down to cost and quality: a strong reputation brings in more of the right applicants, and a weak or unclear one makes every role harder to fill. The same reasoning sits behind why employer branding matters, which looks at it from the retention side, because people who joined knowing what they were signing up for tend to stay.

The mechanics are worth understanding. How employer branding affects recruitment shows up in the number and quality of applications, how many offers get accepted, and how long roles sit open. And how employer branding helps in attracting talent goes into the candidate's side of it: what a person actually looks at, in what order, before they decide a job is worth an application.

It's also worth knowing what UK employers are really doing about it. The CIPD's employer brand insight draws on its Resourcing and talent planning survey and says four in five organisations are taking some action to improve their brand. It also says only 14% took steps to measure the impact. That gap is where a lot of money gets spent on guesswork.

What goes into an employer brand?

Less than people fear, and more than a careers page. What employer branding includes is a mix of the things candidates and staff see directly: your job adverts, your website, your reviews, your induction, your managers, the way you treat people who leave, and the content you put out about all of it. Film is one ingredient. It isn't the whole recipe, and it can't make up for a poor experience on the inside.

Underneath sits the thing everything else draws from. An employer brand proposition is a plain statement of what you offer people in return for their work and why it's different from the place down the road. Pay is part of it, but only part. Training, flexibility, the quality of the people, the pride in what you make: those are what a proposition is built from. If you can't write yours in a few honest sentences, a film will struggle to carry it.

From there you can plan. An employer branding strategy pulls the proposition, the audiences you're trying to reach and the channels you'll use into one plan, with a view on what success looks like. The day to day pieces of that plan are employer branding activities: posts, events, open days, careers content, films, awards entries, the way you handle graduate schemes. And when you bundle some of those into a push with a start and an end, an employer branding campaign is what you've got.

Who owns employer branding, and how do you build it?

This causes more argument than it should. Whether employer branding is marketing or HR usually depends on who's got the budget and who's got the relationships. HR knows what the jobs are really like and what candidates ask. Marketing knows how to make something people want to watch. The best work I've seen happens when the two sit in the same room before anyone books a camera, and the person who signs it off can say yes without a three week approval chain.

If HR and marketing both think the other one owns the culture film, congratulations, you own a very expensive misunderstanding.

To build it, start with listening, not making. How to build employer branding begins with finding out what your current staff would say, what your leavers said on the way out, and what candidates who turned you down gave as the reason. Then you work out the proposition, pick the two or three places you'll show it, and make things that are true. The mistake I see most is starting with the video and working backwards to a message.

LinkedIn is where most UK professional hiring conversations now happen, so it gets its own answer in how to do employer branding on LinkedIn. The short version is that the company page matters less than the people on it. A film cut into short pieces suits the platform well, because it gives your staff something worth sharing rather than a job advert they feel awkward about posting.

Candidates aren't looking for a perfect employer. They're looking for one that's telling them the truth.

How do your own people become part of it?

Candidates trust staff more than they trust a company page. That's the idea behind employee advocacy: your own people sharing, talking about and vouching for the business in their own voices. It's different from asking everyone to repost the latest press release, and anyone who's tried the second version will know how that goes.

Why employee advocacy is important comes back to reach and credibility. Your people's networks are bigger than your page's following, and what they say reads as more believable. The CIPD article above makes the same point, saying personal posts often get significantly more engagement than content shared by company pages. In practice that means the right thing to hand your staff is something they're proud to share, and a good film of their own workplace often is.

The platform changes how it plays out. Employee advocacy on social media covers the general picture across the channels, with the usual cautions about guidelines and consent. Employee advocacy on LinkedIn is the version most UK employers actually run, because it's where colleagues, clients and future candidates all overlap. And if you need the business case for a sceptical finance director, how an employee advocacy programme benefits a company sets out what a programme can and can't deliver.

One thing I'd say from the shoots: advocacy follows pride. People share a film when they come across well in it and when it looks like the place they work. When they wince at it, they won't post it, however many internal emails you send.

What is a culture film, and how do the types differ?

A culture film shows what it's like inside an organisation: how people work together, what they care about and what a normal day feels like. The three names you'll hear for it overlap heavily, and each has its own answer so you can see where they differ. A corporate culture video tends to be about the company as a whole and the values it says it holds. A workplace culture video is closer to the ground, concentrating on the place and the day to day. And an organisational culture video is the term you'll meet in larger, public sector and charity settings, where the audience includes staff, funders and regulators as well as candidates.

Whichever name you use, the test is the same. Does it look like a particular place, with particular people, or could it be any office anywhere? Stock music, a drone shot of the car park and a manager saying everyone's like family is the quickest route to the second. I've written about the different approaches in brand documentary versus corporate video, and for culture films the documentary approach nearly always wins, because staff recognise it as true.

A culture film also does a job beyond hiring. New starters can see what they've joined, existing staff can see themselves in it, and clients get a sense of who they're dealing with. If you're thinking about the induction end of that, employee onboarding videos covers it.

What is a recruitment video, and how do you make a good one?

A recruitment video is a film made to help the right people apply for a role or a type of role, and to help the wrong ones decide it isn't for them. That second job is the underrated one. A film that puts off people who'd have left in three months is saving you money. I've gone into the wider category, including the agency side, in recruitment and employer brand videos and recruitment video for agencies and HR.

How do you make one?

How to make a recruitment video follows a fairly simple order. Decide who it's for and what you want them to do. Pick two or three real people who do the job and are happy to be filmed. Visit the workplace before the shoot and see when it's at its busiest. Interview people in their own space, then film them working. Edit for honesty, not polish. Everything else is detail, and the detail is where the money goes.

Quality is a separate question, and how to make a good recruitment video answers it. A good one has specifics, because specifics are what candidates remember: the early start, the lunch spot, the machine everyone argues about, the manager who sits with new people on day one. It also lets people talk in their own words. If someone's reading a script, viewers can tell in about four seconds. Helping staff relax in front of a camera is half my job, and how to give a good interview answer and how to prepare for being filmed are worth sending to anyone you've asked to take part.

How long should it be, and should it have music?

Shorter than you think, with one exception. How long a recruitment video should be depends on where it sits. A cut for social feeds should be well under a minute. A main film on your careers page can run two to four minutes if it holds attention. Longer pieces with whole interviews can live on YouTube for the candidates who are properly interested. Cut one shoot into several lengths rather than one long compromise, as I explain in how to turn one brand film into a year of content.

Music is the other question that comes up every time. Whether recruiting videos should have music is mostly about restraint. Quiet, simple music under the footage can help the pace, but heavy, upbeat tracks make a real workplace look like an advert and bury the voices. Whatever you use, it has to be licensed for commercial use. A track from your personal streaming account doesn't count, and music licensing for brand videos explains what to check.

What does a good one look like in practice?

I can't show you a recruitment video that isn't ours, but I can describe how the approach plays out on shoots. For the manufacturing case study, we filmed on a working shop floor with the people who make the parts. Nobody needed to be told what to say, because they knew the product better than any copywriter. That's the kind of footage a candidate believes.

Small, craft businesses show it even more clearly. In the Carreducker film, two shoemakers explain a six month process, and you come away understanding what it's like to do that job. Film like that works as an employer brand piece even when nobody planned it as one. And in the char.gy B Corp film, an interview-led format explained what the company stood for in plain language, which is exactly what values-led candidates look for.

On the day itself, the work is practical. We agree who's being filmed and make sure everyone has said yes freely, with no pressure and no penalty for declining. Under UK GDPR, you should be clear with staff about how their image will be used and for how long, and it's worth putting that in writing. We keep the shoot short so it doesn't wreck anyone's working day. Then we let people talk. The best line in a culture film is rarely the one in the brief. It's the throwaway comment from someone who forgot the camera was there.

Cost is the question that sits under all of this. A single film is a very different spend from a day of content cut into a dozen pieces, and how much a brand film costs in the UK sets out how to think about it. Take care, too, to show the people who actually work there. If your film only shows one type of person and your workforce doesn't look like that, candidates will notice, and so will anyone thinking about the Equality Act.

Where do you start?

Start with the proposition, not the camera. Write down, in plain sentences, what you'd honestly tell a good candidate about working for you, including the hard parts. Ask five people who work for you whether it sounds right. If they recognise it, you've got the beginning of a film. If they wince, fix the thing first and film it afterwards.

If you'd like help finding the people and the moments worth filming, have a look at the films page to see how we work, and when you're ready, the easiest way to start is getting in touch. If you want the storytelling thinking behind it, the brand storytelling guide covers it.

Every question in this guide

The thirty questions below each have their own deep dive. Pick the one you're stuck on.

faqs.q: What's the difference between employer branding and recruitment marketing?
faqs.a: Employer branding is the lasting reputation and promise of what working for you is like. Recruitment marketing is the short term activity that promotes specific roles to candidates. The first should shape the second. If your adverts say one thing and your reputation says another, candidates will believe the reputation, so get the brand right before spending on ads.

faqs.q: Do small businesses need an employer brand?
faqs.a: Yes, because you've already got one, whether you manage it or not. Small firms often have an advantage: candidates can meet the actual founder and see the actual team. You don't need a large budget. You need an honest description of what it's like to work there and a few real people willing to say so on camera.

faqs.q: How do I measure whether employer branding is working?
faqs.a: Pick a few numbers you already have: applications per role, offer acceptance rate, time to hire, early leavers and referrals from staff. Note where candidates say they first heard of you. Compare before and after a change. CIPD says only 14% of organisations measure impact, so even a simple tracking sheet puts you ahead.

faqs.q: Can a culture film put people off applying?
faqs.a: It can, and that's often a good result. A film that shows early starts, physical work or a fast pace honestly will deter people who'd have hated the job, which saves you the cost of a bad hire. What matters is that the people who do apply are the right ones and arrive with accurate expectations.

items.title: What is employer branding? A UK guide for businesses
items.excerpt: Employer branding is a business's reputation as a place to work, plus the effort to shape it. What it's made of, who owns it and where film fits.
items.coverAlt: A welder in navy overalls and a breathing helmet works a bright weld in front of a red curtain
items.body:
Employer branding is how a business is seen as a place to work: its reputation with current staff, past staff and people who might join, and the deliberate effort to shape that reputation so the right people apply and stay. Every employer has one whether it manages it or not. Employer branding is the work of managing it on purpose.

This is the foundation post in a series on employer brand and culture films, so it covers the whole idea once, at a sensible depth: where the term came from, what an employer brand is made of, how it differs from your company brand, who owns it, and where film fits. The sibling posts go deeper on single questions: the cost case is in why employer branding is important, the jargon is in what it means, the no-frills version is in simple words, and the hiring view is in recruitment.

Where does the term employer branding come from?

It's older than most people assume. In 1996 two academics, Tim Ambler and Simon Barrow, published a paper at London Business School called The Employer Brand. They'd interviewed senior executives at 27 UK companies and asked what would happen if the techniques used to manage a consumer brand were applied to people management. Their definition of the employer brand has stuck: the package of functional, economic and psychological benefits provided by employment, and identified with the employing company.

Read that slowly and it's a fairly plain idea. Functional is the work itself, the tools, the training. Economic is pay, pension, holiday. Psychological is how it feels to belong there: the pride, the trust, the sense that someone notices when you do well. A job is all three at once, and the employer brand is what people believe about that bundle before they've signed anything.

Nearly three decades on, the idea has moved from academic paper to a line in most HR job titles. The substance hasn't changed much. People choose where to work using something close to the way they choose what to buy: they form a picture from what they hear, what they see, and what they can't easily check.

What is an employer brand actually made of?

I find it easiest to split it into three layers. They're related, but they behave differently, and mixing them up is where most confusion starts.

Reputation

What people say about you when you're not in the room. Former staff talking to friends, reviews on Glassdoor, Indeed and Google, comments under a LinkedIn post, what the local recruiter tells candidates. You don't write this layer. You earn it, and you can only influence it indirectly.

Proposition

What you promise. Often called the employer value proposition, or EVP, it's the short, honest answer to why someone would work for you rather than the business down the road. Pay and benefits are part of it, but so are things like how much responsibility people get early, how flexible the hours are, and what kind of people they'd be working with. I'd send you to our post on the employer brand proposition for the detail.

Experience

What actually happens. The interview process, how fast anyone replies, the first week, the way a manager reacts when something goes wrong. This is the layer that decides whether the other two are believed. A glossy proposition on the careers page followed by a three week silence after interview doesn't build an employer brand. It builds a review.

An employer brand is a promise, a reputation and an experience, and the experience is the one that gets quoted.

If those three line up, you have a strong employer brand almost by accident. If they don't, the gap between what you say and what people experience is the thing to fix, and no amount of nicer photography will close it.

Why does it matter in the UK right now?

Because hiring hasn't gone away, even in a softer jobs market. The government's Employer Skills Survey 2024, which interviewed 22,712 employers across the UK, found that 17% had a vacancy at the time, and that just over a quarter (27%) of all vacancies were skill-shortage vacancies, meaning roles where applicants lacked the skills or experience needed. That's lower than 2022, when it was over a third, but it's still more than one in four.

I'm not going to stretch one statistic into a full business case here. That's the job of our post on why employer branding is important. The short version is that when roles are hard to fill, the businesses that look like a straightforward, honest place to work get the first conversation, and that's worth having before you need it.

How is employer branding different from your company brand?

They share a lot, and they should never contradict each other. Your company brand speaks mainly to customers: what you sell, why you're good at it, why to trust you. Your employer brand speaks to people deciding whether to give you their working life. Same business, same values, different question being asked.

The audiences also overlap more than people expect. A customer reads your careers page to see if you're the sort of firm they want to buy from. A candidate reads your customer reviews to see if the business is doing well. A supplier asks a mutual friend about you. Treating them as sealed boxes is how you end up with a polished consumer brand and a staff turnover problem.

What differs is the evidence people want. Customers want proof the product works. Candidates want proof the people are real, the manager is decent and the job matches the advert. That's one reason film suits employer brand work so well. You can't fake a colleague's expression when they talk about a Monday morning.

Who is responsible for it?

In practice it falls between two chairs. HR owns the policies, the hiring process and the people experience. Marketing owns the brand, the channels and the production budget. Neither can do it alone, and in a small business it's usually the owner doing both badly on a Sunday night. There's a full argument on this in is employer branding marketing or HR, but my view from sitting in those meetings is simple: HR owns the truth, marketing owns the telling, and someone senior has to make sure the two meet.

Employer branding is the only discipline where the whole organisation has a say and nobody thinks it's their department.

It also belongs to your staff more than to either department. Every employee is a daily source of evidence about what it's like to work for you, and their word carries more weight than yours. That's the idea behind employee advocacy, which gets its own treatment in this series.

Does a small business really have an employer brand?

Yes, and often a stronger one than it realises. Most UK businesses are small, and most of them recruit on reputation and word of mouth. The plumber who treats his apprentices well, the workshop where people stay for twenty years, the restaurant that's known locally for fair tips and sane rotas. That's an employer brand. It just hasn't been written down or filmed yet.

What a small firm lacks is usually the proof. A bigger competitor has a careers site, a video and a content team. You have the better workplace and nothing visible to show for it. That's a fixable problem, and it's the one I see most often when we film with small and mid-sized teams. If you want the practical route, how to build employer branding and what an employer branding strategy looks like are the next reads.

What does employer branding include?

A lot of things, some obvious and some not. The careers page, job adverts and the way they're written, social media, the interview and onboarding process, how you treat people who don't get the job, reviews and how you respond to them, internal communications, and the stories staff tell outside work. The full inventory is in what does employer branding include, and the day-to-day work is in employer branding activities.

What matters at this stage is knowing that it's a spread of touchpoints rather than one campaign. A film is one touchpoint. A good one carries more weight than most because it shows people rather than describing them, but it can't make up for a poor interview process.

Where do films fit into an employer brand?

Film does one job exceptionally well: it lets a candidate meet the people before they apply. A short documentary-style piece with a real team member explaining what the job involves, what's hard about it and why they stay will tell a candidate more in three minutes than a page of values.

The examples I'd point to from our own work are small ones. Our film for Virtus Energy and NexBlue was built around an installer talking about the actual work, filmed on live jobs between visits, and that's the shape a recruitment film wants to take as well. The Carreducker shoemakers film shows two makers who trained together and now teach the trade. Nobody is selling a job in it, but it's easy to see why an apprentice would want to work there.

For the longer view, our guide to recruitment and employer brand videos covers formats and the rules to respect. If you're ready to think about the film itself, what is a recruitment video is the right next step, and our brand films page shows how we work.

What do employers get wrong about employer branding?

I've watched the same mistakes on shoot days and in briefing calls for years, so these are patterns rather than one-offs.

  • Starting with the video. A film should show an employer brand you already have. If the honest answer to "why work here?" is still a blank, the film will be generic, and candidates can tell.
  • Writing it in the voice of the board. Staff don't say "we're a dynamic, fast-growing organisation". They say "the team's good and the van's usually clean". Use their words.
  • Casting only the polished. The most senior person is rarely the most convincing. Pick people who are honest and at ease.
  • Overselling. Candidates who feel misled leave in the first quarter and write the review on the way out.
  • Treating it as a one-off. The brand lives in the everyday. A refreshed film every few years helps, but it can't carry things on its own.

Underneath all of that is the same point: the strongest employer brands are accurate. They describe the place as it is and attract people who like that. If you can say what it's really like to work for you and you're comfortable with the answer, you're most of the way there.

What should you do next?

Ask five people who work for you why they joined and why they've stayed, separately, and write down what they say without editing it. That's the raw material for your proposition, and it'll usually surprise you. Then look at your last three job adverts and your interview process through a candidate's eyes. Where the story and the experience don't match, fix that before you make anything.

Once you know the truth about the place, a film becomes straightforward to plan. If you'd like to talk it through, get in touch, and if we don't think a film is the right move for you yet, we'll say so.

faqs.q: What is employer branding in one sentence?
faqs.a: Employer branding is the reputation a business has as a place to work, plus the deliberate effort to shape it so the right people apply, accept and stay. It covers what current and former staff say, what you promise in job adverts and on your careers page, and what the hiring process and first weeks actually feel like for a new starter.

faqs.q: Do small businesses need employer branding?
faqs.a: Yes, because every business that hires has an employer brand already, formed by what staff and applicants say about it. Small firms often have a good one but nothing visible to prove it. A few honest staff stories, a clear job description and a short film showing the team can be enough to compete with much larger employers.

faqs.q: Is employer branding the same as recruitment marketing?
faqs.a: No. Recruitment marketing is the set of campaigns and adverts that promote specific vacancies. Employer branding is the wider reputation and promise that those campaigns draw on. If the brand is weak, marketing a vacancy gets expensive and the people it brings in are less likely to stay. Good recruitment marketing is one part of employer branding.

faqs.q: Who invented the term employer brand?
faqs.a: The term was set out by Tim Ambler and Simon Barrow of London Business School in 1996. They researched how 27 UK companies managed their people and proposed applying brand management techniques to employment. They defined the employer brand as the package of functional, economic and psychological benefits provided by employment and identified with the employing company.

stat.title: Share of UK vacancies that were skill-shortage vacancies
stat.takeaway: Hiring got a little easier between 2022 and 2024, but more than one in four vacancies still went unfilled for lack of the right skills, so being the employer people want to talk to still counts.
